topics.name: Algebraic Expressions
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Algebraic Expressions Apply the index laws to positive, negative, fractional and zero indices, and manipulate surds including rationalising denominators (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1/2.2, AQA 7357 B1-B2, OCR A H640 2.01 Expand single and double brackets, recognising and deploying the difference of two squares and perfect square expansions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.1, AQA 7357 B3 Factorise quadratics with a = 1 and a is not 1 using the AC method, and factorise expressions by grouping (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B3 Simplify, multiply, divide, add and subtract algebraic fractions by factorising and cancelling whole factors only (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8 Divide polynomials by linear expressions using long division or the remainder theorem, and use the factor theorem to extract linear factors and unknown coefficients (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B4 Combine these skills fluently to prove simple statements and simplify harder expressions under timed exam conditions (AO2/AO3) Collect like terms: only terms with identical variables and powers combine - 3x^2y and 3xy^2 are not like terms. Index laws: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b), x^a / x^b = x^(a-b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^0 = 1, x^(-a) = 1/x^a. Difference of two squares a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); perfect squares a^2 +/- 2ab + b^2 = (a +/- b)^2. In algebraic fractions, factorise numerator and denominator fully, then cancel common FACTORS only - never terms joined by + or -. Factor theorem: f(a) = 0 means (x - a) is a factor; remainder theorem: remainder on division by (x - a) is f(a). Index law A rule for manipulating powers of the same base: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b), x^a / x^b = x^(a-b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^0 = 1, x^(-a) = 1/x^a. Surd An irrational root left in exact form, such as sqrt(2) or 3sqrt(5); answers demanding exact form must keep surds unevaluated. Rationalising the denominator Removing a surd from a denominator by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate, using (a + sqrt(b))(a - sqrt(b)) = a^2 - b. Difference of two squares The identity a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b); recognising it instantly saves several lines of working. Perfect square expansion (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 and (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2; note the middle term is 2ab, not b^2 alone. Algebraic fraction A fraction whose numerator, denominator or both contain algebraic expressions; only whole factors of the entire numerator may cancel with the denominator. Polynomial long division Writing dividend = divisor x quotient + remainder, dividing term by term in descending powers of x. Factor theorem f(a) = 0 if and only if (x - a) is a factor of f(x); used to extract linear factors and to find unknown coefficients. Remainder theorem The remainder when f(x) is divided by (x - a) is f(a); when divided by (ax - b) it is f(b/a), with no division carried out. Almost every pure mathematics paper opens with an algebraic manipulation worth 3-6 marks, and those marks are lost through slips, not through difficulty. The index laws (Edexcel 9MA0 Topics 2.1-2.2; AQA 7357 B1-B2; OCR A H640 2.01; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA AS Pure Mathematics) are non-negotiable: x^a x x^b = x^(a+b), x^a / x^b = x^(a-b), (x^a)^b = x^(ab), x^0 = 1 and x^(-a) = 1/x^a. Negative indices send the power downstairs; fractional indices convert to roots, so x^(1/2) = sqrt(x), x^(1/3) = cuberoot(x) and, in general, x^(m/n) = (nth root of x)^m. The A* habit is to convert everything to index form before combining, rather than juggling roots and powers at the same time. Surds are irrational roots kept in exact form. Two results do all the work: sqrt(a) x sqrt(b) = sqrt(ab) and sqrt(a)/sqrt(b) = sqrt(a/b). To rationalise a denominator of the form a + sqrt(b), multiply top and bottom by the conjugate a - sqrt(b), because (a + sqrt(b))(a - sqrt(b)) = a^2 - b, which is rational. Papers routinely test surds and indices together. Worked example: simplifying a compound index expression Simplify (4x^2 y^(-1))^(3/2) / (2x^3 y)^(1/2), giving the answer with positive indices. Line 1: Numerator: (4x^2 y^(-1))^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) x^3 y^(-3/2) = 8x^3 y^(-3/2), using (x^a)^b = x^(ab) and 4^(3/2) = (sqrt(4))^3 = 8. Line 2: Denominator: (2x^3 y)^(1/2) = 2^(1/2) x^(3/2) y^(1/2). Line 3: Divide: (8 / 2^(1/2)) x^(3 - 3/2) y^(-3/2 - 1/2) = (8/sqrt(2)) x^(3/2) y^(-2). Line 4: Rationalise 8/sqrt(2) = 8sqrt(2)/2 = 4sqrt(2), and flip y^(-2): answer 4sqrt(2) x^(3/2) / y^2. Expanding uses the distributive law: every term inside the bracket is multiplied by the term outside. For double brackets, FOIL (first, outer, inner, last) guarantees no pair is missed: (3x - 2)(x + 4) = 3x^2 + 12x - 2x - 8 = 3x^2 + 10x - 8. Three identities should be automatic rather than re-derived: the difference of two squares a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b), and the perfect squares (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 and (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2. The classic mark-losing errors are all sign or structure slips: writing (x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 9 (forgetting 2ab), mishandling a negative multiplier so that -2(x - 1)^2 becomes 2x^2 - 4x + 2 instead of -2x^2 + 4x - 2, and failing to spot differences of two squares in disguise, such as (x - sqrt(3))(x + sqrt(3)) = x^2 - 3 or (2x - 5)(2x + 5) = 4x^2 - 25. Factorising reverses the process. When a = 1, find two numbers with product c and sum b. When a is not 1, use the AC method : for 6x^2 + 13x + 6, compute ac = 36 and look for two numbers with product 36 and sum 13, namely 9 and 4, so 6x^2 + 13x + 6 = 6x^2 + 9x + 4x + 6 = 3x(2x + 3) + 2(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)(3x + 2). Factorising by grouping is the same pairing idea applied to four terms: x^3 + 2x^2 + 3x + 6 = x^2(x + 2) + 3(x + 2) = (x + 2)(x^2 + 3). Always finish by factorising completely : (x^2 - 4)(x + 5) is not fully factorised until written (x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 5). Worked example: expand and simplify with a perfect square Expand and simplify (3x - 2)(x + 4) - (x - 1)^2. Line 1: (3x - 2)(x + 4) = 3x^2 + 12x - 2x - 8 = 3x^2 + 10x - 8. Line 2: (x - 1)^2 = x^2 - 2x + 1, so - (x - 1)^2 = -x^2 + 2x - 1. Line 3: Subtract: (3x^2 + 10x - 8) - (x^2 - 2x + 1) = 2x^2 + 12x - 9. The single governing rule: cancel factors, never terms . In (x^2 + 3x)/x^2, the numerator factorises to x(x + 3), the x cancels with one x downstairs, and the fraction simplifies to (x + 3)/x. But 3 in (x + 3)/x^2 is a term , not a factor, so nothing cancels. The instant check: substitute x = 1 into the original and the simplified form - if the values differ, an illegal cancellation has happened. To multiply fractions, factorise everything first, then multiply numerators and denominators and cancel across the whole product. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction. To add or subtract, rewrite both fractions over a common denominator before combining numerators, then factorise the result to see whether it cancels. Worked example: simplifying a difference of two fractions Simplify (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4). Line 1: x^3 - 8 is a difference of two cubes: x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4). Line 2: x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2). Line 3: Cancel the common factor (x - 2): (x^3 - 8)/(x^2 - 4) = (x^2 + 2x + 4)/(x + 2), for x is not 2 and x is not -2. Worked example: adding fractions with different denominators Write 3/(x - 1) + 2/(x + 2) as a single fraction. Line 1: Common denominator: (x - 1)(x + 2). Line 2: 3(x + 2)/((x - 1)(x + 2)) + 2(x - 1)/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = (3x + 6 + 2x - 2)/((x - 1)(x + 2)). Line 3: Combine like terms: (5x + 4)/((x - 1)(x + 2)). The numerator has no common factor with the denominator, so this is fully simplified. These skills feed directly into partial fractions in Year 2 (Edexcel 9MA0 2.5; AQA 7357 B8), where a proper rational function is split into simpler fractions before integration - and partial fraction questions are marked almost entirely on correct factorisation and common-denominator work. Long division writes dividend = divisor x quotient + remainder . Divide term by term in descending powers: to divide 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 3x - 1 by x - 2, ask what 2x^3 / x is (2x^2), multiply back, subtract, and repeat. The result is 2x^2 - x + 1 with remainder 1, i.e. 2x^3 - 5x^2 + 3x - 1 = (x - 2)(2x^2 - x + 1) + 1. The factor theorem (Edexcel 9MA0 2.5; AQA 7357 B4; OCR A H640 6.01; CCEA AS1/A21) converts division into substitution: f(a) = 0 if and only if (x - a) is a factor. It is used in two ways. First, to show a given linear expression is a factor - evaluate and show zero. Second, to find unknown coefficients: if (x - 3) is a factor of x^3 - 4x^2 + kx + 6, then f(3) = 27 - 36 + 3k + 6 = 0, so 3k = 3 and k = 1. The remainder theorem finds the remainder without dividing: the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x - a) is f(a), and when divided by (ax - b) it is f(b/a). For the division above, f(2) = 2(8) - 5(4) + 3(2) - 1 = 1, confirming the remainder - a two-line check worth doing in the exam. Worked example: factor theorem plus full factorisation Given f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 4x + 4, show that (x - 2) is a factor and factorise f(x) completely. Line 1: f(2) = 2(8) - 3(4) - 4(2) + 4 = 16 - 12 - 8 + 4 = 0, so (x - 2) is a factor by the factor theorem. Line 2: Divide: f(x) = (x - 2)(2x^2 + x - 2), obtained by long division or by matching coefficients. Line 3: Factorise the quadratic by the AC method: 2x^2 + x - 2 = (2x - 1)(x + 1), since ac = -4 and the pair 2, -1 has product -4 and sum 1. Line 4: f(x) = (x - 2)(2x - 1)(x + 1) - three linear factors, fully factorised. Once a cubic is factorised, its roots and its sketch follow immediately, and equating coefficients (comparing x^2, x and constant terms on both sides of an identity) is the algebraic alternative to division that examiners accept fully. This topic is the opening question of pure papers on every board: typically questions 1-3 of Edexcel 9MA0 Paper 1 or Paper 2, AQA 7357 Paper 1, OCR A H640 Paper 1, WJEC/Eduqas Unit 1 and CCEA AS1/A21, worth 3-8 marks each. Command words are precise. Expand and simplify demands one final collected expression. Factorise completely demands every bracket linear (or irreducible quadratic), so check for a hidden difference of two squares. Show that demands every line of working be visible - do not skip the substitution step in a factor theorem argument. Hence means the previous result must be used. Five A* habits: (1) give exact answers with surds and fractions unevaluated unless a decimal is demanded; (2) convert roots to fractional indices before combining; (3) write a minus sign before a bracket and then distribute it - subtracting a bracket is where most marks die; (4) after any cancellation, substitute x = 1 into original and simplified forms to verify; (5) when factorising, state the zero substitutions that justify each factor, since many mark schemes award the method mark for f(a) = 0 alone. Typical whole-paper chains: an index simplification (2-3 marks) leading into solving an equation like 9^x = 3^(x + 1); or a factor theorem question feeding a coordinate geometry or integration part later in the same paper. Practising the manipulation with the follow-on part trains the fluency the papers reward: e.g. if (x - 2) is a factor of f(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 8 and the remainder when f(x) is divided by (x - 1) is -12, then f(2) = 4a + 2b = 0 and f(1) = a + b - 9 = -12, giving a + b = -3 and 2a + b = 0, so a = 3, b = -6. Two simultaneous equations from two theorem substitutions is a standard A* pattern.

topics.name: Quadratic Equations
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Quadratic Equations Solve quadratic equations by factorising, including when the coefficient of x^2 is not 1 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3 Complete the square for a = 1 and a is not 1, and use the completed square form to find exact roots and turning points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3 Use the quadratic formula to solve any quadratic, leaving answers in exact surd form (AO1) Interpret the discriminant to determine the number and nature of roots, including unknown-coefficient problems (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.3, AQA 7357 B3 Use the relationships between roots and coefficients: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha beta = c/a (AO2) Solve quadratic inequalities graphically and algebraically, giving answers in correct set notation (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.4, AQA 7357 B3 Solve hidden quadratic equations by substitution, back-substituting with the range of the substituted variable checked (AO2/AO3) Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a is not 0; factorising when a = 1 uses two numbers with product c and sum b; when a is not 1, use the AC method. Completing the square: x^2 + bx = (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2; for a is not 1, factor a out first. Quadratic formula: x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a; always works, required for surd-form answers. Discriminant b^2 - 4ac: > 0 two distinct real roots; = 0 one repeated root (tangency); < 0 no real roots. Sum of roots -b/a, product c/a. Hidden quadratics: substitute u = x^2, u = sin(theta), u = e^x and solve in u, then back-substitute and CHECK the range of the substituted variable. Quadratic equation An equation of standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a is not 0, having at most two real roots. Root A value of x for which the quadratic equals zero; the x-intercepts of the parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c. Discriminant The quantity b^2 - 4ac: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, negative gives no real roots. Completing the square Rewriting ax^2 + bx + c as a(x + b/2a)^2 + (c - b^2/4a), exposing the turning point and enabling exact surd solutions. Turning point (vertex) The point where the parabola changes direction; a minimum for a > 0 and a maximum for a < 0, located at x = -b/2a. Quadratic inequality An inequality such as x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0; solved by sketching the parabola and reading off where it satisfies the inequality. Sum and product of roots For roots alpha and beta of ax^2 + bx + c = 0: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha beta = c/a. Hidden quadratic An equation in a substituted variable, such as 2sin^2(theta) - 5sin(theta) - 3 = 0, solved by setting u = sin(theta) and back-substituting. Every board examines quadratic solving early and often (Edexcel 9MA0 2.3; AQA 7357 B3; OCR A H640 3.01; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA AS Pure Mathematics), and the first decision is method. Factorising is fastest when an integer factor pair exists: for a = 1, find two numbers with product c and sum b; for a is not 1, use the AC method - for 2x^2 - 5x - 3, compute ac = -6 and find two numbers with product -6 and sum -5, namely -6 and 1, so 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = (2x + 1)(x - 3). Completing the square is required when the question asks for the vertex or exact surd roots. The quadratic formula x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/2a always works and is the expected method when a question requests surd form or when factorising is impractical. Method marks are awarded for correct factorisation or a correct substitution into the formula, and accuracy marks for the roots - so write the formula substitution explicitly, even when using a calculator, because the substitution line is where the method mark lives. Worked example: factorising when a is not 1 Solve 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0. Line 1: ac = -6; two numbers with product -6 and sum -5: -6 and 1 (M1). Line 2: 2x^2 - 6x + x - 3 = 2x(x - 3) + 1(x - 3) = (2x + 1)(x - 3) (A1). Line 3: (2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0, so x = -1/2 or x = 3 (A1). Check roots by substitution: 2(9) - 5(3) - 3 = 0 and 2(1/4) - 5(-1/2) - 3 = 1/2 + 5/2 - 3 = 0. Both check out, so the factorisation is verified - a 20-second safety net. Completing the square rewrites the quadratic so the structure is visible: x^2 + bx = (x + b/2)^2 - (b/2)^2, and in general ax^2 + bx + c = a[(x + b/2a)^2] + (c - b^2/4a). Three uses: (1) solving with exact surd roots; (2) reading the turning point - the minimum of a(x + p)^2 + q is at (-p, q) for a > 0; (3) deriving the quadratic formula and discriminant results from scratch. The half-coefficient discipline: halve the coefficient of x, square it, and subtract it. Sign errors here are the most common mark loss, especially with negative b and with a leading coefficient that must be factored out first. Worked example: exact surd roots Solve x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0 by completing the square, giving exact answers. Line 1: Half of -4 is -2; squared is 4. x^2 - 4x + 1 = (x - 2)^2 - 4 + 1 = (x - 2)^2 - 3 (M1 A1). Line 2: (x - 2)^2 = 3, so x - 2 = +/- sqrt(3) (M1). Line 3: x = 2 +/- sqrt(3), i.e. x = 2 + sqrt(3) or x = 2 - sqrt(3) (A1: exact surd form). Worked example: vertex from completed square form Write 2x^2 - 8x + 5 in the form a(x + p)^2 + q and state the minimum point. Line 1: Factor out 2: 2(x^2 - 4x) + 5 (M1). Line 2: Complete the square inside: 2[(x - 2)^2 - 4] + 5 = 2(x - 2)^2 - 8 + 5 = 2(x - 2)^2 - 3 (A1). Line 3: Minimum at (2, -3), since 2(x - 2)^2 >= 0 with equality when x = 2 (A1). The completed square form also proves the discriminant results: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 rearranges to (x + b/2a)^2 = (b^2 - 4ac)/4a^2, and the left side is a square, so a real solution exists only when b^2 - 4ac >= 0 - this derivation is itself a common exam question. The discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines the nature of the roots without solving: greater than 0 gives two distinct real roots; equal to 0 gives one repeated root, which is exactly the condition for a line to be tangent to a curve; below 0 gives no real roots. Exam questions reverse this: given a condition on the roots, form an inequality in an unknown coefficient and solve it. Two edge cases separate A* candidates. First, when the unknown is the coefficient of x^2, the equation may cease to be quadratic: kx^2 + 4x + k = 0 with k = 0 becomes the linear equation 4x = 0, which does have a (single) real root - so k = 0 must be excluded if the question demands a quadratic with two distinct roots. Second, tangency language: a line tangent to a curve means exactly one intersection point, hence discriminant zero after substitution. Worked example: unknown coefficient with a quadratic condition Find the set of values of k for which kx^2 + 4x + (k - 3) = 0 has two distinct real roots. Line 1: Two distinct real roots require b^2 - 4ac > 0: 16 - 4k(k - 3) > 0 (M1). Line 2: 16 - 4k^2 + 12k > 0, so k^2 - 3k - 4 Line 3: (k - 4)(k + 1) Line 4: k is not 0, otherwise the equation is linear, so the final answer is -1 Worked example: roots and coefficients The equation 2x^2 + bx + 5 = 0 has roots alpha and beta such that alpha + beta = alpha beta. Find b. Line 1: Sum of roots: alpha + beta = -b/2 (M1). Line 2: Product of roots: alpha beta = 5/2 (M1). Line 3: Given alpha + beta = alpha beta: -b/2 = 5/2, so b = -5 (A1). Harder variants combine the two ideas: for which k does kx^2 + 8x + k = 0 have roots whose product equals twice their sum? Here alpha beta = c/a = 1 and alpha + beta = -8/k, so 1 = 2(-8/k), giving k = -16. Setting up the ratio equation from sum and product is the transferable A* skill. Quadratic inequalities (Edexcel 9MA0 2.4; AQA 7357 B3; OCR A H640 2.01) are solved by sketching, never by algebra alone. The routine: (1) rearrange so the quadratic is on one side; (2) solve the corresponding equation for the critical values ; (3) sketch the parabola - upward for a > 0; (4) read off the region where the inequality holds; (5) write the answer in correct notation, with strict inequalities for > and = and For x^2 - 5x + 6 > 0: critical values x = 2 and x = 3; the parabola opens upward, so it is positive outside the roots: x 3. Reversing to between its roots. Combined inequalities intersect solution sets: find k such that k^2 - 3k - 4 and k > 0: the first gives -1 0, so 0 Sketching from completed square form ties the topic together: y = 2(x - 2)^2 - 3 has minimum (2, -3), y-intercept 5 (set x = 0), and roots found by setting the square equal to 3: x = 2 +/- sqrt(3/2). A sketch annotated with intercepts and the turning point earns full marks on sketch questions, and the roots should be labelled with exact values. A hidden quadratic is any equation that becomes quadratic under a substitution: u = x^2 for quartics like x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0; u = sin(theta) for trigonometric equations; u = e^x for exponential equations; u = 3^x for 3^(2x) - 12(3^x) + 27 = 0. The method: substitute, solve the quadratic in u, then back-substitute and check the range of the substituted variable - this check is where marks are won and lost, because solutions in u may be impossible in the original variable. Worked example: hidden quadratic with a trigonometric substitution Solve 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = 0, and hence solve 2sin^2(theta) - 5sin(theta) - 3 = 0 for 0 Line 1: From the first part: 2x^2 - 5x - 3 = (2x + 1)(x - 3) = 0, so x = -1/2 or x = 3 (M1 A1). Line 2: Substitute u = sin(theta): sin(theta) = -1/2 or sin(theta) = 3 (M1: substitution). Line 3: sin(theta) = 3 is impossible since sin(theta) is between -1 and 1, so reject it (B1: range check). Line 4: sin(theta) = -1/2: reference angle pi/6, solutions in quadrants 3 and 4: theta = pi + pi/6 = 7pi/6 and theta = 2pi - pi/6 = 11pi/6 (M1 A1 A1). Exam technique across the topic: (1) write the substitution explicitly - the M1 depends on it; (2) never skip the range check; (3) for equation chains (solve, hence solve), use the first result rather than re-solving; (4) keep surd answers exact until a decimal is requested; (5) when a discriminant inequality arises, watch the sign flip when dividing by a negative and watch the k = 0 edge case. Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 2.3-2.4, AQA 7357 B3, OCR A H640 3.01 and 2.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS Unit 1 algebra, CCEA AS1/A21 - the techniques are identical, only the question wording differs.

topics.name: Coordinate Geometry
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Coordinate Geometry Find the equation of a line from a gradient and point or from two points, in y = mx + c or ax + by + c = 0 form (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1 Calculate distances and midpoints, and use the parallel (m1 = m2) and perpendicular (m1 m2 = -1) conditions (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1, AQA 7357 C1 Find the equation of a circle from its centre and radius, and recover centre and radius by completing the square from the expanded form (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2 Use circle properties: the radius is perpendicular to the tangent, and the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.6, AQA 7357 C2 Find intersections of lines with lines and lines with circles, interpreting a zero discriminant as tangency and deriving exact chord lengths (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 3.1/3.6 Determine loci of points satisfying distance conditions and prove geometric facts using gradients and distances (AO2/AO3) Gradient m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1); line through (x1, y1): y - y1 = m(x - x1). Distance d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2); midpoint M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). Parallel lines have equal gradients; perpendicular lines have gradients multiplying to -1 (m1 x m2 = -1). Circle: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 with centre (a, b), radius r; radius is perpendicular to the tangent; the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre. Line-circle intersection: substitute and examine the resulting quadratic - discriminant zero means tangency; chord length follows from the two roots. Gradient The steepness of a line: m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), the change in y per unit change in x. Midpoint The point halfway along a segment: M = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2). Distance formula The distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2), from Pythagoras. Perpendicular bisector The line through the midpoint of a segment at right angles to it; every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints, and for a chord it passes through the circle's centre. Equation of a circle The circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2. Tangent A line touching a circle or curve at exactly one point; it is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Chord A line segment joining two points on a circle; the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. Locus The set of points satisfying a geometric condition; equidistance from a point and a line gives a parabola, from two points a perpendicular bisector. Straight-line work underpins half the pure paper (Edexcel 9MA0 3.1; AQA 7357 C1; OCR A H640 4.01; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA AS Pure Mathematics). The gradient between two points is m = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), and the equation of a line comes in two interchangeable forms: point-slope y - y1 = m(x - x1) and slope-intercept y = mx + c. Exam answers usually prefer ax + by + c = 0 form when a question says give your answer in the form ax + by + c = 0 - multiply through and collect every term on one side. Two conditions do the geometric work: parallel lines have equal gradients (m1 = m2) and perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is -1 (m1 x m2 = -1), so a perpendicular gradient is the negative reciprocal. For a line 2x + 3y = 6, rewrite as y = -2x/3 + 2 to read the gradient -2/3; any perpendicular line has gradient 3/2. Worked example: perpendicular bisector Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the line joining A(-1, 4) and B(5, -2). Line 1: Midpoint of AB = ((-1 + 5)/2, (4 - 2)/2) = (2, 1) (M1). Line 2: Gradient of AB = (-2 - 4)/(5 - (-1)) = -6/6 = -1 (M1). Line 3: Perpendicular gradient = -1/(-1) = 1 (A1). Line 4: Through (2, 1): y - 1 = 1(x - 2), so y = x - 1 (A1). Check the answer: any point on y = x - 1 should be equidistant from A and B - testing (2, 1) gives distance sqrt(9 + 9) = sqrt(18) to both, confirming the bisector. The circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2 (Edexcel 9MA0 3.6; AQA 7357 C2; OCR A H640 5.01; CCEA AS1/A21). Two directions of travel: (1) given centre and radius, write the equation; (2) given the expanded form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, complete the square in x and in y to recover the centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c). Centre and radius questions award method marks for the completing-the-square lines, so show them. A circle can be specified without its centre: as the circle on a given diameter , where the centre is the midpoint of the diameter's endpoints and the radius is half the distance between them. This construction appears constantly in exam questions. Worked example: circle from a diameter Find the equation of the circle with diameter endpoints A(1, 2) and B(5, 6), and find the tangent at A. Line 1: Centre = midpoint of AB = ((1 + 5)/2, (2 + 6)/2) = (3, 4) (M1). Line 2: Radius = half of AB: AB = sqrt((5 - 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2) = sqrt(32), so r^2 = 32/4 = 8 (M1 A1). Line 3: Circle: (x - 3)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 8 (A1). Line 4: Gradient of the radius from centre (3, 4) to A(1, 2): (2 - 4)/(1 - 3) = 1 (M1). Line 5: Tangent gradient = -1 (perpendicular condition). Tangent at A: y - 2 = -1(x - 1), so y = -x + 3 (A1). Note the efficient habit: keep r^2 as a value rather than computing r, since the equation only needs r^2. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales), which is why a diameter-endpoint question often asks to prove a triangle is right-angled. Three circle properties are examinable (Edexcel 9MA0 3.6; AQA 7357 C2; OCR A H640 5.01): (1) the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact - the workhorse for tangent equations; (2) the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre - the workhorse for finding a centre from a chord; (3) the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees. Tangency can also be established algebraically: substitute the line into the circle, and a repeated root (discriminant zero) proves the line touches at exactly one point. Worked example: proving tangency algebraically Show that the line 3x + 4y = 25 is a tangent to the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25, and find the point of contact. Line 1: Substitute x = (25 - 4y)/3: ((25 - 4y)/3)^2 + y^2 = 25 (M1: substitution). Line 2: Multiply by 9: (25 - 4y)^2 + 9y^2 = 225, so 625 - 200y + 16y^2 + 9y^2 = 225 (M1). Line 3: 25y^2 - 200y + 400 = 0, so y^2 - 8y + 16 = 0, i.e. (y - 4)^2 = 0 (A1: repeated root). Line 4: The discriminant is zero, so there is exactly one intersection point: the line is a tangent (A1: conclusion). Line 5: Point of contact: y = 4, x = (25 - 16)/3 = 3, i.e. (3, 4) (A1). Worked example: tangent at a point using the radius Find the tangent to the circle (x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 = 25 at the point (5, 3). Line 1: Radius from centre (2, -1) to (5, 3): gradient (3 - (-1))/(5 - 2) = 4/3 (M1). Line 2: Tangent gradient = -3/4 (A1: perpendicular). Line 3: y - 3 = -(3/4)(x - 5), so 4y - 12 = -3x + 15, i.e. 3x + 4y = 27 (A1). To find a centre from a chord: the centre lies on the chord's perpendicular bisector - combine with a second chord (or a point and the radius) to pin down the centre by intersecting two bisectors. Intersections are simultaneous equation problems. Line with line: solve the pair directly. Line with circle: substitute the line's expression for y (or x) into the circle to get a quadratic in one variable; its roots give the intersection points. Two outcomes matter: two distinct roots mean the line cuts the circle (a chord), a repeated root means tangency, and no real roots mean the line misses. Chord lengths can be found without ever computing both points in full: if the quadratic in x has roots x1 and x2 and the line has gradient m, then the chord length is sqrt(1 + m^2) |x1 - x2| - but in practice, finding both points and using the distance formula is safer under exam pressure. Worked example: exact chord length The line y = 2x + 1 intersects the circle (x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 10 at points A and B. Find the exact length AB. Line 1: Substitute: (x - 1)^2 + (2x + 1 - 2)^2 = 10, so (x - 1)^2 + (2x - 1)^2 = 10 (M1). Line 2: x^2 - 2x + 1 + 4x^2 - 4x + 1 = 10, giving 5x^2 - 6x - 8 = 0 (A1). Line 3: Factorising: (5x + 4)(x - 2) = 0, so x = 2 or x = -4/5 (A1). Line 4: Points: A(2, 5) and B(-4/5, -3/5) (M1: y = 2x + 1 for each). Line 5: AB = sqrt((2 + 4/5)^2 + (5 + 3/5)^2) = sqrt((14/5)^2 + (28/5)^2) = sqrt(980/25) = sqrt(980)/5 = 14sqrt(5)/5 (A1: exact form). Keep every step exact: fractions, surds and squared terms should stay unevaluated until the final line, since rounding early destroys exact answers and drops accuracy marks. When the quadratic in x does not factorise nicely, use the quadratic formula for the two roots and continue exactly as before - the chord length method does not depend on the roots being rational. A locus question translates a geometric condition into an equation. Equidistance from two points gives the perpendicular bisector; equidistance from a point and a line gives a parabola . The method: write the distance to each object, equate, square to remove the roots, and simplify. Worked example: a parabola locus Find the locus of points equidistant from the point (2, 3) and the line y = -1. Line 1: Distance to the point: sqrt((x - 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2) (M1). Line 2: Distance to the line y = -1: |y + 1| (M1). Line 3: Equate and square: (x - 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2 = (y + 1)^2 (A1). Line 4: Expand: (x - 2)^2 + y^2 - 6y + 9 = y^2 + 2y + 1, so (x - 2)^2 = 8y - 8 (A1). Line 5: y = 1 + (x - 2)^2/8: a parabola with vertex (2, 1), focus (2, 3) and directrix y = -1 (A1). Geometric proof problems use gradients and distances: to prove a triangle is right-angled, either show two gradients multiply to -1 or show the sides satisfy Pythagoras (a^2 + b^2 = c^2 with the longest side as c). For A(1, 1), B(2, 2) and C(4, 0): gradient of AB is 1, gradient of BC is (0 - 2)/(4 - 2) = -1, and 1 x (-1) = -1, so the angle at B is 90 degrees. Exam technique: (1) write the completing-the-square or gradient lines explicitly - method marks live there; (2) keep r^2 unradiquified; (3) when a question says show that a line is a tangent, the expected proof is a zero discriminant, not a sketch; (4) use exact fractions throughout; (5) finish circle questions by checking the point lies on the circle (substitute into the equation). Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 3, AQA 7357 C1-C2, OCR A H640 4.01 and 5.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS Unit 1 geometry, CCEA AS1/A21 - identical techniques, differing wording.

topics.name: Trigonometry
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Trigonometry Work in radians and degrees, using s = r(theta) and A = 1/2 r^2 (theta) for arcs and sectors, and recall exact values for 0, pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2 (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1-5.2, AQA 7357 E1 Sketch sin, cos and tan graphs and their transformations y = a sin(bx + c) + d, stating amplitude, period and phase (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.1, AQA 7357 E1 Use the core identities sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 and tan = sin/cos to solve equations and prove identities (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4 Apply compound angle, double angle and R-formula results, including expressing a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) as R sin(theta + alpha) (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.5, AQA 7357 E6 Solve trigonometric equations in a given interval, using the CAST diagram or graphs and rejecting impossible solutions (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.4, AQA 7357 E4 Apply the sine rule (including the ambiguous case), cosine rule and area = 1/2 ab sin C to triangles (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 5.3, AQA 7357 E3 Use inverse trigonometric functions with their domains and ranges, and small-angle approximations (AO1/AO2) Exact values: sin: 0, 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, 1; cos: 1, sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1/2, 0 for pi/6 steps from 0 to pi/2; tan = sin/cos. Core identity: sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1; tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta) when cos(theta) is not 0. Compound angles: sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B; cos(A +/- B) = cos A cos B -/+ sin A sin B; double angle: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A in three forms. R-formula: a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = R sin(theta + alpha), R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2), tan(alpha) = b/a; maximum R, minimum -R. Sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C (ambiguous case SSA); cosine rule a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A; area = 1/2 ab sin C. Radian The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius; pi radians = 180 degrees. Exact value The precise surd or rational form of a trigonometric ratio at a standard angle, such as sin(pi/6) = 1/2 and cos(pi/3) = 1/2, tan(pi/4) = 1. Compound angle formulae sin(A +/- B) = sin A cos B +/- cos A sin B; cos(A +/- B) = cos A cos B -/+ sin A sin B; tan(A +/- B) = (tan A +/- tan B)/(1 -/+ tan A tan B). Double angle formulae sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A). R-formula a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = R sin(theta + alpha) with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and tan(alpha) = b/a; exposes the maximum R and minimum -R. Sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; used when two angles and a side, or two sides and a non-included angle, are known. Cosine rule a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A; used when two sides and the included angle are known, or all three sides to find an angle. Ambiguous case In the sine rule with two sides and a non-included angle (SSA), two different triangles can satisfy the data - check for a second solution. Inverse trigonometric functions arcsin has range [-pi/2, pi/2], arccos has range [0, pi], arctan has range (-pi/2, pi/2); each returns the principal value. A-level trigonometry is done in radians by default (Edexcel 9MA0 5.1-5.2; AQA 7357 E1-E2; OCR A H640 9.01; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA AS Pure Mathematics): pi radians = 180 degrees, so pi/6 = 30 degrees, pi/4 = 45 degrees, pi/3 = 60 degrees, pi/2 = 90 degrees. Radians make arc length and sector area clean: arc length s = r(theta) and sector area A = 1/2 r^2 (theta), with theta in radians - no 360-degree factor needed. Convert always when a question mixes degrees and radians, and keep the calculator in the right mode: degree-mode calculators silently give wrong values in calculus questions. Exact values are recall material, not derivation material. The sin row climbs 0, 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(3)/2, 1 across 0, pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2; the cos row runs in reverse; tan = sin/cos gives 0, 1/sqrt(3), 1, sqrt(3), undefined. Answers demanding exact form must keep the surds - 0.866 loses the mark. The graphs: y = sin x and y = cos x have amplitude 1 and period 2pi, with cos x = sin(x + pi/2); y = tan x has period pi and vertical asymptotes where cos x = 0, at pi/2 + k(pi). Transformations follow the general pattern y = a sin(bx + c) + d: amplitude |a|, period 2pi/|b|, phase shift -c/b, vertical shift d. So y = 2cos(2x - pi/3) has amplitude 2, period pi and phase shift pi/6 to the right - a max of 2 occurs at x = pi/6 + k(pi). Inverse functions restrict to principal values: arcsin x has range [-pi/2, pi/2], arccos x has range [0, pi], arctan x has range (-pi/2, pi/2). These restrictions matter when solving equations involving inverse functions, since the inverse only returns one branch. Two identities drive almost everything (Edexcel 9MA0 5.4; AQA 7357 E4; OCR A H640 10.01): sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1 and tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta) . The identity is used in two directions: to replace sin^2 with 1 - cos^2 (or vice versa) when an equation mixes both, and to prove identities. The solving routine: (1) isolate or factorise to get a single trig function equal to a constant; (2) find the reference (acute) angle; (3) use the CAST diagram or a graph to find all solutions in the interval; (4) check every solution lies in the required interval. Worked example: factorising a trig equation Solve 2cos^2(theta) + sin(theta) - 1 = 0 for 0 Line 1: Replace cos^2(theta) with 1 - sin^2(theta): 2(1 - sin^2(theta)) + sin(theta) - 1 = 0 (M1: identity substitution). Line 2: -2sin^2(theta) + sin(theta) + 1 = 0, i.e. 2sin^2(theta) - sin(theta) - 1 = 0 (A1). Line 3: Factorising: (2sin(theta) + 1)(sin(theta) - 1) = 0, so sin(theta) = -1/2 or sin(theta) = 1 (M1). Line 4: sin(theta) = 1: theta = pi/2 (A1). sin(theta) = -1/2: reference angle pi/6, sine negative in quadrants 3 and 4, so theta = 7pi/6 and theta = 11pi/6 (A1 A1). Two habits protect marks: never divide by a trig factor - cos(theta)(4sin(theta) - sqrt(3)) = 0 must be factorised, not divided by cos(theta), because dividing destroys the cos(theta) = 0 solutions; and always sketch or CAST before listing solutions, since the interval determines how many there are. Worked example: never divide by a trig factor Solve 2sin(2theta) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) for 0 Line 1: 2(2sin(theta)cos(theta)) = sqrt(3)cos(theta) (M1: double angle). Line 2: 4sin(theta)cos(theta) - sqrt(3)cos(theta) = 0, so cos(theta)(4sin(theta) - sqrt(3)) = 0 (M1: factorise, do not divide). Line 3: cos(theta) = 0: theta = pi/2, 3pi/2 (A1). Line 4: sin(theta) = sqrt(3)/4 = 0.4330: theta = arcsin(0.4330) = 0.448 and theta = pi - 0.448 = 2.694 (A1 A1). The compound angle formulae (Edexcel 9MA0 5.5; AQA 7357 E6; OCR A H640 10.01) expand sin(A +/- B), cos(A +/- B) and tan(A +/- B); the double angle formulae follow by setting B = A. sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2sin^2 A (three interchangeable forms - choose the one matching the rest of the equation); tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A), derived by substituting A = B into the tan compound formula and using tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta). The R-formula converts a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) into a single shifted wave: a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = R sin(theta + alpha) with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and tan(alpha) = b/a. The payoffs: the maximum of the expression is R, the minimum is -R, and equations of the form a sin(theta) + b cos(theta) = c become one-step inverse sine problems. For a cos form, use R cos(theta - alpha) with tan(alpha) = b/a. Worked example: R-formula with max and min Write 5cos(theta) - 12sin(theta) in the form R cos(theta + alpha) with R > 0 and 0 Line 1: R cos(theta + alpha) = R cos(theta)cos(alpha) - R sin(theta)sin(alpha) (M1: expand). Line 2: Compare: R cos(alpha) = 5 and R sin(alpha) = 12 (M1). Line 3: R^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, so R = 13 (A1). tan(alpha) = 12/5, so alpha = arctan(12/5) = 1.176 radians (A1). Line 4: 5cos(theta) - 12sin(theta) = 13cos(theta + 1.176); maximum of cos is 1, so the maximum value is 13 (A1). Know the direction of the shift: R sin(theta + alpha) shifts the sine wave left by alpha; using the wrong sign flips the quadrant of alpha and loses the accuracy marks. When a question asks where the maximum occurs, set theta + alpha = pi/2 and solve. Non-right-angled triangles (Edexcel 9MA0 5.3; AQA 7357 E3; OCR A H640 9.01; CCEA AS1/A21) use three results. The sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C applies when you know two angles and a side, or two sides and a non-included angle - the latter is the ambiguous case , where two triangles can fit the data. The cosine rule a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A applies when two sides and the included angle are known, or all three sides (to find an angle by rearranging to cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/2bc). The area is 1/2 ab sin C for any pair of sides and the included angle. Worked example: cosine rule and area In triangle ABC, AB = 8 cm, BC = 11 cm and angle ABC = 72 degrees. Find AC and the area. Line 1: The included angle at B sits between AB and BC: AC^2 = 8^2 + 11^2 - 2(8)(11)cos(72 degrees) (M1: cosine rule). Line 2: = 64 + 121 - 176(0.3090) = 185 - 54.4 = 130.6 (M1). Line 3: AC = sqrt(130.6) = 11.4 cm (A1: 3 s.f.). Line 4: Area = 1/2 (8)(11)sin(72 degrees) = 44(0.9511) = 41.8 cm^2 (A1). Worked example: sine rule with two sides and a non-included angle In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 9 and angle C = 60 degrees. Find c and the area. Line 1: The angle is included between a and b, so use the cosine rule: c^2 = 7^2 + 9^2 - 2(7)(9)cos(60 degrees) = 49 + 81 - 63 = 67 (M1 A1). Line 2: c = sqrt(67) = 8.19 (A1). Line 3: Area = 1/2 ab sin C = 1/2 (7)(9)sin(60 degrees) = 31.5 x (sqrt(3)/2) = 27.3 (A1). Ambiguous-case discipline: with the sine rule in the form sin B = b sin A/a, the acute solution for B may not be the only one - the obtuse supplement 180 degrees - B is also valid provided the angles still sum below 180 degrees. State both when the data allows, or justify the single solution. Identity proofs follow one discipline: start from the more complicated side and reduce it to the other, never moving terms across the equals sign as if solving. The universal strategy: convert everything to sin and cos using tan(theta) = sin(theta)/cos(theta), then look for the sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 substitution. Worked example: proving a double angle identity Prove that tan(2theta) = 2tan(theta)/(1 - tan^2(theta)). Line 1: sin(2theta) = 2sin(theta)cos(theta) and cos(2theta) = cos^2(theta) - sin^2(theta) (M1: double angles). Line 2: tan(2theta) = sin(2theta)/cos(2theta) = 2sin(theta)cos(theta)/(cos^2(theta) - sin^2(theta)) (M1: tan as sin/cos). Line 3: Divide numerator and denominator by cos^2(theta): 2tan(theta)/(1 - tan^2(theta)) (A1: reduction complete, valid where cos(theta) is not 0). Exact values with inverse functions combine the ideas: sin(arcsin(3/5) + arccos(4/5)) - both inverse values equal the same angle (36.87 degrees, since sin = 3/5 and cos = 4/5 there), so the expression is sin(2 x 36.87 degrees) = 2(3/5)(4/5) = 24/25. Convert inverse values to a right triangle, then apply a compound or double angle formula. Exam technique: (1) keep the calculator in the mode the question uses - radians unless degrees are stated; (2) never divide by a trig factor; (3) give exact surd answers unless decimals are requested, and give decimals to 3 s.f. otherwise; (4) check all solutions lie in the interval, including the boundary behaviour at pi/2 asymptotes; (5) for R-formula questions, state R and alpha explicitly before using them. Small-angle approximations (sin(theta) = theta, cos(theta) = 1 - theta^2/2, tan(theta) = theta for small theta in radians) appear in derivation questions - know them. Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 5, AQA 7357 E1-E6, OCR A H640 9.01 and 10.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS Unit 1 trigonometry, CCEA AS1/A21 - identical techniques, differing wording.

topics.name: Differentiation
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Differentiation Differentiate x^n from first principles for positive integer n and understand the first principles definition of the derivative (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.1, AQA 7357 G1 Apply the power rule to polynomials and to negative and fractional powers (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.2, AQA 7357 G2 Apply the sum, product, quotient and chain rules, including to e^x, ln x, sin x, cos x and tan x (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.5, AQA 7357 G2 Find equations of tangents and normals, using the perpendicular condition for the normal (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.3, AQA 7357 G3 Find and classify stationary points using the second derivative, including points of inflection (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.4, AQA 7357 G3 Solve optimisation problems, justifying maxima and minima, and use implicit differentiation and connected rates of change (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 7.6-7.7, AQA 7357 G3-G4 Power rule: d/dx(x^n) = n x^(n-1) for all real n; sum and difference differentiate term by term. Product rule: d/dx(fg) = f'g + fg'; quotient rule: d/dx(f/g) = (f'g - fg')/g^2; chain rule: d/dx(f(g(x))) = f'(g(x)) x g'(x). Standard derivatives: e^x, ln x = 1/x, sin x = cos x, cos x = -sin x, tan x = sec^2 x. Stationary points: f'(x) = 0. Second derivative test: f'' < 0 maximum, f'' > 0 minimum; inflection requires f'' = 0 with sign change of f'. Tangent gradient f'(x1); normal gradient -1/f'(x1). Implicit: differentiate term by term, y-terms get dy/dx factors. Connected rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). Derivative The gradient function f'(x) = dy/dx, measuring the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x. Differentiation from first principles f'(x) = limit as h tends to 0 of (f(x + h) - f(x))/h: the limit of the chord gradient as the chord shrinks to a point. Stationary point A point where f'(x) = 0: a maximum, a minimum or a stationary point of inflection. Second derivative f''(x), the rate of change of the gradient; f'' > 0 at a stationary point indicates a minimum, f'' < 0 a maximum. Point of inflection A point where the curve changes concavity; a stationary point of inflection has f' = 0 AND f'' = 0 with f' changing sign. Tangent and normal The tangent at (x1, y1) has gradient f'(x1); the normal is perpendicular, with gradient -1/f'(x1) (vertical if f'(x1) = 0). Implicit differentiation Differentiating an equation not in y = f(x) form, term by term with respect to x, applying the chain rule to terms in y and solving for dy/dx. Connected rates of change The chain rule applied to rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx) x (dx/dt), linking how fast one quantity changes to another. Differentiation from first principles (Edexcel 9MA0 7.1; AQA 7357 G1; OCR A H640 11.01) defines the derivative as the limit of chord gradients: f'(x) = lim as h -> 0 of (f(x + h) - f(x))/h. Exam questions ask for specific functions - x^2, x^3, 1/x, x^2 + x - or a general polynomial, and the mark scheme awards marks for the correct expansion, the cancellation of h, and taking the limit correctly. Worked example: x^2 from first principles Line 1: (f(x + h) - f(x))/h = ((x + h)^2 - x^2)/h (M1: correct setup). Line 2: = (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2)/h = (2xh + h^2)/h (M1: expand, cancel x^2). Line 3: = 2x + h, valid for h is not 0 (A1: cancellation of h shown). Line 4: As h -> 0, this tends to 2x, so d/dx(x^2) = 2x (A1: limit taken). The power rule (Edexcel 9MA0 7.2; AQA 7357 G2) extends to all real n: d/dx(x^n) = n x^(n-1). It handles negative and fractional powers as readily as positive integers: sqrt(x) = x^(1/2) differentiates to (1/2)x^(-1/2) = 1/(2sqrt(x)), and 1/x = x^(-1) differentiates to -x^(-2) = -1/x^2. The A* habit: rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers before differentiating, and rewrite the answer in the form the question asks for. Sum and difference rules follow term by term, so polynomials differentiate mechanically - errors come from sign slips on negative powers, not from difficulty. Notation matters in proofs and applied questions alike: f'(x), dy/dx and d/dx of an expression all mean the same operation, but applied questions expect dy/dt style rates, and mixing notation mid-solution reads badly to examiners. Three rules handle every composite or combined function (Edexcel 9MA0 7.5; AQA 7357 G2; OCR A H640 11.01/16.01). The product rule : d/dx(fg) = f'g + fg'. The quotient rule : d/dx(f/g) = (f'g - fg')/g^2 - note the order in the numerator, f' first. The chain rule : differentiate the outside function at the inside function, then multiply by the derivative of the inside: d/dx(f(g(x))) = f'(g(x)) x g'(x). With u = g(x), the chain rule reads dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx. The standard derivatives to recall (Edexcel 9MA0 7.2): d/dx(e^x) = e^x; d/dx(ln x) = 1/x; d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = -sin x; d/dx(tan x) = sec^2 x. With constants: d/dx(e^(3x)) = 3e^(3x), d/dx(sin(2x + 1)) = 2cos(2x + 1) - the chain rule supplies the internal factor. Worked example: product rule with a chain rule inside Differentiate y = x^2 sqrt(2x + 1), simplifying your answer. Line 1: u = x^2 and v = (2x + 1)^(1/2), so du/dx = 2x and dv/dx = (1/2)(2x + 1)^(-1/2) x 2 = (2x + 1)^(-1/2) (M1: product rule setup, chain on v). Line 2: dy/dx = 2x(2x + 1)^(1/2) + x^2(2x + 1)^(-1/2) (M1: product rule applied). Line 3: Common denominator: dy/dx = [2x(2x + 1) + x^2]/(2x + 1)^(1/2) = (5x^2 + 2x)/sqrt(2x + 1) (A1). Line 4: Factorise: dy/dx = x(5x + 2)/sqrt(2x + 1) (A1: simplified form). Rule choice is a decision, not a guess: two factors multiplied - product rule; a ratio - quotient rule; a function inside a function - chain rule; and combinations nest the rules inside each other. Writing u and v (or u and the inside function) explicitly earns the method mark even if the algebra later slips. Worked example: quotient rule Differentiate y = sin(x)/x^2 and simplify your answer. Line 1: u = sin(x), v = x^2; du/dx = cos(x), dv/dx = 2x (M1: setup). Line 2: Quotient rule: dy/dx = (cos(x) x x^2 - sin(x) x 2x)/x^4 (M1: applied with f' first). Line 3: Simplify: dy/dx = (x cos(x) - 2sin(x))/x^3 (A1: factor x cancelled). The quotient rule is the product rule with a sign flipped and a denominator added - but mixing them up is common, so memorise the numerator order f'g - fg' with the derivative of the top function first. The tangent to y = f(x) at (x1, y1) has gradient f'(x1) and equation y - y1 = f'(x1)(x - x1). The normal is perpendicular: gradient -1/f'(x1). The edge case worth knowing: when f'(x1) = 0, the tangent is horizontal and the normal is the vertical line x = x1 - no reciprocal exists, so write the vertical line directly. Stationary points satisfy f'(x) = 0 (Edexcel 9MA0 7.4; AQA 7357 G3; OCR A H640 11.01). Classification uses the second derivative test : f'' 0 means a minimum. A point of inflection with f' = 0 needs f'' = 0 and a sign change in f' - the second derivative test is inconclusive there, and the sign of f' either side settles it. Worked example: stationary points and their nature Find the stationary points of y = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5 and determine their nature. Line 1: dy/dx = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1) (M1: differentiate, factorise). Line 2: dy/dx = 0 at x = 3 and x = -1 (A1: both stationary points found). Line 3: d^2y/dx^2 = 6x - 6. At x = 3: 12 > 0, so a minimum (M1: second derivative test). Line 4: At x = -1: -12 Line 5: y(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 5 = -22 and y(-1) = -1 - 3 + 9 + 5 = 10: minimum at (3, -22), maximum at (-1, 10) (A1: coordinates). Always give the coordinates of stationary points, not just the x-values - mark schemes award the accuracy mark for the y-coordinate, and forgetting it is the most common drop in this question type. Optimisation questions (Edexcel 9MA0 7.4; AQA 7357 G3; OCR A H640 16.01) ask for a maximum or minimum of a modelled quantity. The routine: (1) write the quantity as a function of one variable, using a constraint to eliminate the second variable; (2) differentiate and set the derivative to zero; (3) solve; (4) justify the nature with the second derivative or a sign check; (5) answer in context with units, checking the value lies in the sensible domain. Worked example: minimum surface area A closed rectangular box has a square base and volume 500 cm^3. Find its minimum surface area. Line 1: Let the base side be x and the height h. Volume: x^2 h = 500, so h = 500/x^2 (M1: constraint used to eliminate h). Line 2: Surface area: S = x^2 + 4xh = x^2 + 4x(500/x^2) = x^2 + 2000/x (M1: single-variable expression). Line 3: dS/dx = 2x - 2000/x^2. Setting to zero: 2x^3 = 2000, so x = 10 (A1: critical value). Line 4: d^2S/dx^2 = 2 + 4000/x^3, which is positive at x = 10, so a minimum (A1: justification). Line 5: h = 500/100 = 5; S = 100 + 200 = 300 cm^2 (A1: answer in context). Three discipline points: eliminate the extra variable before differentiating - differentiating a two-variable expression earns nothing; justify the nature of the stationary point explicitly (the second derivative line is a mark); and check the domain - a negative or zero base side is meaningless, and some optimisation problems have their maximum at an endpoint rather than a stationary point, so test the sensible endpoints when the model restricts the domain. Implicit differentiation (Edexcel 9MA0 7.6; AQA 7357 G3; OCR A H640 16.01) handles curves not written as y = f(x). Differentiate every term with respect to x; for terms in y, the chain rule appends a dy/dx factor (d/dx of y^2 is 2y dy/dx; of xy is y + x dy/dx by the product rule). Then collect the dy/dx terms and solve. Worked example: implicit gradient A curve is defined by x^2 + 2xy + 3y^2 = 6. Find the gradient at the point (1, 1). Line 1: 2x + (2y + 2x dy/dx) + 6y dy/dx = 0 (M1: implicit differentiation, product rule on xy). Line 2: Collect: (2x + 6y) dy/dx = -(2x + 2y), so dy/dx = -(x + y)/(x + 3y) (A1: solved for dy/dx). Line 3: At (1, 1): dy/dx = -(1 + 1)/(1 + 3) = -2/4 = -1/2 (A1: evaluated). Connected rates of change apply the chain rule to rates: dy/dt = (dy/dx) x (dx/dt). For a sphere with radius growing at 0.5 cm/s: V = (4/3)(pi)r^3, so dV/dt = 4(pi)r^2 x dr/dt = 4(pi)(100)(0.5) = 200(pi) = 628 cm^3/s when r = 10 - differentiate first, then substitute, never the reverse. Exam technique: (1) for from-first-principles questions, show the limit notation and the cancellation of h explicitly; (2) write u and v before applying the product or quotient rule; (3) give stationary point coordinates; (4) in optimisation, state the model and the constraint before differentiating, and justify the maximum or minimum; (5) in implicit work, the dy/dx factor on y-terms is the method mark. Also know the shapes: a positive cubic has an N-shape with max then min (or one stationary point of inflection when the roots of f' coincide), and a negative cubic reverses it - sketching before classifying catches sign errors. Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 7, AQA 7357 G1-G4, OCR A H640 11.01 and 16.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS/A2 Units, CCEA AS1/A21 - identical techniques, differing wording.

topics.name: Integration
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Integration Integrate polynomials and negative powers with the power rule, and recall the standard results for 1/x, e^x and basic trigonometric functions (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.1, AQA 7357 H1 Integrate composite functions using the reverse chain rule and substitution, changing limits correctly in definite integrals (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.2/8.5, AQA 7357 H2 Apply integration by parts, choosing u sensibly and repeating where needed (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.5, AQA 7357 H3 Evaluate definite integrals and find areas under and between curves, splitting where the curve crosses the axis (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.3, AQA 7357 H4 Calculate volumes of revolution about the x-axis and y-axis (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.4, AQA 7357 H4 Form and solve differential equations by separation of variables, finding particular solutions from initial conditions (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 8.6, AQA 7357 H5 Power rule: the integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n not -1; special: 1/x gives ln|x| + C, e^x gives e^x + C. Trig: the integral of sin x dx = -cos x + C; cos x dx = sin x + C; sec^2 x dx = tan x + C - always check the sign on sine. Reverse chain rule: the integral of f'(x)[f(x)]^n dx = [f(x)]^(n+1)/(n+1) + C; the integral of f'(x)e^(f(x)) dx = e^(f(x)) + C. Substitution: u = f(x), dx = du/f'(x), and CHANGE the limits for definite integrals. By parts: the integral of u dv = uv - the integral of v du; choose u by LIATE. Definite integral F(b) - F(a) measures signed area: split where f crosses the axis. Area between curves: the integral of (top - bottom) dx. Volumes: V = (pi) times the integral of y^2 dx (x-axis) or (pi) times the integral of x^2 dy (y-axis). Indefinite integral The reverse of differentiation: a family of functions differing by a constant, written with the + C. Constant of integration The arbitrary constant C added to every indefinite integral, since differentiating any constant gives zero. Definite integral The integral with limits, evaluated as F(b) - F(a); it measures signed area between the curve and the axis. Integration by substitution Reversing the chain rule: let u = f(x), rewrite dx = du/f'(x), and change the limits when the integral is definite. Integration by parts The reverse of the product rule: the integral of u (dv/dx) = uv - the integral of v (du/dx); choose u by the LIATE order. Volume of revolution The volume formed by rotating a curve about an axis: V = (pi) times the integral of y^2 dx about the x-axis, or (pi) times the integral of x^2 dy about the y-axis. Differential equation An equation involving a derivative, such as dy/dx = 2xy; solved by separating the variables and integrating both sides. Particular solution The member of the solution family fixed by an initial or boundary condition, which determines the constant of integration. Integration is the reverse of differentiation plus a constant of integration (Edexcel 9MA0 8.1; AQA 7357 H1; OCR A H640 12.01). The power rule: the integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for any n except -1 - raise the power by one and divide by the new power. The two exceptions and extras are recall material: the integral of 1/x dx = ln|x| + C (note the modulus); the integral of e^x dx = e^x + C; and the trigonometric results the integral of sin x dx = -cos x + C, the integral of cos x dx = sin x + C, and the integral of sec^2 x dx = tan x + C. The sign on the sine integral is the classic slip - check it by differentiating your answer, since d/dx(-cos x) = sin x confirms it. A definite integral has limits and evaluates to a number: the integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), with no constant needed. It measures signed area: regions below the axis contribute negatively, so area questions split the integral where the curve crosses the axis. Polynomials integrate term by term exactly as they differentiate, so fluency here is mechanical - the marks are lost in the exceptions (the modulus in ln|x|, the sign on -cos x) and in the techniques that follow. Writing the antiderivative line explicitly before substituting limits earns the method mark - jumping straight to a number is where marks are lost. Worked example: basic definite integral Evaluate the integral from 1 to 3 of (2x + 1/x) dx. Line 1: Antiderivative: x^2 + ln|x| (M1: power rule plus ln result). Line 2: Substitute limits: (9 + ln 3) - (1 + ln 1) = 8 + ln 3 (A1). Line 3: = 8 + 1.0986 = 9.10 (A1: 3 s.f. if decimals requested; 8 + ln 3 is the exact form). The reverse chain rule handles integrals where a derivative sits alongside a function of itself: the integral of f'(x)[f(x)]^n dx = [f(x)]^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, and the integral of f'(x)e^(f(x)) dx = e^(f(x)) + C. Spot the pattern first - if the derivative of the inner function (up to a constant) multiplies the outer function, the reverse chain rule is the fast route, no substitution needed. Substitution (Edexcel 9MA0 8.5; AQA 7357 H2; OCR A H640 17.01) is the general version: let u = f(x), compute du/dx, rewrite dx = du/(du/dx), and replace every x in the integrand. For definite integrals, change the limits from x-values to u-values - then the integral is entirely in u and no back-substitution is needed. Forgetting the limit change is the most common error, and it silently produces a wrong answer if the integrand is also back-substituted inconsistently. Worked example: substitution with limit change Evaluate the integral from 0 to 2 of x sqrt(4 - x^2) dx using the substitution u = 4 - x^2. Line 1: du/dx = -2x, so x dx = -du/2 (M1: substitution set up). Line 2: Limits: x = 0 gives u = 4; x = 2 gives u = 0 (M1: limits changed). Line 3: Integral becomes the integral from 4 to 0 of u^(1/2) (-1/2) du = (1/2) times the integral from 0 to 4 of u^(1/2) du (A1: flipped and simplified). Line 4: = (1/2)[(2/3)u^(3/2)] from 0 to 4 = (1/3)(8) = 8/3 (A1: exact answer). Worked example: reverse chain rule spot Evaluate the integral from 0 to 1 of x/(1 + x^2)^2 dx. Line 1: The derivative of 1 + x^2 is 2x, which matches the numerator up to a constant (M1: reverse chain spot). Line 2: Antiderivative: -1/(2(1 + x^2)) (A1). Line 3: Limits: [-1/(2(1 + x^2))] from 0 to 1 = -1/4 - (-1/2) = 1/4 (A1). Integration by parts (Edexcel 9MA0 8.5; AQA 7357 H3; OCR A H640 17.01) reverses the product rule: the integral of u (dv/dx) dx = uv - the integral of v (du/dx) dx. Choosing u follows the LIATE order - Logs, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential - pick u as the earliest category present, because u must simplify when differentiated and dv/dx must survive integration. Logs go first: ln x differentiates to the clean 1/x; exponentials go last: e^x integrates to itself without simplifying. Worked example: log first Use integration by parts to find the integral of x ln x dx. Line 1: u = ln x, dv/dx = x, so du/dx = 1/x and v = x^2/2 (M1: LIATE choice of u). Line 2: Integral = (x^2/2) ln x - the integral of (x^2/2)(1/x) dx (M1: formula applied). Line 3: = (x^2/2) ln x - the integral of x/2 dx = (x^2/2) ln x - x^2/4 + C (A1). Worked example: algebraic before trig Find the integral of x cos x dx. Line 1: u = x (algebraic), dv/dx = cos x, so du/dx = 1 and v = sin x (M1). Line 2: Integral = x sin x - the integral of sin x dx (M1). Line 3: = x sin x + cos x + C (A1: sign on the sine integral). Some integrals need by parts twice : the integral of x^2 e^x dx = x^2 e^x - the integral of 2x e^x dx, and the remaining integral needs by parts again, giving x^2 e^x - 2x e^x + 2 e^x + C = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C. The classic cyclic case is the integral of e^x sin x dx, where applying by parts twice returns the original integral, which is then solved algebraically. Keep the same u-type on the second application, or the algebra cycles without progress. The definite integral measures signed area, so area questions need care where the curve crosses the axis (Edexcel 9MA0 8.3; AQA 7357 H4; OCR A H640 12.01/17.01). Find where f(x) = 0, split the integral at those points, and add the absolute values. The area between two curves is the integral of (top - bottom) dx over the interval between their intersections - find the intersections first, and check which curve is on top in that interval. Worked example: area under a curve crossing the axis The region R is bounded by y = 4 - x^2 and the x-axis. Find the exact area of R. Line 1: Intersections: 4 - x^2 = 0, so x = -2 and x = 2 (M1: limits found). Line 2: The curve is above the axis throughout (-2, 2), so area = the integral from -2 to 2 of (4 - x^2) dx (M1). Line 3: Antiderivative: 4x - x^3/3; at 2: 8 - 8/3 = 16/3; at -2: -8 + 8/3 = -16/3 (A1). Line 4: Area = 16/3 - (-16/3) = 32/3 (A1: exact). Worked example: volume of revolution The curve y = sqrt(x) from x = 0 to x = 4 is rotated a full turn about the x-axis. Find the exact volume formed. Line 1: V = (pi) times the integral from 0 to 4 of y^2 dx = (pi) times the integral from 0 to 4 of x dx (M1: formula, y^2 = x). Line 2: = (pi)[x^2/2] from 0 to 4 = (pi)(8) = 8(pi) (A1: exact volume, units cubed). For rotation about the y-axis, use V = (pi) times the integral of x^2 dy with the y-limits, rewriting the curve as x = f(y) first. Volumes always carry the (pi) factor and units cubed - dropping the (pi) or integrating y instead of y^2 are the two standard errors. For a region between two curves rotated about the axis, the washer method applies: V = (pi) times the integral of (R^2 - r^2) dx, where R is the outer radius (the top curve) and r the inner radius (the bottom curve) - integrate the difference of the squares , not the square of the difference. A differential equation involving dy/dx is solved by separation of variables (Edexcel 9MA0 8.6; AQA 7357 H5; OCR A H640 17.01): move every y term to the dy side and every x term to the dx side, integrate both sides, and use an initial condition to find C. A general solution keeps C arbitrary; a particular solution fixes it from the condition. Worked example: separable equation with an initial condition Solve dy/dx = 2xy, given that y = 3 when x = 0. Line 1: Separate: (1/y) dy = 2x dx (M1: variables separated). Line 2: Integrate: ln|y| = x^2 + C (A1: both sides integrated). Line 3: Exponentiate: y = A e^(x^2), absorbing the constant (M1: general solution). Line 4: Initial condition: y(0) = 3 gives A = 3, so y = 3e^(x^2) (A1: particular solution). Exam technique across the topic: (1) write the antiderivative line explicitly before substituting limits - the method mark lives there; (2) change limits when substituting in a definite integral, or back-substitute consistently - mixing the two produces silent errors; (3) check every indefinite integral by differentiating the answer (the -cos x check); (4) in area questions, split at axis crossings and add absolute values; (5) in volume questions, keep the (pi) and integrate y^2, not y; (6) in differential equations, separate cleanly, keep ln|y| with the modulus, and state the particular solution in the form asked. Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 8, AQA 7357 H1-H5, OCR A H640 12.01 and 17.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS/A2 Units, CCEA AS1/A21 - identical techniques, differing wording.

topics.name: Vectors
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Vectors Represent vectors in 2D and 3D using components and unit vectors, and calculate magnitudes and direction angles (AO1) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 Section J, OCR A H640 14.01 Add, subtract and scalar-multiply vectors, and use position vectors to find displacements, midpoints and collinear points (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J1-J2 Calculate the scalar (dot) product in component and magnitude form, and determine angles between vectors and conditions for perpendicularity and parallelism (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J2-J3 Find the vector and Cartesian equations of a line in 2D and 3D, and determine whether lines are parallel, intersecting or skew (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 J3 Solve geometric problems using vectors, proving properties such as right angles, parallelograms and collinearity (AO2/AO3) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, OCR A H640 14.01 Connect vectors to kinematics (velocity and displacement as vector quantities) and understand scalar triple product contexts as a Further Mathematics extension (AO2) Magnitude: |a| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) in 2D and sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) in 3D; unit vector in the direction of a: a/|a|. Displacement from A to B: AB = b - a (subtract position vectors: end minus start). Scalar product: a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) = x1x2 + y1y2 + z1z2; perpendicular exactly when a . b = 0; parallel when components are in the same ratio. Vector equation of a line: r = a + t d (or r = a + t(b - a) through two points); Cartesian form (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n. In 3D, intersecting lines: solve two equations for t and s, then CHECK the third equation - failure means the lines are skew. Vector A quantity with magnitude and direction, written as a column or in component form xi + yj + zk; distinguished from a scalar, which has magnitude only. Magnitude The length of a vector: for a = (x, y) it is sqrt(x^2 + y^2), and for a = (x, y, z) it is sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2), denoted |a|. Unit vector A vector of magnitude 1; the unit vector in the direction of a is a/|a|. The standard unit vectors i, j and k point along the coordinate axes. Position vector The vector from the origin to a point, written OP or p; the displacement from A to B is AB = b - a, the difference of position vectors. Scalar (dot) product a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) = x1x2 + y1y2 + z1z2; a scalar measuring how much two vectors align, zero exactly when they are perpendicular. Direction vector Any vector parallel to a line, giving its direction; the line through point A with direction d has vector equation r = a + t d. Vector equation of a line r = a + t d, where a is the position vector of a point on the line, d a direction vector and t a scalar parameter. Skew lines Lines in three dimensions that are not parallel but never meet; they have no common solution despite having non-parallel directions. A vector carries magnitude and direction; a scalar carries magnitude only. In component form, a vector in the plane is a = x i + y j (or the column (x, y)), and in three dimensions a = x i + y j + z k (Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10; AQA 7357 Section J; OCR A H640 14.01; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA include 3D vectors at A-level). The magnitude is the length: |a| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) in 2D, extending to sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) in 3D by three-dimensional Pythagoras. The unit vector in the direction of a is a/|a| - dividing by the magnitude keeps the direction but gives length 1. Questions ask for a unit vector in a given direction, or for the direction angle: in 2D, tan(theta) = y/x with the quadrant read from the signs of the components. Two vectors are equal exactly when all corresponding components match - the algebraic statement behind geometric arguments. The standard unit vectors i, j, k point along the axes, so (3, 2, 4) = 3i + 2j + 4k; converting between the two notations is routine but worth doing carefully, since a dropped component is a silent error. Worked example: magnitude and direction Find the magnitude of a = 2i - j + 2k, and a unit vector in the direction of a. Line 1: |a| = sqrt(2^2 + (-1)^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(4 + 1 + 4) = sqrt(9) = 3 (M1 A1). Line 2: Unit vector: a/|a| = (2i - j + 2k)/3 = (2/3)i - (1/3)j + (2/3)k (A1). Line 3: Check: the magnitude of the unit vector is sqrt(4/9 + 1/9 + 4/9) = 1 (A1: verified). Vector addition is component-wise, with the triangle law as its picture: a + b takes you along a then along b. Subtraction reverses the second vector; scalar multiplication scales the length (and reverses the direction when the scalar is negative). Two results do the geometric work: the displacement from A to B is AB = b - a (end position minus start position), and a point M is the midpoint of AB when its position vector is m = (a + b)/2. Position vectors turn geometry into algebra. Three points are collinear when the displacement between one pair is a scalar multiple of the displacement between another pair, AND the lines share a point - AB = t BC for some scalar t. Parallelogram problems use the property that diagonals bisect each other, or that opposite sides are equal as vectors: ABCD is a parallelogram when AB = DC. Worked example: displacement, distance and collinearity The points P, Q and R have position vectors p = (1, 2), q = (3, 4) and r = (5, 6). Show that P, Q and R are collinear. Line 1: PQ = q - p = (3 - 1, 4 - 2) = (2, 2) (M1). Line 2: QR = r - q = (5 - 3, 6 - 4) = (2, 2) (M1). Line 3: QR = 1 x PQ, so the displacements are parallel (A1). Line 4: The displacements share the point Q, so P, Q and R lie on one straight line (A1: collinearity concluded). Watch the direction discipline: AB means from A to B, so it is b - a, not a - b - reversing it loses the direction and, in angle questions, the sign of the answer. In mechanics, the same arithmetic drives displacement and velocity vectors, so this section is shared ground with the applied papers. The scalar (dot) product (Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10; AQA 7357 J2-J3; OCR A H640 14.01) has two equivalent forms: a . b = |a||b|cos(theta) and a . b = x1x2 + y1y2 + z1z2 (the sum of the products of corresponding components). Equating them gives the angle between vectors: cos(theta) = (a . b)/(|a||b|). The dot product is a scalar , not a vector - a common confusion in definitions. Two special cases do the geometric work: vectors are perpendicular exactly when a . b = 0 (cos(90 degrees) = 0), and parallel when their components are in the same ratio (b = t a, giving |cos(theta)| = 1). Perpendicularity questions ask for an unknown component: set the dot product to zero and solve. Worked example: angle between two 3D vectors Find the angle between a = (1, 2, 2) and b = (2, 1, 0). Line 1: a . b = (1)(2) + (2)(1) + (2)(0) = 4 (M1). Line 2: |a| = sqrt(1 + 4 + 4) = 3 and |b| = sqrt(4 + 1) = sqrt(5) (M1). Line 3: cos(theta) = 4/(3sqrt(5)) = 0.5963 (A1). Line 4: theta = arccos(0.5963) = 0.932 radians = 53.4 degrees (A1). Worked example: perpendicular vectors with an unknown Find the value of x for which a = (2, -1, 3) and b = (1, x, -2) are perpendicular. Line 1: Perpendicular requires a . b = 0 (M1). Line 2: (2)(1) + (-1)(x) + (3)(-2) = 2 - x - 6 = -x - 4 (A1). Line 3: -x - 4 = 0, so x = -4 (A1). The dot product also powers geometric proofs: a right angle in a triangle is proved by showing two side vectors have zero dot product, which is often faster than gradients or Pythagoras, and it works in 3D where gradients do not. The line through point A with position vector a and direction d has vector equation r = a + t d , where t is a scalar parameter: as t runs over all reals, r runs along the line. Through two points A and B, the direction is d = b - a, so r = a + t(b - a). The Cartesian form converts the components: for d = (l, m, n), the line is (x - x1)/l = (y - y1)/m = (z - z1)/n - each component divided by its direction component. A zero direction component means that coordinate is constant on the line, so the Cartesian fraction for it is omitted. In 3D, intersecting lines are found by equating components: two equations solve for t and s, and the third equation must be checked - if it fails, the lines are skew (not parallel, never meeting). The third-equation check is the mark-winning step: skipping it, or claiming intersection from two equations alone, loses the conclusion mark. Worked example: intersection of two 3D lines Line 1: r1 = (1, 2, 2) + t(1, 1, 0). Line 2: r2 = (1, 5, 1) + s(2, -1, 1). Find their intersection or show they are skew. Line 1: Equate components: 1 + t = 1 + 2s and 2 + t = 5 - s (M1: equations formed). Line 2: From the first: t = 2s. Substituting into the second: 2 + 2s = 5 - s, so 3s = 3, s = 1 and t = 2 (A1). Line 3: Check the third equation: z-coordinate of r1 at t = 2 is 2 + 0 = 2; of r2 at s = 1 is 1 + 1 = 2. They agree (A1: third equation verified). Line 4: The lines intersect at r = (3, 4, 2) (A1: point stated). Parallel lines have proportional direction vectors; identical lines have proportional directions AND a shared point - check whether one line's point satisfies the other's equation to distinguish parallel from coincident. These line ideas feed directly into Further Mathematics (where the scalar product finds angles between lines and the shortest-distance problems live) and into mechanics, where velocity vectors follow r = r0 + v t. Vector questions reward clean algebra and correct notation. Typical applications: proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram (show AB = DC as vectors), proving a right angle (zero dot product), finding a midpoint or a ratio point (m = (a + b)/2, or r = (b a + a b)/(a + b) style weighted averages for ratio divisions), and kinematics links - a velocity vector v means position moves as r(t) = r0 + v t, so speed is |v| and displacement over time t is v t. Scalar triple product contexts : the product a . (b x c), where b x c is the vector (cross) product, measures the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b and c - and it is zero exactly when the three vectors are coplanar. The cross product itself, with |b x c| = |b||c|sin(theta), gives the area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors (half of it, a triangle). The cross product and triple product are formally assessed in Further Mathematics , not single A-level Maths - but the contexts appear as motivation, and knowing that |a||b|sin(theta) measures parallelogram area helps with geometry questions that ask for areas from two side vectors. Worked example: geometry with position vectors A(1, 1), B(4, 2) and C(6, 5) are three vertices of parallelogram ABCD, in order. Find D. Line 1: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = DC as vectors (opposite sides equal and parallel) (M1: property quoted). Line 2: AB = b - a = (4 - 1, 2 - 1) = (3, 1) (A1). Line 3: DC = c - d = (3, 1), so d = c - (3, 1) = (6, 5) - (3, 1) = (3, 4) (A1). Line 4: Check with the diagonals: midpoint of AC = ((1 + 6)/2, (1 + 5)/2) = (3.5, 3) and midpoint of BD = ((4 + 3)/2, (2 + 4)/2) = (3.5, 3) - equal, confirming D = (3, 4) (A1: verified). Exam technique: (1) write AB as b - a before doing anything else - direction errors are the biggest single loss; (2) keep surds exact; (3) in 3D line intersections, always check the third equation and state skew or intersecting explicitly; (4) quote the property used (parallelogram, perpendicular, collinear) before the algebra; (5) for angle questions, give the answer in degrees or radians as the question demands, to 1 d.p. or 3 s.f. Board coverage: Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 10, AQA 7357 Section J, OCR A H640 14.01, WJEC/Eduqas AS/A2 vectors, CCEA AS1/A21 - all include 2D and 3D vectors, the scalar product and vector equations of lines.

topics.name: Algebraic Methods and Proof
topics.subject: mathematics
topics.searchText: mathematics Mathematics Algebraic Methods and Proof Understand and use the structure of mathematical proof, proceeding from given assumptions through a chain of valid logical steps to the conclusion (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 Topic 1, AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01 Prove statements by deduction and by exhaustion, and prove algebraic identities using the equivalence sign (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, Edexcel 9MA0 1.1-1.2 Disprove a statement by counter-example, selecting one value satisfying the conditions for which the claim fails (AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 1.3, AQA 7357 A1 Carry out proofs by contradiction, including the irrationality of sqrt(2) and the infinitude of the primes (AO2) - AQA 7357 A1, OCR A H640 1.01; Edexcel tests contradiction-style arguments in past papers Decompose proper rational functions into partial fractions with distinct and repeated linear factors, dividing improper fractions first (AO1/AO2) - Edexcel 9MA0 2.5, AQA 7357 B8 Select and justify the correct proof technique and write arguments in full sentences showing every logical step (AO2/AO3) Deduction chains known facts into the conclusion; exhaustion proves every case in a finite split; a single counter-example disproves a general claim. Contradiction: assume the statement false, derive an impossible consequence, conclude the original statement is true. Identities use the equivalence sign and hold for all values of the variable; manipulate each side independently. Partial fraction forms: A/(ax+b) + B/(cx+d) for distinct linear factors; A/(ax+b) + B/(ax+b)^2 for a repeated factor; divide improper fractions first. Proofs are marked on structure: state the assumption or case split, show every logical step, state the contradiction or conclusion explicitly.
