Original writing: one piece for a real audience and purpose; the commentary must reflect on choices (lexis, syntax, tone, structure) against audience and purpose and connect to style models - reflection, not narration of process. Pitfalls that cost marks: overbroad scope, data dumping, description without analysis, theory listed but never applied, no ethics section, commentary written as 'what I did'. Language investigation The AQA 7702/C research project: an independent study of an area of language diversity or change, maximum 2,000 words excluding data and quotations, marked out of 70 (AO1 20, AO2 20, AO3 20, AO4 10). Original writing The second AQA NEA task: one 750-word piece written for a clearly defined audience and purpose (e.g. feature article, speech, campaign leaflet or short fiction), assessed for AO5 (expertise and creativity in the use of English). Commentary The 750-word reflection accompanying the original writing: justifies stylistic, lexical and structural choices against audience and purpose and connects to style models, assessed for AO4 (15 marks) alongside the piece's AO5 (15 marks). Naturally occurring data Language produced for real communication (conversations, online forums, signage) rather than gathered for the study - prized for validity but harder to collect and transcribe. Elicited data Language prompted by the researcher for the study (interviews, questionnaires, reading tasks, test sentences) - easier to control and compare, but risks artificiality and the observer's paradox. Corpus A principled collection of machine-readable texts (e.g. the BNC or COCA) searchable for frequency and collocation - the natural data source for language change and word-formation projects where scale matters. Informed consent Participants (or parents/carers for minors) must know what the research involves, agree to take part and be free to withdraw - the core ethical requirement for recorded spoken data. Anonymisation Removing or replacing names, places and identifying details in transcripts and write-ups so participants cannot be recognised; standard practice is pseudonyms at first mention plus secure storage and deletion of files. Triangulation Corroborating findings across methods or data types (e.g. frequency counts plus close discourse analysis of extracts) so conclusions rest on more than one line of evidence. Academic poster The OCR H470/03 one-page visual summary of the independent research - title, data, methodology, findings and conclusions - marked alongside the research project. The NEA is marked as independent research, so the first A* decision is scope. AQA 7702/C allows an investigation into any area of language diversity or change - typically gender, change, power, region, occupation or acquisition - within 2,000 words excluding data and quotations; OCR H470/03 gives the same free choice for a longer project with an academic poster. Two thousand words is roughly four sides of argument: a project that tries to cover 'language and gender' produces a survey; one that asks a precise question produces an argument. Gender: 'How are women politicians represented differently from men in 2024 UK broadsheet headlines?' - bounded data, a clear comparison, direct links to representation work (marked lexis, semantic derogation, agency). Change: 'How has the semantic field of X shifted between the BNC (1994) and a 2024 web corpus?' - corpus evidence gives the quantitative spine and links change to usage (AO2). Power: 'How does doctor-patient talk distribute authority in recorded GP consultations?' - asymmetry, directives, terminology and turn-taking. Region: 'How do adolescents in two contrasting locations perform local identity through dialect lexis and prosodics?' - matched samples make the comparison workable. Occupation: 'How does classroom teacher talk manage turn-taking and control?' - or hospital handovers, legal registers, service encounters. Acquisition: 'How does a child aged 2-3 acquire question and negation formation?' - longitudinal or cross-sectional data, with parental consent essential. Scoping rules: frame the title as a question or hypothesis with named variables ('How does X do Y in Z?'); fix data type, sample size and date range before writing; reserve at least 70% of the word count for analysis rather than context or methodology; and check the question is answerable with data you can actually access - overambition is the single most common reason investigations underperform. Hypothesis vs research question: quantitative-leaning projects (change, corpus work) suit a testable hypothesis - 'use of X increases across the two samples' - while qualitative-leaning projects (power, identity, representation) suit an open question with sub-aims. Either way, state the variables explicitly, and expect to refine the wording after a pilot read-through of the data: a title written before the data exists is a guess, and examiners can tell. OCR projects allow a wider spread of areas, including comparison of spoken and written modes, but the same rule holds: the title must promise an argument the data can actually deliver. Data: three families. Naturally occurring data (recorded conversations, forums, signage) is prized for validity but hard to collect and transcribe, and Labov's observer's paradox - informants shifting style when watched - must be acknowledged. Elicited data (interviews, reading tasks, test sentences) is controllable and comparable but risks artificiality. Corpora (BNC, COCA) give searchable frequency and collocation evidence - ideal for change projects. Transcription is a methodological choice in itself: orthographic transcription with select notation (pauses, overlap, stress) is the workable middle ground; full transcripts belong in an appendix and do not count towards the word limit, though the analysis of them does. Ethics (AO3): informed consent - written, and from parents/carers where participants are minors; gatekeeper permission (e.g. headteacher) for school-based collection; anonymisation with pseudonyms and removal of identifying details; the right to withdraw at any point, including after recording; secure storage and deletion of data files; and no deception about how the data will be used. State these explicitly and justify them - examiners credit ethics only when they are applied to your data, not listed generically. Analysis: choose the frameworks before collecting, so the data answers the question. Work the levels the question demands - lexis and semantics for representation projects, grammar and pragmatics for power and occupation, phonology/prosodics for region, grammatical stages for acquisition - and mix quantitative evidence (frequency counts, percentages) with close discourse analysis of short contrasting extracts. This triangulation is what turns a data description into an argument: the counts show the pattern, the extracts show how it works. Sampling and scale: justify sample size and composition - ten consultations, two age-matched friendship groups, 200 headlines across two years - and say why that is enough: depth beats coverage in a 2,000-word study, but the sample must still support the comparison the title promises. Note representativeness limits honestly (one practice, one region) and build them into the conclusion rather than hoping examiners miss them. For spoken data, fix the transcription conventions up front - orthographic with selected notation for pauses, overlap and stress; Jefferson conventions only where prosody is central to the question - and state them: transcription is a methodological decision examiners expect to see justified, not housekeeping. Data protection: store recordings and transcripts securely (password-protected, school or college systems only), delete files after certification, and build anonymity in from the outset - pseudonyms applied at the transcription stage - so anonymisation is designed into the project rather than bolted on at the end. Investigation structure: introduction (context, rationale, precise aims or hypothesis), methodology (data, sampling, ethics), analysis (two or three sections organised by framework), conclusion (synthesis, limitations, extension). AO profile (AQA, 70 marks): AO1 20 - accurate, consistent framework terminology and coherent academic expression; AO2 20 - linguistic concepts, methods and research used critically on your data; AO3 20 - contextual factors (mode, audience, purpose, situation, era) shaping the language; AO4 10 - connections made across your texts or extracts. Weight the writing accordingly: a quarter of words on context and a half on analysis is the rough A* ratio. Original writing (30 marks): one 750-word piece for a defined audience and purpose - a feature article, campaign leaflet, speech or short fiction - assessed for AO5 (15): sustained control of register, lexis, syntax and structure for that audience. The commentary (750 words) earns AO4 (15): analyse your own choices as if analysing an unseen text - genre conventions followed and subverted, lexical and syntactic decisions justified against audience and purpose, connections to style models. The commentary must reflect , not narrate: 'the imperative in the opening line positions the reader as instructed because...' earns AO4; 'first I drafted, then I edited' earns nothing. OCR H470/03: the same research skills assessed through a longer project plus the academic poster - a one-page visual summary of title, data, methodology, findings and conclusions. Treat the poster as a pitch to an examiner: it must stand alone, so distil the argument (question, headline findings, one quantified example), not the process. Using research sources (AO2): two or three sources, each with a job: one framing concept (e.g. Fairclough's power in discourse for an institutional-talk project), one empirical study whose findings your data supports or complicates, and one critique you test against your own evidence. Every citation must touch the data: 'Fairclough's synthetic personalisation is visible in the GP's collective we' earns AO2; 'Fairclough wrote about power' earns nothing. For the original writing, choose real style models and reference them in the commentary - the AO4 marks reward explicit connections between your piece and the models, not vague nods to 'the genre'. The pitfalls are predictable, which makes them avoidable: Overbroad scope: 'language and gender' as a topic, not a question - the data cannot support it, so AO3 stays shallow and the analysis becomes a survey. Fix: name variables, data and context in the title. Data dumping: long transcripts narrated extract by extract without framework terminology - caps AO1. Fix: quantify the pattern, then close-analyse two or three short contrasting extracts. Theory listing: research cited as background ('Lakoff said...') but never applied to the data - caps AO2. Fix: weave two or three sources into the analysis, each used on your own evidence. Generic ethics: 'consent was obtained' without saying how, from whom, or why - loses AO3 methodology marks. Fix: state the mechanics applied to your participants. Commentary narration: a process account of writing the piece - earns neither AO4 nor AO5. Fix: analyse your own text's choices against audience and purpose. Weak conclusion: restating findings instead of answering the title question. Fix: synthesise into a direct answer, then note limitations and an extension. A* habits: draft the question first and pilot your coding on a small sample before collecting everything; keep a research log so the methodology writes itself; integrate theory into analysis paragraphs (claim, evidence, concept); write the commentary as textual analysis of your own piece; and use your supervisor's feedback window - most centres allow one set of draft comments, and spending it on the analysis section (not the introduction) is the highest-yield choice. Timing: the NEA runs across the year with fixed submission dates, so collect data early - access to participants is the slowest step - draft the analysis in stages as data arrives, and write the commentary last: it analyses choices, so it cannot be written before the piece is final. Check the board's current specification and your centre's guidance for word limits, word-count rules and deadlines - they are fixed, and ignoring them costs marks no analysis can recover. Reading the mark scheme like an examiner: before writing, find the board's exemplar materials and marked scripts - they show exactly what the top band rewards. The investigation mark scheme is AO-banded, so audit every draft paragraph against the four AOs: does it apply terminology (AO1), use research critically (AO2), address context (AO3), make connections (AO4)? A paragraph with no AO attached is description, however fluent. For the original writing, the top band rewards a piece that could genuinely be published for its stated audience - so test the draft against that standard, and write a commentary that proves the control was deliberate.

topics.name: Cell Structure
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Cell Structure Label and state the function of every eukaryotic organelle from light- and electron-microscope images (AQA 3.2.1.1; OCR 2.1.1) Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and describe viral structure (AQA 3.2.1.1; OCR 2.1.1) Explain the fluid mosaic model and each transport mechanism, including water potential calculations (AQA 3.2.1.2/3.2.3; OCR 2.1.5) Describe mitosis, calculate a mitotic index, and explain how meiosis generates variation (AQA 3.2.2, 3.4.3; OCR 2.1.6) Link cell specialisation to function in erythrocytes, sperm and epithelia Apply microscopy maths: magnification, resolution, graticule calibration and image-size calculations Nucleus: DNA + nucleolus; mitochondrion: aerobic respiration with cristae; RER/SER: protein/lipid synthesis; Golgi: modify and package; lysosome: hydrolytic enzymes; chloroplast: photosynthesis; vacuole: turgor Prokaryote: no nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA + plasmids, peptidoglycan wall; eukaryote: 80S ribosomes, linear histone-bound DNA, membrane-bound organelles Transport: simple diffusion (small, non-polar), facilitated diffusion (channel/carrier proteins), active transport (ATP, against gradient), osmosis (water, down water-potential gradient), co-transport, endo/exocytosis Mitosis: prophase-metaphase-anaphase-telophase gives two identical diploid cells; meiosis: two divisions, crossing over and independent assortment give haploid gametes and variation Organelle A membrane-bound or distinct structural component of a cell specialised for a particular function, e.g. mitochondrion, chloroplast, Golgi apparatus. Prokaryote Unicellular organism with no true nucleus or membrane-bound organelles: circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes and usually a peptidoglycan cell wall. Magnification The number of times larger an image appears compared with the actual object size; magnification = image size / actual size. Resolution The minimum distance between two objects at which they can still be distinguished as separate; determined by the wavelength of the illumination (electrons allow ~0.1-0.2 nm). Fluid mosaic model Model of the cell-surface membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer (lipids move laterally) studded with a mosaic of integral and peripheral proteins, cholesterol, glycoproteins and glycolipids. Water potential (ψ) The pressure created by water molecules, measured in kPa; the tendency of water molecules to move out of a solution. Pure water is 0 kPa and all solutions have negative values; water moves from higher (less negative) to lower water potential. Mitotic index The proportion of cells in a field of view undergoing mitosis: mitotic index = number of cells with visible chromosomes ÷ total number of cells observed. Stem cell An undifferentiated cell that can divide by mitosis repeatedly and differentiate into specialised cells; classified as totipotent, pluripotent or multipotent by range of cell types it can produce. Binary fission Asexual reproduction of prokaryotes in which the circular DNA replicates and the cell divides into two genetically identical daughter cells. Tissue A group of similar cells specialised for the same function, organised together, e.g. squamous epithelium, xylem, muscle. Exams routinely present an unlabelled electron micrograph and ask you to identify organelles and link each to a function . The safest answers connect structure to process, not just location: Organelle Structural features to quote Function link that earns marks Nucleus Double membrane (nuclear envelope) with pores; chromatin; nucleolus Pores allow mRNA out; nucleolus makes ribosomes; contains genetic material Mitochondrion Double membrane; inner folded into cristae; matrix Cristae give large surface area for the electron transport chain; matrix holds Krebs-cycle enzymes; own circular DNA and ribosomes Rough ER Membrane sheets studded with ribosomes Folds and transports proteins made on its ribosomes Smooth ER Membrane tubes, no ribosomes Lipid and phospholipid synthesis and transport Golgi apparatus Stack of flattened membrane sacs; vesicles pinch off Modifies (e.g. adds sugars), sorts and packages proteins; makes lysosomes Lysosome Single membrane, hydrolytic enzymes (lysozyme) Digest worn organelles and engulfed pathogens; can release enzymes for cell death Chloroplast Double membrane; thylakoid membranes stacked into grana; stroma; starch grains Thylakoids hold photosystems for the light-dependent reaction; stroma contains Calvin-cycle enzymes Cell-surface membrane Phospholipid bilayer + proteins (fluid mosaic) Controls entry and exit; cell recognition Ribosome 80S, no membrane Site of translation (protein synthesis) Centrioles Two bundles of microtubules (animals only) Organise the spindle in cell division Vacuole (plants) Tonoplast membrane; cell sap Stores solutes; water entry makes cells turgid for support The classic six-marker is mitochondrial structure enabling efficient aerobic respiration : double membrane isolates reactions; cristae maximise surface area for respiratory enzymes and the electron transport chain; the narrow intermembrane space builds a steep proton gradient for chemiosmosis; the matrix contains the Krebs-cycle enzymes, DNA and ribosomes so the organelle can make some of its own proteins quickly. Practise writing that as linked structure-function pairs because the mark scheme awards each pair, not description alone. Compare prokaryotes with eukaryotes in the terms the mark schemes use: prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles and no true nucleus - their single circular DNA molecule (not associated with histones) lies free in the cytoplasm along with plasmids, which carry non-essential genes such as antibiotic resistance; ribosomes are 70S (smaller than the 80S of eukaryotes); the cell wall is peptidoglycan (murein) , not cellulose; many have a capsule of slime, pili and flagella without the 9+2 microtubule arrangement. Reproduction is by binary fission : DNA replication followed by division roughly every 20 minutes in ideal conditions. Viruses sit outside both groups: a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope stolen from the host membrane and attachment proteins (e.g. HIV has reverse transcriptase). Viruses are acellular and can only reproduce inside host cells. Microscopy maths is guaranteed easy marks. Optical microscopes resolve to about 0.2 μm and magnify to about ×1500; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) pass electrons through ultrathin sections for ~0.1 nm resolution and 2D internal detail; scanning electron microscopes (SEM) scan surfaces for 3D topography at ~20 nm. Always convert to the same units before dividing: magnification = measured image size ÷ actual size , and actual size = image size ÷ magnification . For graticule calibration: at ×100 the eyepiece graticule may be 100 divisions; if each stage-micrometer division is 10 μm and 10 graticule divisions span one stage division, one eyepiece division = 10 μm at that objective - recalculate for each objective lens. In drawings, a clean single line, no shading, and a correctly calculated scale bar or ×magnification gain the practical marks (AQA RP1; OCR PAG1). The fluid mosaic model explains everything the examiners ask about membranes: phospholipids move laterally (fluid) while proteins are scattered through the bilayer (mosaic). The hydrophobic fatty-acid core makes the membrane selectively permeable : small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, lipid-soluble vitamins) diffuse straight through, whereas polar molecules and ions need protein pathways. Cholesterol slots between phospholipids, regulating fluidity and stability; glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer face act as antigens and receptors for cell recognition and signalling. Temperature questions: at low temperatures the membrane loses fluidity; above ~40 °C proteins denature and the bilayer disrupts, increasing permeability - the basis of the beetroot practical (AQA RP4; OCR PAG3) where you measure pigment leakage with a colorimeter and explain increased permeability with heat/solvent/ethanol via disruption of the bilayer and denaturation of membrane proteins. Know the five transport mechanisms as definition + example + energy source: Simple diffusion : net passive movement down a concentration gradient, no ATP, rate rises with gradient and surface area (Fick's law). Facilitated diffusion : passive movement through channel or carrier proteins; saturates when all carriers are occupied, so rate plateaus. Osmosis : passive diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane from higher to lower water potential (ψ). Plant cells in dilute solution become turgid (wall resists, no lysis); animal cells lyse. In concentrated solution plant cells are plasmolysed ; the incipient plasmolysis point estimates ψ (AQA RP3 calibration curve with sucrose solutions). Active transport : movement against the gradient through carrier proteins driven by ATP hydrolysis ; e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) maintains ion gradients for nerve impulses. Co-transport : one substance's downhill movement drives another's uphill movement on the same carrier - the Na⁺-glucose co-transporter in the ileum (Na⁺/K⁺ pump lowers intracellular Na⁺, Na⁺ diffuses in from the lumen dragging glucose against its gradient, glucose leaves by facilitated diffusion). Large-scale transport uses endocytosis (membrane engulfs material into vesicles; phagocytosis is a special case) and exocytosis (vesicles fuse with the membrane, e.g. neurotransmitter release) - both active processes requiring ATP. When asked to distinguish mechanisms, always name the energy source and the direction relative to the gradient; that pairing earns the second mark in most schemes. The cell cycle is interphase (G₁ growth, S - DNA replicates, G₂ growth and organelle synthesis) followed by M phase (mitosis + cytokinesis) . In mitosis: prophase - chromosomes condense into two sister chromatids joined at centromeres, the nuclear envelope breaks down and the spindle forms; metaphase - chromosomes line up on the equator, attached to spindle fibres by their centromeres; anaphase - spindle fibres shorten, pulling sister chromatids to opposite poles (centromeres divide); telophase - nuclear envelopes reform and chromosomes decondense; cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm to give two genetically identical diploid cells . Prokaryotes divide by binary fission instead; viruses are not cells and replicate inside hosts. Mitotic index calculations from a stained root-tip squash (AQA RP2; OCR PAG4) are common: count only cells with visible condensed chromosomes in the numerator, and state safety points (wear gloves/goggles, iodine or toluidine blue stain, macerate the tip to spread cells). Interphase cells vastly outnumber mitotic cells, so expect a small index; a high index in a tumour sample underlies cancer chemotherapy that targets rapidly dividing cells. Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid cells from one diploid cell via two divisions. After interphase I, meiosis I separates homologous chromosome pairs (prophase I: crossing over between homologous chromatids at chiasmata creates new allele combinations; metaphase I: independent assortment of homologous pairs at the equator), halving the chromosome number; meiosis II separates sister chromatids like mitosis. The exam loves the two variation sources: crossing over (recombination of alleles between chromatids) and independent assortment (2ⁿ combinations - for humans 2²³ ≈ 8 million per gamete), plus random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Non-disjunction (failure of homologs or chromatids to separate) produces gametes with an extra or missing chromosome (e.g. trisomy 21). Compare with mitosis in a table if asked for differences: number of divisions, daughter cells produced, ploidy, genetic identity, role in life cycle. Specialised cells are adapted so their structure matches function - quote adaptations, not just names. Erythrocytes : biconcave disc (large surface area to volume for gas exchange, flexible to squeeze through capillaries), no nucleus or mitochondria (more room for haemoglobin), packed with haemoglobin that binds oxygen. Sperm : acrosome with hydrolytic enzymes to penetrate the egg, many mitochondria in the mid-piece for ATP to power the flagellum, haploid nucleus, minimal cytoplasm for streamlining. Ciliated epithelium : cilia beat to move mucus in the airways; goblet cells secrete mucus trapping pathogens. Palisade cells : many chloroplasts, thin walls, large vacuole. Root hair cells : projections increase surface area for water and mineral uptake. Levels of organisation are always examinable: specialised cells form tissues (similar cells with the same function), tissues form organs (several tissues working together, e.g. the stomach: muscle, epithelium, secretory tissue), organs form systems (digestive, circulatory). Stem cells supply new specialised cells: totipotent cells (early embryo/zygote) can become any cell type including extra-embryonic tissue; pluripotent cells (inner cell mass of the blastocyst) form all somatic cell types; multipotent cells (e.g. bone marrow) form a limited range of related cells. In mature animals most cells are permanently in G₀; plants retain meristems. Stem-cell uses (bone marrow transplants, regenerative medicine, iPS cells made by reprogramming adult cells with transcription factors) and their ethics (embryo destruction vs. medical benefit) link this sub-topic to gene-expression content - expect a discussion question for 3+ marks on why iPS cells avoid the ethical objections of embryo use.

topics.name: Biological Molecules and Respiration
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Biological Molecules and Respiration Describe the structure of monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides, triglycerides and phospholipids, and state the biochemical tests (AQA 3.1.1-3.1.3; OCR 2.1.2) Explain protein structure levels and enzyme action via the induced fit model (AQA 3.1.4; OCR 2.1.4) Interpret Km, Vmax and the effects of competitive and non-competitive inhibitors from rate graphs Detail glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation with locations and yields (AQA 3.5.2; OCR 5.2.1) Explain chemiosmosis and calculate theoretical vs actual ATP yield per glucose; calculate RQ values Compare anaerobic respiration in animals (lactate) and yeast (ethanol) and explain the lower yield Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP, 2 NADH. Link reaction (matrix): pyruvate → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH. Krebs (matrix): per acetyl CoA → 2CO₂ + 3NADH + FADH₂ + ATP Oxidative phosphorylation: NADH/FADH₂ donate electrons to the ETC; proton pumping builds the gradient; H⁺ flows through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis); O₂ is the terminal electron acceptor Theoretical yield ~32 ATP per glucose; actual 30-32 due to proton leak, shuttle costs and ATP spent transporting pyruvate/ADP Anaerobic: animals pyruvate → lactate (lactate dehydrogenase, regenerates NAD⁺); yeast pyruvate → ethanol + CO₂ Enzymes: induced fit lowers activation energy; competitive inhibitors raise Km (Vmax unchanged); non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax Tests: Benedict's (reducing sugar), Benedict's after HCl/NaHCO₃ (non-reducing), iodine (starch), Biuret (protein), emulsion (lipid) Monomer A small single molecular unit that can join to others in repeating chains; biological monomers include monosaccharides, amino acids and nucleotides. Condensation reaction A reaction joining two molecules with the formation of a covalent bond and the release of a molecule of water. Hydrolysis reaction A reaction breaking a covalent bond using a molecule of water; digestion and polymer breakdown use hydrolysis. Glycosidic bond A covalent bond formed between two monosaccharides in a condensation reaction (e.g. 1,4-bonds in amylose, 1,6-bonds at glycogen branch points). Ester bond The bond formed between glycerol and a fatty acid in a condensation reaction; three ester bonds join each triglyceride. Induced fit model Model of enzyme action in which substrate binding induces a conformational change in the active site that stresses bonds and lowers activation energy; explains enzyme specificity. Km (Michaelis constant) The substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is half Vmax; a lower Km indicates higher enzyme-substrate affinity. Vmax The maximum rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction, reached when all active sites are saturated with substrate. Chemiosmosis ATP synthesis driven by the flow of protons down an electrochemical gradient across a membrane (inner mitochondrial membrane or thylakoid) through ATP synthase. Respiratory quotient (RQ) RQ = CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ consumed; ~1.0 for carbohydrate, ~0.7 for lipid, ~0.9 for protein, and can exceed 1 with anaerobic fermentation. Monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose) are monomers joined by condensation reactions releasing water to form glycosidic bonds ; hydrolysis reverses this. α-glucose monomers join into starch (amylose: unbranched 1,4-bonds, coiled helix; amylopectin: branched 1,4- and 1,6-bonds) and glycogen (more highly branched, animals). The storage-function link is a guaranteed four-marker: insoluble so it does not affect water potential or draw water into cells; compact so lots of glucose fits into a small volume; branched so many terminal ends allow rapid simultaneous enzymatic hydrolysis when glucose demand is high; α-glycosidic bonds are easily hydrolysed by amylase/maltase. Cellulose contrasts: β-glucose in unbranched straight chains with hydrogen bonds between chains forming microfibrils - structural, not storage. Triglycerides are one glycerol + three fatty acids joined by three ester bonds in condensation reactions. Function links: hydrophobic energy store releasing more energy per gram than carbohydrate (more C-H bonds to oxidise); insoluble storage; metabolic water source (e.g. camel hump, desert eggs); low mass. Phospholipids have one fatty acid replaced by a hydrophilic phosphate group - hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tails - explaining bilayer formation in membranes. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds (straight chains, pack tightly, solid at room temperature); unsaturated have double bonds (kinked chains, lower melting point, oils). Tests are free marks - quote the sequence and positive result: Benedict's : heat with Benedict's reagent, brick-red precipitate = reducing sugar (green→yellow→red grades concentration with a colorimeter); non-reducing sugar : boil with dilute HCl to hydrolyse glycosidic bonds, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, re-test with Benedict's - positive means non-reducing sugar was present; iodine/potassium iodide : blue-black = starch; Biuret : NaOH then copper sulfate, purple = protein (peptide bonds); emulsion test : dissolve in ethanol, add to water, white emulsion = lipid. AQA RP6 and OCR PAG6 test the colorimetric calibration-curve technique. Amino acids have an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and variable R-group on a central carbon; peptide bonds join amino acids in condensation reactions. Know the four structure levels with the bonds that stabilise each: primary - unique amino-acid sequence (peptide bonds); secondary - hydrogen bonding into α-helix or β-pleated sheet; tertiary - 3D folding via hydrogen, ionic and disulfide bonds between R-groups, determining active-site shape; quaternary - multiple polypeptide chains (haemoglobin: 4 chains + haem prosthetic groups). Tertiary structure is what enzymes and inhibitors attack - link any denaturation question to disruption of hydrogen/ionic bonds changing active-site shape. Induced fit beats lock-and-key in mark schemes: the active site is close to complementary but changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, putting the enzyme-substrate complex under stress that lowers activation energy . Enzymes are biological catalysts, globular proteins, specific to substrates. Rate factors: temperature - more kinetic energy, more successful collisions, rate rises to an optimum (~37 °C in humans), then hydrogen/ionic bonds vibrate too much and break, denaturing the active site so rate falls sharply; pH - deviation from the optimum changes H⁺/OH⁻ concentrations, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds, denaturing the enzyme (often irreversibly at extremes); substrate concentration - rate rises to Vmax when all active sites are saturated; enzyme concentration - proportional rise if substrate is non-limiting. Km and Vmax interpretation : Km is the substrate concentration at half-Vmax; lower Km = higher affinity. Competitive inhibitors bind the active site reversibly, competing with substrate: raising substrate concentration overcomes inhibition, so Vmax unchanged, Km increased . Non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site, changing tertiary conformation so the active site is no longer complementary: substrate concentration cannot help, so Vmax decreased, Km effectively unchanged (for the fraction of uninhibited enzyme). Statins (competitive, HMG-CoA reductase) and cyanide (non-competitive, cytochrome c oxidase) are the stock examples. Metabolic pathways are regulated by feedback inhibition : the end product inhibits the first enzyme of the pathway when it accumulates (e.g. isoleucine inhibiting threonine deaminase), and by allosteric effectors that switch enzymes between active/inactive conformations - link these to homeostatic control of respiration rate. ATP is a nucleotide derivative : adenine + ribose + three phosphates. Energy is released in small, manageable packets when the terminal phosphate bond is hydrolysed by ATPase to ADP + Pi (30.6 kJ mol⁻¹), and ATP is resynthesised from ADP + Pi using energy from respiration. Properties that suit its role: small (moves easily), water-soluble, releases energy in small amounts, quickly resynthesised, and couples energy-releasing to energy-requiring reactions via transfer of the terminal phosphate. Phosphorylation of substrates (e.g. glucose → glucose phosphate in glycolysis) also makes them more reactive. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and is anaerobic-compatible: (1) glucose is phosphorylated using 2 ATP to fructose bisphosphate (6C); (2) it splits into two triose phosphate (3C) molecules; (3) each TP is oxidised (losing H to NAD ) and converted to pyruvate , producing 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation . Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate . Substrate-level phosphorylation = direct transfer of a phosphate from an intermediate to ADP (contrast with oxidative phosphorylation via the proton gradient). The link reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix : pyruvate is actively transported into the matrix, oxidatively decarboxylated - each pyruvate loses CO₂, loses H to NAD (forming NADH) and combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA (2C). Per glucose: 2 CO₂ + 2 NADH. The 2C acetyl group then feeds the Krebs cycle , also in the matrix: acetyl CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C); citrate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated in a series of redox reactions regenerating oxaloacetate. Per turn: 2 CO₂, 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (by substrate-level phosphorylation) ; per glucose (two turns): 4 CO₂, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP. Coenzymes NAD and FAD carry H atoms (electrons) to the electron transport chain; remember that dehydrogenation is oxidation. When asked to state where each stage occurs and its products , a quick table of stage/location/yields is the fastest full-mark format. Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the folded inner mitochondrial membrane : NADH and FADH₂ deliver electrons (from their H atoms) to the electron transport chain of protein complexes I-IV. As electrons pass along the carriers of decreasing energy, energy released pumps H⁺ from the matrix into the intermembrane space , building a steep electrochemical gradient. Protons then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase channels, and this flow ( chemiosmosis ) drives phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor : it combines with electrons and protons to form water (½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O). Without oxygen, electrons stop flowing, the proton gradient dissipates, NADH cannot be reoxidised, and oxidative phosphorylation ceases - explaining both cyanide poisoning (inhibits complex IV) and the far lower anaerobic yield. ATP yield per glucose : glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link 2 NADH; Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂. Each NADH yields ~2.5 ATP and each FADH₂ ~1.5 ATP via chemiosmosis, giving a theoretical ~32 ATP. Actual yields (30-32) are lower because: some protons leak back across the inner membrane without making ATP; energy is spent shuttling NADH from the cytoplasm into the mitochondrion (glycerol-3-phosphate vs malate-aspartate shuttles yield different returns); and ATP is used to actively transport pyruvate and ADP across the mitochondrial membranes. Exam questions may ask you to calculate yield from NADH/FADH₂ numbers or to explain why the theoretical maximum is not reached - learn both directions. Respirometers measure oxygen consumption (a manometer fluid moves as O₂ is consumed and CO₂ is absorbed by soda lime): link rate of oxygen uptake to rate of respiration, and control temperature with a water bath. RQ calculations : for tripalmitin C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 72.5 O₂ → 51 CO₂ + 49 H₂O, RQ = 51 ÷ 72.5 = 0.70 . RQ near 1.0 = carbohydrate substrate; below 1 = lipid/protein; above 1 = some anaerobic respiration occurring. These interpretation questions appear regularly on OCR (5.2.1) and WJEC C1 papers. When oxygen is limiting, glycolysis continues but the link reaction, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation stop because NADH cannot unload its electrons. Anaerobic pathways regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep producing its net 2 ATP. In animals : pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD⁺, catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase in muscle during intense exercise. Lactate accumulates, lowering pH; it is transported in the blood to the liver and oxidised back to pyruvate (or converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis) - the oxygen debt. Blood lactate assays and muscle fatigue questions expect this. In yeast (fermentation) : pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂ (pyruvate decarboxylase), then acetaldehyde + NADH → ethanol + NAD⁺ (ethanol dehydrogenase) - the basis of brewing and of AQA RP-style investigations into yeast respiration rate under different variables. Why anaerobic yields far less ATP : glucose is only partially oxidised - the energy-rich hydrogen in pyruvate/lactate is never transferred to the ETC, so only the 2 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis are made, versus ~32 aerobically; the large chemiosmotic yield from oxidising 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂ is lost. In animals the lactate pathway also costs ATP later (liver conversion), and lactate acidosis impairs muscle contraction - an exam staple linking respiration to muscle physiology (Edexcel T7, WJEC). Regulation of respiration completes the topic: phosphofructokinase (an early glycolytic enzyme) is allosterically inhibited by high ATP and citrate, and activated by high AMP/ADP, so glycolysis slows when energy charge is high - a concrete feedback-inhibition example worth quoting. Mitochondrial diseases that impair the ETC reduce ATP yield and raise dependence on anaerobic pathways; uncouplers (e.g. DNP) dissipate the proton gradient, so respiration continues without ATP production, releasing energy as heat - questions use these to test whether you really understand chemiosmosis rather than recite stages.

topics.name: Exchange and Transport
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Exchange and Transport Explain surface area to volume ratio and the features of efficient exchange surfaces (AQA 3.3.1; OCR 3.1.1) Describe gas exchange in the alveoli, insects, fish and plants, and ventilation mechanics (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 3.1.1) Describe digestion, absorption and co-transport of glucose in the ileum (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel A T1/T2) Describe the heart structure, cardiac cycle and blood vessels; explain tissue fluid formation (AQA 3.3.4; OCR 3.1.2) Explain transpiration and the cohesion-tension theory; describe phloem translocation by mass flow (AQA 3.3.4.2; OCR 3.1.3) Calculate cardiac output, ventilation rate and interpret potometer data As size increases SA:V falls; efficient exchange surfaces: large area, thin, good gradient (Fick's law); mass transport systems overcome diffusion limits Lungs: alveoli (large SA, thin squamous epithelium), capillary network, ventilation maintains gradient; insect tracheae: spiracles; fish: gill lamellae, counter-current; plants: stomata, mesophyll Ileum absorption: microvilli, Na⁺-glucose co-transport (Na⁺/K⁺ pump → Na⁺ diffuses in dragging glucose → facilitated diffusion out) Cardiac cycle: SAN → AVN → bundle of His → Purkyne fibres; systole/diastole; valves prevent backflow; cardiac output = HR × SV Tissue fluid: hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out at arterial end; proteins stay in (oncotic pressure pulls water back); lymph drains excess Xylem: cohesion-tension, transpiration pull, lignified walls; phloem: mass flow from source to sink; sucrose loaded actively at source Surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) The relationship between an organism's surface area and its volume; as size increases, SA:V decreases, so large organisms need exchange and transport systems. Fick's law Rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of exchange surface; exchange surfaces are adapted to maximise the numerator and minimise thickness. Tidal volume The volume of air breathed in and out at rest (~0.5 dm³); ventilation rate = tidal volume × breathing rate per minute. Cardiac output The volume of blood pumped by one ventricle per minute: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (dm³ min⁻¹). Tissue fluid Fluid forced out of capillaries at the arterial end by hydrostatic pressure, bathing cells and supplying them with oxygen and nutrients; excess returns via the lymphatic system. Transpiration The loss of water vapour from plant leaves by evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion through stomata down a water-potential gradient. Cohesion-tension theory Theory of water movement in xylem: water evaporates from leaves (transpiration pull), and cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) plus adhesion to walls maintains an unbroken water column under tension. Mass flow The bulk movement of fluids driven by a pressure gradient; phloem sap flows from source (high hydrostatic pressure) to sink (low pressure) in mass flow. Potometer Apparatus measuring water uptake by a shoot, used as an estimate of transpiration rate (OCR PAG8). Counter-current exchange Exchange system in which water and blood flow in opposite directions, maintaining a diffusion gradient along the whole length of the gill lamellae. As organisms get larger, surface area increases more slowly than volume , so the SA:V ratio falls . Small organisms exchange everything across their body surface by diffusion alone; larger organisms cannot - the diffusion distance is too great and the surface too small, so they need specialised exchange surfaces plus mass transport systems to carry substances between the exchange surface and cells. Heat loss shows the same pattern: small organisms (high SA:V) lose heat faster and need high metabolic rates; large organisms conserve heat. Fick's law gives the three features examiners want in every exchange-surface answer: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness - so efficient exchange surfaces have (1) a large surface area (folds, villi, lamellae, alveoli); (2) a thin barrier (often one-cell thick squamous epithelium); and (3) a steep concentration/diffusion gradient maintained (ventilation, blood flow, counter-current flow). Quote Fick's law explicitly and link each structure to one of its three terms - that structure-function pairing is what the mark scheme awards. Mammalian lungs : the trachea divides into bronchi, then bronchioles, ending in alveoli - the exchange surface. Adaptations to quote: ~300 million alveoli give a huge surface area ; walls are one cell thick (squamous epithelium) plus one-cell-thick capillary endothelium, so the diffusion barrier is ~two cells; a dense capillary network maintains the gradient by rapidly removing oxygenated blood; ventilation maintains a high O₂/low CO₂ gradient; alveoli are moist so gases dissolve. Ventilation (inspiration) : diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostal muscles contract, ribs move up and out - thoracic volume increases, pressure falls below atmospheric, air flows in. Expiration : diaphragm relaxes, internal intercostals contract, volume decreases, pressure rises, air flows out (passive at rest). Tidal volume ~0.5 dm³; ventilation rate = tidal volume × breaths per minute ; spirometer traces and calculations appear on OCR (3.1.1) and WJEC papers. Emphysema (destroyed alveolar walls, reduced surface area, less elastic recoil) and fibrosis (thickened walls) are stock application questions linking structure to reduced gas exchange. Insects : air enters through spiracles (open/close to limit water loss) into tracheae reinforced with chitin, branching into tracheoles ending in fluid-filled tips in contact with cells; gases diffuse directly to tissues - no blood transport of O₂. Water loss is minimised by spiracle closure, hairs and a waterproof cuticle. Fish : water flows unidirectionally over gill filaments and lamellae (large surface area, thin, rich capillary supply); counter-current exchange - water and blood flow in opposite directions , so a diffusion gradient is maintained along the whole lamella and ~80% of water's O₂ is extracted (vs ~50% with parallel flow) - explain this as maintaining the gradient at every point, the classic A* point. Plants : gases diffuse through stomata (guard cells open/close) into air spaces in the spongy mesophyll ; the flat, thin leaf gives a large SA:V; stomatal closure balances gas exchange against water loss - link to xerophytes (rolled leaves, hairs, sunken stomata) in dry habitats. Required practical: AQA RP5 (dissection of lungs/gills/insect to show exchange structures); OCR PAG9 (dissection). Spirometer traces and lung-volume terms earn regular marks on OCR and WJEC: tidal volume (air per breath at rest, ~0.5 dm³), inspiratory/expiratory reserve volumes (extra air above/below tidal), vital capacity (max in + max out) and residual volume (air that cannot be exhaled); ventilation rate = tidal volume × breaths per minute - calculate, don't just define. Disease application questions link structure to reduced gas exchange: emphysema (smoking/alveolar macrophage damage destroys alveolar walls - less surface area and less elastic recoil, so ventilation becomes laboured), fibrosis (scar tissue thickens the exchange barrier - longer diffusion distance), asthma (bronchiole constriction and mucus narrow the airways, reducing airflow). Quote Fick's law terms in each answer: which term (area, thickness, gradient) the disease changes. Digestion hydrolyses polymers to monomers: amylase (saliva, pancreas) hydrolyses starch to maltose, maltase (membrane-bound in ileum epithelium) to glucose; lipase (pancreas) hydrolyses lipids to fatty acids + monoglycerides, aided by bile salts emulsifying lipids into micelles (large surface area for lipase); endopeptidases/exopeptidases and dipeptidases hydrolyse proteins to amino acids. Absorption in the ileum uses the villi/microvilli (folded membrane - large surface area, thin epithelium, dense capillary and lacteal supply): amino acids and monosaccharides enter by specific transport; monoglycerides/fatty acids re-form triglycerides in the epithelium and enter the lacteal as chylomicrons. The co-transport of glucose is the classic mechanism question (from the existing site content, AQA 3.3.3): (1) Na⁺/K⁺ pump (ATPase) actively transports Na⁺ out of the epithelial cell into the blood, lowering intracellular Na⁺; (2) Na⁺ diffuses down its gradient from the lumen into the cell via sodium-glucose co-transporter proteins , dragging glucose against its gradient; (3) glucose exits into the blood by facilitated diffusion . Cystic fibrosis (defective Cl⁻ channel, thick mucus, impaired absorption) is the stock application on Edexcel T2. Water absorption follows osmosis down the water potential gradient created by solute uptake. The heart is a double pump: right side sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs, left side (thicker myocardium) sends oxygenated blood to the body. The cardiac cycle : (1) diastole - atria and ventricles relax; atrioventricular valves open, semilunar valves close; blood fills the atria and ventricles; (2) atrial systole - the SAN (sinoatrial node, the pacemaker) initiates contraction, atria contract, pushing remaining blood into ventricles; (3) ventricular systole - impulse reaches the AVN , passes down the bundle of His and Purkyne fibres (delay at AVN allows atria to empty; Purkyne fibres ensure contraction from the apex upwards); ventricles contract, AV valves close (first sound), semilunar valves open, blood ejected into aorta/pulmonary artery. Valves prevent backflow . Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume - calculations guaranteed. Pressure graphs (aorta, ventricle, atrium) and valve-state interpretation are standard six-markers. Control of heart rate: medulla receives signals from baroreceptors (pressure) and chemoreceptors (CO₂/pH) - sympathetic nerves increase rate, vagus (parasympathetic) decreases it; adrenaline increases rate (link to homeostasis topic). Blood vessels : arteries - thick muscular/elastic walls, high pressure, elastic recoil maintains pulse flow; arterioles - muscle controls flow to organs; capillaries - one-cell-thick endothelium, narrow, for exchange; veins - thin walls, low pressure, valves preventing backflow. Tissue fluid formation : at the arterial end , hydrostatic pressure (higher than the water potential of the plasma) forces fluid and small solutes out through capillary gaps - plasma proteins stay in , making the plasma water potential more negative; at the venous end , hydrostatic pressure has fallen and oncotic (water-potential) pressure pulls fluid back in; the lymphatic system drains the excess , returning it to the blood near the heart. Oedema questions follow from this balance. Pressure-change graphs are the standard interpretation question: the aortic pressure lags behind ventricular pressure (the valve must open first), the atrial pressure stays low, and valve closure sounds mark the boundaries of systole - read which valve is open/closed from which pressure is higher, not from memory of the order. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume ; during exercise heart rate and stroke volume both rise (venous return increases, more blood fills the ventricles, stretching the myocardium - the Starling mechanism gives a stronger contraction), so cardiac output can rise fourfold to deliver more oxygen to respiring muscle; after exercise, parasympathetic control restores the resting rate. Arterial blood pressure is maintained by elastic recoil between beats; hypertension damages arteries and increases heart workload - the link to cardiovascular disease questions on Edexcel T1 and WJEC. Xylem carries water and mineral ions from roots to leaves - one-way, dead, hollow, lignified cells forming continuous tubes. Movement is explained by the cohesion-tension theory : water evaporates from mesophyll cells into air spaces and diffuses out of stomata ( transpiration ), lowering the water potential of leaf cells; water moves from xylem into mesophyll by osmosis, creating transpiration pull (tension) in the xylem column; cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonding) and adhesion to xylem walls keep the column unbroken and under tension, pulling water up from the roots; root pressure contributes at the base. Transpiration rate factors: light (stomata open), temperature (more evaporation, more kinetic energy, lower water potential of air), humidity (smaller gradient), air movement (removes humid layer). Potometer (OCR PAG8) measures water uptake as an estimate of transpiration: cut shoot underwater, seal airtight, measure bubble movement; quote controls (same shoot, still air, constant temperature) and limitations (uptake ≠ transpiration exactly, cut surfaces). Xerophytic adaptations (marram grass, cacti): rolled leaves, sunken stomata, hairs, thick waxy cuticle - all reduce the water-potential gradient and air movement at the stomata. Phloem translocates sucrose and amino acids from sources (leaves, storage organs releasing sugars) to sinks (roots, growing tips, fruits) by mass flow , in both directions over time. Mechanism: sucrose is actively loaded into companion cells/seive tube elements at the source (H⁺ gradient from ATP-driven H⁺ pumping, sucrose co-transport), lowering the water potential of the phloem; water enters by osmosis from the xylem, raising hydrostatic pressure at the source ; at the sink, sucrose is unloaded (actively or by diffusion), water potential rises, water leaves, pressure falls ; sap then flows en masse from high to low pressure . Evidence: ringing experiments (ringed bark accumulates sugar above the ring, swelling below is absent), aphid stylets (sap exudes under pressure), radioactively labelled CO₂ traced to sinks. Compare xylem vs phloem in a table if asked: direction, contents, living/dead cells, driving force, evidence.

topics.name: DNA, Genes and Protein Synthesis
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology DNA, Genes and Protein Synthesis Describe DNA and RNA structure and explain why DNA is suited to carrying information (AQA 3.1.5.1; OCR 2.1.3.1) Describe semi-conservative replication and the evidence from the Meselson-Stahl experiment (AQA 3.1.5.2; OCR 2.1.3.2) Explain the features of the genetic code (triplet, non-overlapping, degenerate, universal) (AQA 3.4.1) Describe transcription and post-transcriptional modification in eukaryotes (AQA 3.4.2; OCR 2.1.3.3) Describe translation with codon-anticodon pairing and peptide bond formation (AQA 3.4.2; OCR 2.1.3.3) Explain how gene mutations (substitution, insertion, deletion) alter protein structure (AQA 3.8.1; OCR 6.1.1) DNA: antiparallel strands, A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds), sugar-phosphate backbone of phosphodiester bonds; RNA: ribose, uracil, single-stranded Replication: helicase unwinds and unzips; DNA polymerase synthesises 5'→3' (leading continuous, lagging in Okazaki fragments joined by ligase) Transcription: RNA polymerase, template strand, pre-mRNA spliced (introns out) in eukaryotes Translation: ribosome reads codons; tRNA anticodons deliver amino acids; peptide bonds form the polypeptide Mutations: substitution (silent/missense/nonsense), insertion/deletion (frameshift); mutagens increase rate Nucleotide A monomer of nucleic acids: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (A/T/C/G in DNA, A/U/C/G in RNA). Gene A base sequence of DNA that codes for the amino-acid sequence of a polypeptide or a functional RNA (e.g. tRNA, rRNA). Codon A triplet of mRNA bases coding for one amino acid; 64 codons exist, including the start codon (AUG) and three stop codons. Anticodon The triplet of bases on a tRNA molecule complementary to a specific mRNA codon; pairs by complementary base pairing during translation. Degenerate code The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet codon, so some mutations are silent. Semi-conservative replication DNA replication in which each daughter molecule retains one original (conserved) parental strand and one newly synthesised strand. Exon A coding region of a eukaryotic gene that remains in mature mRNA after splicing and is translated. Intron A non-coding region of a eukaryotic gene that is transcribed into pre-mRNA but removed by splicing before translation. Frameshift mutation An insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three, which shifts the reading frame and changes every codon downstream. Gene mutation A change in the base sequence of a chromosome - substitution, insertion, deletion, duplication or inversion - arising spontaneously in replication or induced by mutagens. A DNA nucleotide = deoxyribose (pentose sugar) + phosphate group + nitrogenous base (A, T, C or G). Nucleotides join by condensation between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next, forming a sugar-phosphate backbone linked by phosphodiester bonds . Two polynucleotide strands run antiparallel (one 5'→3', one 3'→5') and twist into a double helix, held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A-T (2 hydrogen bonds), G-C (3 hydrogen bonds) . Complementary base pairing plus the constant width of paired bases makes DNA stable yet able to unzip. RNA contrasts in four ways: ribose sugar (not deoxyribose), uracil replaces thymine, single-stranded , shorter. mRNA (carries the code from nucleus to ribosome), tRNA (cloverleaf, anticodon, amino-acid binding site) and rRNA (ribosomal structure) all feature in mark schemes. Know the structure-function links examiners award: the double helix stores large amounts of information in a compact stable form; hydrogen bonds are weak enough to allow unzipping for replication and transcription; complementary base pairing enables accurate copying; phosphodiester bonds give backbone strength; the sequence of bases codes the amino-acid sequence of polypeptides. ATP is a nucleotide derivative (adenine + ribose + three phosphates) - expect a link question between DNA nucleotides and ATP structure. Base classification matters for exam precision: purines (adenine, guanine - double-ring, larger) pair with pyrimidines (thymine, cytosine - single-ring, smaller), keeping the double helix a constant width; hydrogen bonding numbers (A-T 2, G-C 3) explain why G-C rich DNA is more stable and melts at higher temperatures. In eukaryotes, DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, then coils into chromosomes - this packaging is what epigenetic modification (histone acetylation/methylation) adjusts to switch genes on or off. Prokaryotic DNA is naked (no histones) and circular. Also note that most eukaryotic DNA is non-coding : introns, regulatory sequences and repeats; only a small fraction codes for polypeptides, and the coding regions are the genes at their loci on homologous chromosomes. The full sequence earns marks in order: (1) DNA helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases; (2) the two exposed antiparallel strands each act as a template ; (3) free DNA nucleotides are attracted to their complementary exposed bases (A-T, G-C) and hydrogen-bond into place; (4) DNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds , synthesising each new strand 5'→3' ; (5) because the strands are antiparallel, the leading strand is synthesised continuously while the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase ; (6) each daughter molecule contains one conserved parental strand and one newly built strand - hence semi-conservative . Evidence: the Meselson-Stahl experiment grew E. coli in heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), then transferred to light (¹⁴N); after one generation all DNA was intermediate density, after two, half intermediate and half light - only semi-conservative replication predicts this. Exam questions often test why the experiment excludes conservative and dispersive models, so know the predicted banding patterns. Add the conditions and error-control detail: replication happens during S phase of interphase before cell division, requiring free nucleotides, ATP, helicase, polymerase and ligase. Complementary base pairing makes replication highly accurate : A always pairs with T and G with C, and DNA polymerase proof-reads newly added nucleotides, excising mismatches - mutations persist only when errors escape repair. When asked to evaluate the Meselson-Stahl evidence, state the three predictions: a conservative model predicts one heavy and one light band after one generation; a dispersive model predicts intermediate DNA at every generation that gets progressively lighter; only the observed pattern (intermediate after one generation, half intermediate and half light after two) fits semi-conservative replication. DNA replication in prokaryotes is similar but starts from a single origin and proceeds in both directions around the circular chromosome. A gene is a base sequence coding for a polypeptide or functional RNA. Eukaryotic genes contain introns (non-coding) and exons (coding); prokaryotic DNA has no introns. The genetic code is: triplet (three bases = one codon = one amino acid), non-overlapping (each base belongs to only one codon), degenerate (most amino acids have multiple codons - so some substitutions are silent), and universal (same codons code the same amino acids in all organisms - the basis of genetic engineering). A gene on a chromosome sits at a locus ; homologous chromosomes carry the same genes at the same loci but may carry different alleles. Transcription : (1) RNA polymerase binds the promoter region and unwinds/unzips the DNA; (2) free RNA nucleotides pair with the exposed template strand (uracil pairs with adenine); (3) RNA polymerase joins them with phosphodiester bonds to make pre-mRNA ; (4) in eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is spliced to remove introns, and modified with a 5' cap and poly-A tail, producing mature mRNA; (5) the mRNA leaves via a nuclear pore. Only the template strand is copied because the code must match the sense strand when translated. Prokaryotes produce mRNA directly (no splicing) and translation can begin immediately - a comparison the exam uses. Alternative splicing of exons lets one gene code several polypeptides, increasing diversity of gene products in humans. Two strand roles examiners test: only the template strand is transcribed (the sense strand carries the same sequence as the mRNA, in T/U terms); RNA polymerase moves along the template in the 3' to 5' direction , synthesising mRNA 5' to 3'. The promoter is the DNA sequence RNA polymerase binds to start transcription - transcription factors (see gene-expression topic) control this access, so a gene's expression depends on which factors are active, not just the gene's presence. Contrast eukaryotic and prokaryotic protein synthesis in one line each if asked: eukaryotes transcribe in the nucleus, splice the pre-mRNA, then translate in the cytoplasm; prokaryotes have no nucleus, produce mRNA directly with no splicing, and translation can begin before transcription finishes - this speed underlies rapid bacterial responses to environmental change. Translation occurs on the ribosome in the cytoplasm (or on rough ER for secreted proteins): (1) the ribosome attaches to the start codon (AUG) of mRNA; (2) tRNA molecules, each carrying a specific amino acid, have anticodons complementary to mRNA codons ; (3) the ribosome moves along the mRNA, and two tRNAs occupy the ribosome at once so the ribosome can catalyse peptide bond formation between adjacent amino acids (using ATP to attach amino acids to tRNA first); (4) tRNA leaves, emptied, and is reused; (5) translation stops at a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA), releasing the polypeptide , which folds into its tertiary structure (assisted by chaperones in some cases). Codon-anticodon pairing by complementary base pairing guarantees the amino-acid sequence matches the gene. The polypeptide may then be modified in the Golgi (e.g. glycosylation) - link this back to cell-structure content for synthesis-and-secretion questions. tRNA earns its own marks: a single strand of ~80 nucleotides folded into a cloverleaf shape held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, with an anticodon at one end and an amino-acid binding site at the other; ATP and activating enzymes attach each amino acid to its specific tRNA - the energy in that bond later supplies peptide-bond formation. Ribosomes consist of a large and a small subunit of rRNA and protein: the small subunit binds mRNA, the large subunit holds the tRNAs and catalyses peptide bonds. Several ribosomes can translate one mRNA simultaneously (a polysome ), producing many copies of the polypeptide quickly. The completed polypeptide is often modified after translation - folded, with sugars added in the Golgi, or cleaved into active fragments (e.g. insulin from pro-insulin) - before becoming a functional protein. Gene mutations change the base sequence of a chromosome. They arise spontaneously during DNA replication (base pairing errors) or are induced by mutagens - UV radiation, ionising radiation, and chemicals such as tar in tobacco smoke. Types and their consequences: substitution - one base replaced: silent if the new codon codes the same amino acid (degenerate code), missense if a different amino acid is inserted (may alter tertiary structure, e.g. sickle-cell anaemia from a single substitution in haemoglobin), nonsense if a stop codon is created (truncated, non-functional protein); insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three - frameshift : the reading frame shifts so every codon downstream changes, inserting wrong amino acids and often creating a premature stop codon; duplication - a base sequence repeated; inversion - a sequence reversed. Chromosome mutations include deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation of whole sections, and non-disjunction producing aneuploidy (e.g. trisomy 21). Mutations in gametes are inherited and fuel genetic diversity and evolution; mutations in somatic cells (not inherited) can produce cancer if they affect genes controlling cell division (proto-oncogenes, tumour-suppressor genes - see gene-expression topic). Because the code is degenerate and non-overlapping, substitutions are often silent while insertions/deletions are catastrophic - a classic comparison question. Beneficial mutations (e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria, lactose tolerance in humans) show mutation as the source of new alleles on which natural selection acts, linking this sub-topic to genetics, evolution and ecosystems. Mutagens increase the mutation rate: ultraviolet light causes thymine dimers in DNA; ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma) breaks chromosomes and damages bases; chemicals such as tar in tobacco smoke and mustard gas are alkylating agents. Cells possess DNA repair mechanisms (excision repair enzymes) that correct most damage, but unrepaired mutations become permanent and are copied in every future replication. Repeat-expansion mutations (e.g. Huntington's disease - extra CAG repeats) show that inserting multiples of three also mutates proteins by inserting extra amino acids without a frameshift. Distinguish somatic mutations (body cells - not inherited, can cause cancer) from germ-line mutations (gametes - inherited, source of new alleles on which selection acts). Rates vary: most base pairs replicate faithfully, but with billions of bases per cell division, spontaneous mutations occur constantly - the raw material of genetic diversity.

topics.name: Gene Expression and Technology
topics.subject: biology
topics.searchText: biology Biology Gene Expression and Technology Explain how transcription factors, oestrogen and siRNA control gene expression (AQA 3.8.2.1-3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1) Describe epigenetic control: DNA methylation and histone acetylation, and the epigenome (AQA 3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1) Distinguish totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells and describe their sources and uses (AQA 3.8.2.2; OCR 6.1.1) Describe making recombinant DNA: reverse transcriptase, restriction endonucleases, DNA ligase, vectors and marker genes (AQA 3.8.4.1-3.8.4.2; OCR 6.1.3) Detail PCR stages and explain gel electrophoresis, DNA probes and DNA sequencing (AQA 3.8.4.3-3.8.4.4; OCR 6.1.3) Describe genome projects, proteomics and evaluate ethical issues of gene technology and gene therapy Transcription factors bind promoters: stimulatory or inhibitory; oestrogen binds ER in cytoplasm, complex acts as transcription factor Epigenome: DNA methylation of CpG islands condenses chromatin (silences); histone acetylation loosens chromatin (activates); heritable without changing base sequence siRNA: binds RISC, guides to complementary mRNA, cleaves it - prevents translation Stem cells: totipotent (zygote) → pluripotent (blastocyst) → multipotent (bone marrow); iPS cells made by reprogramming with transcription factors Recombinant DNA: reverse transcriptase (mRNA → cDNA), restriction endonucleases (sticky ends), DNA ligase (seals), plasmid vectors, marker genes PCR: 95 °C denaturation, 55 °C annealing, 72 °C extension by Taq polymerase; doubles DNA each cycle Gel electrophoresis: DNA fragments move to the anode; shorter fragments travel further - separates by size Transcription factor A protein that binds to specific DNA regions (promoters) and either stimulates or inhibits transcription of a gene by controlling RNA polymerase access. Epigenetics Heritable changes in gene expression caused by mechanisms other than changes to the DNA base sequence, e.g. DNA methylation and histone modification; the epigenome is the chemical layer controlling gene expression. Totipotent stem cell A stem cell that can differentiate into all body cell types plus extra-embryonic tissue (placenta); found in the first few divisions of the embryo (zygote). Pluripotent stem cell A stem cell from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst that can differentiate into all somatic (body) cell types but not extra-embryonic tissue. Restriction endonuclease An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific palindromic recognition site, leaving either blunt or staggered (sticky) ends used in recombinant DNA technology. Sticky ends Staggered, complementary single-stranded ends produced when restriction endonucleases cut DNA; they anneal by complementary base pairing to join DNA fragments. Vector A carrier (usually a bacterial plasmid or virus) used to transfer a target gene into a host cell; contains marker genes to identify successful uptake. cDNA Complementary DNA made from mature mRNA using reverse transcriptase; contains no introns, so bacteria can translate it. Primer A short single-stranded DNA sequence that binds complementarily to the 3' end of a target DNA strand, providing the starting point for DNA polymerase in PCR. DNA probe A short single-stranded DNA fragment, labelled with a radioactive or fluorescent tag, that hybridises to a complementary target sequence to locate specific alleles or genes. Every cell contains the same genome, yet only some genes are translated - control of gene expression explains differentiation and cell specialisation. Transcription factors are proteins that bind specific DNA sequences (promoters) and control whether RNA polymerase can transcribe a gene: stimulatory factors enable transcription; inhibitory factors block it. Oestrogen is the stock example of an external signal controlling transcription: it is lipid-soluble, diffuses through the cell-surface membrane, binds a complementary receptor (ER) in the cytoplasm, causing the receptor to change shape and release an inhibitory molecule; the oestrogen-receptor complex then enters the nucleus and binds promoter regions, acting as a transcription factor that activates target genes (e.g. in some breast cancers, over-expression drives uncontrolled cell division). siRNA controls expression after transcription: double-stranded siRNA unwinds and associates with RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex); one strand guides RISC to a complementary mRNA , which RISC cleaves , so translation cannot occur - RNA interference, usable therapeutically to silence disease genes. Epigenetics is heritable change in gene expression without altering the base sequence , controlled by the epigenome - a layer of chemical tags on DNA and histones. Two mechanisms are examinable: DNA methylation - methyl groups (-CH₃) added to cytosine in CpG islands attract proteins that condense chromatin (heterochromatin), blocking RNA polymerase access and silencing transcription; histone acetylation - acetyl groups added to histone lysine residues loosen the DNA-histone packing (euchromatin), giving RNA polymerase access and activating transcription. Deacetylation condenses chromatin again. Epigenetic changes are heritable through cell division and sometimes between generations , and link environmental factors to disease: e.g. methylation changes in cancer (tumour-suppressor genes silenced, oncogenes activated), smoking-induced epigenetic marks. The epigenome is reversible - drugs can inhibit methylation enzymes or histone deacetylases, an A* discussion point. When asked to explain epigenetic control, always state the mechanism (methyl/acetyl), the chromatin state (condensed/loosened), and the outcome (transcription on/off) - three linked marks. Epigenetic tags can be inherited across generations - examples studied include famine exposure (Dutch Hunger Winter) leaving methylation marks in offspring, and maternal care altering methylation of stress-response genes - showing how the environment in one generation changes gene expression in the next without changing the base sequence; this bridges genetics and evolution questions, since epigenetic variation is another heritable layer on which selection can act. Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that divide by mitosis and differentiate. Classify them precisely - the three-tier definition earns full marks: totipotent - can differentiate into all body cell types plus extra-embryonic tissue (placenta) ; only the zygote and first few divisions (up to the 8-cell stage). Pluripotent - from the inner cell mass of the blastocyst ; differentiate into all somatic cell types but not placental tissue; source of embryonic stem cells. Multipotent - e.g. bone marrow (haematopoietic) stem cells; differentiate into a limited range of related cells (blood cells). During differentiation, most genes are switched off (heterochromatin) so only genes needed for the cell's function are expressed - the mechanism linking stem cells to transcription control above. iPS cells (induced pluripotent stem cells) are adult somatic cells reprogrammed back to pluripotency by introducing extra transcription factors: they divide endlessly like embryonic stem cells but avoid destroying embryos , sidestepping the main ethical objection, and can be made from the patient's own cells to avoid immune rejection. Uses: bone marrow transplants for leukaemia/lymphoma, regenerative medicine (growing tissues/organs), studying differentiation, testing drugs without animal/human trials. Ethics debate expects balance: embryo destruction vs. medical benefit; consent and ownership of embryos; safety (uncontrolled division, tumour risk); alternatives (iPS, adult stem cells). Expression is also controlled post-transcriptionally and post-translationally : splicing and RNAi (above), and protein activation (e.g. phosphorylation, as in the cAMP second-messenger cascade in homeostasis). In prokaryotes, the lac operon (OCR 6.1.1; WJEC) is the classic model: lactose (allolactose) binds the repressor, releasing it from the operator so RNA polymerase transcribes the structural genes (β-galactosidase, lactose permease); glucose scarcity raises cAMP which helps CAP binding - transcription only when lactose present and glucose absent. Learn the operon sequence if your board lists it (OCR and WJEC do; AQA does not). Recombinant DNA combines DNA from different organisms; because the genetic code is universal , a gene transplanted between species still produces the same protein. Obtaining the target gene : (1) reverse transcriptase - isolate mRNA for the target protein (abundant in specialised cells, e.g. β-cells for insulin), use reverse transcriptase (from retroviruses) to make cDNA ; cDNA contains no introns , so bacteria (which cannot splice) can translate it, and single-stranded cDNA is made double-stranded with DNA polymerase; (2) restriction endonucleases - cut the gene from DNA at a specific palindromic recognition site , leaving staggered sticky ends ; (3) a gene machine synthesises the gene directly from a known sequence (from genome databases). Inserting into a vector : the same restriction enzyme cuts a plasmid at a single site, producing complementary sticky ends; gene and plasmid anneal by complementary base pairing, and DNA ligase seals the sugar-phosphate backbones with phosphodiester bonds, producing recombinant DNA . Transforming cells : plasmids are returned to host bacteria (e.g. E. coli) via Ca²⁺ and heat shock (or electroporation), making membranes permeable; marker genes identify successful uptake - fluorescent markers (GFP), antibiotic-resistance markers (survivors grown on antibiotic agar carry the plasmid) or enzyme markers; replica plating distinguishes plasmids with the target gene. Fermenters culture transformed bacteria to mass-produce protein (insulin, factor VIII, vaccines). In vivo (vectors, bacteria) vs in vitro (PCR) comparison is a standard six-marker: in vivo is slow but accurate (proof-reading enzymes, low error rate), copies large fragments, produces modified proteins (post-translational modification possible in bacteria is limited - note insulin is made as pro-insulin), and carries little risk of contamination; in vitro (PCR) is rapid, automatable, needs only tiny DNA samples, but has a higher error rate (Taq lacks proof-reading) and produces many identical copies without modification. Ethics of recombinant DNA and transgenic organisms: benefits (mass cheap insulin, GM crops with higher yield/nutrition, gene therapy); concerns (antibiotic-resistance marker genes spreading to pathogens, GM gene flow to wild populations, animal welfare, corporate control of seeds); evaluation questions want both sides plus a justified conclusion. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) amplifies DNA in vitro in three repeating stages: (1) denaturation at ~95 °C - hydrogen bonds break, separating the double helix into single strands; (2) annealing at ~55 °C - short single-stranded primers bind complementarily to the 3' ends of the target sequences, providing the starting point for DNA synthesis (and preventing re-annealing of the template strands); (3) extension at ~72 °C - Taq polymerase (thermostable, from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus ) adds free nucleotides (dNTPs) to synthesise complementary strands. Each cycle doubles the DNA (2ⁿ after n cycles: ~1 billion copies after 30 cycles). A thermal cycler automates the temperature cycling. Exam questions ask for the role of primers and Taq exactly as above, and why Taq is needed (does not denature at 95 °C).
