Model comparisons: diamond vs graphite — both giant covalent, both high MP because covalent bonds must break to melt, but graphite conducts (delocalised electrons between layers, which can also slide giving lubricating softness) while diamond does not (all four electrons in σ bonds). MgO vs NaCl — higher charges, smaller ions, stronger lattice. HF vs HCl — H-bonding vs dipole-dipole/London only. I₂(s) vs NaCl(s) — weak London forces between I₂ molecules vs strong electrostatic forces in the lattice. Graphene and fullerenes are sometimes asked about: graphene is a single layer of graphite with delocalised electrons making it conductive and extremely strong; fullerenes are simple molecular (C₆₀), so low melting points despite covalent bonds within each sphere. Structure–property questions are marked by the causal chain: structure type → which forces/bonds must be overcome → energy required → property observed. Always name the force, never just say 'strong bonds'. Exam technique for structure-property questions: the mark scheme is built from a causal chain — name the structure type, name the exact force or bond broken on melting/boiling, link to the energy required, conclude the property. 'Strong bonds' scores nothing: it must be 'strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions' or 'strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice' or 'weak London forces between molecules'. Conductivity answers must identify the mobile charge carrier (delocalised electrons in metals/graphite; mobile ions when molten/dissolved) and state why it is immobile in the other state. When comparing two substances, answer both halves: why A is high AND why B is low — half-comparisons lose half the marks. Drawing conventions: dot-and-cross diagrams show outer shells only with bonding pairs overlapping; displayed formulae show every bond; skeletal formulae omit C and H labels on the chain. Fluency converting between the three is assumed at A-level and tested indirectly throughout organic chemistry.

topics.name: Energetics and Kinetics
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Energetics and Kinetics Define standard enthalpy changes and perform calorimetry calculations using q = mcΔT Apply Hess's law using formation and combustion cycles, and calculate ΔH from mean bond enthalpies with limitations Construct Born-Haber cycles to find lattice enthalpies and explain differences between theoretical and experimental values Calculate ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, determine feasibility and the temperature threshold Use collision theory and Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions to explain the effects of temperature, concentration and catalysts Determine rate equations and orders by the initial-rates method and calculate k with units Use the Arrhenius equation, half-life relationships and ln k vs 1/T plots to find Ea Enthalpy change (ΔH) The heat energy change of a reaction at constant pressure, in kJ mol⁻¹. Standard enthalpy of formation The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions (100 kPa, 298 K). Standard enthalpy of combustion The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions; always exothermic. Hess's law The total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken. Lattice enthalpy of formation The enthalpy change when one mole of solid ionic lattice forms from gaseous ions; always exothermic. Activation energy (Ea) The minimum energy colliding molecules need for a collision to be effective and lead to reaction. Order of reaction The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation, determined experimentally. Half-life (t½) The time for the concentration of a reactant to halve; constant for first-order reactions, t½ = ln2/k. Gibbs free energy (ΔG) ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; a reaction is thermodynamically feasible when ΔG ≤ 0. Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat energy change at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings (ΔH negative; products lower than reactants; temperature rises) — combustion, oxidation, neutralisation. Endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH positive; products higher; temperature falls) — thermal decomposition, dissolving some salts. Standard conditions for all standard enthalpies: 100 kPa, 298 K, and 1 mol dm⁻³ for solutions; ΔH f ° of elements in their standard states is 0. Definitions to memorise exactly (each says 'one mole'): enthalpy of formation — one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states; enthalpy of combustion — one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen, always exothermic; enthalpy of neutralisation — one mole of water forms from an acid and alkali, −57.1 kJ/mol for strong acid–strong base; enthalpy of atomisation — one mole of gaseous atoms forms from an element in its standard state, always endothermic. Calorimetry (required practical: measuring enthalpy of combustion or neutralisation): q = mcΔT, where m is the mass of solution heated (assume density 1 g cm⁻³) and c is specific heat capacity (4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water). Convert to ΔH by dividing by moles: ΔH = −q/n (negative for exothermic). Sources of error for combustion: heat loss to surroundings and apparatus, incomplete combustion (soot), evaporation of fuel, heat capacity of the container not accounted for — all make the measured value less exothermic than data-book values. Improvements: lid, draught shields, flame close to can, or a bomb calorimeter. Energy level diagrams : y-axis enthalpy, reactants left, products right; exothermic products lower, endothermic products higher. An energy profile additionally shows the activation energy hump and, with a catalyst, a lower hump via an alternative route (two smaller humps). ΔH is the difference in levels; E a is the hump height from reactants. Label both correctly — confusing them is a classic lost mark. Hess's law : the total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, because enthalpy is a state function. Two standard cycles are examined. (1) Formation cycle — used when combustion data are given: ΔH r = ΣΔH c (reactants) − ΣΔH c (products). Watch the direction: combustion arrows point away from the reactants/products down to common combustion products (CO₂ + H₂O). (2) Combustion-cycle alternative / formation-data cycle — when ΔH f ° data are given: ΔH r = ΣΔH f °(products) − ΣΔH f °(reactants). Worked example (from formation data): for C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l), given ΔH f °(C₂H₅OH) = −277, ΔH f °(CO₂) = −394, ΔH f °(H₂O) = −286 kJ/mol: ΔH c = [(2 × −394) + (3 × −286)] − [−277] = (−788 − 858) + 277 = −1369 kJ/mol. Method marks: correct cycle, correct direction, correct multiples, final value with sign and units. Bond enthalpy method: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) — breaking bonds is endothermic, forming is exothermic. Example: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) with H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 243, H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol: ΔH = (436 + 243) − (2 × 431) = −183 kJ/mol. Limitations (standard explain question): mean bond enthalpies are averages over many different compounds containing that bond, and apply strictly only to gaseous molecules, so they ignore the specific molecular environment — calculations from ΔH f ° data are more accurate because they are measured for the exact substance under standard conditions. If any reactant or product is liquid/solid, you cannot use mean bond enthalpies without an extra atomisation step. Lattice enthalpy of formation : the enthalpy change when one mole of solid ionic lattice forms from its gaseous ions under standard conditions — always exothermic (e.g. Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s), −787 kJ/mol). The lattice dissociation enthalpy is the reverse, always endothermic. It cannot be measured directly, so a Born-Haber cycle is used: ΔH f ° = ΔH at (metal) + ΣIE(metal) + ΔH at (non-metal) + ΣEA(non-metal) + ΔH latt . Each stage: atomise the metal (endothermic), ionise it (IEs endothermic, larger for each successive electron), atomise the non-metal, add electrons (first EA usually exothermic; second EA always endothermic — energy needed to force an electron onto an already negative ion), then form the lattice. Worked example: calculate lattice enthalpy of NaCl given ΔH f °(NaCl) = −411, ΔH at (Na) = +107, ΔH at (Cl) = +122, IE₁(Na) = +496, EA₁(Cl) = −349 kJ/mol: −411 = 107 + 122 + 496 − 349 + ΔH latt , so ΔH latt = −411 − 376 = −787 kJ/mol. Sign discipline is everything — state whether the answer is formation (negative) or dissociation (positive) enthalpy. Comparing lattice enthalpies: more exothermic when ions are smaller and more highly charged (MgO >> NaCl). A gap between the theoretical lattice enthalpy (calculated assuming a perfect ionic model) and the experimental Born-Haber value indicates covalent character caused by polarisation of the anion — larger, more highly charged anions (e.g. AgI) polarise more, showing the purely ionic model fails. Enthalpy of solution : ΔH sol = −ΔH latt (dissociation) + ΣΔH hyd — equivalently ΔH latt (formation) + ΣΔH hyd . Hydration enthalpy is always exothermic and more exothermic for smaller, higher-charge ions (Li⁺ most exothermic in Group 1, decreasing down the group). Dissolving is feasible when ΔH sol is exothermic, or when TΔS outweighs an endothermic ΔH sol . Gibbs free energy : ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin, ΔS converted to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Reaction thermodynamically feasible when ΔG ≤ 0. Example: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ/mol, ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: feasible when T ≥ ΔH/ΔS = 178000/161 = 1106 K (833 °C). Entropy increases on: melting, boiling (large), dissolving gases out of solution, more gas moles produced. Feasible ≠ spontaneous — rate and activation energy still matter (kinetic control). Collision theory : reactions occur when molecules collide with at least the activation energy (E a ) and with correct orientation — only then is a collision effective . Factors increasing rate: concentration/pressure — more molecules per unit volume, more frequent collisions; temperature — molecules move faster, more frequent collisions and (much more importantly) a far higher proportion exceed E a ; surface area (solids) — more exposed particles; catalyst — alternative route with lower E a . The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shows the number of molecules with a given energy: starts at the origin (no molecules with zero energy), peaks at the most probable energy, and never touches the x-axis at high energy. When temperature rises, the peak shifts right and flattens — the total area (number of molecules) is unchanged, but the area beyond E a increases disproportionately, giving an exponentially faster reaction. Drawing marks: label axes, draw the E a line, shade/hatch the extra area beyond E a at the higher temperature. With a catalyst, draw a lower E a line — a much larger area of the unchanged distribution now exceeds it. Required practical (rates): follow reaction rate by measuring gas volume (gas syringe), mass loss (balance) or colour change/turbidity (disappearing cross), then vary concentration or temperature while keeping everything else constant. Classic experiment: Mg + HCl, or Na₂S₂O₃ + HCl with the disappearing cross. Control variables, plot rate against concentration, repeat and average; state the main error sources (reaction starts before sealing/inserting, timing of the endpoint is subjective) and improvements (bung ready, data-logger, fixed cross distance). Rate equations must be determined experimentally — orders cannot be deduced from the equation: rate = k[A] m [B] n ; overall order = m + n. Zero order: rate independent of [A] (horizontal concentration–time graph). First order : rate ∝ [A]; concentration–time graph shows constant half-life — t ½ = ln2/k ; ln[A] = −kt + ln[A]₀ gives a straight line when ln[A] is plotted against t. Second order : rate ∝ [A]²; 1/[A] vs t is linear; half-life doubles as concentration halves. Determining orders: the initial-rates method — vary one concentration while holding others constant and compare initial rates (e.g. from tangents at t = 0 or the disappearing-cross method). If doubling [A] doubles the rate, order 1 in A; quadruples, order 2; no change, order 0. Once orders are known, substitute concentrations and rates into the rate equation to calculate k with units: s⁻¹ for first order, mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹ for second, mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹ for third overall. Clock reactions approximate initial rate using the time for a fixed small amount of product to appear (rate ∝ 1/t). The Arrhenius equation : k = Ae −Ea/RT . Rearranged: ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A , so plotting ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient −Ea/R and intercept ln A. Exam calculations: given two rate constants at two temperatures, use ln(k₂/k₁) = −Ea/R × (1/T₂ − 1/T₁). A typical answer: Ea = R × gradient × (−1), with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and temperatures in kelvin. Increasing temperature raises k because a greater proportion of molecules exceed E a — the exponential term is the key explanation. Mechanisms and rate equations connect at A2: in a multi-step mechanism, the rate-determining (slowest) step controls the rate equation; species in the rate-determining step (and species feeding into it via fast pre-equilibrium) appear in the rate equation. If rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr], the rate-determining step involves only the halogenoalkane — evidence for an SN1 mechanism (see Organic Chemistry: Mechanisms).

topics.name: Equilibria and Redox
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Equilibria and Redox Apply Le Chatelier's principle to concentration, pressure and temperature changes, including industrial compromise conditions Write Kc and Kp expressions, calculate equilibrium constants from ICE tables and partial pressures, and assign units Explain why only temperature changes K, and why catalysts do not affect equilibrium position Assign oxidation states and construct balanced half-equations and full redox equations in acidic and alkaline conditions Calculate E°cell from standard electrode potentials and predict feasibility and reaction direction Describe electrochemical cells, salt bridges and cell notation, and evaluate fuel cells and rechargeable batteries Dynamic equilibrium Forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates in a closed system, so concentrations remain constant. Le Chatelier's principle When a change in concentration, pressure or temperature is applied, the equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Kc Equilibrium constant in concentrations, products over reactants, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient. Kp Equilibrium constant in partial pressures; pA = mole fraction × total pressure. Partial pressure The pressure a gas would exert if it alone occupied the volume: mole fraction × total pressure. Oxidation number A measure of electron loss/gain assigned by rules; increase = oxidation, decrease = reduction. Standard electrode potential (E°) The potential of a half-cell measured against the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions (298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³, 100 kPa). Disproportionation A reaction in which one element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl₂ in water. Fuel cell A cell that generates electricity continuously from the reaction of a fuel (e.g. H₂) with oxygen; products at point of use are water. A dynamic equilibrium exists in a closed system when forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates: concentrations stay constant, but both reactions continue. Le Chatelier's principle : when a change in concentration, pressure or temperature is applied, the equilibrium position shifts to oppose the change. Concentration: adding a species shifts equilibrium to consume it; removing shifts to replace it. Pressure (gases only): increasing pressure shifts to the side with fewer gas moles. Temperature: heating shifts in the endothermic direction — for an exothermic forward reaction, yield falls as temperature rises. Only temperature changes the value of Kc or Kp ; concentration and pressure change the position but not K, because the system re-establishes the same ratio. A catalyst speeds both directions equally — faster equilibrium, no change in position or K. Kc = [products]/[reactants] at equilibrium, each concentration raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient. For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b. Units: count powers — e.g. for esterification CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, Kc has no units (equal moles each side). Homogeneous equilibria have all species in the same state; heterogeneous equilibria involve different states — pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from K expressions because their concentrations are constant. ICE-table calculations: given initial moles and the equilibrium amount of one species, fill the change row (x per coefficient), deduce equilibrium moles, divide by volume for concentrations, substitute into Kc. Exam tip: state the change as ±(coefficient × x) explicitly — that row carries the method marks. Industrial context: Haber process (450 °C compromise temperature, ~200 atm, Fe catalyst — low temperature favoured by equilibrium but too slow, so a compromise is chosen); Contact process for SO₃ (~2 atm because yield is already high; V₂O₅ catalyst). Kp is the equilibrium constant for gas equilibria expressed in partial pressures. Partial pressure of gas A: pA = mole fraction of A × total pressure , where mole fraction = moles of A / total moles of gas. Kp = product of p( products )^coefficients / p( reactants )^coefficients. Example for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g): Kp = p(SO₃)² / [p(SO₂)² × p(O₂)] , units: (kPa)²/(kPa)³ = kPa⁻¹. Worked example: 2.00 mol SO₂ and 1.00 mol O₂ reach equilibrium with 1.20 mol SO₃ formed at total pressure P. Change row: SO₂ −1.20, O₂ −0.60, SO₃ +1.20; equilibrium moles: 0.80, 0.40, 1.20; total = 2.40. Mole fractions: 1/3, 1/6, 1/2. Partial pressures: P/3, P/6, P/2. Kp = (P/2)² / [(P/3)² × (P/6)] = (P²/4) / (P³/54) = 13.5/P kPa⁻¹. Method marks: change row, mole fractions, substitution, units. Temperature is the only variable that alters Kp. Raising pressure at constant temperature leaves Kp unchanged but shifts position to fewer gas moles. The relationship Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn where Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of gaseous reactants links the two constants (more heavily used by some boards, e.g. WJEC/CCEA). When asked to predict the effect of a change on yield, first compare gas moles; when asked about K, first ask whether temperature changed. Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain ( OIL RIG ); an oxidising agent gains electrons (is itself reduced), a reducing agent loses electrons. Oxidation state rules: free element = 0; Group 1 = +1; Group 2 = +2; Al = +3; O = −2 except in peroxides (−1) and OF₂ (+2); H = +1 except in metal hydrides (−1); F always −1. The sum of oxidation states equals the overall charge. Nomenclature: oxidation states in Roman numerals — iron(III) means Fe³⁺, manganate(VII) Mn in +7. Half-equations — method: (1) balance the main species; (2) balance O with H₂O; (3) balance H with H⁺ (acidic conditions); (4) balance charge with electrons on the correct side. Example: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ gives MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. In alkaline conditions, balance as if acidic then add OH⁻ to both sides to cancel H⁺ (forming water) — e.g. for ClO⁻ → Cl₂ in alkaline solution. Combining half-equations: multiply so electrons cancel, then add and cancel common species. Classic redox titration equation: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺ (manganate(VII) oxidising Fe(II), self-indicating — purple to colourless at the endpoint). Work out oxidation state changes: Mn +7 → +2 (gain 5e⁻), Fe +2 → +3 (lose 1e⁻), so 5 Fe²⁺ per MnO₄⁻. Disproportionation: one species is both oxidised and reduced — chlorine in water: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HClO + HCl (0 → +1 and −1), the basis of water treatment. An electrochemical cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy from two redox half-cells connected by a wire (external circuit) and a salt bridge (usually KNO₃ — mobile ions complete the circuit without reacting). In cell notation, the more negative electrode is written on the left: Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu. Oxidation occurs at the anode (negative in a galvanic cell), reduction at the cathode. The standard hydrogen electrode (Pt | H₂(g, 100 kPa) | H⁺(1 mol dm⁻³), E° = 0.00 V) is the reference against which all standard electrode potentials are measured under standard conditions. E°cell = E°(reduction at cathode) − E°(reduction at anode) — always subtract the more negative (or less positive) reduction potential. Example: Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu with E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V > 0 → spontaneous; Zn is oxidised, Cu²⁺ reduced, overall Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. A reaction is feasible when E°cell > 0 ; the more positive E°, the stronger the oxidising agent (more readily reduced). Limitations: E° values are standard (298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³, 100 kPa) and predict thermodynamic feasibility only — they say nothing about rate (activation energy) or the actual conditions. Under non-standard conditions the Nernst equation applies: E = E° − (0.059/n) log Q at 298 K (Q = reaction quotient; for the half-cell Mⁿ⁺/M, Q = 1/[Mⁿ⁺]). Increasing the concentration of the metal ion makes E more positive. At equilibrium E°cell = 0 and E°cell = (0.059/n) log K links cell potential to the equilibrium constant. Commercial cells : fuel cells — H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O; alkaline version has anode H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻, cathode ½O₂ + H₂O + 2e⁻ → 2OH⁻; advantages: higher efficiency and only water produced at point of use; limitation: H₂ storage/transport, energy cost of producing H₂. Rechargeable cells (Li-ion, NiMH, lead-acid): reversible redox — charging reverses the reaction by forcing electrons the other way. Non-rechargeable : irreversible reactions (e.g. zinc-carbon). Environmental arguments (recycling, lithium mining, hydrogen from renewable electricity) are standard 3-mark evaluation points. Non-standard condition example: a Cu²⁺/Cu half-cell with [Cu²⁺] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³ (standard 1.0): E = E° − (0.059/2) log(1/[Cu²⁺]) = +0.34 − (0.0295 × 2) = +0.28 V — the more dilute ion solution gives a less positive potential. Concentration cells (same electrode, different concentrations) generate a voltage purely from the concentration difference; the spontaneous direction increases the concentration of the dilute half-cell until E reaches 0 at equilibrium. When predicting direction from E° values with non-standard conditions, compare the actual E values rather than E° — a reaction feasible under standard conditions can be reversed by concentrating products or diluting reactants. Exam technique: quote the Nernst equation with n (electrons transferred) identified for the specific half-cell — MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ has n = 5, Cu²⁺/Cu n = 2 — then substitute carefully, taking the log of the correct quotient. Industrial processes are the applied 6-marker of this topic: predict the conditions Le Chatelier's principle would favour, then explain why industry chooses a compromise. Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol): equilibrium favours high pressure (4 → 2 gas moles) and low temperature (exothermic forward reaction), but low temperature is too slow and very high pressure is expensive and dangerous. Industry uses ~450 °C (compromise between yield and rate) and ~200 atm with an iron catalyst; the ammonia is cooled and liquefied as it forms, and unreacted N₂/H₂ recycled — recycling shifts the effective position right without changing K. Contact process (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = −196 kJ/mol): ~450 °C, ~2 atm (yield already ~99% at low pressure, so higher pressure is not worth the cost), V₂O₅ catalyst. Methanol production (CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, ΔH = −90 kJ/mol): similar compromise logic; ethanol hydration (C₂H₄ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₅OH, ΔH = −42 kJ/mol): excess steam shifts position right, ~300 °C, 60 atm, H₃PO₄ catalyst. Writing the evaluation: (1) state the equilibrium-favoured condition with the mole-count or exothermic-direction reasoning; (2) state the kinetic problem (too slow at the equilibrium-favourable temperature); (3) state the cost/safety factor (high pressure expensive, containment); (4) conclude the compromise condition and catalyst. Each step earns a mark — '450 °C because it is a compromise' alone does not. Catalyst evaluation: does not change yield or K, but allows a lower temperature for the same rate, saving energy and reducing the yield penalty of higher temperature. Exam traps: confusing 'yield' with 'rate' in answers (pressure increases both here, but for exothermic reactions temperature raises rate while lowering yield); forgetting that only temperature changes K; omitting that a catalyst speeds both directions equally. When asked 'explain the effect on K of increasing temperature', answer with the direction of the endothermic change: for an exothermic forward reaction, K decreases as temperature rises because the equilibrium shifts left. Link back to ΔG = ΔH − TΔS for the thermodynamic perspective: K falls as T rises for exothermic reactions because the equilibrium constant relates to ΔG by ΔG = −RT ln K.

topics.name: Acids, Bases and Buffers
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Acids, Bases and Buffers Apply Brønsted-Lowry theory, identify conjugate pairs and amphoteric species Calculate pH of strong acids and strong bases using Kw, including diprotic acids and Ba(OH)₂ Calculate weak acid pH and Ka from pH data using the √(Ka·[HA]) approximation and state its validity Explain buffer action with equations and calculate buffer pH using [H⁺] = Ka([HA]/[A⁻]) Describe blood buffering by the carbonic acid/hydrogencarbonate system Interpret pH titration curves, justify indicator choice and determine Ka from the half-equivalence point Brønsted-Lowry acid A proton (H⁺) donor, e.g. HCl, CH₃COOH. Brønsted-Lowry base A proton (H⁺) acceptor, e.g. NH₃, OH⁻. Conjugate pair Two species differing by one H⁺, e.g. CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻; the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Kw (ionic product of water) Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K; increases with temperature as ionisation is endothermic. Ka (acid dissociation constant) Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] for a weak acid HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻; larger Ka = stronger acid. pKa −log₁₀ Ka; smaller pKa = stronger acid. At half-equivalence pH = pKa. Buffer solution A solution that maintains approximately constant pH when small quantities of acid or base are added; a weak acid plus its conjugate base. Equivalence point The volume at which acid and base have reacted exactly — the near-vertical section of the pH curve. Amphoteric species A species that can act as both an acid and a base, e.g. H₂O, HCO₃⁻. Brønsted-Lowry : an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor, a base is a proton acceptor. In the equilibrium CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺, ethanoic acid donates a proton and water accepts it. Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺: CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O. An amphoteric species can act as both — water donates to bases (H₂O → OH⁻) and accepts from acids (H₂O → H₃O⁺). Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) dissociate completely; weak acids (ethanoic, carbonic) dissociate partially — the ⇌ arrow distinguishes them. pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] ; [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖʰ. Strong acid calculations: [H⁺] equals the acid concentration (for HCl) or twice it (H₂SO₄ gives 2H⁺ — check whether the question intends full dissociation of both protons). Strong bases : [OH⁻] equals concentration for NaOH, twice for Ba(OH)₂. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K — the ionic product of water. Convert [OH⁻] to [H⁺] via Kw, then to pH. Worked example: pH of 0.050 mol dm⁻³ Ba(OH)₂ at 298 K: [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.050 = 0.100; [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴/0.100 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³; pH = 13.00. Water's ionisation (2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻) is endothermic , so Kw increases with temperature and the pH of pure water falls below 7 at higher temperature — water stays neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻]; neutrality is defined by equality, not by pH 7. This distinction is a classic A* point: pH 7 is neutral only at 298 K. Further pH calculation examples to rehearse: (1) pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl: [H⁺] = 0.010, pH = 2.00. (2) pH of 0.0050 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ (assume full dissociation): [H⁺] = 0.010, pH = 2.00 — the factor of 2 matters; check whether the question specifies both protons dissociate. (3) dilution: diluting 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl by ×100 gives 0.00100 mol dm⁻³, pH rises from 1.00 to 3.00 — each ×10 dilution raises pH by 1 for strong acids. (4) [H⁺] from pH: pH 4.20 → [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴·²⁰ = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵. For strong bases, the two-step Kw route is always required — writing pH = 14 + log[OH⁻] without the Kw step loses the working marks; state Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ explicitly and quote units (mol² dm⁻⁶). At temperatures other than 298 K the question gives the new Kw — use it as given; do not assume 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. The acid dissociation constant for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] ; pKa = −log₁₀ Ka . Larger Ka (smaller pKa) = stronger acid. For a weak acid, the approximation [H⁺] = [A⁻] (dissociation is tiny compared with [HA]) gives [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka × [HA]) , so pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] and Ka ≈ [H⁺]²/[HA]. Worked examples: (1) pH of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵): [H⁺] = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.32 × 10⁻³; pH = 2.88. (2) Ka from pH: 0.150 mol dm⁻³ propanoic acid has pH 2.82: [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁸² = 1.51 × 10⁻³; Ka = (1.51 × 10⁻³)²/0.150 = 1.52 × 10⁻⁵. Approximation validity — the standard 4-marker: two approximations are made. (1) [H⁺] from water is negligible (Kw tiny) — valid for all but very weak/very dilute acids. (2) [HA] at equilibrium ≈ [HA] initial — valid only when dissociation is small: if [H⁺] > 5% of [HA], the approximation fails and the quadratic must be solved properly. Very dilute weak acids (e.g. 0.001 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic) violate approximation (2) — state the check: (5 × [H⁺]/[HA]) A buffer solution maintains approximately constant pH when small quantities of acid or base are added. An acidic buffer is made from a weak acid plus its conjugate base — either a salt (e.g. CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa) or partial neutralisation (excess weak acid + NaOH). The buffer contains large, roughly equal reservoirs of HA and A⁻, with the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ pushed far left by the added A⁻. Buffer action — the mechanism in words: when acid is added, the H⁺ reacts with the conjugate base reservoir: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH — equilibrium shifts left, removing most added H⁺, so [H⁺] (and pH) barely change. When base is added, the OH⁻ reacts with the weak acid reservoir: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O — equilibrium shifts right, replacing H⁺. The pH changes only slightly as long as both reservoirs remain large; a buffer is exhausted when one reservoir is consumed. Buffer pH calculation : [H⁺] = Ka × ([HA]/[A⁻]), so pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]) (Henderson-Hasselbalch). Worked example (from the specification style): calculate the pH of a buffer with 0.20 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵) and 0.15 mol dm⁻³ sodium ethanoate: [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × (0.20/0.15) = 2.32 × 10⁻⁵; pH = 4.63. Made-by-neutralisation questions: work out moles of HA remaining (initial minus reacted) and moles of A⁻ formed, then substitute into [H⁺] = Ka × n(HA)/n(A⁻) — mole ratios replace concentrations (same volume cancels). Blood buffering : blood pH is controlled at 7.35-7.45 by the carbonic acid/hydrogencarbonate buffer (H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, carbonic acid formed from dissolved CO₂). Acidosis (excess H⁺) is countered by HCO₃⁻ removing it (H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂ exhaled); alkalosis (excess OH⁻) is countered by H₂CO₃ neutralising it. The link between respiration rate and blood pH (CO₂ levels) is the standard applied question: faster breathing removes CO₂, shifting equilibrium left, lowering [H⁺] and raising pH. Buffer capacity and dilution — the finer points examiners test: diluting a buffer with water scales [HA] and [A⁻] by the same factor, so the ratio [HA]/[A⁻] is unchanged and the pH stays the same — but the buffer capacity falls (smaller reservoirs of each species, so fewer moles of added acid/base can be absorbed before exhaustion). Strong acid/concentrated-base additions beyond the capacity overwhelm the buffer and the pH changes substantially — buffers resist small additions only. When a buffer is made by partial neutralisation, check that neither reservoir is fully consumed: if the NaOH moles exceed the HA moles, no buffer forms (excess strong base, pH from [OH⁻] via Kw instead). Comparing two buffers of the same pH but different concentrations: same pH (same ratio) but the more concentrated one has greater capacity — a standard A* discrimination. Writing buffer answers: state the reservoirs present, give the reaction with the added species, state the equilibrium shift and conclude 'pH changes only slightly' — the full chain earns all marks. A pH titration curve plots pH against titrant volume. The equivalence point is the near-vertical section; curve shapes depend on the acid-base pair: strong-strong (pH 1 → 13, huge vertical section centred at 7); weak acid-strong base (vertical section above 7 — salt hydrolysis: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻); strong acid-weak base (vertical below 7); weak-weak (shallow, no vertical section). The flat region before equivalence is the buffer zone — in a weak acid titration the HA/A⁻ pair formed in the flask buffers the solution around half-equivalence. Indicator choice : the indicator's colour-change range must lie entirely within the vertical section — phenolphthalein (8.3-10.0) for weak acid-strong base; methyl orange (3.1-4.4) for strong acid-weak base; either for strong-strong; neither for weak-weak. Indicators are themselves weak acids whose conjugate pair has different colours (HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻); the range is where both colours coexist. Determining Ka experimentally (standard 6-marker): titrate a weak acid with a strong base, measuring pH with a calibrated pH meter. At half the equivalence volume, [HA] = [A⁻] , so pH = pKa — read the pH at half-equivalence and take Ka = 10⁻ᵖᵏᵃ. Method: find the equivalence volume from the vertical section (or from a preliminary titration), halve it, read the pH there, convert. Improvements: pH meter calibrated with buffers, temperature controlled (Ka depends on T), small increments near equivalence. Cross-links: this is the experimental side of the titration page's curve analysis, and the buffer zone explanation mirrors the buffer section above. Salt solutions are not all neutral: the ions can hydrolyse water. NaCl (from strong acid + strong base) is neutral — neither ion reacts with water. CH₃COONa (weak acid + strong base) is basic : the ethanoate ion accepts a proton — CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻ — so [OH⁻] rises and pH > 7. NH₄Cl (strong acid + weak base) is acidic : NH₄⁺ donates a proton — NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ — so pH Multi-step calculation style (AQA Paper 1 favourite): a buffer made by mixing solutions, or a titration part-way to equivalence. Method: (1) moles of each species from concentration × volume/1000; (2) apply the reaction (neutralisation) to find remaining HA and formed A⁻; (3) substitute mole ratios into [H⁺] = Ka × n(HA)/n(A⁻) — volumes cancel because both species share the flask volume; (4) convert to pH. Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH mixed with 10.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH: moles HA = 2.50 × 10⁻³, OH⁻ = 1.00 × 10⁻³; remaining HA = 1.50 × 10⁻³, A⁻ formed = 1.00 × 10⁻³; [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × (1.50/1.00) = 2.61 × 10⁻⁵; pH = 4.58. Exam technique: read whether the question wants pH, pKa or Ka and answer exactly that; keep unrounded values through the calculation and round only at the end (quoting pH to 2 decimal places); state assumptions ([H⁺] from water negligible; [HA] unchanged — valid when dissociation

topics.name: Periodicity and Group Chemistry
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Periodicity and Group Chemistry Explain trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and melting point across Period 3, linking melting points to structure and bonding Describe Group 2 reactions with water, oxygen and acids, and explain the reactivity trend using ionisation energies Explain the opposing solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates and their uses (antacids, barium meals, lime cycle) Describe Group 7 trends, displacement reactions and the halide tests with AgNO₃ and NH₃ Explain chlorine's disproportionation in water and NaOH, and evaluate water chlorination benefits and risks Classify Period 3 oxides as basic, acidic or amphoteric and write equations for their reactions with water and acids/bases Periodicity The repeating pattern of physical and chemical properties of the elements across periods, arising from repeating outer electron configurations. Displacement reaction A more reactive halogen displaces the halide ion of a less reactive halogen from solution; the halogen is reduced and the halide oxidised. Disproportionation A redox reaction in which one element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, e.g. Cl₂ → Cl⁻ + ClO⁻ in NaOH. Amphoteric A substance that reacts with both acids and bases, e.g. Al₂O₃. Basic oxide An oxide that reacts with water to form an alkaline solution or neutralises acids, e.g. Na₂O, MgO. Acidic oxide An oxide that reacts with water to form an acidic solution or reacts with bases, e.g. SO₂, P₄O₁₀, SiO₂. Oxidising power The tendency of a species to gain electrons (be reduced); decreases down Group 7 as atomic radius and shielding increase. Disproportionation product For chlorine in cold dilute NaOH: NaCl (−1) and NaClO (+1) — bleach. Periodicity is the repeating pattern of physical and chemical properties across periods. Atomic radius decreases across a period : nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same outer shell, so attraction on the outer electrons strengthens and pulls the shell in. Radius increases down a group : each element has an extra full inner shell and more shielding. Ionic radius mirrors this: cations are smaller than their atoms (one shell lost), anions larger (extra repulsion in the filled outer shell); ions with the same electron configuration shrink as nuclear charge rises (N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺). First ionisation energy increases across a period (rising Z eff , constant shielding) with two dips: aluminium below magnesium (3p electron in a higher-energy sub-shell) and sulfur below phosphorus (paired 3p electrons repel). It decreases down a group (extra shell: more distance and shielding). Full explanations with the three factors (nuclear charge, distance, shielding) are the standard 4-marker. Melting points across Period 3 explain structure types: Na, Mg, Al — metallic, MP rises left to right (ion charge +1 → +3 and more delocalised electrons per atom → stronger metallic bonding; Al melts highest of the three). Si — giant covalent, highest MP of the period (strong covalent bonds must break). P₄, S₈, Cl₂ — simple molecular, low MPs depending on molecules per mole/electrons (S₈ > P₄ > Cl₂: more electrons, stronger London forces). Ar — monatomic, lowest. The Na→Ar MP graph is the standard interpretation question: identify the structure type from the shape of the graph and justify each by the forces broken on melting. Group 2 (alkaline earth) metals form 2+ ions by losing two s electrons; reactivity increases down the group (ionisation energies fall: extra shell, more shielding — outer electrons lost more easily). Reactions: with water — Mg reacts very slowly with cold water (faster with steam: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂), Ca reacts steadily with cold water (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂), Ba vigorously; with oxygen — 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (bright white flame); with dilute acids — Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, rate increasing down the group. Group 2 oxides are basic , reacting with water to form alkaline hydroxides: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂. Hydroxide solubility increases down the group (Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ very soluble) while sulfate solubility decreases down the group (MgSO₄ soluble, BaSO₄ insoluble). The solubility trends link to hydration/lattice enthalpies: down the group the ions get larger, the hydration enthalpy becomes less exothermic — the balance with lattice enthalpy differs for hydroxides and sulfates, giving opposite trends. BaSO₄'s insolubility is the basis of the sulfate test (white precipitate with Ba²⁺) and of barium meals (BaSO₄ too insoluble to be toxic, X-ray contrast agent). Uses to quote: Mg(OH)₂ as an antacid (milk of magnesia — neutralises excess stomach acid); Ca(OH)₂ in agriculture (lime, neutralises acidic soil); CaCO₃ in the lime cycle (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ on heating; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂; Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O); BaSO₄ in medicine. Trend explanations must always invoke ionisation energy, atomic radius and shielding — 'reacts more vigorously because outer electrons are lost more easily down the group'. Writing trend explanations for full marks: every Group 2/Group 7 trend answer needs the causal chain — state the trend, name the factor that changes (ionic/atomic radius, shielding, nuclear charge), link to the chemistry (electrons lost more easily, attraction for incoming electron weaker), conclude. 'Barium reacts faster because it is more reactive' scores nothing; 'barium's outer electrons are lost more easily because its larger atomic radius and greater shielding reduce the attraction of the nucleus, so the first two ionisation energies are lower' scores fully. Displacement answers must name the redox change: the displacing halogen gains electrons (reduced, oxidation number 0 → −1) and the halide loses them (oxidised, −1 → 0) — writing only the colour change loses the chemistry marks. Where equations are requested, include state symbols and the correct balancing (Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂) — ionic equations are expected, not full formula equations with spectator ions. Group 7 (halogens) exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) with increasing melting/boiling points down the group (more electrons, stronger London forces: Cl₂ gas, Br₂ liquid, I₂ solid at room temperature). Reactivity and oxidising power decrease down the group : atomic radius and shielding increase, so the attraction for the incoming electron falls — the ability to gain an electron (be reduced) weakens. Electronegativity likewise falls down the group. Displacement reactions : a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide. Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻ (Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, solution turns orange; Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, brown); Br₂ displaces I⁻ only; I₂ displaces none. This is redox — the displacing halogen is reduced, the halide oxidised. The trend is confirmed by E° values: E°(F₂/F⁻) = +2.87 V down to E°(I₂/I⁻) = +0.54 V. Disproportionation — the same element simultaneously oxidised and reduced — is the key reaction of chlorine: in water, Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO (chlorine 0 → −1 and +1); with cold dilute NaOH, Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (also 0 → −1/+1), making household bleach (NaClO). Benefits of chlorinating water: kills bacteria, preventing waterborne disease; risks: HClO can react with organic matter forming potentially carcinogenic chlorinated hydrocarbons — the benefit/risk evaluation is a standard 4-6 marker. Adding a small amount of NaOH reduces the risk while keeping disinfection. Halide tests : add dilute HNO₃ (removes interfering CO₃²⁻/OH⁻), then AgNO₃: AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow , all insoluble; solubility decreases down the group. Confirm with dilute NH₃ (dissolves AgCl only) then conc. NH₃ (dissolves AgBr, not AgI). The nitric acid step matters — using HCl would add Cl⁻ and give a false white precipitate. Halide ion reducing power increases down the group (larger ions lose electrons more easily): concentrated H₂SO₄ tests show NaCl gives HCl only (no redox), NaBr gives HBr + Br₂ (SO₂ produced), NaI gives HI + I₂ + H₂S/H₂SO₄ reduced further — fumes and colour changes identify the halide. Period 3 oxides show the periodic shift from ionic to covalent bonding: Na₂O and MgO are ionic (giant lattices, high melting points: 1275 °C and 2852 °C); Al₂O₃ is ionic but with significant covalent character (polarisation of O²⁻ by the small, highly charged Al³⁺ — amphoteric); SiO₂ is giant covalent (very high MP, 1610 °C); P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃ are simple molecular (low MPs: 340 °C, sublimes, 17 °C). Melting point falls sharply after Al₂O₃ as bonding changes from giant to molecular. Acid-base behaviour : Na₂O and MgO are basic — react with water giving alkaline solutions (Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH, pH ~14; MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂, pH ~9 sparingly soluble) and neutralise acids (Na₂O + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O). SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂ and SO₃ are acidic — react with water/alkalis giving acidic solutions (SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃, pH ~1; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄, pH ~0-1; P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄; SiO₂ reacts with hot concentrated NaOH: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O). Al₂O₃ is amphoteric — reacts with both acids (Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O) and bases (Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2NaAl(OH)₄) but is insoluble in water. Acidic character increases across the period because electronegativity difference between element and oxygen falls — bonding shifts covalent. Explanations earn marks by linking bonding to behaviour: ionic oxides contain O²⁻ which accepts protons (basic); covalent oxides of non-metals form oxyacids because the E–O bond polarises water. The classic exam answer: explain why Na₂O has a higher melting point than SO₃ — giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic forces vs simple molecular with weak London forces. Also quote environmental chemistry: SO₂ from burning fossil fuels causes acid rain (dissolves in atmospheric water as H₂SO₃/H₂SO₄); MgO/CaO used in flue gas desulfurisation to remove SO₂. Linking oxide behaviour to structure earns the evaluation marks: ionic oxides (Na₂O, MgO) contain O²⁻ ions which are strong proton acceptors — hence basic; covalent oxides of non-metals (SO₃, P₄O₁₀) form oxyacids because the polarised E–O bonds transfer proton character to water — hence acidic. The trend across the period mirrors electronegativity: as the element becomes more electronegative, the difference with oxygen falls, bonding becomes covalent and the oxide becomes acidic. Al₂O₃ sits at the crossover — its small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the oxide ion, giving covalent character and amphoteric behaviour (reacts with both acids and bases). Environmental applications complete the standard answers: SO₂/SO₃ from fossil-fuel combustion dissolve in atmospheric moisture forming acid rain (H₂SO₃/H₂SO₄); MgO and CaO remove SO₂ from flue gases (flue gas desulfurisation: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃); CO₂ from combustion slightly acidifies rainwater (carbonic acid) — quote these links because application marks are embedded in most Period 3 oxide questions. Required practical (AQA RP4, OCR PAG4): use test-tube reactions to identify cations and anions and to compare trends. Standard identification scheme: cations — add NaOH(aq) dropwise then in excess: Mg²⁺ gives a white precipitate insoluble in excess; Ca²⁺ slight white precipitate (often none at low concentration); Al³⁺ white precipitate dissolving in excess NaOH (amphoteric hydroxide: Al(OH)₃ + OH⁻ → [Al(OH)₄]⁻); NH₄⁺ warm with NaOH and test the gas with damp red litmus (turns blue — ammonia released: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O); Group 1 cations flame tests (Li crimson, Na yellow, K lilac). Anions — sulfate: acidify with HNO₃ then BaCl₂/Ba(NO₃)₂, white precipitate BaSO₄; halides: HNO₃ then AgNO₃ (white/cream/yellow); carbonate: dilute acid fizzing (CO₂ turns limewater milky); hydroxide: pH paper/red litmus blue. Trend experiments to describe: comparing Group 2 metals with water (rate of fizzing increases Mg → Ca → Ba) and measuring the pH of the resulting hydroxide solutions (rises down the group as hydroxides become more soluble); halogen displacement in solution (Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻; observe orange/brown colour changes) — the observations confirm the oxidising-power trend. Writing up: state the reagent, the observation with colour, and the conclusion (ion identified) — 'white precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH' identifies Mg²⁺, but 'white precipitate' alone is ambiguous with Ca²⁺/Al³⁺ before the excess test. Exam technique: safety points earn marks — gloves/goggles for concentrated NaOH; fume cupboard for halogens (Cl₂ toxic); never mix AgNO₃ with ammonia carelessly. Precision points: use fresh samples, control volumes, repeat observations. The identification scheme rewards knowing the 'excess' step — dissolving the Al(OH)₃ precipitate is the discriminating observation between Al³⁺ and Mg²⁺, and it links directly to the amphoteric behaviour of Al₂O₃/Al(OH)₃ covered in Period 3 oxides.

topics.name: Organic Chemistry: Mechanisms
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Organic Chemistry: Mechanisms Name organic compounds and identify functional groups, structural/E-Z/optical isomerism Describe the free-radical substitution mechanism with initiation, propagation and termination steps Describe electrophilic addition mechanisms step by step, applying Markovnikov's rule and carbocation stability Compare SN1 and SN2 mechanisms with curly-arrow conventions, rate laws and stereochemical outcomes Describe the elimination mechanism with ethanolic KOH and the oxidation sequence of alcohols including required practical apparatus Describe nucleophilic addition to carbonyls with HCN and NaBH₄, and aromatic substitution (nitration, Friedel-Crafts) including electrophile generation Nucleophile An electron-pair donor that attacks electron-deficient (δ+) carbon atoms, e.g. OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃. Electrophile An electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions such as C=C bonds, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂. Homolytic fission Bond breaking in which each atom takes one electron, forming two radicals. Heterolytic fission Bond breaking in which both electrons go to one atom, forming a cation and an anion. Carbocation A positively charged carbon ion; stability increases with substitution (3° > 2° > 1°) due to alkyl inductive donation. SN1 mechanism Stepwise nucleophilic substitution: C–X bond breaks first (rate-determining) forming a planar carbocation, then nucleophile attacks — racemic product, rate = k[halogenoalkane]. SN2 mechanism Concerted nucleophilic substitution: nucleophile attacks 180° to the leaving group as C–X breaks — inversion of configuration, rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]. Markovnikov's rule In electrophilic addition to an unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, so the more stable carbocation forms. Elimination (dehydrohalogenation) Loss of HX from a halogenoalkane using hot ethanolic KOH, forming an alkene. Arenium (Wheland) intermediate The carbocation formed when an electrophile bonds to benzene, with the positive charge delocalised over five carbons; stability restored by deprotonation. IUPAC naming : find the longest carbon chain containing the highest-priority functional group, number from the end giving the lowest locants, name substituents as prefixes in alphabetical order and the functional group as a suffix. Priority order (high to low): carboxylic acid > ester > acyl chloride > amide > nitrile > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine > alkene > alkane. Examples: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol; CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl propanoate (acid part as base name, alkyl part as prefix). Functional groups and their reactions: alkanes (free-radical substitution); alkenes (electrophilic addition); halogenoalkanes (nucleophilic substitution, elimination); alcohols (substitution, elimination, oxidation, esterification); aldehydes/ketones (nucleophilic addition, oxidation of aldehydes); carboxylic acids (esterification, reduction); esters (hydrolysis); amines (bases, nucleophiles); nitriles (reduction, hydrolysis). Skeletal formulae show bonds as lines with vertices as carbons — be fluent converting between displayed, structural and skeletal forms. Isomerism : structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom ordering (chain, position, functional-group isomerism). E/Z (geometric) isomerism requires a C=C bond with restricted rotation and two different groups on each carbon: Z when the highest-priority groups (CIP rules — higher atomic number first) are on the same side, E when opposite. But-2-ene has cis (Z) and trans (E) forms. Optical isomerism : a chiral carbon (four different groups) gives non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers) rotating plane-polarised light equally in opposite directions; racemic mixtures are 50:50 and optically inactive. SN1 products are racemic (planar carbocation attacked from both sides) — a classic A* link between mechanisms and stereochemistry. Free-radical substitution (alkanes + halogens, UV light): three stages. Initiation: UV supplies energy for homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond — each atom takes one electron, forming two radicals: Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → CH₃• + HCl (radical abstracts H, new radical forms), then CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (radical regenerated — chain reaction). Termination: any two radicals combine: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl; CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆. Curly-arrow convention: radicals use single-headed 'fish-hook' arrows showing one-electron movement; a dot represents the unpaired electron. Limitations to quote: further substitution (poly-substitution giving CH₂Cl₂ etc.) and mixture of products at termination — limiting CH₄ excess favours monosubstitution. Ozone depletion mechanism (CFCl₃ → Cl• + CFCl₂•; Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂) uses the same radical chain logic. Electrophilic addition (alkenes): the C=C π bond is electron-rich and attracts electrophiles. Mechanism for propene + HBr, step by step: (1) the π electron pair forms a bond to the H of H–Br; simultaneously (or immediately after) the H–Br bond breaks heterolytically — both electrons go to Br. Curly arrows: from the π bond to the H, and from the H–Br bond to Br. (2) A carbocation forms on one alkene carbon; Markovnikov's rule : H adds to the carbon already carrying more hydrogens, so the positive charge sits on the more substituted carbon (secondary/tertiary carbocations are stabilised by electron-donating alkyl groups via the inductive effect). (3) The Br⁻ lone pair donates to the positive carbon, forming the C–Br bond: product 2-bromopropane (major). Minor product 1-bromopropane arises via the primary carbocation. With Br₂ no polar solvent needed — Br₂ is polarised as it approaches the electron-rich π bond. Exam tip: always draw the intermediate carbocation with the positive charge, and justify the major product by carbocation stability. Hydration of alkenes (H₃PO₄ catalyst, steam) follows the same electrophilic-addition mechanism to make alcohols industrially. Nucleophiles are electron-pair donors (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O) attacking electron-deficient δ+ carbon bonded to a halogen (C–X is polar: X more electronegative). SN2 — substitution nucleophilic bimolecular — is concerted , one step: (1) the nucleophile's lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon from the side opposite (180° to) the leaving group ; (2) simultaneously the C–X bond breaks heterolytically, both electrons to X. Curly arrows: from nucleophile lone pair to carbon, and from C–X bond to X. A transition state shows partial bonds C···Nu and C···X with a dashed wedge — the 'umbrella turning inside out'. Rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]; favoured by primary halogenoalkanes (little steric hindrance, no stable carbocation) and polar aprotic solvents. Inversion of configuration occurs at a chiral centre. SN1 — substitution nucleophilic unimolecular — is stepwise : (1) the C–X bond breaks first, heterolytically, forming a planar carbocation intermediate — rate-determining step; (2) the nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation from either side equally, giving a racemic mixture if the carbon was chiral. Rate = k[halogenoalkane] only. Favoured by tertiary halogenoalkanes (carbocation stabilised by three alkyl groups' inductive effect; steric hindrance blocks backside attack). Standard exam comparison: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts by SN1, 1-bromobutane by SN2 — justify by carbocation stability AND steric hindrance for full marks. Conditions: hydrolysis with warm aqueous NaOH (or water, slower) gives alcohols; with KCN in ethanol gives nitriles (extends chain by one C); with excess ethanolic NH₃ gives amines (excess NH₃ minimises further substitution). Bond enthalpy trend: C–I weakest, hydrolyses fastest — rate measured by AgNO₃/ethanol (AgI precipitate fastest, AgCl slowest), a required OCR/AQA rate comparison. Nucleophilicity order in polar protic solvents: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ (weaker bond, more polarisable). Elimination (dehydrohalogenation): halogenoalkane + hot, concentrated ethanolic KOH (reflux) → alkene + KBr + H₂O. Step-by-step mechanism (E2): (1) the hydroxide lone pair abstracts a β-hydrogen (on the carbon adjacent to the C–X carbon); (2) the C–H bond electron pair forms a C=C π bond between the α and β carbons; (3) simultaneously the C–X bond breaks heterolytically to X⁻. Curly arrows: OH⁻ lone pair to the β-H, C–H bond to the C–C gap (forming π), C–X bond to X. Aqueous KOH gives substitution (alcohol); ethanolic KOH gives elimination — condition determines mechanism, standard comparison question. With asymmetric halogenoalkanes, the major alkene has more alkyl groups (more stable — Zaitsev-type preference). Oxidation of alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange → green, Cr³⁺): primary alcohols → aldehydes (distil immediately, to prevent further oxidation) → carboxylic acids (reflux with excess oxidant); secondary → ketones; tertiary resist oxidation (no C–H on the carbinol carbon, so no hydrogen to remove). Oxidation mechanism concept: loss of two H (one from O–H, one from C–H) forming the new C=O. Distinguishing tests: aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent ([Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺) giving a silver mirror and Fehling's gives brick-red Cu₂O; ketones give no reaction. 2,4-DNP (Brady's reagent) gives an orange precipitate with any C=O, confirming carbonyl presence but not distinguishing aldehyde from ketone. Distinguishing the alcohol classes: oxidise then test, or use iodoform (CH₃CHOH– and CH₃CO– give yellow CHI₃ precipitate with I₂/NaOH). Required practical (AQA RP5 / OCR PAG5) : distillation of a primary alcohol oxidation product. Apparatus: round-bottom flask, still head with thermometer, condenser, receiver. Thermometer bulb level with the side-arm so it reads the vapour temperature; collect the fraction boiling at the aldehyde's boiling point. Sealing: anti-bumping granules prevent violent boiling. Then test the distillate with Tollens'/Fehling's to show incomplete oxidation produced aldehyde, or reflux further to convert to the acid. Preparation of purified organic solids (recrystallisation) is covered under Titrations and Analytical Techniques. Nucleophilic addition to carbonyls: the C=O is polarised (O more electronegative → C δ+), so nucleophiles attack the carbon. Mechanism for carbonyl + HCN (NaCN/H₂SO₄ catalyst), step by step: (1) the CN⁻ lone pair attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the π bond pair moves onto the oxygen — curly arrow from CN⁻ lone pair to C, from C=O π bond to O — forming an alkoxide intermediate with O⁻; (2) the alkoxide oxygen abstracts a proton from HCN: arrow from O⁻ lone pair to H, from H–CN bond to CN⁻ (regenerating CN⁻ — catalyst). Product: hydroxynitrile (extends chain by one carbon, creates a chiral centre when the two groups on C differ — racemic mixture because planar C=O is attacked from both sides). Ketones react more slowly than aldehydes: two alkyl groups donate electron density, reducing the δ+ character, and sterically hinder attack. Reduction: NaBH₄ provides H⁻ (hydride) — same nucleophilic-addition mechanism: aldehydes → primary alcohols, ketones → secondary alcohols. Carboxylic acids need LiAlH₄ (stronger). Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol, conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst, reflux → ester + water; mechanism involves protonating the C=O, alcohol addition, then loss of water. Ester hydrolysis: hot aqueous acid (reversible, gives acid + alcohol) or hot aqueous alkali — saponification , irreversible, gives carboxylate salt + alcohol (basis of soap-making from fats). Aromatic chemistry : benzene's delocalised π-system (6 electrons over 6 carbons) makes it stable — evidence against Kekulé: hydrogenation enthalpy −208 kJ/mol vs expected −360 kJ/mol for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene; equal C–C bond lengths (0.139 nm, between single and double); reluctance to undergo addition. Nitration mechanism , step by step: (1) electrophile generation: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ (conc. acids, 50–60 °C); (2) attack: the π-electron pair of one C=C in benzene bonds to NO₂⁺, forming the arenium (Wheland) intermediate — a carbocation with the positive charge delocalised over five carbons (horseshoe); (3) deprotonation: HSO₄⁻ removes the H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, the C–H bond electrons restore the delocalised ring — nitrobenzene + H₂SO₄ (catalyst regenerated). Higher temperatures promote dinitration; −NO₂ deactivates the ring (electron-withdrawing), so further substitution needs harsher conditions. Friedel-Crafts acylation : RCOCl + AlCl₃ → RCO⁺ (acylium ion) + AlCl₄⁻; the acylium ion attacks the ring as in nitration; AlCl₃ is regenerated on deprotonation (catalyst). Products: aryl ketones (e.g. benzene + CH₃COCl → phenylethanone). Acylation is used in synthesis because it prevents multiple acylation (the ketone deactivates the ring) and fixes chain length. Directing effects : electron-donating groups (−OH, −NH₂, alkyl) activate the ring and direct 2,4-substitution; electron-withdrawing (−NO₂, −COR) deactivate and direct 3-substitution. Phenol is more reactive than benzene (O lone pair delocalised into the ring, increasing electron density) and reacts with bromine water without a catalyst (white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol).

topics.name: Analysis: NMR, IR and Mass Spectrometry
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Analysis: NMR, IR and Mass Spectrometry Deduce relative molecular mass from the molecular ion peak and use isotope peaks (M+1, Cl, Br) to identify elements Interpret fragmentation patterns using common fragment losses (15, 29, 31, 43, 45) Use high-resolution mass spectrometry to distinguish compounds with the same integer M_r Identify functional groups from IR absorptions, including broadness of O-H bands and the fingerprint region Interpret ¹H NMR spectra using chemical shifts, integration, splitting (n+1 rule) and the D₂O shake Count carbon environments from ¹³C NMR and combine all techniques to determine structures with justified assignments Molecular ion (M⁺•) The ion formed by loss of one electron from a molecule in electron-impact MS; its m/z equals the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation Break-up of the molecular ion into smaller charged fragments, whose pattern identifies the molecule. Fingerprint region The IR region below ~1500 cm⁻¹ unique to each compound; matching it confirms identity. Chemical shift (δ) The resonant frequency position of a nucleus relative to TMS, measured in ppm. TMS (tetramethylsilane) The NMR standard: single sharp peak at δ = 0, inert, non-toxic, volatile. Spin-spin splitting Splitting of a NMR signal into n+1 peaks by n non-equivalent protons on adjacent atoms. Integration trace The NMR peak areas, proportional to the relative number of protons in each environment. D₂O shake Addition of deuterium oxide that exchanges with labile O–H/N–H protons, removing their signals — identifies OH/NH peaks. High-resolution MS MS measuring m/z to 4 decimal places, distinguishing compounds of the same integer mass. In electron-impact mass spectrometry the molecule is bombarded with high-energy electrons, knocking out an electron to form the molecular ion M⁺• . The m/z of this peak (using z = +1) equals the relative molecular mass — the first reading to take from any spectrum. Isotopic peaks help identify elements: an M+1 peak (from ¹³C, ~1.1% per carbon) indicates the number of carbons — 7% M+1 means ~7 carbons; chlorine gives 3:1 doublets and bromine 1:1 doublets in fragments (see Atomic Structure). Fragmentation : the molecular ion breaks into smaller cations and radicals; only charged fragments are detected. The pattern of fragment peaks identifies the molecule. Common fragments to memorise: 15 = CH₃⁺, 29 = C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺, 31 = CH₂OH⁺, 43 = CH₃CO⁺ or C₃H₇⁺, 45 = COOH⁺, 77 = C₆H₅⁺ (phenyl) . Loss of 18 = water, loss of 28 = CO or ethene, loss of 31/32 = methanol/methoxy. A fragment at M−15 shows loss of a methyl group; at M−45 loss of COOH suggests a carboxylic acid. High-resolution mass spectrometry measures m/z to four decimal places, distinguishing compounds with the same integer mass: C₃H₈O (58.0731), C₂H₄O₂ (58.0367) and C₂H₆N₂ (58.0531) all give M⁺ = 58 at low resolution but separate with high-resolution data. Exam questions give exact isotopic masses (¹²C = 12.0000, ¹H = 1.0078, ¹⁶O = 15.9949, ¹⁴N = 14.0031) and ask you to compute the precise M+ and match to a listed formula — add the mass contributions carefully, keeping four decimal places. Interpreting full mass spectra — method for A* answers: (1) take M⁺ as the M r (careful: the tallest peak is the base peak, usually a stable fragment, not the molecular ion — a small peak at high m/z may be M⁺); (2) check isotope patterns for Cl (3:1) and Br (1:1) — their presence tells you how many halogen atoms are in the molecule; (3) work out each fragment's formula from the m/z and identify the loss; (4) assemble a structure consistent with the fragments. Example: a spectrum with M⁺ = 92 and a 3:1 doublet at 89/94 would suggest one Cl; a fragment at m/z 31 (CH₂OH⁺) points to an alcohol. M+1 peaks: ~1.1% per carbon means a compound with M⁺ = 100 and M+1 at ~7.7% has about 7 carbons — quoted ratios in exams are always consistent with the formula given, so use them as a cross-check. Bonds absorb IR radiation at characteristic wavenumbers, vibrating more strongly when the frequency matches their natural frequency. Absorptions to know: O–H (alcohol) broad 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; O–H (carboxylic acid) very broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹; C=O sharp/strong 1680–1750 cm⁻¹; C–H 2850–3000 cm⁻¹; N–H 3300–3500 cm⁻¹; C–N 1000–1300 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹; C–O 1000–1300 cm⁻¹ . The fingerprint region (below 1500 cm⁻¹) is unique to each compound — a match between an unknown's spectrum and a database spectrum confirms identity. Broadness matters: hydrogen-bonded O–H groups absorb over a wide range, so a very broad band spanning 2500–3300 identifies a carboxylic acid; a sharper band above 3200 identifies an alcohol. C=O is the most reliable diagnostic — a strong sharp peak near 1700 cm⁻¹ signals aldehyde, ketone, acid, ester, acyl chloride or amide; combine with other peaks to decide which (ester: C=O plus C–O; acid: C=O plus very broad O–H; aldehyde: C=O plus C–H aldehydic doublet ~2720/2820). Applications: breathalysers measure IR absorption by C–H/O–H bonds of ethanol in breath; IR spectroscopy monitors pollutant gases (CO, NO, hydrocarbons) by their characteristic absorptions. Exam technique: quote the wavenumber, the bond, the shape of the absorption, and the functional group implied. When identifying an unknown from IR alone, state which absorptions are present and absent — the absence of C=O rules out all carbonyl compounds at once. Common IR misidentifications to avoid: an O–H band alone does not distinguish alcohol from acid — check the range (broad 3200-3600 alcohol; very broad 2500-3300 acid, overlapping the C–H region). A C=O peak with no other diagnostic could be aldehyde, ketone, acid, ester, acyl chloride or amide — use supporting evidence: acid gives the very broad O–H; ester gives C–O at 1000-1300; aldehyde gives the aldehydic C–H doublet near 2720-2820 cm⁻¹. Water in a sample shows a broad O–H band — drying agents matter before running spectra of alcohols. When the question asks which absorption is 'most useful for identification', answer C=O (sharp, strong, reliable range) or the fingerprint region (unique match) — justify the choice. Remember the units: wavenumber in cm⁻¹, always quoted with the bond and shape (sharp/broad/strong). ¹H NMR exploits nuclear spin: protons in different chemical environments resonate at different frequencies in a strong magnetic field. Chemical shift (δ) is measured in ppm relative to TMS (tetramethylsilane) at δ = 0 ppm. TMS is used because it gives a single sharp peak (12 equivalent H), is inert, non-toxic and volatile (easily removed). Higher δ means more deshielded protons — near electronegative atoms or π systems. Chemical shift ranges: δ 0.7–1.2 alkyl C–H; δ 2.2–3.0 C–H next to C=O or C=C; δ 3.1–4.2 C–H next to O (alcohol/ester); δ 4.7–5.7 =C–H alkene; δ 6.0–9.0 aromatic H; δ 9.0–10.0 aldehyde; δ 10–12 carboxylic acid O–H; δ 1.0–5.0 alcohol O–H (variable, hydrogen-bonded). Integration : the area under each peak (shown as an integration trace) is proportional to the relative number of protons in that environment — ratios 3:2:1 indicate groups like CH₃/CH₂/OH. Spin-spin splitting (n+1 rule): a signal is split into n+1 peaks by n non-equivalent protons on adjacent carbons — singlet (0), doublet (1), triplet (2), quartet (3). Classic patterns: triplet + quartet with 3:2 integration = ethyl group CH₃CH₂–; two equivalent methyls next to no H = singlet integrating 6H. Splitting only occurs between non-equivalent neighbours — equivalent protons do not split each other; O–H and N–H protons usually appear as singlets (rapid exchange). D₂O shake : adding D₂O exchanges labile O–H and N–H protons (R–OH + D₂O → R–OD + HOD), so their signals disappear from the spectrum — identifying OH/NH peaks unambiguously. Exam workflow for structure determination: (1) molecular formula from MS; (2) degree of unsaturation (rings/double bonds); (3) IR identifies functional groups; (4) number of ¹H signals = number of proton environments; (5) integration gives H ratios; (6) splitting identifies neighbours; (7) assemble and check against all data. ¹³C NMR is simpler: the number of distinct signals equals the number of unique carbon environments . Symmetry reduces signals — propanone CH₃COCH₃ gives 2 signals (two equivalent CH₃, one C=O), but propanal CH₃CH₂CHO gives 3. Chemical shift ranges: δ 5–50 alkyl C; δ 50–90 C–O; δ 90–150 alkene/aromatic C; δ 160–210 C=O; δ 190–220 aldehyde C=O . A peak near δ 200 with no other C=O clue suggests aldehyde/ketone; δ 170 with an ester/acid fragment suggests acid/ester/amide. Model answer (combining all techniques): identify C₃H₆O₂ showing IR 1715 cm⁻¹, broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹, ¹H NMR triplet δ 1.1 (3H), quartet δ 2.4 (2H), singlet δ 11.5 (1H). (1) IR: 1715 (C=O) + very broad 2500–3300 (acid O–H) → carboxylic acid −COOH. (2) ¹H NMR: δ 11.5 singlet confirms the −COOH proton. (3) Triplet δ 1.1 (3H) + quartet δ 2.4 (2H) = ethyl group CH₃CH₂−. Structure: propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH — consistent with M r 74 and all data. Method marks are given for each deduction step, not just the final structure. Sequencing logic for multi-technique questions: MS gives M r and fragments; IR gives functional groups; ¹³C NMR counts carbon environments; ¹H NMR gives proton environments, ratios and neighbours; D₂O removes labile protons. Cross-check: the assembled structure must account for every signal — if a δ 2.4 quartet is unexplained, the structure is wrong. A* students state the evidence for each assignment explicitly ('δ 9.8 confirms CHO') because marks are awarded for justification. Splitting-pattern library beyond the basics: triplet + quartet (3:2) = CH₃CH₂–; doublet + septet (6:1) = CH–(CH₃)₂ (isopropyl); singlet integrating 6H = two equivalent CH₃ next to no H (e.g. propanone); singlet integrating 9H = C(CH₃)₃; doublet + quartet (3:1 with one H each) = CH₃CH(OH)–. The n+1 rule applies only to protons on adjacent carbons — CH₃ next to C=O is not split by it (no H on the carbonyl carbon). Equivalent protons never split each other. Integration ratios are relative, not absolute: 3:2:1 with a 6H total means 2H/1.3H/0.7H in reality scaled — exams give whole-number ratios you divide by the smallest. When two environments overlap in shift, the exam data avoids ambiguity — trust the given splitting and integration over memory of shift tables, and state which data each assignment uses. The combined-techniques question (AQA Paper 3, OCR, Edexcel) rewards a fixed workflow applied under time pressure: (1) molecular formula from M⁺ (check M+1 for carbon count, Cl/Br doublets); (2) functional groups from IR (C=O, O–H ranges, fingerprint match); (3) number of ¹H signals = proton environments; number of ¹³C signals = carbon environments; (4) integration ratios give relative numbers of each H; (5) splitting (n+1) identifies adjacent groups; (6) D₂O shake locates labile O–H/N–H; (7) assemble the structure and verify every datum is explained. Write the evidence for each assignment ('δ 9.8 confirms CHO', 'triplet/quartet 3:2 confirms ethyl') — justification marks are the difference between grades. If two structures fit, find the discriminating datum: a chemical shift range, a splitting pattern, or an IR band that only one explains. Planning synthesis with analysis: exam questions ask how you would confirm a product's identity and purity after preparation — melting point (sharp, matches data book, mixed melting point confirms identity), TLC (single spot, Rf matches standard), IR (expected absorptions present, starting-material absorptions absent — e.g. no broad acid O–H if you made the ester), and boiling point for liquids. Percentage yield and atom economy link the synthesis to analysis: yield = actual/theoretical × 100; atom economy = M r of desired product / total M r of all products × 100. Observing an impure product (low melting point, multiple TLC spots) means recrystallisation is needed before analysis — the techniques feed each other. Required practicals referenced: making a pure organic solid (recrystallisation, melting point), preparing an ester and purifying by distillation, and using TLC to separate plant pigments or amino acids — describe the apparatus (Buchner funnel, still head, TLC chamber) and the safety points (fume cupboard for volatile solvents) because practical-write-up marks are embedded in these questions.

topics.name: Titrations and Analytical Techniques
topics.subject: chemistry
topics.searchText: chemistry Chemistry Titrations and Analytical Techniques Describe the full titration procedure including rinsing rules, meniscus reading and concordant titres Make a standard solution and calculate concentrations, dilutions and percentage purity from titration data Perform redox titration calculations with MnO₄⁻/Fe²⁺ and I₂/S₂O₃²⁻, explaining the self-indicating endpoint and acid choice Sketch and interpret pH titration curves for all four acid-base combinations and justify indicator choice Use the half-equivalence point (pH = pKa) to determine Ka experimentally Describe recrystallisation, TLC (Rf values) and melting point purity tests, explaining how purity is checked Standard solution A solution of accurately known concentration, made by dissolving an exact mass of a primary standard in a volumetric flask. Concordant titres Titres agreeing within 0.10 cm³, averaged to give the mean titre. Equivalence point The volume of titrant at which the reaction is exactly complete — the near-vertical section of a pH titration curve. End point The volume at which the indicator changes colour; coincides with the equivalence point when the indicator is chosen correctly. Buffer solution A solution that maintains approximately constant pH when small quantities of acid or base are added. Rf value Distance moved by a substance divided by distance moved by the solvent front in chromatography; always ≤ 1. Recrystallisation Purification by dissolving a solid in the minimum hot solvent, cooling to crystallise, filtering and drying — impurities remain in solution. Self-indicating titrant A titrant that shows its own endpoint by colour change, e.g. purple MnO₄⁻ turning colourless/pale pink. Mixed melting point Melting point of a mixture of prepared solid and pure standard; unchanged sharp melting point confirms identity. A titration determines the unknown concentration of a solution by reacting it with a standard solution of known concentration. Required practical (AQA RP1, OCR PAG1/2): make a standard solution and use it to find the concentration of an unknown acid/base. Method step by step: (1) weigh the solid by difference (mass of bottle + solid, then bottle) and dissolve in a beaker with deionised water; (2) transfer to a volumetric flask using a funnel, rinse the beaker into the flask, add water to the graduation mark (bottom of meniscus on the line), stopper and invert repeatedly to homogenise; (3) rinse the burette with the standard solution (then fill, record initial reading to 0.05 cm³); pipette 25.0 cm³ of the unknown into a conical flask with 2-3 drops of indicator; (4) run in titrant swirling continuously, adding dropwise near the endpoint until a permanent colour change remains; (5) repeat until concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³) and take the mean of concordant values only. Accuracy rules that earn marks: rinse the burette with the solution it will hold (residual water dilutes it); rinse the pipette with the solution it transfers; rinse the conical flask with deionised water only (residual water does not change moles of acid present); remove the funnel before reading; read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; white tile under the flask to see the colour change. Uncertainties: each burette reading ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³; percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty/measurement) × 100 — a small titre (e.g. 10 cm³) carries a large percentage error, so use a larger titre or a more concentrated solution. Reduce uncertainty: titrate a larger volume, use a lower concentration titrant, or a smaller-graduation burette. Indicators: phenolphthalein (colourless → pink, range 8.3-10.0) and methyl orange (red → yellow, range 3.1-4.4). Choose the indicator whose range lies entirely within the near-vertical section of the titration curve: strong acid-strong base works with either; weak acid-strong base needs phenolphthalein; strong acid-weak base needs methyl orange; weak acid-weak base has no sharp vertical section — neither indicator is suitable. A standard solution is one of known concentration, made by dissolving an exact mass of a primary standard (pure, stable, not hygroscopic — e.g. anhydrous sodium carbonate, not NaOH which absorbs water) in a volumetric flask. Moles = mass/M r ; concentration = moles/volume (dm³). Concentration conversions: g dm⁻³ ÷ M r = mol dm⁻³. Core titration calculation: (1) moles of titrant = concentration × volume/1000; (2) moles of unknown from the equation's ratio; (3) concentration = moles × 1000/volume. Worked example: 25.0 cm³ of HCl of unknown concentration is neutralised by a mean titre of 22.30 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (1:1 ratio). Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 22.30/1000 = 2.23 × 10⁻³ mol. Moles HCl = 2.23 × 10⁻³. [HCl] = 2.23 × 10⁻³ × 1000/25.0 = 0.0892 mol dm⁻³. Dilutions: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂; if the sample was diluted first, scale back by the dilution factor. Purity questions: percentage purity = (moles found × M r / mass used) × 100. Water of crystallisation: find the anhydrous salt moles from the titre, subtract from the mass used to get the water mass, divide by 18 for moles, then divide both by the smaller to get x in M x ·xH₂O. Exam tip: always write the balanced equation first and state the ratio — most lost marks come from wrong ratios (e.g. 2:1 for H₂SO₄) or dm³/cm³ slips.
