Rounding underflows precision at the mantissa's tail; very large exponents overflow to infinity, very small underflow to zero. Also know fixed-point contrast: fast, exact for a fixed scale (money in pence), but a fixed range/precision split — floating point trades both dynamically, which is why it dominates general arithmetic. ASCII is 7-bit: 128 codes, enough for English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes. 'A' = 65 (01000001), 'a' = 97, and the examinable trick: digit characters are codes 48–57, so code - 48 converts a character digit to its numeric value. Unicode assigns a code point to every character in every script plus emoji; UTF-8 is variable-length (1–4 bytes, ASCII-compatible: the first 128 code points use 1 byte identical to ASCII), UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes. The comparison question: ASCII cannot represent non-Latin scripts (one code set of 128); Unicode's variable-length UTF-8 keeps English text at 1 byte (backward compatible) while allowing any code point — state both halves of the trade-off. Error detection: a parity bit makes the count of 1s even (even parity) or odd; on receipt the parity is recomputed and a mismatch flags an error. It detects single-bit (odd numbers of) errors but cannot locate or correct them, and even numbers of errors slip through — the exact evaluation to give. A checksum goes further: arithmetic over the bytes (e.g. sum mod 256) sent with the data; stronger detection, still no correction — correction needs redundancy (e.g. retransmission, or error-correcting codes). Bitmaps store a grid of pixels, each with a colour code. Resolution = width x height in pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel (1-bit = 2 colours, 8-bit = 256, 24-bit = 16.7 million). File size calculation — memorise and practise: Bitmap: 1024 x 768 pixels at 24-bit colour = 1024 x 768 x 24 bits = 18,874,368 bits = 2,359,296 bytes = 2.25 MiB (divide by 1024 twice) Bitmap drawbacks to quote: file size grows with resolution x depth regardless of image content, and scaling up loses quality (pixels become visible blocks). Vector graphics store drawing objects : a list such as [circle, x=40, y=60, r=15, colour=red] , rendered by the drawing software. Advantages: small files for simple diagrams; scaling to any size with no quality loss (objects are redrawn); each object editable independently. Limitation: unsuitable for photographs — a photo's pixel detail cannot be described as a short list of shapes, so bitmaps win there. The exam comparison is exactly that pairing. Sound is sampled: an analogue wave's amplitude is measured at a fixed sample rate (Hz, samples per second) and each sample stored at a fixed sample resolution (bits per sample). CD quality: 44,100 Hz, 16-bit, stereo (2 channels). File size: 60 seconds at 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo: 44100 x 16 x 60 x 2 bits = 84,672,000 bits = 10,584,000 bytes ≈ 10.1 MiB Trade-offs to quote: higher sample rate and resolution capture the wave more faithfully (closer approximation, higher bandwidth sounds) but increase file size proportionally; the Nyquist principle — sample at more than twice the highest frequency present — explains why 44.1 kHz covers the ~20 kHz limit of human hearing. Lower rates introduce aliasing distortion (high frequencies masquerade as low ones). Compression reduces the number of bits needed to store or transmit data (OCR 1.3.1). Lossless compression reconstructs the original exactly (required for text, code, executables); lossy discards detail humans barely perceive (JPEG, MP3, streaming video) and achieves far higher ratios. The examinable fact: lossless for data where every bit matters, lossy where perceptual approximation is acceptable — with a reason in each case. Run-length encoding (RLE) — lossless — replaces runs of identical values with (count, value) pairs. Worked example, a 1-bit bitmap row: Original (24 pixels): 000000001111111100000011 RLE: 8x0, 8x1, 6x0, 2x1 Stored (4 bits per pair): 8,0 8,1 6,0 2,1 -> 32 bits vs 24... loss! Count the marking subtlety: with 4-bit counts and 1-bit values, each pair costs 5 bits, so four pairs = 20 bits when RLE gains : long runs (flat backgrounds, scans of text, fax images). When data alternates rapidly (ABABAB...), RLE stores a pair per character and expands the file — still lossless, but bigger. Be ready to compute the break-even: with n-bit counts and v-bit values, a run of length k compresses when k x original-bit-depth > n + v. Dictionary (LZ-family) compression — lossless — builds a dictionary of repeated substrings as it scans, replacing each repeat with a short codeword/index. Worked sketch on the cat sat on the mat : Scan: 'the ' seen -> dictionary[254] = 'the ' 'the cat sat on the mat' -> the cat sat on [254]mat (second 'the ' replaced by an index) Repeated phrases collapse to 1-byte (or few-bit) references; the dictionary itself is stored (or rebuilt during decompression, as in LZ77/LZW) so the process is fully reversible. Properties to quote: lossless; excellent on text and structured data with repetition; poor on already-compressed or random data (no repeats to factor out — and can even add overhead); decompression must be able to rebuild or reference the dictionary, so implementations either store it or derive it deterministically. Evaluation paragraph to reuse in essays: compression trades processing time for space/bandwidth — compressing and decompressing cost CPU, so it pays off when data is stored long-term or transmitted over slow links, and can be counterproductive for data compressed once and used once on a fast local bus. Also connect to error detection: compressed data is more fragile — a single corrupted bit can derail the dictionary, which is why compressed streams carry checksums.

topics.name: Computer Systems and Architecture
topics.subject: computer-science
topics.searchText: computer-science Computer Science Computer Systems and Architecture Describe the role of the ALU, control unit and registers (PC, ACC, MAR, MDR, CIR, status register) and the system buses (AQA 4.4.1, OCR 1.1.1) Trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle step by step using register transfer notation, and explain pipelining and its hazards (OCR 1.1.1) Describe the memory hierarchy and explain cache operation (hit/miss) and virtual memory (paging, page faults) (AQA 4.4.1, OCR 1.1.3) Explain operating system functions: memory management, scheduling algorithms, interrupt handling (OCR 1.2.1, WJEC 1.5) Compare CISC and RISC processor design and parallel architectures (SIMD, MIMD, multicore, GPU) (OCR 1.1.2) Calculate performance using Amdahl's law and analyse the effect of clock speed and core count CPU: ALU (arithmetic/logic + flags), CU (decode + control signals); registers: PC (next instruction address), ACC (ALU results), MAR (address), MDR (data), CIR (current instruction), SR (flags) (AQA 4.4.1, OCR 1.1.1) Buses: address bus unidirectional (CPU to memory), data bus bidirectional, control bus carries commands; wider address bus = more addressable memory FDE: fetch (PC to MAR, memory to MDR, to CIR, PC incremented), decode (CU interprets opcode), execute (ALU/data movement) Pipelining overlaps fetch/decode/execute; hazards: data (result not ready), control (branches), structural (resource conflict) Memory hierarchy: registers > L1 > L2 > L3 cache > RAM > SSD > HDD; cost per byte falls, size grows going down Virtual memory: pages swapped between RAM and disk via a page table; page fault stalls the process; thrashing degrades performance OS functions: memory management (paging, segmentation), scheduling (round robin, FCFS, SJF, SRTN, multilevel feedback), interrupt handling, resource allocation (OCR 1.2.1) CISC vs RISC: complex microcoded instructions vs simple load/store one-cycle instructions with many registers; RISC suits pipelining Parallel: SIMD (one instruction, multiple data), MIMD (multicore); Amdahl: speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/n) Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) The CPU component that performs arithmetic and logical operations, and updates the status register flags. Control Unit (CU) The CPU component that decodes instructions and coordinates the control signals that sequence the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Program counter (PC) The register holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched. Status register The register holding condition flag bits (carry, negative, overflow, zero) set by the ALU and tested by branch instructions. Bus A shared set of parallel wires: the address bus carries addresses (unidirectional), the data bus carries data (bidirectional), the control bus carries commands. Cache Small, fast memory between the CPU and RAM holding copies of frequently-used data; a hit avoids a slow RAM access. Virtual memory An OS technique using an area of secondary storage as an extension of RAM, moving pages between the two via a page table. Interrupt A signal that causes the CPU to suspend the current program, save its state and run an interrupt service routine (e.g. I/O completion, timer). CISC Complex Instruction Set Computer: many complex, variable-length instructions, microcode interpretation, fewer registers. RISC Reduced Instruction Set Computer: simple fixed-length instructions executed in one cycle, load/store architecture, many registers, suited to pipelining. The standard 6-marker here is 'describe the role of the following registers...' (AQA 4.4.1, OCR 1.1.1, WJEC 1.4). Learn this table exactly — the purposes below are the mark-scheme wording: Register Purpose Program counter (PC) Holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched Current instruction register (CIR) Holds the instruction currently being decoded/executed Memory address register (MAR) Holds the address of the memory location about to be read/written Memory data register (MDR) Holds the data just read from, or about to be written to, that address Accumulator (ACC) Holds the result of ALU operations Status register (SR) Holds flags (carry, negative, overflow, zero) set by the ALU and tested by branches The classic trap: PC holds the address of the next instruction (not the current one), and MAR holds an address while MDR holds the data at that address. Pairs go together in traces: MAR/MDR for memory access, PC/CIR for instruction flow. The other components: the ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic (AND, OR, shifts), and sets the status flags; the control unit decodes the opcode in the CIR and generates the control signals that sequence every other component; the clock synchronises them; general-purpose registers hold intermediate values (RISC designs have many, CISC few). Buses carry everything between them. Three buses, three examinable facts: the address bus is unidirectional (CPU to memory) and its width determines the addressable memory — 32 address lines address 2^32 bytes = 4 GiB; the data bus is bidirectional and its width determines how much data moves per transfer — 64 lines move 8 bytes at a time; the control bus carries command and timing signals (read, write, clock, interrupt request). Exam question pattern: 'Explain how the width of the address bus affects performance.' Answer: each additional line doubles the addressable space (2^w), not the speed directly — but more addressable memory allows more RAM and less swapping, which improves performance indirectly. State that distinction and you separate yourself from candidates who say 'wider bus = faster'. The FDE cycle (OCR 1.1.1, AQA 4.4.1) repeats for every instruction. Learn the register transfers in order — this exact sequence is the mark scheme: 1. FETCH MAR Double-bracket notation: MAR copies the contents of PC into MAR; MDR copies the contents of the memory location whose address is in MAR — the nested brackets mean 'dereference the address'. Exam trap: PC is incremented during fetch , before decode, so it already points at the next instruction while the current one executes; branch instructions then overwrite PC during execute, which is how jumps work. Worked micro-trace for ADD #5 (immediate operand 5): fetch — MAR gets PC, PC increments, CIR gets ADD #5; decode — CU recognises an immediate add; execute — ACC LOAD 200 (direct addressing): fetch as above; decode; execute — MAR Pipelining overlaps the three stages: while one instruction executes, the next is decoded and a third fetched — so an ideal pipeline completes about one instruction per cycle instead of three cycles per instruction. Hazards break the flow, and exams ask you to name and exemplify all three: Data hazard — an instruction needs a result the previous instruction has not yet produced: ADD R1, R2, R3 followed immediately by ADD R4, R1, R5 — R1 is not ready. Fixed by stalling (pipeline bubbles) or forwarding the result directly between stages. Control hazard — a branch invalidates instructions already fetched: if the branch is taken, the prefetched instructions are wrong and must be flushed. Fixed by branch prediction (guess and roll back if wrong). Structural hazard — two instructions need the same hardware resource at once (e.g. one memory port for both fetch and data access). Fixed by duplicating resources (separate instruction/data caches — the Harvard-style split). Exam question pattern: 'Explain what a data hazard is and how a pipelined processor deals with it.' Full-credit: define the dependency (consecutive instructions, second needs the first's result before it is written back), give the two-instruction example, then state stall-and-forward as the fix. Memory is arranged by the trade-off speed versus cost versus size — fastest and smallest at the top: Level Typical access time Typical size Registers bytes (tens of registers) L1 cache ~1 ns tens of KiB L2/L3 cache ~4–20 ns hundreds of KiB – tens of MiB RAM (main memory) ~100 ns GiB SSD ~100 microseconds hundreds of GiB HDD ~10 ms Terabytes Cache holds copies of recently and frequently used data. On a hit , the CPU reads from cache — no wait. On a miss , the data is fetched from RAM (a stall of ~100 cycles) and cached for reuse. Why cache improves performance: programs exhibit locality of reference — temporal locality (recently used data is used again: loop counters, accumulators) and spatial locality (nearby addresses are used together: sequential instructions, array traversal) — so a small cache captures a large fraction of accesses. Quote both locality terms; they are the explanation marks. Cache policies worth one line each: cache replacement replaces the least recently used line; write policies decide when cached writes reach RAM (write-through immediately, write-back lazily with a dirty bit). Virtual memory extends RAM using secondary storage: memory is divided into fixed-size pages ; a page table maps virtual addresses to physical frames; pages not currently in RAM live on disk. When a process accesses a page that is not in RAM — a page fault — the OS suspends the process, loads the page from disk, updates the page table and resumes. If pages are replaced too aggressively (RAM too small for the working set), the system thrashes : constantly swapping pages in and out and doing almost no useful work — the classic evaluation point. Exam question pattern: 'Explain how virtual memory allows a program larger than physical RAM to run, and why excessive reliance on it degrades performance.' Answer: pages of the program are swapped between RAM and disk via the page table on demand (page faults), so the program's full address space need not be resident; disk access is orders of magnitude slower than RAM, so heavy swapping (thrashing) dominates execution time. Also know why the OS needs memory management at all: multiple programs run concurrently, so memory must be partitioned and protected — one process must not read or write another's memory; paging provides that isolation via the page table (each process has its own mapping), which is the link between the hardware and the OS section below. The OS is the layer between hardware and applications, and its examinable functions fall into four groups (OCR 1.2.1, WJEC 1.5, AQA 4.4.4). Memory management: allocates and deallocates memory to processes; implements paging (fixed-size pages, any page fits any frame — no external fragmentation, small internal fragmentation in the last page) and segmentation (variable-sized logical units such as code, stack, heap — matches program structure but suffers external fragmentation); manages the page table and virtual memory; enforces protection between processes. The paging-vs-segmentation comparison is the standard question: paging divides memory into fixed-size blocks chosen for hardware convenience; segmentation divides into variable-size logical units chosen for the program's structure; both need the OS to translate addresses, and both enable sharing and protection. Scheduling decides which ready process gets the CPU next. Know the algorithms, their fairness and their failure modes: Algorithm Method Key property Round robin Each process gets a fixed time slice, then rejoins the queue Fair response time; slice too small = overhead, too large = poor responsiveness First come, first served Runs each process to completion in arrival order Simple; short jobs stuck behind long ones (convoy effect) Shortest job first Runs the process with the smallest predicted duration Best average waiting time; needs prediction; long jobs can starve Shortest remaining time Preemptive SJF — preempts if a shorter job arrives Even better waiting time; more context switches; starvation risk Multilevel feedback queues Multiple queues with priorities; processes move between them on behaviour Balances interactive responsiveness with throughput Exam pattern: 'A short interactive task arrives while a long batch job is running. Explain which scheduling algorithm gives the best response time.' Answer: round robin (or multilevel feedback) — the batch job is preempted at its time-slice boundary so the interactive task runs soon; FCFS would make it wait for the whole batch; SJF favours the short task once both are queued but cannot preempt a running job unless implemented as SRTN. Also know preemptive vs non-preemptive : preemptive schedulers can interrupt a running process (timer interrupt); non-preemptive wait for it to yield — and preemption is what makes multitasking possible. Interrupt handling: an interrupt is a signal (I/O completion, timer tick, hardware fault, program error) that suspends the current process. The sequence to reproduce: (1) the processor finishes the current instruction; (2) it saves the current context (PC, status register, registers) on the stack; (3) it loads the interrupt service routine (ISR) address from the interrupt vector table and runs it; (4) on completion the saved context is restored and the interrupted program resumes transparently. Interrupts are what allow the CPU to multiplex between programs and to react to devices without busy-waiting — the exam point: polling wastes cycles checking devices repeatedly, whereas interrupts let the device signal the CPU only when needed. CISC vs RISC (OCR 1.1.2) — the comparison to reproduce in full: Feature CISC RISC Instructions Many, complex, variable length Few, simple, fixed length Execution Multiple cycles; interpreted by microcode One cycle per instruction Memory access Many addressing modes; instructions can access memory directly Load/store architecture — only load/store touch memory Registers Fewer Many Pipelining Harder — variable instruction length Designed for it — uniform stages Compiler Simpler to target; hardware does more Must do more work; hardware simpler Evaluation line to add: modern x86 processors are externally CISC but internally translate to RISC-like micro-operations, so the distinction is about design philosophy, not clean categories; ARM processors (phones, Raspberry Pi) are RISC, chosen for power efficiency — one instruction per cycle and simpler decode burn less energy. Parallel architectures: SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) applies one instruction to many data items at once — graphics pipelines and vector units; MIMD (multiple instruction, multiple data) is multiple independent cores running different instruction streams — general multicore. Also know the GPU as a co-processor: thousands of simple cores specialised for the massively parallel arithmetic of graphics and machine learning, while the CPU handles general sequential control flow; co-processors (maths, floating-point units) offload specific workloads from the main CPU. Amdahl's law quantifies the limit of parallelism: if a fraction p of a program can be parallelised and the rest (1 − p) is serial, the speedup on n cores is: speedup = 1 / ( (1 - p) + p / n ) Worked calculations to memorise (these are the exact exam patterns): 20% serial, 4 cores: speedup = 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/4) = 1 / (0.2 + 0.2) = 2.5x . Even with infinite cores: 1 / 0.2 = 5x — the serial fraction caps everything. 30% serial, 8 cores: 1 / (0.3 + 0.7/8) = 1 / (0.3 + 0.0875) = 1 / 0.3875 ≈ 2.58x . Note how little the extra cores helped beyond 4 — the serial 30% dominates. 50% serial, infinite cores: 1 / 0.5 = 2x — halving the serial fraction doubles the ceiling; doubling cores does not. The conclusion to quote: beyond a few cores, returns diminish sharply and the serial fraction — not the core count — sets the maximum speedup. Exam question pattern: 'Explain why adding more cores eventually stops improving performance.' Answer: only the parallelisable fraction speeds up; the serial portion runs at the same speed regardless, so as n grows the p/n term vanishes and speedup approaches 1/(1-p), a hard ceiling set by the code's serial fraction. Add the counterpoint for evaluation: better single-core performance (clock speed, IPC, cache) helps serial code, whereas more cores only helps parallel code — which is why optimisation priorities depend on the workload.

topics.name: Networks and Databases
topics.subject: computer-science
topics.searchText: computer-science Computer Science Networks and Databases Compare network topologies (star, mesh, bus) and distinguish LAN, WAN, client-server and peer-to-peer models (AQA 4.5.2, OCR 1.3.3) Describe the four layers of the TCP/IP stack and the role of each (AQA 4.5.4, OCR 1.3.3) Compare TCP and UDP, and trace the TCP three-way handshake and DNS resolution steps (AQA 4.5.2, OCR 1.3.3) Explain IP addressing: IPv4 dotted decimal, subnet masks and CIDR notation, and why IPv6 exists (AQA 4.5.2, OCR 1.3.3) Design relational databases: entities, attributes, relationships and keys (primary, foreign, candidate), and enforce referential integrity (AQA 4.6.1, OCR 1.3.2, WJEC 1.9) Normalise a database to 3NF, showing partial and transitive dependencies at each stage (AQA 4.6.2) Write SQL SELECT queries with joins, aggregation and grouping, and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements (AQA 4.6.3, OCR 1.3.2) Explain transaction processing and the ACID properties, including concurrency control (AQA 4.6.2, OCR 1.3.2) Topologies: star (central switch — easy to add nodes, hub is single point of failure), bus (shared cable — collisions), mesh (redundant paths) TCP/IP stack: Application (HTTP, DNS, FTP, SMTP), Transport (TCP/UDP), Internet (IP routing), Link (Ethernet, WiFi) (AQA 4.5.4) TCP: connection-oriented, 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), sequencing, retransmission, flow/congestion control; UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, low latency DNS: resolver asks root → TLD (.co.uk) → authoritative server; recursive vs iterative queries; records A, AAAA, MX, CNAME IPv4: 32-bit dotted decimal with subnet mask/CIDR (/24 = 24 network bits); IPv6: 128-bit hex, vast address space (AQA 4.5.2) Relational DB: entity = table, attribute = column; 1:1, 1:N, M:N relationships resolved with link tables; PK/FK enforce referential integrity (AQA 4.6.1) Normalisation: 1NF atomic, 2NF no partial FD on part of a composite key, 3NF no transitive FD (AQA 4.6.2) SQL: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY; JOIN ... ON; COUNT/SUM/AVG (AQA 4.6.3) ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed changes survive crashes) LAN Local Area Network: a network over a small geographic area (one site), owned by the organisation, with high bandwidth and low latency. WAN Wide Area Network: a network spanning large geographic areas using third-party infrastructure (e.g. leased lines); the internet is the largest WAN. Protocol An agreed set of rules governing communication between devices, defining format, ordering and error handling. TCP Transmission Control Protocol: a connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol with sequencing, acknowledgements, flow and congestion control. UDP User Datagram Protocol: a connectionless transport protocol with no delivery guarantee, ordering or handshake — low overhead and latency. DNS Domain Name System: the hierarchical distributed service resolving domain names to IP addresses via root, TLD and authoritative servers. Primary key An attribute (or combination) uniquely identifying each record in a table; never null and never duplicated. Foreign key An attribute in one table that references the primary key of another, creating the link between tables and enforcing referential integrity. Normalisation The process of structuring tables to remove redundancy: 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependencies, 3NF no transitive dependencies (AQA 4.6.2). Transaction A sequence of database operations treated as one indivisible unit: it either completes fully (commit) or has no effect at all (rollback). Topologies (AQA 4.5.2, WJEC 1.7): star — every node connects to a central switch; easy to add nodes, one cable fault isolates only that node, but the switch is a single point of failure; bus — all nodes share one backbone cable; cheap but collisions rise with traffic and a backbone break kills the network; mesh — nodes interconnect (full or partial); redundant paths give fault tolerance at the cost of cabling; ring — nodes in a loop with token passing. The exam pattern: given a scenario (school, office, safety-critical), name the best topology and justify with cost, fault tolerance and expansion. LAN vs WAN — the one-marker pair: a LAN spans one site, is owned by the organisation, and has high bandwidth/low latency; a WAN spans large distances using third-party (telecom) infrastructure — leased lines and the internet. Client-server vs peer-to-peer: client-server centralises services (files, databases, email) on dedicated servers — central control, security and backups, but the server is a cost and a bottleneck; peer-to-peer shares resources directly between equals — cheap for small networks but no central control, and security/backup are per-machine. The TCP/IP stack (AQA 4.5.4, OCR 1.3.3) has four layers, each using the layer below and serving the layer above: Layer Role Protocols Application Provides network services to programs HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, FTP, SMTP, IMAP Transport End-to-end delivery, port numbers, reliability TCP, UDP Internet Routing packets between networks by IP address IP, ICMP Link Physical transmission on the local network (frames, MAC addresses) Ethernet, WiFi The two examinable points: (1) layering — each layer's services are independent of the implementation of the others, so a protocol can change (WiFi to Ethernet) without touching the layers above, and the same stack works over any physical medium; (2) encapsulation — data moves down the stack gaining a header at each layer (TCP header with ports and sequence numbers, IP header with addresses, Ethernet frame with MAC addresses) and the headers are stripped back off at the receiver. Exam question pattern: 'Explain the purpose of each layer of the TCP/IP stack.' Answer: application provides user-facing services; transport provides end-to-end delivery with ports and (with TCP) reliability; internet routes packets across networks by IP; link handles transmission over the physical local network. Devices to know by role: a switch forwards frames within a LAN using MAC addresses; a router forwards packets between networks using IP addresses; a firewall filters traffic by rules; a wireless access point joins wireless clients to the wired LAN. TCP vs UDP is the highest-frequency comparison in this topic (AQA 4.5.2, OCR 1.3.3). TCP is connection-oriented : a three-way handshake (client SYN → server SYN-ACK → client ACK) establishes the connection; segments are numbered and acknowledged, lost segments are retransmitted, and flow/congestion control pace the sender. UDP is connectionless : no handshake, no ordering, no retransmission — just datagrams with ports. The trade-off sentence to quote: TCP guarantees delivery and order at the cost of overhead and latency; UDP has minimal overhead and latency but no guarantees. Application matching is the standard follow-up: web pages, file transfer and email need every byte intact and in order — TCP. Live video, voice and online games prefer UDP — a lost packet is a momentary glitch, and retransmitting an outdated frame would arrive too late to be useful; DNS queries also use UDP (single small request-response, retried on failure). The exam pattern: 'Explain why UDP rather than TCP is used for live video streaming.' Answer: streaming tolerates small losses but not delay; TCP's retransmission of lost packets would stall playback with late-arriving data, whereas UDP delivers what arrives immediately — lower latency, and a dropped frame is preferable to a delayed one. DNS resolution (AQA 4.5.2) — learn the sequence: The client asks its configured recursive resolver (ISP's DNS server) for www.example.co.uk. The resolver asks a root server , which replies with the address of the .co.uk TLD server . The resolver asks the TLD server, which replies with the authoritative name server for example.co.uk. The resolver asks the authoritative server, which returns the IP address (an A record for IPv4, AAAA for IPv6). The resolver caches the answer (with a TTL) and returns it to the client, which connects to that IP. Records to name: A (name → IPv4), AAAA (name → IPv6), MX (mail server), CNAME (alias). HTTP/HTTPS: HTTP is a request-response application protocol (GET, POST, status codes); HTTPS is HTTP over TLS — the handshake exchanges certificates and establishes session keys before any data flows, giving confidentiality and server authentication. Exam one-liner: HTTPS encrypts the traffic and proves the server's identity via a CA-signed certificate, protecting against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. IP addressing: IPv4 is 32-bit, written dotted decimal (192.168.1.0), with a subnet mask splitting network bits from host bits. CIDR notation appends the network-bit count: /24 = 255.255.255.0 = 24 network bits, 8 host bits, 254 usable hosts. Worked subnetting (the exact exam pattern): Subnet 192.168.1.0/24 into 4 equal subnets: 4 subnets need 2 more network bits: /24 -> /26 New mask: /26 = 255.255.255.192 Subnets: 192.168.1.0/26 (hosts .1 - .62) 192.168.1.64/26 (hosts .65 - .126) 192.168.1.128/26 (hosts .129 - .190) 192.168.1.192/26 (hosts .193 - .254) Method: doubling the number of subnets adds one bit to the mask; each subnet's size halves (here 64 addresses, 62 usable — subtract the network and broadcast addresses). IPv6 exists because 32-bit IPv4 exhausted its ~4.3 billion addresses; IPv6 is 128-bit hex, eliminating the need for NAT, with hierarchical routing and built-in support for autoconfiguration. A relational database stores data in tables (relations): each table is an entity , each column an attribute , each row a record . Relationships between tables are 1:1, 1:N or M:N, and the examinable design rule: an M:N relationship must be resolved with a link (junction) table — e.g. Student ↔ Course is M:N, so create Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID) referencing both. Keys (AQA 4.6.1, OCR 1.3.2): a primary key uniquely identifies each record (never null, never duplicated); a candidate key is any attribute that could serve as the primary key; a foreign key in one table references the primary key of another, forming the link; a composite key combines two or more attributes (link tables commonly use (StudentID, CourseID) as a composite PK). Referential integrity is the constraint that every foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table — you cannot enrol a student who does not exist, and deleting a course must be restricted or cascade to its enrolments. The exam pattern: 'Explain how the design enforces referential integrity.' Answer: the FK in the child table references the PK of the parent; the DBMS rejects inserts/updates with FK values that have no matching PK, and deletion of a referenced parent is restricted or cascades. Why relational at all — the 4-marker: data is stored once (no redundancy), so updates happen in one place and cannot disagree; integrity is enforced by keys and constraints; SQL gives a declarative query language independent of storage; and tables scale to complex many-to-many structures via link tables. Contrast with flat files worth one line: a flat file repeats data across records, so it suffers update anomalies (change a name in one record, disagree with another) and has no built-in integrity. Normalisation (AQA 4.6.2, WJEC 1.9) structures tables to eliminate redundancy. The stages, in mark-scheme wording: 1NF (first normal form): all attributes contain atomic (indivisible) values; no repeating groups. Fix a 'phone numbers' column holding '0121 555, 07700 900' by splitting into a separate Phone table. 2NF: in 1NF and no non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key (partial dependency). Only bites when the key is composite. 3NF: in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (transitive dependency). Worked example — normalise Student(StudentID, Name, CourseID, CourseName, TutorID, TutorName): Functional dependencies: StudentID -> Name, CourseID CourseID -> CourseName, TutorID // course determines its tutor TutorID -> TutorName 1NF: all values atomic - already satisfied. 2NF: key is StudentID alone (no composite key), so no partial dependencies are possible - already in 2NF. 3NF: CourseName and TutorID depend on CourseID, a non-key attribute -> transitive dependency. TutorName depends on TutorID, another non-key attribute -> transitive dependency. Split: Student(StudentID, Name, CourseID) Course(CourseID, CourseName, TutorID) Tutor(TutorID, TutorName) Step-by-step reasoning to reproduce: (1) list the functional dependencies; (2) check 1NF — atomic values; (3) check 2NF — only relevant when a composite key exists, so with a single-attribute key the table is automatically in 2NF (a point that earns the 'explain why 2NF was trivially satisfied' mark); (4) check 3NF — any non-key attribute determined by another non-key attribute must move out with its determinant; (5) verify the final tables: each stores one entity, linked by foreign keys, with zero redundancy — CourseName appears once however many students take the course. The benefits to quote in the 4-marker: no redundancy (each fact stored once), so no update anomalies (changing a tutor's name updates one row); no insertion anomalies (a new course can be added with no students yet); no deletion anomalies (deleting the last student does not erase the course). A second worked pattern — a composite key case: OrderLine(OrderID, ProductID, ProductName, Quantity) — ProductName depends on ProductID alone (part of the composite key OrderID+ProductID), a partial dependency, so 2NF splits out Product(ProductID, ProductName). Exam question pattern: 'Explain the difference between 2NF and 3NF.' Answer: 2NF removes partial dependencies — non-key attributes depending on part of a composite key; 3NF additionally removes transitive dependencies — non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes; both only apply to tables already in the previous normal form. SQL (AQA 4.6.3, OCR 1.3.2) is declarative — you specify what data, not how to retrieve it. The SELECT skeleton, in evaluation order: SELECT attributes // 5. project the columns FROM tables // 1. source tables WHERE condition // 2. filter rows GROUP BY attributes // 3. aggregate rows into groups HAVING condition // 4. filter groups ORDER BY attributes // 6. sort the result Worked query 1 — students with an average grade above 70 (the exact existing exam pattern): SELECT s.Name FROM Student s JOIN Grade g ON s.StudentID = g.StudentID GROUP BY s.StudentID, s.Name HAVING AVG(g.Mark) > 70; Step-by-step: JOIN pairs each student with their grades via the foreign key; GROUP BY collapses to one row per student; AVG computes each student's mean; HAVING filters groups — the marking subtlety is that WHERE cannot contain AVG because WHERE runs before grouping; HAVING runs after. Worked query 2 — multi-table join returning details: SELECT s.Name, c.CourseName, t.TutorName FROM Student s JOIN Course c ON s.CourseID = c.CourseID JOIN Tutor t ON c.TutorID = t.TutorID WHERE s.Name LIKE 'A%' ORDER BY c.CourseName, s.Name; Each JOIN follows one FK link (Student→Course→Tutor); LIKE 'A%' matches names starting with A (% is the wildcard); ORDER BY sorts by course then name. Worked query 3 — DML: INSERT INTO Student (StudentID, Name, CourseID) VALUES (2214, 'Ada', 'CS01'); UPDATE Student SET CourseID = 'CS02' WHERE StudentID = 2214; DELETE FROM Student WHERE StudentID = 2214; Marking points: UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE affects every row — the classic catastrophic one-marker; INSERT must supply every non-null column and respect FK constraints. Transactions and ACID (AQA 4.6.2, OCR 1.3.2): a transaction is a group of operations treated as indivisible. The four properties, each with its example: Atomicity — all operations complete or none do: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another; a crash between the two would corrupt the data, so rollback restores the original state. Consistency — a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another: constraints (keys, check rules) hold before and after. Isolation — concurrent transactions do not interfere: two simultaneous bookings of the last seat cannot both succeed; the DBMS serialises access (locks) so one sees the other's effect. Durability — once committed, changes survive a crash: a write-ahead log lets the DBMS redo committed work after failure. Concurrency failure modes to name: a lost update (two transactions read the same value, both write, one overwrites the other), an inconsistent read , and deadlock (two transactions each hold a lock the other needs — neither proceeds; the DBMS detects and aborts one). Exam pattern: 'Explain why a ticket-booking system must use transactions.' Answer: booking decrements availability and creates the booking — if the system crashes between them the data is inconsistent, so atomicity requires both to succeed or both to roll back; concurrent bookings of the last seat must be isolated so only one succeeds; committed bookings must be durable.

topics.name: Software Development and Legal Issues
topics.subject: computer-science
topics.searchText: computer-science Computer Science Software Development and Legal Issues Compare SDLC models (waterfall, agile, spiral, incremental) and justify a choice for a given project scenario (OCR 1.2.4, AQA 4.9/4.12) Explain the stages of a systematic approach to problem solving: analysis, design, implementation, testing, evaluation (AQA 4.9) Describe programming paradigms — procedural and object-oriented — and apply OOP: classes, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism (OCR 1.2.6, WJEC Unit 4) Compare compilers, interpreters and assemblers, and explain bytecode and virtual machines (OCR 1.2.3, AQA 4.4) Describe testing levels (unit, integration, alpha, beta, acceptance) and types (white box, black box), and select test data (normal, boundary, erroneous) (OCR 1.2.4, AQA 4.9) Explain the legal framework: Data Protection Act 2018, Computer Misuse Act 1990, Copyright Designs and Patents Act 1988, Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (OCR 1.5) Discuss ethical and professional issues in software development, including privacy and non-functional requirements (AQA 4.10, OCR 1.5) SDLC stages: analysis (requirements), design (data structures, interfaces, modules), implementation, testing, evaluation (AQA 4.9, OCR 1.2.4) Waterfall: linear, fixed requirements, cheap to manage — but change is expensive and feedback comes late Agile: iterative sprints, working software early, embraces changing requirements — needs constant customer involvement Spiral: risk-driven iterations (risk analysis each loop); incremental: deliver in stages, each adding functionality OOP: class = attributes + methods; encapsulation hides state, inheritance reuses (is-a), polymorphism = one call, many behaviours (OCR 1.2.6) Compiler: whole-program translation before run — fast execution; interpreter: line-by-line at run time — immediate error reporting; assembler: assembly to machine code (OCR 1.2.3) Testing levels: unit (one subroutine), integration (modules together), alpha (in-house), beta (real users), acceptance (customer sign-off) (OCR 1.2.4) Test data: normal (valid), boundary (edges of valid ranges), erroneous (invalid — must be rejected); white box tests internal paths, black box tests behaviour only Legal: Data Protection Act 2018 (data principles), Computer Misuse Act 1990 (unauthorised access), Copyright Designs & Patents Act 1988, RIPA 2000 (OCR 1.5) SDLC Software Development Life Cycle: the structured stages a software project passes through — analysis, design, implementation, testing, evaluation/maintenance. Waterfall model A linear SDLC where each stage completes before the next begins; requirements are fixed up front, so change is expensive. Agile development An iterative SDLC delivering working software in short sprints, embracing changing requirements and continuous customer feedback. Prototype An early, partial version of a system built to clarify requirements or demonstrate feasibility before full development (AQA 4.12). Paradigm A style or model of programming: procedural (sequence of subroutine calls), object-oriented (objects exchanging messages), declarative/functional. Class A template defining the attributes (data) and methods (behaviour) of a type; an object is an instance of a class. Encapsulation Binding attributes and methods together in a class and hiding internal state (private attributes) behind a public interface. Inheritance A subclass deriving attributes and methods from a superclass, adding or overriding behaviour; an is-a relationship. Polymorphism The same method call behaving differently depending on the object's actual class — each subclass overrides the method with its own implementation. Compiler vs interpreter A compiler translates the whole program to machine code before execution (fast execution, one build); an interpreter translates and executes line by line at run time (slower, immediate errors). The SDLC (OCR 1.2.4, AQA 4.9) is the sequence of stages every project passes through: analysis (establish requirements with the client — the problem, not the solution), design (data structures, algorithms, module structure, UI), implementation (coding to the design), testing (verifying against the requirements), evaluation (does it meet the original goals?) and maintenance (AQA 4.11: corrective — fixing bugs found in use; adaptive — responding to changed environments; perfective — improving it beyond the original spec). Waterfall runs the stages linearly, each completing before the next begins. Strengths: simple to manage, clear milestones, thorough documentation, suits projects with fixed, well-understood requirements (contracted, safety-critical, regulatory). Weaknesses: requirements are frozen up front, so late feedback; a wrong decision in analysis propagates; the customer sees nothing working until the end; change is expensive. The exam one-liner: waterfall assumes requirements are known and stable — it fails when they change. Agile develops in short iterations ( sprints , typically 1–4 weeks), each delivering a working increment reviewed by the customer; requirements are re-prioritised every sprint. Strengths: working software early and often, welcomes changing requirements, continuous customer feedback, risks surface early. Weaknesses: needs constant customer involvement, less predictable final cost/timeline, documentation can be thin, harder to contract. Exam one-liner: agile assumes requirements will change — it embraces that with iteration. Spiral loops through planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation — each loop addressing the biggest current risk; suited to large, high-risk projects where risk analysis per iteration is worth its cost. Incremental delivers the system in stages, each adding functionality to a working core; overlaps with agile but without mandating short sprints or customer ceremonies. Prototyping (AQA 4.12) builds an early partial version — throwaway prototypes clarify requirements and are discarded; evolutionary prototypes grow into the final system; both reduce the risk of building the wrong thing. The 9-marker this topic almost always takes: 'Explain why organisation X should use [model] for project Y.' The full-credit structure: (1) identify Y's defining characteristic — requirements stable or changing? deadline or budget fixed? high-risk? (2) match the model: fixed requirements → waterfall; changing requirements/unclear needs → agile or prototyping; high-risk → spiral; (3) justify with two consequences of the match (e.g. agile delivers working increments early so the client can course-correct, avoiding building the wrong product); (4) concede one weakness and why it is tolerable here. An A* answer argues both sides before concluding. Example conclusion: a startup building an app with unclear market fit should use agile — requirements will change as users give feedback, and short sprints mean the product pivots cheaply; waterfall's frozen requirements would bake in early guesses, and its single end-of-project delivery would arrive after the market moved. A paradigm (OCR 1.2.6) is a style of programming. The examinable set: procedural — programs as sequences of subroutine calls over shared data; object-oriented — programs as interacting objects, each bundling data and behaviour; declarative/functional — programs as expressions and function applications (AQA 4.8: map, filter, fold/reduce), stating what not how . The comparison to quote: procedural suits problems modelled as step-by-step algorithms; OOP suits systems with many entity types interacting (GUIs, simulations, games); functional suits data transformation pipelines. OOP concepts (OCR 1.2.6, WJEC Unit 4) — learn each with its one-line benefit: Class and object: a class defines attributes + methods; an object is an instance. Benefit: one definition, many instances. Encapsulation: attributes are private; access goes through public methods (getters/setters). Benefit: internal state cannot be corrupted by outside code; the implementation can change without breaking callers — the class maintains its own invariants (e.g. a setter rejects negative balances). Inheritance: a subclass extends a superclass (an is-a relationship), reusing its attributes and methods and adding/overriding. Benefit: code reuse; a common interface over related types. Polymorphism: the same method call behaves differently per actual class — each subclass overrides the method. Benefit: code written against the superclass works for all subclasses without conditionals. Worked example — the classic exam design (vehicles): class Vehicle: def __init__(self, wheels): self.wheels = wheels # private in spirit def describe(self): return 'Vehicle with ' + str(self.wheels) + ' wheels' class Car(Vehicle): # Car is-a Vehicle (inheritance) def __init__(self, wheels, plates): super().__init__(wheels) self.plates = plates def describe(self): # overridden (polymorphism) return 'Car, ' + str(self.wheels) + ' wheels, plate ' + self.plates vehicles = [Car(4, 'AB12 CDE'), Vehicle(2)] for v in vehicles: print(v.describe()) # one call, two behaviours Trace: the loop calls describe() on each element without knowing its class; Python dispatches to the actual class's method — output 'Car, 4 wheels, plate AB12 CDE' then 'Vehicle with 2 wheels' . That is polymorphism: the call site is unchanged whether the list holds cars, bikes or trucks — adding a new subclass requires no change to this code, which is the evaluation point examiners want (open/closed principle in spirit). Exam patterns: 'Explain the difference between a class and an object' (class is the template, object is an instance of it); 'Explain why encapsulation improves maintainability' (state is accessed only through methods, so the representation can change freely and invalid values are rejected at the boundary); 'Explain what is meant by inheritance and state one benefit' (subclass derives from superclass, is-a; benefit: reuse of attributes/methods and a common interface). Full marks consistently require the benefit sentence, not just the definition. High-level languages must be translated to machine code (OCR 1.2.3, AQA 4.4). The three translators and their trade-offs: Compiler: translates the whole program to machine code before execution. Fast execution (native code, translated once); reports all syntax errors after a full compile; errors listed with line numbers; the executable runs without the compiler or source. Slower development loop — recompile after every change; error messages can be less immediate. Interpreter: translates and executes line by line at run time. Execution is slower (re-translated every run); stops at the first error — excellent for debugging and learning; needs the interpreter present on every machine. Development is fast: run immediately, no build step. Assembler: translates assembly language (mnemonics such as LDA, ADD) one-to-one into machine code — low level, processor-specific. The comparison to reproduce: 'Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.' Model phrasing: a compiler translates the entire source program into machine code before execution, producing an executable that runs quickly and independently of the compiler, and reporting syntax errors after a full pass; an interpreter translates and executes statements one at a time at run time, so execution is slower but errors are reported immediately and no build step is needed. Bytecode and virtual machines — the A* extension: languages such as Java compile source to bytecode , an intermediate representation executed by the Java Virtual Machine (a bytecode interpreter/JIT compiler). The benefit: platform independence — 'write once, run anywhere': one compiled artefact runs on any machine with a JVM, because the JVM adapts the final translation to each processor. The cost: an extra execution layer, so slower than fully native compilation (partly recovered by JIT). Exam pattern: 'Explain why Java programs can run on many different processors.' Answer: source is compiled to bytecode, an intermediate form not tied to any processor; the JVM on each platform translates bytecode to that processor's machine code at run time, so the same bytecode runs wherever a JVM exists. Also be ready to link translators to the FDE cycle: whatever the translator, the processor ultimately executes machine code fetched instruction by instruction — assembly language is the human-readable form of exactly those instructions (opcode + operand), one mnemonic per machine instruction for the target architecture. Testing levels (OCR 1.2.4, AQA 4.9) — learn the ladder and what each catches: Unit testing: each subroutine tested in isolation with known inputs and expected outputs — catches logic errors early, where they are cheapest to fix. Integration testing: modules tested together — catches interface errors: mismatched parameters, wrong data formats between modules, assumptions one module makes about another. Alpha testing: in-house testing by the development team on the complete system. Beta testing: released to real users outside the team — catches usage patterns and environment differences in-house testing cannot reproduce. Acceptance testing: the customer verifies the system meets the agreed requirements before sign-off. The exam pattern: 'Explain why unit testing alone is not sufficient.' Answer: units can each pass while the system fails — interface errors between them (mismatched parameters, incompatible data formats, misread return values) are only found when modules are tested together, which is integration testing's purpose; and only beta/acceptance testing exposes real-user conditions. Test types: black box testing supplies inputs and checks outputs without seeing the code — testing the specified behaviour; white box (structural) testing designs tests from the code itself, aiming to exercise every branch and path (each if-side, each loop exit). The comparison: white box can prove all paths execute but only tests what the code does (bugs of omission escape); black box tests the requirement but may miss internal branches. Test data — three categories, the guaranteed exam question: Normal: valid, typical values — a mark of 65 in 0–100. Boundary: the edges of validity — 0, 1, 99, 100 for the range 0–100 (and just outside: −1, 101, catching off-by-one errors). Erroneous: invalid input that must be rejected — 'abc', 150, −5; the program must reject gracefully, not crash. Exam pattern: 'A program validates an age between 13 and 19 inclusive. State the test data you would use and the expected outcome for each.' Answer: normal — 16 (accepted); boundary — 13, 19 (accepted), 12, 20 (rejected — just outside catches off-by-one comparison errors); erroneous — 'abc', negative numbers (rejected with an error message). The boundary-just-outside values are what earn the top marks, because they detect the classic vs error. Test-driven development (TDD) — write the test first, watch it fail, write the minimum code to pass, refactor. The benefit to quote: tests encode the requirements before implementation, so the code is verified against the spec continuously and regressions are caught the moment they appear; the cost: more up-front effort, and tests can encode a wrong understanding of the spec as faithfully as the code would. Four UK laws cover the examined ground (OCR 1.5, WJEC 1.10) — learn each with its scope and a scenario: Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR: governs personal data — data relating to identifiable living individuals. Principles: data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified purposes; kept accurate and up to date; kept no longer than necessary; kept secure; and transferred only with adequate protection. Individuals' rights: access their data, correction, erasure. Scenario: a company storing customer records must secure them and delete them when no longer needed; a breach must be reported. Computer Misuse Act 1990: three offences: unauthorised access (accessing someone else's account/system — even without damage); unauthorised access with intent to commit further crime; unauthorised modification (viruses, ransomware, altering data). Scenario: guessing a friend's password is the first offence; deploying ransomware is the third. Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988: protects creative works including software — copying or distributing software without a licence is illegal; proprietary licences restrict use/copying, open-source licences (GPL, MIT) grant it under conditions. Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA): governs surveillance and interception of communications by public bodies — when and how communications data may be accessed and warrants obtained. Exam pattern: 'State the legislation that covers [scenario] and explain its relevance.' Answer structure: name the Act precisely (with year), state its scope in one line, apply it: e.g. an employee accessing customer records without authorisation — Computer Misuse Act 1990, unauthorised access offence; if they then copy the records, Data Protection Act 2018 governs how that personal data may be processed. Ethical issues beyond the law — the evaluation questions ('discuss the ethical issues...') reward balance. The standard axes: privacy (collecting more personal data than necessary; tracking; surveillance vs security benefits), employment (automation displacing roles while creating others), bias and fairness (machine-learning systems trained on biased data making discriminatory decisions), digital divide (unequal access to technology), environmental (energy use of data centres and crypto-mining), and professional behaviour (ACM/BCS codes of conduct: competence, honesty, public interest). The A* structure: give both sides (benefit and harm), then a reasoned judgement: e.g. a facial-recognition system in schools — benefit: security and safeguarding; harms: privacy of minors, consent issues, biased accuracy across demographics; judgement: the intrusion must be proportionate to the benefit, with consent and independent oversight. Non-functional requirements (AQA 4.10) tie the section together: the qualities beyond function the system must meet — performance (response times), usability, security, reliability, capacity, maintainability. The exam point: functional requirements say what the system does; non-functional say how well it must do it, and they are measurable — 'respond within 2 seconds' is testable, 'must be fast' is not. Ethical and legal compliance (DPA security principle, accessibility) are themselves non-functional requirements a design must state explicitly to be evaluated.

topics.name: Markets: Supply and Demand
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics Markets: Supply and Demand Draw and shift demand and supply curves correctly, distinguishing movements along from shifts of the curve Calculate and interpret PED, YED, XED and PES, applying each to pricing, revenue, tax incidence and business strategy Explain the three functions of the price mechanism and the interrelationship between markets (joint, competitive, composite and derived demand) Analyse market equilibrium, shortage and surplus, and evaluate how elasticities determine the speed of adjustment Compare market structures using surplus analysis, showing the deadweight loss of monopoly against perfect competition Evaluate monopoly using dynamic efficiency, economies of scale and X-inefficiency arguments Analyse wage determination using MRP and the monopsony model, and evaluate the effect of a National Minimum Wage Price elasticity of demand (PED) The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price; measures responsiveness of demand to price. Income elasticity of demand (YED) The percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income; positive for normal, negative for inferior goods. Cross elasticity of demand (XED) The percentage change in quantity demanded of good A divided by the percentage change in the price of good B; positive for substitutes, negative for complements. Price elasticity of supply (PES) The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price; determined mainly by the time period and spare capacity. Price mechanism The allocation of resources by prices acting as signals, incentives and rationing devices (Smith's invisible hand). Consumer surplus The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay; the area under demand above price. Allocative efficiency The output level where P = MC, so the value society places on the last unit equals its marginal cost; total surplus is maximised. Derived demand Demand for a factor of production (such as labour) that arises from demand for the good or service it produces. Marginal revenue product (MRP) Marginal physical product multiplied by marginal revenue; the demand curve for labour. Monopsony A market with a single buyer of labour, whose marginal cost of labour lies above the supply curve, depressing wages and employment. The law of demand : as price falls, quantity demanded rises (an inverse relationship), ceteris paribus. Three explanations earn AO1 marks: the income effect (a lower price raises real income, so more can be bought), the substitution effect (the good becomes relatively cheaper than alternatives) and diminishing marginal utility (each extra unit gives less satisfaction, so consumers only buy additional units at a lower price). Determinants of demand : income (normal goods vs inferior goods), tastes and preferences, the price of substitutes (Coke and Pepsi) and complements (printers and ink), expectations of future prices (expected rises bring purchases forward), and the number of buyers. Determinants of supply : costs of production, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, and the number of firms in the market. Movements vs shifts — the single most common source of lost marks: a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve (extension or contraction); a change in any other determinant shifts the whole curve. Before drawing any diagram, ask which variable has changed. Diagram description: axes are price (vertical) against quantity (horizontal); a downward-sloping demand curve D and upward-sloping supply curve S intersect at equilibrium (P*, Q*). If demand shifts right from D1 to D2, at the old price P1 quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (excess demand); price is bid up along both curves to a new equilibrium P2, Q2 — a price rise (extension of supply) with higher quantity. A supply shift works symmetrically: higher costs shift S left, raising price and cutting quantity (stagflation-style outcome in micro form). The price mechanism (Adam Smith's “invisible hand”) performs three functions: signalling — prices convey information about relative scarcity; incentive — higher prices encourage production and discourage consumption; rationing — scarce goods are allocated to those willing and able to pay. Together these allocate resources without central planning; Hayek's “knowledge problem” argument holds that no planner can aggregate dispersed price information. Interrelated markets (AQA 4.1.2.7): joint demand (complements bought together), competitive demand (substitutes), composite demand (one good with several uses, e.g. milk for drinking or cheese), and derived demand (labour is demanded because of the demand for its output). A price change in one market feeds into others — e.g. a wheat price rise raises bread prices and cuts demand for butter — a chain-of-reasoning staple in data-response questions. PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP (negative by the law of demand; quote the absolute value). |PED| Label Meaning > 1 Elastic Quantity responds proportionally more than price Inelastic Quantity responds proportionally less than price = 1 Unitary Proportional response; total revenue constant = 0 Perfectly inelastic Vertical demand curve = ∞ Perfectly elastic Horizontal demand curve (price taker) Determinants of PED : number and closeness of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, the proportion of income spent on the good, habit/addiction, the time period (demand is more elastic in the long run as consumers adjust), and the breadth of the market definition (a single brand has many substitutes; “food” has almost none). Uses of PED : revenue maximisation — raise price while |PED| YED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔIncome . Normal goods have YED > 0 (necessities 0 1); inferior goods have YED 1) suffer most in downturns. This makes demand in cyclical, income-sensitive industries volatile. XED = %ΔQd of A ÷ %ΔP of B . Substitutes have XED > 0 (Coke and Pepsi); complements have XED Worked example (adapted from a real exam-style calculation): a coffee shop raises latte prices by 10% and quantity demanded falls 4% → PED = −0.4, inelastic; total revenue changes by (1.10 × 0.96) − 1 ≈ +5.6%. But if all coffee shops raise prices together, market demand is more elastic (supermarket coffee is a substitute), so the revenue gain shrinks — the difference between a firm's demand curve and the market demand curve is a key evaluation point. PES = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP ; elastic when > 1. Determinants : spare capacity, stock levels, the time period (the crucial one — supply is more elastic in the long run because all factors can be varied and firms can enter or exit), the mobility and availability of factors of production, and the length of the production cycle. Inelastic-supply examples : housing (planning constraints, construction lags), agriculture (growing seasons), and oil (extraction capacity). Consequence: demand shocks translate into large price swings — the wheat price spike after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and UK rent inflation, both reflect inelastic supply meeting shifting demand. Equilibrium occurs where Qd = Qs at P* — the market-clearing price with no tendency to change. A shortage (excess demand) at any price below P* puts upward pressure on price; a surplus (excess supply) above P* puts downward pressure on it, as unsold stocks build. The market is self-correcting, but the speed and size of adjustment depend on both elasticities: the more inelastic the curves, the larger the price change needed to restore equilibrium. Diagram description: at price P1 below equilibrium, draw the horizontal gap between the demand and supply curves — the shortage; an arrow shows price rising to P* where the gap closes. Buffer stock schemes (used historically for commodities such as coffee under the International Coffee Agreement): the agency buys in gluts and sells from stock in shortages to stabilise the price. Evaluation: storage is costly, and if supply shocks persist (repeated bad harvests) the agency exhausts its funds — so buffer stocks manage volatility but cannot abolish it. Exam technique: in data-response questions, always complete the chain — shock → curve shift → new equilibrium price and quantity → extension/contraction on the other curve → welfare implication. Missing the final link is where AO2 marks are dropped; quoting elasticities in the analysis is where AO3 is earned. Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price paid — what consumers were willing to pay minus what they actually pay. Producer surplus is the area above the supply curve and below the price. Total surplus is maximised where allocative efficiency holds: P = MC, so the value society places on the marginal unit equals its marginal cost of production. Any price above MC (monopoly power, indirect tax) or below it (maximum price, subsidy distortions) creates deadweight welfare loss — surplus destroyed with no offsetting gain to anyone. Diagram description (monopoly vs perfect competition): axes price/quantity; a downward-sloping demand curve D with marginal revenue MR below it (MR has twice the slope of a linear demand curve); an upward-sloping MC and U-shaped AC. Under perfect competition the firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve, producing where P = MC; long-run equilibrium is P = minimum AC (normal profit only). The monopolist sets MR = MC at Qm MC. The deadweight loss is the triangle between demand and MC over the output gap Qm to Qpc; consumer surplus falls, part being transferred to the monopolist as supernormal profit, sustained in the long run by barriers to entry (legal barriers such as patents, economies of scale, brand loyalty, control of key inputs, predatory pricing). Structure Firms Product Entry barriers Long-run profit Perfect competition Many, price takers Homogeneous None Normal only (P = min AC) Monopolistic competition Many Differentiated Low Normal (excess capacity) Oligopoly Few, interdependent Homogeneous or differentiated High Supernormal possible (collusion/non-price competition) Monopoly One (25%+ market share definition) Unique/no close substitutes Very high Supernormal sustained Evaluation (the A* framing): static DWL is not the whole story. Dynamic efficiency : supernormal profit funds R&D and innovation (Schumpeter's creative-destruction argument), so monopoly may deliver faster product improvement. Economies of scale : a large monopolist's AC may be far below that of many small competitive firms, so Pm could be lower than the competitive price the model predicts. Price discrimination can raise output closer to the competitive level and share gains with consumers. Counting against monopoly: X-inefficiency (costs drift above minimum AC without competitive pressure) and weak incentives to innovate behind protected markets. Competition authorities therefore judge each case on its merits — market share alone is not evidence of consumer harm. Derived demand : labour is demanded because of the demand for its output. The marginal revenue product (MRP = MPP × MR) curve is the demand for labour; a profit-maximising firm hires where MCL = MRP — in a competitive labour market the wage equals MRP. Wage differentials reflect differences in MRP, human capital and skills, compensating differentials for unpleasant or risky work, and barriers to entry such as professional qualifications. Labour supply to an occupation depends on wages, non-monetary benefits, qualifications required, and participation decisions; at very high wages the income effect can eventually outweigh the substitution effect (the backward-bending supply curve) as workers choose more leisure. Monopsony : a market with a single buyer of labour (a large employer in a small town, or the NHS for certain specialists). Because hiring one more worker requires raising the wage for all workers, the marginal cost of labour (MCL) lies above the upward-sloping supply curve. Unregulated, the monopsonist hires where MCL = MRP, giving employment Q1 and wage W1 (read off the supply curve) — both below the competitive outcome (Wc, Qc where S = MRP): the monopsonist exploits its buyer power. Diagram description: axes wage/employment; upward-sloping labour supply S (= ACL) with MCL above it; downward-sloping MRP (demand). Mark Q1/W1 at MCL = MRP; mark Qc/Wc at S = MRP; shade the under-employment gap. National Minimum/Living Wage intervention: a statutory wage set at Wc (above W1 but below the MCL at Q1) makes the supply of labour horizontal (perfectly elastic) up to Qc — the monopsonist can hire more workers at a constant wage. The wage rises and employment rises: the minimum wage corrects the monopsony distortion. UK data: the National Living Wage rose to £11.44 an hour in April 2024 and £12.21 in April 2025; Low Pay Commission evidence (and the famous Card–Krueger studies) suggests moderate rises have had little negative employment effect, consistent with monopsony power in low-paid labour markets. Trade unions use collective bargaining to push wages above MRP-equivalent levels; in a monopsony a union can offset employer power without costing jobs. Evaluation: the benign outcome holds only if monopsony power genuinely exists — in competitive labour markets a minimum wage above equilibrium causes unemployment (Qs > Qd), concentrated on young and low-skilled workers whose MRP is low; firms may instead cut hours, benefits or training; and enforcement matters where gig-economy misclassification hides true employment relationships. The exam-ready judgement: the effect of a minimum wage depends on the structure of the labour market, its level relative to the market wage, and the state of labour demand.

topics.name: Market Failure and Government Intervention
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics Market Failure and Government Intervention Draw and interpret externality diagrams, identifying Q1, Q*, the welfare loss and which curve shifts Distinguish merit from demerit goods and evaluate interventions for each Explain the free-rider problem for public and quasi-public goods and evaluate state provision Analyse adverse selection and moral hazard, and assess signalling, screening and regulatory remedies Evaluate Pigouvian taxes, subsidies, tradable permits, regulation and price controls using elasticity, information and cost criteria Identify the five causes of government failure and apply them to real interventions Construct balanced judgements weighing the size of market failure against the risk of government failure Market failure When the price mechanism allocates resources inefficiently — MSB does not equal MSC at the market output. Externality A cost or benefit imposed on a third party outside a market transaction, causing a divergence between private and social costs or benefits. Merit good A good that is under-consumed in the free market because of positive externalities and information gaps (e.g. education, vaccination). Demerit good A good that is over-consumed because of negative externalities and imperfect information about long-run costs (e.g. cigarettes). Public good A good that is non-excludable and non-rival in consumption (e.g. national defence), so markets underprovide it. Free-rider problem When non-excludable users cannot be charged, individuals let others pay, so voluntary provision collapses. Adverse selection Pre-contract asymmetric information: higher-risk parties are more likely to enter transactions, so average pricing drives out low-risk customers. Moral hazard Post-contract hidden action: once insured or bailed out, agents take more risks because part of the cost falls on others. Pigouvian tax An indirect tax set equal to the marginal external cost, internalising a negative externality. Government failure When intervention worsens resource allocation compared with the free market, via information gaps, administrative costs, regulatory capture, unintended consequences or rent-seeking. Market failure occurs when the price mechanism allocates resources inefficiently — marginal social benefit does not equal marginal social cost at the market output. Externalities are costs or benefits imposed on third parties outside the transaction, causing a divergence between private and social costs/benefits. A negative production externality (pollution) means MSC > MPC; a positive consumption externality (education, vaccination) means MSB > MPB. Formally: MSC = MPC + MEC and MSB = MPB + MEB. Diagram description (negative production externality): axes price/quantity; MPB = demand (downward-sloping); MPC = supply (upward-sloping); MSC drawn above MPC, vertically separated by the constant marginal external cost. Free market: MPC = MPB at Q1 (overproduction). Social optimum: MSC = MSB at Q* deadweight welfare loss is the triangle between MSC and MSB over that gap. For a positive externality the logic mirrors: MSB above MPB, free market underproduces at Q1 Merit goods (education, healthcare, vaccination) are goods whose consumption generates positive externalities and/or whose benefits are underestimated by consumers due to information gaps — under-consumed in the free market. Demerit goods (cigarettes, gambling) are over-consumed: negative externalities plus imperfect information (consumers underestimate long-run costs). Worked example (real exam-style calculation): a factory pollutes a river with MPC = 20 + Q, MEC = 5, MPB = 100 − Q. Market: MPC = MPB → 20 + Q = 100 − Q → Q = 40. Social optimum: MSC = MSB → 20 + Q + 5 = 100 − Q → Q = 37.5. The Pigouvian tax equals MEC = £5 per unit; at Q = 37.5 price = 100 − 37.5 = 62.5 and tax revenue = 5 × 37.5 = £187.5. Exam technique: always name the externality, identify which curve shifts, mark both Q1 and Q*, and shade the DWL — the diagram carries half the available marks in AQA Paper 1 Section B. A public good has two defining characteristics: non-excludable — it is impossible (or prohibitively costly) to prevent people from consuming it once provided; and non-rival — one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available to others. Examples: national defence, street lighting, flood defences, clean air, the lighthouse (the classic textbook case). Quasi-public goods are partially excludable or partially rival: roads (congestion makes them rival; tolls make them excludable), museums, broadcast TV (encryption), beaches. The free-rider problem : because non-excludable users cannot be charged, each individual has an incentive to let others pay — everyone reasons this way, so voluntary markets underprovide or fail to provide the good entirely. Chain of reasoning: non-excludable → free riders cannot be excluded → no revenue for private providers → profit-maximising firms will not supply → the good is underprovided relative to the social optimum → total surplus is lost (a DWL equal to the forgone benefits). This is a complete market failure: no market price exists to ration provision. Solution: state provision financed by taxation (defence, street lighting) — the government estimates the socially optimal quantity and taxes beneficiaries. Evaluation: the government faces an information gap in valuing public goods — cost–benefit analysis of flood defences or new roads is uncertain, and political incentives (visible projects before elections) distort choice; taxation itself creates deadweight losses; and quasi-public goods can sometimes be charged for (road pricing, subscription TV), which partially restores a market. The complete vs partial distinction (pure public good vs quasi-public good) is the discriminator between high marks: clean air is pure; motorways are quasi and can be priced. Asymmetric information — one party to a transaction knows more than the other — causes two classic failures. Adverse selection (pre-contract, hidden information): high-risk individuals are more likely to buy insurance because they know they will claim, while low-risk people find the average premium too high and stay out; the insurance pool becomes dominated by high-risk clients, premiums rise, more low-risk customers leave — a “death spiral” that can collapse the market (Akerlof's “market for lemons” in used cars). Moral hazard (post-contract, hidden action): once insured, people take more risks or take less care, because part of the cost falls on the insurer — e.g. careless driving after buying comprehensive cover, or banks taking excessive risks expecting bailouts. Market solutions: signalling — the informed party reveals quality (warranties, qualifications, no-claims bonuses, brand reputation); screening — the uninformed party gathers information (application forms, medical exams, driving records); excesses/deductibles — the claimant pays the first part of any loss, deterring high-risk customers and reducing moral hazard; experience rating — premiums adjusted over time to claims history. Government solutions: mandatory disclosure (nutrition labels, financial services regulation), compulsory insurance (motor), and regulation of professional standards (FCA conduct rules). Evaluation: screening is costly and never perfect — information gaps persist; risk-based pricing can make insurance unaffordable for genuinely high-risk groups (genetic testing raises equity and ethical issues, hence the UK moratorium on genetic test results in life insurance); and excesses create their own problem — moral hazard falls but small claims go unclaimed, weakening the insurance function. A well-structured answer defines both forms of information failure, gives one market and one government remedy for each, then evaluates whether the remedy restores efficiency or merely shifts the failure elsewhere. Indirect (Pigouvian) taxes equal to the marginal external cost shift MPC up to MSC, internalising the externality: price rises to P*, output falls to Q*, and the DWL is eliminated. Diagram description: supply shifts left (up) by the tax per unit; the new intersection with demand marks Q*; the vertical gap between old and new supply equals the tax.
