Cultural bias: most classic research used US samples; collectivist cultures show higher conformity (Smith and Bond), so findings may not generalise - though Meeus and Raaijmakers (Netherlands) and Burger (2009, US replication finding 67.5% obedience for men) show the effects are fairly robust. Historical validity: society has changed; Burger's replication and the BBC Prison Study suggest the classic findings are partly period-specific, and modern replication is essential before applying them. Applications: research explains real phenomena - obedience in hierarchical organisations (military, healthcare), minority influence in campaigns (Suffragettes, recycling, energy conservation) and resistance programmes in schools - demonstrating the topic's practical value.

topics.name: Memory
topics.subject: psychology
topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Memory Describe and evaluate the multi-store model (Atkinson-Shiffrin 1968), citing coding, capacity and duration evidence (AQA 4.1.2) Describe and evaluate the working memory model (Baddeley-Hitch 1974): central executive, phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad, episodic buffer (AQA 4.1.2) Distinguish episodic, semantic and procedural LTM with supporting case studies (HM, Clive Wearing) (AQA 4.1.2) Evaluate interference (proactive/retroactive) and retrieval failure as explanations of forgetting (AQA 4.1.2) Evaluate eyewitness testimony research: misleading information and anxiety (Loftus and Palmer, weapon focus) (AQA 4.1.2; OCR Loftus and Palmer 1974) Describe and evaluate the cognitive interview and its effectiveness (AQA 4.1.2) MSM: sensory (iconic/echoic, <1s) → attention → STM (acoustic, 7±2, 18-30s) → rehearsal → LTM (semantic, unlimited); supported by primacy/recency (Glanzer and Cunitz) Evidence for stores: Peterson and Peterson (1959) STM duration; Bahrick et al. (1975) LTM duration; Baddeley (1966) acoustic vs semantic coding; KF case challenges unitary STM WMM: CE (attention/allocation, limited), PL (articulatory process, word-length effect), VSSP (visual/spatial, Logie), EB (added 2000, integrates); supported by dual-task studies and KF Types of LTM: episodic (time-stamped events), semantic (facts), procedural (skills); HM and Clive Wearing: episodic impaired, procedural intact; Tulving PET: episodic right prefrontal, semantic left Forgetting: interference (proactive old→new, retroactive new→old; McGeoch and McDonald; Baddeley and Hitch rugby players), retrieval failure (Godden and Baddeley 1975 divers; Goodwin state cues) EWT: misleading information (Loftus and Palmer 1974 'smashed' 41mph vs 'hit' 34mph; Gabbert et al. 2003 conformity effect 71%), anxiety (weapon focus, Deffenbacher 2004 inverted-U; Christianson and Hubinette better real recall) Cognitive interview: context reinstatement, report everything, reverse order, change perspective; Fisher et al. 1990 more correct details; Kohnken et al. 1999 meta-analysis; enhanced CI used by UK police Encoding The way information is changed into a form the memory system can store: acoustic (sound) in STM, semantic (meaning) in LTM. Capacity The amount of information a store can hold: 7 ± 2 items in STM (Miller 1956), effectively unlimited in LTM. Duration How long information remains in a store: under 30 seconds in STM without rehearsal (Peterson and Peterson 1959), potentially a lifetime in LTM (Bahrick et al. 1975). Multi-store model Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) linear model: sensory memory, STM and LTM as separate unitary stores linked by attention and rehearsal. Working memory model Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) replacement for unitary STM: an active multi-component system comprising the central executive, phonological loop, visuo-spatial sketchpad and (added 2000) episodic buffer. Proactive interference Forgetting when older (previously learned) memories disrupt recall of newer information - old disrupts new. Retroactive interference Forgetting when newer learning disrupts recall of older memories - new disrupts old. Retrieval failure Forgetting that occurs because a memory is available in LTM but the cues needed to access it are absent (cue-dependent forgetting). Encoding specificity principle (Tulving) A retrieval cue is only effective if it was present at encoding - the cue must match the way the memory was originally encoded. Cognitive interview Geiselman and Fisher's method for improving eyewitness recall using four techniques: context reinstatement, report everything, reverse order and change perspective. The multi-store model (MSM) proposes three separate memory stores linked in a linear sequence by attention and rehearsal: sensory memory (iconic for visual, echoic for auditory; very large capacity but duration under one second, unless attention is paid, in which case information passes to...), STM (coding mainly acoustic , capacity of 7 ± 2 items - Miller 1956's 'magic number'; duration of 18-30 seconds - Peterson and Peterson 1959, where 90% of three-consonant trigrams were forgotten after 18 seconds of distraction) and LTM (coding mainly semantic , unlimited capacity, potentially lifelong duration). Information moves from sensory to STM via attention and from STM to LTM via rehearsal : maintenance rehearsal (repetition, keeps in STM) and elaborative rehearsal (linking to existing knowledge, transfers to LTM). Retrieval from LTM returns information to STM for conscious use. Evidence: (1) Glanzer and Cunitz (1966) - the serial position effect : participants recalled words from the start of a list (primacy, LTM via rehearsal) and the end (recency, still in STM) but not the middle; a 30-second counting task before recall abolished the recency effect, supporting a separate STM store. (2) Baddeley (1966) - participants confused acoustically similar words (cat, cap, can) in STM but semantically similar words (great, large, big) in LTM, supporting different coding. (3) Case study KF (motorcycle accident) - impaired verbal STM but intact visual memory, challenging the idea of one unitary STM store. (4) Bahrick et al. (1975) - US graduates recognised yearbook photos up to 48 years later at 90% accuracy, showing LTM duration is potentially lifelong. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - supporting evidence: brain-imaging (different active regions for STM/LTM tasks), case studies (HM, KF) and the serial position effect all converge on multiple stores. Limitation - oversimplified: KF's dissociation (impaired verbal, intact visual STM) contradicts a unitary STM; the working memory model supersedes it. Limitation - rehearsal not the only route: Craik and Lockhart's (1972) levels-of-processing approach and flashbulb memories show information enters LTM without prolonged rehearsal (deep processing matters more than repetition). Limitation - artificial evidence: most support (trigrams, word lists) uses lab tasks with low ecological validity; everyday memory is richer (faces, events). Strength - practical: the model underpins revision technique itself (elaborative rehearsal, chunking) and multi-store logic appears in exam questions on encoding/capacity/duration studies. The working memory model (WMM) replaces unitary STM with an active , multi-component system that manipulates information while performing tasks. Components: (1) the central executive - allocates attention and slave-system resources, has very limited capacity and no modality-specific storage; (2) the phonological loop (PL) - processes speech-based and auditory information, split into the phonological store (holds heard words, 'inner ear', ~2 seconds) and the articulatory process ('inner voice', allows subvocal rehearsal; its limited capacity explains the word-length effect - longer words are harder to recall because they take longer to rehearse, Baddeley et al. 1975); (3) the visuo-spatial sketchpad (VSSP) - processes visual and spatial data, subdivided by Logie (1995) into the visual cache and inner scribe ; (4) the episodic buffer (added 2000) - integrates the CE, PL and VSSP with LTM, providing a limited-capacity 'store' for combined information and explaining how we form integrated episodes. Evidence: (1) Dual-task performance - Baddeley and Hitch found participants could track a moving light (VSSP) while performing a verbal reasoning task (PL) with little interference, but performance collapsed when both tasks used the same component - supporting separate slave systems. (2) Case study KF - impaired verbal STM but intact visual STM supports the PL/VSSP distinction. (3) Brain imaging - different activation areas for verbal (left hemisphere) versus visual (right) tasks. (4) The word-length effect disappears when articulation is suppressed (saying 'the the the'), confirming the articulatory process. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - experimental support: dual-task studies are robust, replicable and directly test the model's predictions; the word-length effect is a reliable laboratory finding. Strength - clinical evidence: KF and other brain-damaged patients support dissociable components, giving the model converging validity across methods. Limitation - central executive underspecified: the CE is 'the most important but least understood component' - vague, unitary and hard to test empirically; some researchers argue it should be subdivided. Limitation - case study generalisability: KF's impairment may involve more than one damaged component (Hitch and others noted other damage); single cases may not generalise. Limitation - LTM interaction: the original model said little about how working memory links to LTM; the 2000 episodic buffer was bolted on partly to fix this, showing the model is incomplete. Tulving (1972, 1985) distinguished three LTM systems. Episodic memory : personal, time-stamped memories of events (your last birthday), consciously recalled and prone to distortion. Semantic memory : general knowledge and facts (capital of France), not time-stamped, constantly updated. Procedural memory : implicit motor skills and actions (riding a bike), recalled without conscious effort and highly resistant to forgetting. Evidence: HM (hippocampus removed to treat epilepsy in 1953) could form no new episodic memories but retained procedural skills and some semantic knowledge; Clive Wearing (herpes encephalitis) similarly lost episodic memory (seconds-long awareness) while remaining able to play the piano - dissociation supporting distinct stores. Tulving's PET scans (1989) : episodic retrieval activated the right prefrontal cortex, semantic the left - physical evidence for separate systems. The case studies also link to the MSM debate: LTM is not a single store. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - converging evidence: clinical cases (HM, Clive Wearing), neuroimaging (Tulving) and everyday dissociations (knowing how vs knowing that) all support separate LTM systems. Strength - practical application: distinctions guide dementia care (procedural memory often spared) and eyewitness research (episodic memory is what EWT measures). Limitation - case study weakness: HM's and Wearing's brain damage was severe and widespread, so clean dissociation is hard to prove; cases may not generalise. Limitation - overlapping categories: semantic and episodic systems interact in everyday recall (a personal memory of a fact lesson), so the divisions may be less neat than the model suggests; some psychologists propose more than three systems. Interference explains forgetting in LTM: memories compete, with proactive interference (old disrupts new - an old phone number intruding on a new one) and retroactive interference (new disrupts old - new parking spot habits making the old one harder to recall). Evidence: McGeoch and McDonald (1931) - participants learned a word list then a second list; when the second list was semantically similar, recall of the first was much worse, showing similarity drives interference. Baddeley and Hitch (1977) - rugby players who had played every match in the season recalled fewer recent games than those who missed matches, showing new games (retroactive interference) displaced older ones. Müller and Pilzecker (1900) showed retroactive interference occurs when new learning follows closely on old (consolidation time). Retrieval failure (cue-dependent forgetting) explains forgetting when a memory is available but lacks access cues: Tulving's encoding specificity principle states a cue only aids recall if it was present at encoding. Godden and Baddeley (1975) - deep-sea divers learned word lists on land or 15ft underwater; matching learning and recall contexts produced much better recall (context-dependent forgetting). Goodwin et al. (1969) - heavy drinkers who learned tasks drunk recalled them better drunk (state-dependent cues). Abernethy (1940) - students tested in the same room by the same teacher performed better. Forgetting can also be explained by decay (trace fades - only really applies to sensory memory) and motivated forgetting/repression (Freud - distressing memories pushed into the unconscious, weak empirical support but relevant to anxiety-based forgetting). Evaluation (AO3): Interference - strength: lab studies (McGeoch and McDonald) and field studies (rugby players) converge; similarity effect is reliable. Interference - limitations: lab studies use artificial word lists (low ecological validity); interference explains only some LTM forgetting and predicts forgetting should be faster the more you learn, which real-life expertise contradicts; research by Anderson (1974) shows interference is strongest when forgetting tests are cued by the competing material. Retrieval failure - strength: robust, replicable evidence (Godden and Baddeley, Goodwin) and clear practical value - the cognitive interview's context reinstatement and exam revision advice (revisit the study environment) derive from it. Retrieval failure - limitations: effects are mainly demonstrable in lab word-list recall; in real life cues are rarely absent entirely; and Baddeley himself argued context effects are weak in everyday memory; the explanation is hard to falsify - we cannot prove whether a memory is gone or merely lacking cues. A* synthesis: the two explanations are complementary rather than competing - interference is about competing material at encoding, retrieval failure about absent cues at retrieval; exam questions often reward noting this. Misleading information (leading questions and post-event discussion) distorts EWT. Loftus and Palmer (1974) : 45 US students watched clips of car accidents and were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed , collided , bumped , hit or contacted - estimates ranged from 41 mph ('smashed') to 32 mph ('contacted') ; a week later, 'smashed' participants falsely recalled broken glass, showing response-bias and memory distortion. Loftus and Zanni (1975) - 'the' versus 'a' broken headlight changed false recollection. Gabbert et al. (2003) - pairs watched different versions of the same event, discussed it, and 71% (versus 0% of controls) incorrectly recalled details they could not have seen - memory conformity (going along to fit in, not true distortion). Anxiety has mixed effects. Weapon focus (Loftus et al. 1987) - participants' eyes fixated on a gun, reducing identification of the holder; anxiety narrows attention onto the threat. Deffenbacher et al. (2004) meta-analysis - an inverted-U (Yerkes-Dodson) relationship: moderate arousal aids accuracy, extreme arousal impairs it. But Christianson and Hubinette (1993) - real bank-employees who were victims of threats recalled more accurately than bystanders, showing real-life emotional involvement can aid memory. Yuille and Cutshall (1986) - witnesses to a real shooting gave accurate accounts 4-5 months later, and misleading questions had little effect - challenging lab findings. The cognitive interview (CI) (Geiselman and Fisher, 1985) uses four techniques: context reinstatement (recreate the scene, weather, feelings - uses retrieval-failure logic), report everything (all details, however trivial - triggers may cue others), reverse order (recall backwards - disrupts schemas and prevents dishonesty) and change perspective (view events from another witness's position - disrupts schema expectations). The enhanced CI (Fisher) adds social techniques (building rapport, minimising distractions). Evidence: Fisher et al. (1990) - detectives trained in the CI elicited 47% more correct information from real witnesses in Miami; Kohnken et al. (1999) meta-analysis of 50 studies - CI produced significantly more correct details than standard interviews (34% average increase). Evaluation (AO3): Misleading information - limitations: lab clips lack real-world stress (ecological validity), participants know they are in a study (demand characteristics); Loftus's findings reflect response bias as much as true memory change; but Yuille and Cutshall's real-shooting study shows lab effects may not transfer. Misleading information - strength: robust replicable evidence with huge practical impact - police now avoid leading questions, and the legal system recognises post-event discussion contamination. Anxiety - contradiction: weapon-focus studies suggest anxiety harms accuracy while Christianson and Hubinette suggest it helps - the inverted-U resolves this but individual differences (trait anxiety) moderate effects. CI - strengths: strong empirical support (Fisher, Kohnken) and real police adoption; individual techniques are effective in isolation. CI - limitations: change perspective demands speculation and can increase recall of incorrect details; the full CI is time-consuming and requires expensive training, so UK forces typically use the enhanced CI with selected elements; Kohnken et al. also found increased errors alongside more correct information.

topics.name: Attachment
topics.subject: psychology
topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Attachment Describe caregiver-infant interactions: reciprocity, interactional synchrony; Schaffer's stages of attachment (AQA 4.1.3) Evaluate animal studies of attachment: Lorenz (imprinting) and Harlow (wire/cloth mothers) (AQA 4.1.3) Compare learning theory and Bowlby's evolutionary explanation of attachment, with critical period, monotropy and IWM (AQA 4.1.3) Describe and evaluate Ainsworth's Strange Situation and attachment types A/B/C (D) (AQA 4.1.3) Evaluate cultural variations in attachment (van IJzendoorn, Takahashi) (AQA 4.1.3) Evaluate maternal deprivation (44 thieves), institutionalisation and Romanian orphan research (Rutter, ERA); influence on later relationships (AQA 4.1.3) Interactions: reciprocity (two-way turn-taking, Brazelton 'dance'), interactional synchrony (mirrored actions/emotions, Meltzoff and Moore 1977); support bonding, hard to observe accurately Schaffer (1964, Glasgow, 60 infants): asocial (0-6 weeks), indiscriminate (6 weeks-6 months, accepts anyone), specific (7 months+, one special attachment, separation/stranger anxiety), multiple (10-11 months+) Animal studies: Lorenz (1935) goslings imprinted on first moving object, critical period, irreversible; Harlow (1958) rhesus monkeys preferred cloth 'contact comfort' mother over wire milk mother Learning theory: Dollard and Miller - classical (food = UCS) + operant (feeding as primary reinforcer); Bowlby evolutionary: monotropy, critical period 0-2.5yrs, IWM, social releasers, continuity hypothesis Ainsworth (1971, Baltimore): secure B 66%, insecure-avoidant A 22%, insecure-resistant C 12%; disorganised (D, Main and Solomon 1990); measures proximity-seeking, separation anxiety, stranger anxiety, reunion behaviour Cultural variations: van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) meta-analysis - secure most common everywhere but variations (China/Japan more resistant, Germany more avoidant); Takahashi (1990) Japanese infants harder to test Maternal deprivation: Bowlby 44 thieves (1944) - 86% affectionless psychopaths had prolonged early separation; institutionalisation: Rutter ERA (Romanian orphans) - disinhibited attachment, but adoption before 6 months largely reversed effects Attachment A close two-way emotional bond between two people (usually infant and caregiver) in which each seeks closeness and feels distress on separation. Reciprocity Two-way turn-taking interaction between caregiver and infant, where each responds to the other's signals (Brazelton: 'dance-like'). Interactional synchrony Mirroring of each other's actions and emotions in a coordinated, simultaneous way (Meltzoff and Moore 1977: infants imitated adult tongue protrusion and facial expressions). Monotropy Bowlby's claim that infants form one special attachment (usually to the mother) which is of central importance to development; all later attachments build on it. Critical period The biologically determined window (Bowlby: around 6 months to 2.5 years) within which an attachment must form or development may be permanently damaged. Internal working model (IWM) A mental representation of the first attachment relationship that acts as a template for all later relationships (parenting, peer, romantic - Hazan and Shaver). Social releaser Innate infant behaviours (crying, smiling, cute features) that elicit caregiving responses from adults and trigger the attachment process. Imprinting Lorenz's term for rapid, irreversible attachment formed by precocial animals (goslings) to the first moving object seen within a critical period after hatching. Institutionalisation The effects of growing up in an institution (e.g. an orphanage): disinhibited attachment, intellectual underfunctioning and delayed physical development (Rutter's ERA study). Maternal deprivation Bowlby's term for the loss of the mother-figure's emotional care (separation or failure to form), proposed to cause delinquency, affectionless psychopathy and developmental delay. Attachment forms through early caregiver-infant interactions. Reciprocity is two-way turn-taking: each partner responds to the other's signals and adjusts their behaviour in turn (Brazelton et al. 1975 described it as a 'dance' - the infant responds to the caregiver's timing, and the caregiver to the infant's). Interactional synchrony is mirroring: caregiver and infant coordinate their actions and emotions in simultaneous, rhythm-matched ways - Meltzoff and Moore (1977) found infants as young as 2-3 weeks imitated an adult's tongue protrusion, mouth opening and facial expressions, suggesting innate imitation. Isabella et al. (1989) found more synchrony predicted a stronger attachment. These interactions are hard to observe (infant behaviour is subtle) - researchers use filmed observations with multiple observers to improve inter-rater reliability. Schaffer (1964, Glasgow longitudinal study) : 60 working-class infants visited monthly for a year, mothers reporting separation anxiety (protest at caregiver leaving) and stranger anxiety (protest at unfamiliar people). Four stages : (1) asocial (0-6 weeks) - responses to objects and people are similar; (2) indiscriminate attachment (6 weeks-6 months) - preference for people over objects, accepts care from anyone; (3) specific attachment (7 months+) - one special attachment forms (usually mother), separation and stranger anxiety appear; (4) multiple attachments (10-11 months+) - secondary attachments form (father, grandparents, siblings). Fathers : Schaffer found 75% of infants formed an attachment with the father by 18 months; Grossmann and Grossmann (2002) found fathers' play (stimulation) mattered more than their emotional care, suggesting fathers take a different role; Field (1978) found primary-caregiver fathers showed as much interactional synchrony as mothers, suggesting the father's role depends on responsiveness, not gender. Evaluation (AO3): Methodological strength: longitudinal design (same infants over time) shows individual development, and mothers were observers (reducing stranger effects) - but this risks social desirability bias in reports. Limitation - observer bias: infants cannot report; inferring attachment from crying is subjective, and filming improves reliability but infant movements (mouth movements) are hard to code (Meltzoff and Moore acknowledged this). Limitation - cultural bias: Schaffer's stages are based on 1960s Glasgow working-class families; the multiple-attachment stage timing differs across cultures (in collectivist families, multiple attachments form earlier - Tronick's Efe study). Support from Meltzoff and Moore: controlled filmed observation with blinded observers supports interactional synchrony; but critics (e.g. the 'tongue protrusion is just imitation' debate) argue infant responses may be reflexive, not social - Koepke et al. failed to replicate, though Meltzoff and Moore countered that their replication was flawed. Lorenz (1935) - imprinting : random division of a goose clutch; half hatched with their mother, half in an incubator with Lorenz as the first moving object. Findings: incubator goslings followed Lorenz and ignored the real mother; imprinting occurred within a critical period (12-17 hours after hatching) and was irreversible ; goslings imprinted on Lorenz later tried to mate with humans ( sexual imprinting ). Lorenz concluded attachment is innate and biologically programmed. Harlow (1958) - contact comfort : 16 rhesus monkeys separated from mothers at birth and raised with two surrogate 'mothers': one wire mesh (milk) and one covered in soft cloth. Findings: monkeys spent most time with the cloth mother , visiting the wire mother only to feed - contact comfort matters more than food; when frightened, the monkeys ran to the cloth mother; monkeys raised by surrogates showed abnormal social and sexual behaviour and were abusive (or indifferent) parents later - supporting the idea that early attachment shapes later development (internal working model). Harlow set a critical period of 90 days: monkeys deprived beyond this were permanently damaged. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - support for innate attachment and contact comfort: both studies challenge the 'cupboard love' (food-based) learning-theory account - goslings imprinted on a non-food object and monkeys chose comfort over food. Limitation - generalisability: geese are precocial and monkeys' attachment differs from human attachment; imprinting has no direct human equivalent (though Klappenbach noted evidence of human 'imprinting-like' phenomena - e.g. Bassett 2005, babies born without programming for attachment). Counter: monkeys are close relatives of humans, so Harlow's findings inform human development better than rodent studies would. Limitation - ethics (Harlow): severe, lasting harm was inflicted on monkeys (isolation, abusive parenting), which would breach modern BPS guidelines; Lorenz's study was less harmful (relocation). Strength - practical application: Harlow's findings influenced orphanage care (attachment figures, comfort) and animal welfare legislation; both studies support Bowlby's evolutionary framework. Learning theory (Dollard and Miller, 1950) - the 'cupboard love' explanation: attachment is learned through association and reinforcement. Classical conditioning : food (unconditioned stimulus) produces pleasure (unconditioned response); the caregiver (neutral stimulus) is paired with feeding, becoming a conditioned stimulus producing pleasure - attachment forms. Operant conditioning : the infant is fed when it cries (negative reinforcement - crying stops discomfort), and the caregiver is rewarded by the infant's smile (positive reinforcement). Feeding is a primary reinforcer and the caregiver a secondary reinforcer . Bowlby's evolutionary theory (1969) : attachment is innate, evolved because it aids survival (protection from predators, nourishment). Key claims: monotropy (one special attachment, usually to the mother, of central importance); the critical period (around 6 months to 2.5 years - attachment must form or development is damaged); social releasers (innate infant behaviours - crying, smiling, cute faces - that elicit caregiving); the internal working model (a template of the first attachment shaping all later relationships) and the continuity hypothesis (secure early attachment predicts secure later relationships). Evaluation (AO3): Learning theory - limitation: contradicted by animal studies - Lorenz's goslings imprinted without food and Harlow's monkeys preferred comfort over milk; Schaffer and Emerson (1964) found 39% of infants' primary attachments were not to the person who fed them , directly refuting cupboard love. Learning theory - strength: some elements are valid - reinforcement clearly shapes some infant-caregiver behaviour (feeding soothes), and the theory is scientific (testable, based on conditioning principles); but it is reductionist, ignoring the infant's active social role. Bowlby - support: Lorenz and Harlow support innate attachment and critical periods; Hazan and Shaver (1987) - the love quiz found adults' romantic attachment styles matched their early attachment types, supporting the internal working model; Bailey et al. (2007) - mothers' attachment style predicted their infants' attachment (IWM continuity). Bowlby - limitations: monotropy is overstated - Rutter argued all attachment figures matter (not just the mother), and Schaffer found multiple attachments were common and healthy; the critical period is better described as a sensitive period - Romanian orphan research shows late adoption can largely reverse early damage; the theory risks maternal determinism (pressuring women to stay home) and is partly based on 1940s mothers working in wartime factories. Temperament alternative (Kagan): infants' innate personality (temperament) may drive attachment quality rather than caregiver sensitivity - a confound in sensitivity-based explanations. Ainsworth's Strange Situation (1971, Baltimore) is a controlled observation of infants aged 12-18 months with their mother and a stranger, using eight episodes (including two separations and two reunions) to measure proximity-seeking , exploration (safe-base behaviour), separation anxiety , stranger anxiety and reunion behaviour . Types: secure (Type B, ~66% of US infants) - mother used as safe base, moderate separation and stranger anxiety, seeks and is comforted on reunion; insecure-avoidant (Type A, ~22%) - high exploration, low separation/stranger anxiety, ignores mother on reunion (associated with rejecting, unresponsive caregiving); insecure-resistant (Type C, ~12%) - low exploration, high separation/stranger anxiety, ambivalent reunion (seeks contact but resists comfort; associated with inconsistent caregiving). Main and Solomon (1990) later added disorganised (Type D) - no consistent pattern, associated with abuse. Cultural variations : van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg (1988) meta-analysis of 32 studies across 8 countries - secure attachment was the most common type everywhere , but variations existed: China and Japan showed higher resistant (C) rates, West Germany higher avoidant (A) rates; variation within countries was 1.5 times greater than between countries, suggesting culture affects caregiving style, not the attachment process itself. Takahashi (1990) - 60 middle-class Japanese infants: virtually no avoidant attachments and 32% resistant; 90% of Japanese infants were so distressed by the final separation episode (the seventh) that it was stopped - showing the Strange Situation is culturally biased (Japanese infants are rarely left alone, so the procedure over-measures anxiety). Grossmann and Grossmann (German study) - more avoidant attachments, consistent with German culture's valuing of independence. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - reliability: highly standardised procedure with consistent coding categories; inter-rater reliability is high (observers agree on type), and the meta-analysis supports replication across cultures. Limitation - ecological validity: artificial setting (lab, strangers, separations imposed); infants' behaviour may differ in natural home settings. Limitation - cultural bias: designed on US middle-class samples; imposed etic - Takahashi's finding that the procedure distressed Japanese infants shows it measures anxiety, not attachment, in some cultures; Temperament (Kagan) is a confound - infant personality, not caregiving, may drive type. Limitation - the caregiver's role: the Strange Situation measures attachment to the mother only; multiple attachments are ignored. Support - predictive validity: attachment type predicts later outcomes (friendship, romantic relationships, mental health), suggesting the categories capture something real. Maternal deprivation (Bowlby, 1944, 44 Thieves) : Bowlby compared 44 adolescent thieves (referred to a child guidance clinic) with 44 emotionally disturbed but non-delinquent controls. Findings: 86% of the affectionless psychopaths (unable to feel guilt or empathy) had experienced prolonged early separation from their mothers (before age 5), versus few controls; 39% of thieves overall had separations versus 5% of controls. Bowlby concluded prolonged separation causes affectionless psychopathy , delinquency and developmental delay - the basis of his maternal deprivation hypothesis. Institutionalisation and Romanian orphans : Rutter et al.'s English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) study (1998, 2010) followed 165 Romanian orphans adopted into UK families (severe institutional deprivation under Ceausescu) against 52 UK adoptees. Findings: orphans adopted before 6 months showed near-normal development; those adopted after 6 months showed disinhibited attachment (indiscriminate friendliness to strangers), intellectual underfunctioning (lower IQ, ~4 points per 6 months of deprivation) and delayed physical growth; effects persisted to age 11-23 but were partially reversed. Zeanah et al. (2009, Bucharest Early Intervention Project) : institutionalised children showed more disorganised (D) attachments than fostered children, supporting the damage of institutional care. Key institutional effects: disinhibited attachment, intellectual underfunctioning and delayed physical development. Influence on later relationships (IWM) : Hazan and Shaver (1987) - the 'love quiz' of 620 adults found early attachment types predicted adult romantic styles (secure adults trusted partners; avoidant feared intimacy); McCarthy (1999) - insecure-resistant women had the worst adult friendships and relationships; Bailey et al. (2007) - mothers' attachment style predicted how they parented their own infants (IWM continuity). Evaluation (AO3): 44 Thieves - limitations: Bowlby conducted the interviews himself (researcher bias), the 'affectionless psychopathy' diagnosis was subjective, retrospective data (mothers may have misremembered separations), and the study is correlational - confounding variables (poverty, trauma) could explain delinquency; the sample was small and biased (already disturbed). ERA - strengths: a natural experiment (adoption could not be manipulated), longitudinal (persistence over time), and a matched control group - high validity for measuring institutionalisation effects. ERA - practical application: informed adoption policy (adoptions before 6 months prioritised) and improved orphanage care worldwide. Counterpoint - recovery: Rutter emphasised resilience : adoption before 6 months largely reversed effects, so the critical period is better described as a sensitive period; late-adopted children also improved over time (though disinhibited attachment persisted). Confounding variables (ERA): Romanian orphans suffered malnutrition, disease and neglect as well as emotional deprivation - Rutter separated these (he identified 'deprivation' itself as the key factor via the ERA and his earlier 4-to-1 ratio), but full separation of variables is impossible.

topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Psychopathology Explain and evaluate four definitions of abnormality: statistical infrequency, deviation from social norms, failure to function adequately, deviation from ideal mental health (AQA 4.1.4) Describe phobia characteristics (behavioural, emotional, cognitive) and the two-process model; evaluate systematic desensitisation and flooding (AQA 4.1.4) Describe depression characteristics and cognitive explanations (Beck's negative triad, Ellis's ABC) with treatments (CBT, behavioural activation, SSRIs) (AQA 4.1.4) Describe OCD characteristics and biological explanations (COMT, SLC1A1, basal ganglia, serotonin) with treatments (ERP, SSRIs) (AQA 4.1.4) Evaluate diagnosis and classification: DSM-5/ICD-11 reliability, validity, comorbidity, culture-bound syndromes (AQA 4.1.4) Definitions: statistical (rare, IQ<70), social norms (culture-specific), failure to function (Rosenhan and Seligman), ideal mental health (Jahoda's six criteria) Phobias: two-process model (classical acquisition, operant maintenance via avoidance), preparedness (Seligman); treatments: systematic desensitisation (hierarchy + relaxation), flooding, CBT Depression: Beck (negative triad, schemas, distortions), Ellis (ABC model), learned helplessness (Seligman); biological: 5-HTT gene, serotonin, cortisol/HPA axis; treatments: CBT, behavioural activation, SSRIs (6-8 weeks) OCD: obsessions (intrusive thoughts), compulsions (repetitive rituals); biological: COMT and SLC1A1 genes, basal ganglia, serotonin-dopamine circuits; cognitive: thought-action fusion, inflated responsibility; treatments: ERP, SSRIs Classification: DSM-5 (APA, 2013), ICD-11 (WHO); reliability (inter-rater), validity (construct/predictive), comorbidity (depression + anxiety), culture-bound syndromes Treatments compared: SD (systematic, slow, effective for specific phobias), flooding (fast, high drop-out), CBT (gold standard, cognitive + behavioural), SSRIs (cheap, side effects, symptoms only) Statistical infrequency Defining abnormality as behaviour or traits that are rare in the population (e.g. IQ below 70, 2% of people), measured objectively against a normal distribution. Deviation from social norms Defining abnormality as behaviour that violates the unstated rules of a society; norms are culture-specific and change over time. Failure to function adequately Defining abnormality by inability to cope with everyday living: distress, maladaptive behaviour, irrationality, unpredictability (Rosenhan and Seligman's seven criteria). Deviation from ideal mental health Jahoda's (1958) definition: abnormality is the absence of six criteria - self-attitudes, personal growth, integration, autonomy, accurate reality perception and environmental mastery. Two-process model Mowrer's explanation of phobias: fear is acquired by classical conditioning (neutral stimulus paired with trauma) and maintained by operant conditioning (avoidance negatively reinforces the fear). Systematic desensitisation (SD) Behavioural therapy using counter-conditioning: an anxiety hierarchy is built, relaxation is taught, and the client works up the hierarchy until the CS no longer produces fear. Flooding Behavioural therapy exposing the client to their phobic stimulus at maximum intensity immediately, without avoidance, until the adrenaline-fuelled fear response extinguishes. Negative cognitive triad (Beck) Beck's (1967) three negative views central to depression: a negative view of the self, the world and the future, produced by negative schemas and cognitive distortions. ERP (exposure and response prevention) Behavioural treatment for OCD: exposure to the obsessive trigger while preventing the compulsive response, so anxiety declines and the compulsion extinguishes. SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) Biological drugs (e.g. fluoxetine) that block serotonin reuptake at the synapse, increasing serotonin availability to reduce depression and OCD symptoms. Statistical infrequency : behaviour or traits that are rare are abnormal - any measurable characteristic can be plotted on a normal distribution and behaviours more than two standard deviations from the mean (about 2% of people) are classed as abnormal, e.g. IQ below 70 (intellectual disability) or above 130. Deviation from social norms : behaviour violating the unstated rules of a society is abnormal - norms are culture-specific and change over time (homosexuality was classified as a disorder until 1973 in the DSM-II revision); antisocial personality disorder involves impulsive, aggressive behaviour that breaks social norms. Failure to function adequately (Rosenhan and Seligman, 1989): abnormality is judged by the inability to cope with everyday living, signalled by observer discomfort, maladaptive behaviour, unpredictability, irrationality, personal distress and violation of moral standards; the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) operationalises it. Deviation from ideal mental health (Jahoda, 1958): abnormality is the absence of six criteria for positive mental health - self-attitudes (high self-esteem), personal growth (self-actualisation), integration (coping with stress), autonomy (independence), accurate reality perception and environmental mastery ; lacking any criterion indicates abnormality. Evaluation (AO3): Statistical infrequency - strengths: objective, measurable and based on the normal distribution; useful for research and screening (IQ cut-offs guide diagnoses). Statistical infrequency - limitations: labels desirable rarities as abnormal (high IQ); not all rare behaviours are disorders (left-handedness); arbitrary cut-offs; some disorders (mild depression) are statistically common . Social norms - strengths/limitations: considers social context, but norms are culture-specific (hearing voices is valued in some cultures, diagnosed as schizophrenia in the UK) and change over time; risks abusing the label to control non-conformity. Failure to function - strengths/limitations: respects the individual's own experience and captures the 'at what cost?' question, but functioning is judged subjectively (who decides?) and it risks discriminating against people who live unconventional but happy lives (e.g. extreme sports, unusual lifestyles). Ideal mental health - strengths/limitations: positive, holistic and goal-focused (like Jahoda's humanistic background), but the criteria are so demanding that few people would qualify as 'healthy' at any one time, and the criteria are culture-bound (autonomy is a Western value). Characteristics of phobias: behavioural - panic (crying, running), avoidance of the phobic stimulus, endurance (staying with high anxiety); emotional - persistent, excessive and unreasonable fear and anxiety; cognitive - irrational beliefs about the stimulus (e.g. 'all dogs are dangerous'), selective attention to the threat, recognition that the fear is excessive. DSM-5 requires the fear to be persistent (6 months+) and to interfere with functioning. Explanations : the two-process model (Mowrer, 1947) - fear is acquired by classical conditioning : a neutral stimulus (spider) is paired with a frightening unconditioned stimulus (being bitten), so the spider becomes a conditioned stimulus eliciting fear (conditioned response) - supported by the Little Albert experiment (Watson and Rayner, 1920) , where a baby was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise. Fear is maintained by operant conditioning : avoiding the stimulus reduces anxiety ( negative reinforcement ), so the phobia persists. Preparedness (Seligman, 1971) : humans are biologically prepared to fear evolutionarily relevant threats (snakes, heights, dark) rather than modern ones (cars, electrical sockets) - explaining why some phobias are far more common and why they resist extinction. Treatments : systematic desensitisation (Wolpe, 1958) - counter-conditioning: an anxiety hierarchy (stimuli ranked from least to most feared) is built; the client is taught relaxation (reciprocal inhibition - relaxation and fear cannot coexist); the client works up the hierarchy pairing relaxation with each level until the conditioned stimulus no longer elicits fear. Flooding - immediate exposure to the most feared stimulus at maximum intensity without avoidance, until the adrenaline-driven fear response exhausts itself ( extinction ). CBT - exposure plus cognitive restructuring of irrational beliefs. Evaluation (AO3): Two-process model - strength: explains both acquisition and maintenance, and has direct application (SD targets the learned association; flooding targets avoidance) - Watson and Rayner's Little Albert supports conditioning of fear. Two-process model - limitations: ignores cognition (irrational beliefs) - CBT addresses this; not all traumatic encounters produce phobias (Di Gallo's data on accident survivors) and not all phobias follow trauma ( preparedness explains why snakes are feared more than flowers); the model cannot explain individual differences. SD - strengths: effective for specific phobias (McGrath: ~75% of patients responded; Capafons: acrophobia patients reported lower fear); suitable for patients with learning difficulties (unlike CBT); low drop-out because exposure is gradual. SD - limitations: slower than flooding (multiple sessions); less effective for generalized anxieties and social phobias; symptom substitution is a criticism from psychodynamic approaches (fear may resurface elsewhere). Flooding - strengths/limitations: fast and cost-effective (Ohman found flooding more effective than SD for some phobias), but highly distressing, producing high drop-out and ethical concerns (informed consent, protection from harm); less effective for complex phobias with cognitive components. Characteristics of depression (major depressive disorder): behavioural - low activity levels, disruption to sleep and eating, aggression/self-harm; emotional - lowered mood, anger, lowered self-esteem; cognitive - poor concentration, dwelling on the negative, absolutist thinking ('black-and-white' thinking). Cognitive explanations : Beck (1967) - the negative triad : a negative view of the self ('I am worthless'), the world ('nothing goes right') and the future ('it will never improve'), produced by negative schemas (formed in childhood through bad experiences) and cognitive distortions (overgeneralisation, catastrophising, minimising positives), which maintain a vicious cycle of negative thinking. Ellis (1962) - the ABC model : an Activating event (failing a test) triggers irrational Beliefs ('I must succeed at everything'), producing emotional Consequences (depression); 'musturbatory' irrational beliefs (must, ought, should) cause unhealthy emotions. Learned helplessness (Seligman, 1974) - repeated uncontrollable negative events teach the person that outcomes are independent of effort, producing passivity and depression. Treatments : CBT (Beck's cognitive therapy) - identify and challenge negative thoughts ( cognitive restructuring ), test irrational beliefs against reality, and use behavioural activation (planning pleasant, achievable activities) and homework ('patient as scientist'). Ellis's REBT - disputing irrational beliefs (logical, empirical, pragmatic disputation), effective argument and behavioural techniques. SSRIs (fluoxetine) - block serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin availability; take 6-8 weeks to work; combined with CBT under NICE guidelines for best outcomes. Evaluation (AO3): Cognitive explanations - strengths: strong supporting evidence (Clark and Beck 2010: depressed people show biased processing), direct practical application in CBT, and they take account of the person's experience (unlike the purely biological model). Cognitive explanations - limitations: causal direction is unclear - negative thoughts may be a consequence rather than a cause of depression (reactive depression follows real loss); some depression has clear biological bases (the 5-HTT gene, cortisol/HPA axis dysfunction), so the cognitive account is incomplete; Ellis's ABC is simplistic (ignores biological factors and context). CBT - strengths: March et al. (2007) found CBT was as effective as antidepressants and the combination most effective; effects persist after treatment (unlike drugs), giving lower relapse; patient empowerment. CBT - limitations: time-consuming, requires motivation and expensive training; not suitable for severe depression (patients cannot engage); individual differences - CBT suits reflective patients (suits 'inner' depression), while drug therapy suits those unable to talk. SSRIs - evaluation: meta-analyses show moderate benefit over placebo (strongest for moderate-to-severe depression), they are cheap and less time-consuming than CBT, but side effects (nausea, insomnia, sexual dysfunction) cause discontinuation, they treat symptoms not causes (relapse common after stopping) and the placebo difference is modest for mild depression. Characteristics of OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder): behavioural - compulsions are repetitive (hand-washing, checking, counting) and reduce anxiety temporarily; emotional - intense anxiety and distress from obsessions and compulsions; cognitive - obsessions are intrusive, recurrent, unwanted thoughts (contamination, harm), and sufferers recognise they are irrational. OCD involves obsessions, compulsions or both; DSM-5 requires them to be time-consuming (1 hour+) or distressing. Biological explanations : genetic - the COMT gene (regulates dopamine; a variation produces higher dopamine levels, associated with OCD) and the SLC1A1 gene (regulates serotonin transport; mutations increase OCD risk) - Nestadt et al. (2010) found OCD heritability of 68% (MZ twins ~68% concordance versus DZ ~31%, van Grootheest); neural - abnormal serotonin levels (low serotonin linked to obsessions) and dopamine over-activity; brain circuits - the basal ganglia (specifically the caudate nucleus, filtering impulses) and the orbitofrontal cortex (worry circuit, sends worry signals to the caudate): a hyperactive OFC and impaired caudate produce obsessive thoughts - Saxena et al. (2002) found higher OFC activity in OCD patients. Cognitive explanations : sufferers have inflated responsibility (believing they can prevent harm) and thought-action fusion (believing that thinking about an action is morally equivalent to performing it) - obsessions become more distressing, and compulsions are performed to neutralise the thought; Salkovskis's model explains why rituals repeat. Treatments : ERP (exposure and response prevention) - exposure to the obsessive trigger while preventing the compulsive response, so anxiety declines (extinction); SSRIs - increase serotonin availability (first-line drug); benzodiazepines (short-term anxiety relief, GABA enhancement) and ECT/deep brain stimulation for severe, resistant cases. Evaluation (AO3): Biological - strengths: twin and family studies (Nestadt 68% heritability) support genetic contribution; drug therapies targeting serotonin work for many patients, indirectly supporting the neural explanation. Biological - limitations: MZ concordance is not 100%, so the environment always contributes; gene association studies are correlational and COMT/SLC1A1 explain only a small proportion of cases; the neural evidence is inconclusive - cause and effect are unclear (abnormal serotonin may be a consequence, not a cause, of OCD); and the biological account is reductionist (ignores cognitive and environmental factors). Cognitive - strengths: explains individual differences in OCD symptoms (inflated responsibility varies) and has practical application (CBT targets thought-action fusion). Cognitive - limitations: hard to test causally (thoughts precede or follow compulsions?); some sufferers lack inflated responsibility; less strong evidence than for depression. ERP - evaluation: strong evidence of effectiveness (Albucher et al.: ERP produces large symptom reductions; NICE recommends ERP for OCD), but it is highly distressing (high drop-out), time-consuming and requires specialist training; not all patients benefit, and relapse can occur. SSRIs for OCD - evaluation: effective for many (60% symptom reduction on average in trials), cheap and easy to administer, but side effects, 6-12 week delay, and symptoms return after stopping; combining SSRIs with ERP is most effective. Classification systems : the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association, 2013) and the ICD-11 (World Health Organization) classify mental disorders by symptom criteria. Reliability (consistency of diagnosis): inter-rater reliability - two clinicians should reach the same diagnosis; improvements in DSM-5 criteria raised reliability for some disorders, but comorbidity (diagnosing two or more disorders together, e.g. depression + anxiety) lowers reliability, since overlapping symptoms make classification ambiguous. Validity : construct validity (does the diagnosis capture the disorder as it really is?) and predictive validity (does diagnosis predict treatment response and outcome?). Culture-bound syndromes (e.g. taijin kyofusho in Japan - fear of offending others with one's body) show classification is culture-bound, and symptoms may express differently across cultures. General evaluation of treatments (AO3) - a bank of points usable across treatment essay questions: Psychological vs biological: psychological treatments (CBT, SD, ERP) address causes (cognitive distortions, learned associations) and produce lasting change with lower relapse; biological treatments (SSRIs, benzodiazepines) are cheaper, faster and suit patients unable to engage with talking therapies, but treat symptoms only. Combined treatment: NICE guidelines recommend combining CBT with drug therapy for depression and OCD - March et al. (2007) found the combination most effective for adolescents. Ethics: flooding and ERP raise protection-from-harm issues (high distress, drop-out); drugs raise informed consent (side effects) and dependency (benzodiazepines are addictive). Methodological issues in treatment research: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard but suffer from placebo effects, demand characteristics and publication bias (studies showing drug effectiveness are more likely to be published - Kirsch et al. argued placebo effects explain much of SSRI benefit for mild depression). Individual differences: severity, patient preference and history determine treatment choice; severe depression may preclude CBT, and specific phobias suit SD/flooding more than CBT.

topics.name: Research Methods and Statistics
topics.subject: psychology
topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Research Methods and Statistics Design experiments: lab, field, natural, quasi; operationalise IV/DV; control extraneous variables, demand characteristics and investigator effects (AQA 4.2.3) Choose and justify experimental designs (independent measures, repeated measures, matched pairs) with counterbalancing and random allocation (AQA 4.2.3) Describe non-experimental methods (observations, self-report, correlations, case studies) and sampling techniques (random, stratified, systematic, opportunity, volunteer) (AQA 4.2.3) Apply BPS ethical guidelines and evaluate reliability (test-retest, inter-rater) and validity (internal, external, ecological, construct) (AQA 4.2.3) Compute and interpret descriptive statistics, distributions and levels of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval) (AQA 4.2.3) Conduct hypothesis testing: probability, significance, critical values, type I/II errors; choose the correct inferential test from the seven (AQA 4.2.3) Explain features of science (falsifiability, replicability, objectivity) and the peer review process (AQA 4.2.3) Experiments: lab (control, low EV), field (natural setting, less control), natural (IV occurs naturally), quasi (IV pre-existing); operationalise IV/DV; control extraneous/confounding variables Designs: independent measures (different people per condition, no order effects but participant variables), repeated measures (same people, no participant variables but order effects - counterbalance), matched pairs (matched on key variables) Sampling: random (unbiased, needs target population list), stratified (proportional subgroups, most representative), systematic (every nth), opportunity (convenient, biased), volunteer (self-selecting, biased but willing) Ethics (BPS): informed consent, deception (cost-benefit + debrief), protection from harm, right to withdraw, confidentiality, privacy; presumpptive consent, retrospective consent Descriptive stats: mean (sensitive, uses all data), median (skewed data), mode (nominal); SD (precise spread), range (crude); distributions: normal (symmetrical, bell curve), positive/negative skew Hypothesis testing: null/alternative hypotheses, p ≤ 0.05 significance, calculated vs critical value, one-/two-tailed; type I error (false positive, lenient) vs type II (false negative, stringent) Choosing the test: difference vs correlation/association × related/unrelated design × nominal/ordinal/interval data → chi-square, sign test, Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon, related/unrelated t, Spearman's rho, Pearson's r Features of science: theory construction, falsifiability (Popper), replicability, objectivity, empirical methods, paradigm shifts (Kuhn); peer review checks validity before publication Operationalisation Defining variables precisely so they can be measured - e.g. 'memory' operationalised as 'number of words recalled from a 15-word list in 60 seconds'. Demand characteristics Cues in a study that lead participants to guess the aim and change their behaviour (please-you or screw-you effects), reducing internal validity. Counterbalancing The ABBA technique: half the participants experience condition A then B, the other half B then A, spreading order effects (practice, fatigue) evenly across conditions. Standard deviation A measure of dispersion showing the average spread of scores around the mean; a large SD indicates values are spread out, a small SD that they cluster near the mean. Levels of measurement The type of data collected: nominal (categories/frequencies), ordinal (ranked/ordered data), interval (equal units with a true zero-free scale, e.g. seconds, temperature). Probability and significance Probability (p) is the likelihood results occurred by chance; results are significant if p is at or below the significance level (0.05 by convention - 5% or less chance of results being due to chance). Type I error A false positive: wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis - claiming an effect exists when it does not; caused by a significance level that is too lenient (e.g. p < 0.10; the 'optimistic' error). Type II error A false negative: wrongly accepting a false null hypothesis - missing a real effect; caused by a significance level that is too stringent (e.g. p < 0.01 when 0.05 was acceptable; the 'pessimistic' error). Peer review Assessment of psychological research by independent experts before publication, checking validity, significance and originality to allocate research funding and maintain quality. Falsifiability (Popper) A key feature of science: theories must be capable of being proven wrong by evidence; psychology's theories must generate testable (and therefore falsifiable) predictions. Experiments test cause and effect by manipulating an independent variable (IV) and measuring a dependent variable (DV). Both must be operationalised (defined precisely so they can be measured). Types of experiment : lab (artificial setting, high control, high internal validity but low ecological validity and demand characteristics), field (natural setting, higher ecological validity but less control and ethical issues - consent), natural (the IV occurs naturally, e.g. a disaster - high ecological validity, no manipulation, rare events, confounding variables) and quasi (the IV is pre-existing and not manipulated, e.g. gender, age - no random allocation, so causation is weaker). Variables and controls : extraneous variables (any variable other than the IV affecting the DV - situational: noise, time of day; participant: age, intelligence) must be controlled or they become confounding variables (variables that systematically vary with the IV, making it impossible to tell which caused the DV change). Control techniques: standardisation (same procedure/materials for all), randomisation (random order of tasks/conditions), random allocation (assigning participants to conditions by chance, spreading participant variables evenly), counterbalancing (ABBA technique for order effects) and single/double-blind procedures (participants/researchers unaware of condition, reducing demand characteristics and investigator effects). Demand characteristics - cues letting participants guess the aim (Orne: please-you effects) - and investigator effects (researcher's behaviour influencing results, e.g. Rosenthal and Fode's 'clever Hans' effect) both threaten internal validity; single-blind and double-blind designs control them. Experimental designs : independent measures (different participants in each condition - no order effects, but participant variables confound and more participants are needed; controlled by random allocation); repeated measures (same participants in all conditions - participant variables controlled, fewer participants needed, but order effects (practice, fatigue, boredom) confound - controlled by counterbalancing or leaving a gap between conditions); matched pairs (different participants matched on key variables such as age or IQ - controls participant variables without order effects, but matching is time-consuming and imperfect). Evaluation (AO3): Lab experiments: high control (internal validity, replicability) but low ecological validity, demand characteristics and artificiality; field experiments improve ecological validity at the cost of control and consent. Repeated measures: participant variables controlled and economical, but order effects require counterbalancing; demand characteristics more likely (participants experience both conditions and may guess the aim). Independent measures: no order effects and fewer demand characteristics, but needs more participants and participant variables threaten validity - random allocation controls this. Matched pairs: best of both, but matching is never perfect and it is time-consuming. Observations : watching and recording behaviour. Naturalistic (real environment, high ecological validity, low control) versus controlled (structured setting, control over variables); covert (participants unaware - no demand characteristics but ethical issues) versus overt (aware - consent obtained but reactivity); participant (researcher joins the group - rich insight but loss of objectivity) versus non-participant (researcher observes from outside - objective but less insight). Behavioural categories must be operationalised (specific, observable actions) and event sampling (counting every occurrence) or time sampling (recording at intervals) used; inter-rater reliability checks consistency between observers. Self-report techniques : questionnaires (open questions - rich qualitative data, hard to analyse; closed questions - quantitative, easy to analyse but restricted; social desirability bias and response bias/acquiescence are key weaknesses) and interviews (structured - standardised questions, replicable; unstructured - flexible, rich data but interviewer bias and hard to replicate). Correlations : measuring the association between two co-variables (no IV manipulation, so no cause and effect - a third variable may explain the relationship); positive (both increase), negative (one increases, other decreases), zero (no relationship); presented as scattergrams with a correlation coefficient (-1 to +1). Case studies : in-depth study of one individual or small group (HM, Clive Wearing) - rich, detailed, unusual cases that cannot be generated experimentally, but small samples, researcher bias and poor generalisability. Sampling techniques for selecting a representative sample from the target population: random (every member has an equal chance - unbiased and generalisable, but needs a full list and may still be unrepresentative by chance); stratified (subgroups in proportion to the population, randomly selected - most representative, but time-consuming); systematic (every nth person from a list - objective, but may coincide with a pattern); opportunity (whoever is available - quick and easy but biased towards the researcher's location and unrepresentative); volunteer (self-selecting - willing and engaged, but volunteer bias: more motivated, extroverted, may respond differently). Evaluation (AO3): Observations: naturalistic has high ecological validity but low control; inter-rater reliability and operationalised categories improve objectivity; covert observations raise consent issues. Self-report: rich data and direct access to thoughts, but social desirability bias, response bias and dishonesty threaten validity; pilot studies and anonymity reduce these. Correlations: useful for exploring relationships and generating hypotheses (basis of further research), but no causation, no IV manipulation, and a third-variable problem. Sampling: random and stratified are most representative but impractical; opportunity and volunteer are practical but biased - exam answers must justify the choice for the study in question. Pilot studies and content analysis: pilots improve the design before it matters (ecological validity of procedure), while content analysis converts rich qualitative material into analysable data - both are standard AQA application scenarios; content analysis's subjectivity in coding is the key limitation. Further non-experimental techniques : a pilot study is a small-scale trial run before the main study, checking the procedure works, questions are understood and timings are right - saving money and time by catching design flaws early; it also trains observers for inter-rater reliability. Content analysis systematically converts qualitative material (documents, media, transcripts) into quantitative data using coding units (categories of content counted across the material) - non-invasive and high in external validity, but the researcher's interpretation of coding units risks subjectivity; thematic analysis (identifying themes rather than counting) keeps the qualitative richness but is harder to replicate. Case study defence : unusual cases (HM, Clive Wearing) generate data experiments cannot, but generalisability is limited - the standard A* trade-off in methods essays. Ethics (BPS Code of Ethics and Conduct) : informed consent (participants must know the aim and agree; alternatives: presumptive consent - asking similar people, prior general consent , retrospective consent ); deception (misleading participants - only acceptable if justified by the cost-benefit ratio and followed by debriefing ); protection from harm (physical and psychological; participants must leave as they arrived); right to withdraw (during and after the study); confidentiality (no names, use numbers; the Data Protection Act); privacy (no observations in private spaces without consent). Reliability (consistency): test-retest (same test on two occasions, high correlation ≥ 0.8 = reliable), inter-rater/inter-observer (two observers agree), split-half (two halves of a test correlate). Improved by: standardised procedures, operationalised behavioural categories, trained observers and pilot studies. Validity (accuracy): internal (did the IV cause the DV change? - threatened by demand characteristics, confounding variables, investigator effects); external (generalisable to other settings/populations/eras); ecological (real-life applicability); temporal (applicable across eras); construct (does the test measure the concept it claims to?); face (does it look valid?); concurrent (agrees with an established measure). Improved by: control groups, standardisation, single-blind procedures, natural settings and operationalisation. Features of science (AQA 4.2.3): theory construction (hypotheses derived from theories), falsifiability (Popper - theories must be testable and capable of being disproven; psychology's theories must generate testable predictions), replicability (findings must be repeatable - the basis of reliability), objectivity (bias-free measurement, empirical methods), empirical methods (evidence from observation/experiment, not speculation) and paradigms and paradigm shifts (Kuhn - a science has a shared framework; psychology may be a 'pre-science' because it lacks a single paradigm). Peer review : research is assessed by independent experts before publication to check validity , significance and originality ; it allocates research funding and maintains quality, but it is imperfect - reviewers may be biased (against unconventional findings, or in favour of their own field), anonymity can hide personal attacks, and publication bias favours positive results (the 'file drawer problem'). Psychological report structure (AQA 4.2.3): abstract (~150-word summary of aim, method, results, conclusions), introduction (literature review leading to aims and hypotheses), method (design, sample, materials/apparatus, procedure - detailed enough to replicate), results (descriptive and inferential statistics, tables/graphs; qualitative analysis if applicable), discussion (interpretation, evaluation, implications, further research), references (full APA format: Author, A. A. (Year). Title of article. Journal Name , Volume (Issue), pages.) Descriptive statistics summarise data. Measures of central tendency : mean (sum ÷ number - uses all data, most sensitive, but distorted by outliers); median (middle value - unaffected by outliers, best for skewed data, but ignores some values); mode (most frequent - usable for nominal data, but may be bimodal and unrepresentative). Measures of dispersion : standard deviation (average spread around the mean - precise, uses all values, but distorted by outliers and harder to calculate) and range (highest minus lowest - quick and easy, but crude: distorted by a single outlier and ignores the distribution in between). Percentages and ratios are also used for summarising frequencies. Distributions : a normal distribution is symmetrical and bell-shaped, with the mean, median and mode all at the midpoint (e.g. height, IQ); a positive skew has a long tail to the right (most scores at the low end - the mean is pulled above the median; use the median); a negative skew has a long tail to the left (most scores at the high end - the mean is pulled below the median). Exam questions often ask you to identify the distribution and choose the appropriate measure of central tendency. Levels of measurement : nominal (categories/frequencies - e.g. gender, blood type; mode only; chi-square, sign test), ordinal (ranked/ordered data, unequal units - e.g. Likert scales, rankings, ratings; median, range; non-parametric tests) and interval (equal units on a scale with no true zero - e.g. seconds, temperature in °C, test scores; mean, SD; parametric tests). The level of measurement determines which inferential test is appropriate - the standard first question when choosing a test. Graphs and presentation : bar charts (categories, bars separated - nominal data), histograms (continuous data, bars touching - interval), scattergrams (correlations), line graphs (trends over time), tables (raw and summary data). The choice of graph matches the level of measurement - bar charts for nominal, scattergrams for correlations, histograms for interval distributions. Hypotheses : the null hypothesis (H0) predicts no difference/relationship ('there will be no difference...'); the alternative/experimental hypothesis (H1) predicts a difference/relationship - directional (one-tailed) if it states which way ('music will improve recall' - only used when prior research justifies the direction) or non-directional (two-tailed) ('music will affect recall'). Hypotheses must be operationalised and testable. Hypothesis testing and significance : the researcher sets a significance level (p ≤ 0.05 by convention - the probability of results occurring by chance is 5% or less), calculates the test statistic (calculated value) and compares it with the critical value from statistical tables. For most tests (t-tests, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Spearman, Pearson), results are significant if the calculated value equals or exceeds the critical value; for the sign test (and chi-square with one degree of freedom), significance requires the calculated value to be equal to or less than the critical value. The decision depends on: significance level (0.05 or 0.01), one- or two-tailed test, degrees of freedom (df = N-1 for related tests, N1+N2-2 for unrelated t-tests, (rows-1) × (columns-1) for chi-square) and N (sample size). Conclusions must state whether the null hypothesis is rejected or retained and report p (e.g. 'p ≤ 0.05, so the null hypothesis is rejected - music significantly improved recall'). Type I and type II errors : a type I error is a false positive - wrongly rejecting a true null hypothesis (claiming an effect exists when it does not); it occurs when the significance level is too lenient (e.g. using p type II error is a false negative - wrongly accepting a false null hypothesis (missing a real effect); it occurs when the level is too stringent (e.g. using p Choosing the inferential test - three questions decide which of the seven tests to use: (1) test of difference, correlation or association? (2) related (repeated measures/matched pairs) or unrelated (independent measures) design? (3) level of measurement: nominal, ordinal or interval? Test Purpose Design Data level Chi-square (χ²) Association/difference Independent (unrelated) Nominal Sign test Difference Related (repeated measures) Nominal (direction of difference) Mann-Whitney U Difference Unrelated (independent measures) Ordinal Wilcoxon (signed ranks) Difference Related (repeated measures/matched pairs) Ordinal Unrelated t-test Difference Unrelated (independent measures) Interval (normal distribution) Related t-test Difference Related (repeated measures/matched pairs) Interval (normal distribution) Spearman's rho Correlation Pairs of scores Ordinal Pearson's r Correlation Pairs of scores Interval (normal distribution) Parametric tests (related and unrelated t, Pearson's r) assume interval data and a normally distributed population - they are more powerful (more likely to detect a real effect) when assumptions are met; non-parametric tests (chi-square, sign test, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Spearman) make no distribution assumptions and suit ordinal/nominal data. The sign test (the simplest, and the one you must be able to compute): (1) record the direction of difference (+/-) between each pair of scores (ignore zeros, reducing N); (2) count the number of less frequent sign (S = the smaller total); (3) compare S with the critical value at p ≤ 0.05 for one/two-tailed; (4) significant if S ≤ critical value .

topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Biopsychology Describe the divisions of the nervous system (CNS, PNS, somatic, autonomic, sympathetic, parasympathetic) and the structure/function of neurons and the reflex arc (AQA 4.2.2) Explain synaptic transmission, including excitation and inhibition, and the endocrine system's fight-or-flight response (AQA 4.2.2) Evaluate localisation of function (Broca, Wernicke, motor/somatosensory cortex) and split-brain research (Sperry 1968) (AQA 4.2.2) Evaluate plasticity and functional recovery after trauma (Maguire taxi drivers), and ways of studying the brain: fMRI, EEG, ERP, post-mortem (AQA 4.2.2) Describe and evaluate biological rhythms: circadian, infradian and ultradian; endogenous pacemakers and exogenous zeitgebers (SCN, melatonin, light) (AQA 4.2.2) Nervous system: CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS; PNS splits into somatic (voluntary, sensory/motor) and autonomic (involuntary) - ANS splits into sympathetic (arousing) and parasympathetic (calming) Neurons: sensory (receptor → CNS, cell body in dorsal root ganglion), relay (within CNS), motor (CNS → effector); structure: dendrites, cell body, axon (myelin, nodes of Ranvier), terminal buttons Reflex arc: stimulus → sensory neuron → relay neuron (spinal cord) → motor neuron → muscle - fast, unconscious, bypasses the brain Synaptic transmission: action potential → Ca²⁺ → vesicle fusion → neurotransmitter release → postsynaptic receptors → EPSP/IPSP; summation (temporal/spatial); recycling via reuptake Endocrine: pituitary (master gland) → adrenal glands (adrenaline/cortisol) → fight-or-flight; hormones are slower than neural but longer-lasting Localisation: motor cortex (frontal), somatosensory (parietal), visual (occipital), auditory (temporal), Broca's area (left frontal, speech production - Tan), Wernicke's area (left temporal, comprehension) Split-brain (Sperry 1968): corpus callosum severed; 'ring' shown to right visual field → named with left hemisphere; left field → selected by touch with right hemisphere; supports lateralisation Plasticity: Maguire et al. (2000) taxi drivers - larger posterior hippocampi; functional recovery: axonal sprouting, denervation supersensitivity, recruit homologous areas Studying the brain: fMRI (blood oxygenation, 1-2mm resolution), EEG (overall electrical activity, sleep/epilepsy), ERPs (averaged responses to stimuli), post-mortem (Broca/Wernicke origins) Rhythms: circadian (~24h, sleep-wake, SCN + melatonin, Siffre cave study), infradian (>24h, menstrual cycle, Stern and McClintock pheromones), ultradian (<24h, sleep stages 90-min cycles, BRAC) Central nervous system (CNS) The brain and spinal cord: the brain coordinates higher functions and the spinal cord relays messages between the brain and body and controls reflexes. Autonomic nervous system (ANS) The PNS division controlling involuntary functions (heart rate, digestion, breathing), split into the sympathetic (arousing) and parasympathetic (calming) branches. Synaptic transmission The process by which neurotransmitters cross the synapse: an action potential triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft, binding receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Excitation and inhibition Neurotransmitter effects on the postsynaptic cell: excitatory neurotransmitters (e.g. adrenaline) depolarise it and increase firing; inhibitory neurotransmitters (e.g. GABA, serotonin) hyperpolarise it and decrease firing. Fight-or-flight response The sympathetic branch's response to threat: the hypothalamus triggers the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline, raising heart rate, blood pressure and glucose for immediate action. Localisation of function The theory that specific brain areas are responsible for specific functions: motor and somatosensory cortices, visual and auditory centres, Broca's and Wernicke's areas. Hemispheric lateralisation The specialisation of each hemisphere: language (Broca's and Wernicke's areas) is usually localised in the left hemisphere; the right hemisphere dominates visual-motor and spatial tasks. Plasticity The brain's ability to change and adapt its structure in response to experience and learning (synaptic connections form and strengthen - Maguire et al. 2000: taxi drivers' posterior hippocampi enlarged). Endogenous pacemakers Internal biological clocks that regulate rhythms - the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus regulates the sleep-wake cycle via the pineal gland's melatonin release. Exogenous zeitgebers External cues that entrain biological rhythms - light resets the SCN daily; social cues (meal times, clocks) entrain sleep and meal patterns. The nervous system divides into the central nervous system (CNS) - the brain and spinal cord (the brain coordinates higher functions: cognition, emotion, planning; the spinal cord relays messages between brain and body and controls reflexes) - and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) , which relays messages to and from the CNS.
