Decision tree A diagram of strategic choices (squares), chance outcomes (circles), probabilities and financial outcomes; the expected value of each option guides the decision. Expected value The sum of each outcome's financial value multiplied by its probability — the weighted average return of a risky option. Force-field analysis (Lewin) A framework listing driving forces for change and restraining forces against it; successful change strengthens drivers and weakens restraints. Strategic drift The gradual divergence between a firm's strategy and the changing environment — typically because the culture and routines that brought past success resist change (Johnson). SWOT audits the strategic position: internal strengths and weaknesses (capabilities, resources, cost base, brand, staff) against external opportunities and threats (market growth, technology, legislation, competitors). Used well, SWOT is not a list but a bridge to strategy: match strengths to opportunities (use a strong brand to enter a new market), convert weaknesses (outsource a weak IT function), and defend against threats that exploit weaknesses (a price war against a high-cost base). Limitations to evaluate: SWOT is static (a snapshot in dynamic markets), subjective (different managers list different items), unweighted (no prioritisation — a minor strength sits beside a critical one) and descriptive rather than analytical unless converted into actions. Examiners penalise SWOT used as a bare list; reward it as the basis for a judgement. PESTEL structures external change: Political — government policy, grants, trade policy, instability. Economic — growth, interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, unemployment, consumer income. Social — demographics, lifestyles, values (environmental awareness, ageing population, remote working). Technological — innovation, automation, e-commerce, AI — creative destruction threatens established business models. Environmental — sustainability pressure, emissions targets, weather and resource scarcity. Legal — employment law, consumer protection, competition regulation, minimum wage. Worked application — the UK electric vehicle industry: political — government grants and bans on new petrol/diesel cars create opportunities; economic — high fuel prices boost EV demand, but cost-of-living pressure may delay purchases; social — environmental awareness and the image of green driving increase adoption; technological — battery range improvements and expanding charging networks reduce barriers; environmental — emissions targets favour EVs, but battery production and disposal raise sustainability questions; legal — clean air zones (ULEZ) and zero-emission vehicle mandates push manufacturers to electrify. Evaluation: most factors create opportunities for EV makers, but threats remain — patchy charging infrastructure and possible subsidy withdrawal — so firms should monitor the external environment continuously rather than treat PESTEL as a one-off snapshot. Link PESTEL to opportunity-cost and risk: every strategic choice is made against a moving external backdrop, which is why strategic analysis is repeated, not one-off. Porter's five forces explain why some industries are more profitable than others — and where a firm's profit is vulnerable: Competitive rivalry — the more rivals of similar size, the fiercer the fight (price wars, promotion wars). Threat of new entrants — low when barriers are high: capital requirements, economies of scale, brand loyalty, regulation, established supply chains. Threat of substitutes — products meeting the same need differently (video streaming vs cinema; plant milk vs dairy) cap prices. Buyer power — strong when buyers are concentrated, price-sensitive or face low switching costs; they squeeze prices and terms. Supplier power — strong when suppliers are concentrated, inputs are unique, or switching suppliers is costly. Worked application — the UK supermarket industry: rivalry is high (Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, Morrisons, Aldi, Lidl — persistent price wars); new entrants are unlikely (huge capital, established supply chains, brand loyalty); substitutes are a moderate threat (convenience stores, online, markets); buyer power is high (price-sensitive shoppers, low switching costs, easy comparison); supplier power is moderate (supermarkets are huge buyers, but branded goods suppliers retain some power). The overall force profile explains why supermarket margins are thin despite enormous scale — five forces links industry structure to profitability, exactly the analysis chain examiners reward. Core competences are the capabilities that give durable competitive advantage, judged by the VRIN criteria: Valuable (creates customer value), Rare (few competitors have it), Inimitable (hard to copy — embedded in culture and routines), Non-substitutable (no alternative achieves the same). Examples: Toyota's production system, Apple's ecosystem integration, Dyson's engineering. Competences built on culture and accumulated learning resist imitation; competences based on a single feature (a price point, one technology) are copied or substituted quickly. Evaluation: competitive advantage erodes — Kodak's film dominance, BlackBerry's keyboard — so strategy must renew competences as the environment shifts; a strength today can become a rigidity tomorrow (strategic drift). Strong answers link the five forces to the chosen generic strategy: in a five-forces-hostile industry, either cost leadership (compete on price) or differentiation (escape price competition) is the route — which is Porter's bridge from analysis to direction. Porter's generic strategies — the two routes to above-average performance: Cost leadership — lowest unit costs in the industry, through economies of scale, process efficiency, standardisation and tight overheads; allows the lowest prices (Ryanair, Aldi, IKEA). Risks: thin margins are vulnerable to cost shocks (fuel, wage inflation) and price wars; cost-cutting can erode quality; imitation erodes the advantage. Differentiation — unique perceived value through brand, quality, service, design or innovation, supporting premium prices (Apple, British Airways, Dyson). Risks: the cost of differentiation may exceed what customers will pay; imitation narrows the difference; downturns shift demand to budget rivals. Focus — either strategy applied to a narrow niche: cost focus (lowest cost within the niche) or differentiation focus (unique value within the niche — Rolls-Royce, specialist B2B suppliers). Risks: niche size limits scale, and larger rivals may enter. Stuck in the middle: firms that commit to neither route underperform both — without low costs they cannot win on price; without differentiation they cannot justify premiums. (Counterpoint to evaluate: some firms blend both — IKEA offers low cost and distinctive design — so 'stuck in the middle' is contestable; Porter's defence is that such firms achieve one advantage at genuine scale.) Bowman's strategic clock extends the analysis along price and perceived value: routes include low price/low value (cheap and cheerful), low price (cost leadership), hybrid (low price with differentiation — IKEA again), differentiation (premium pricing for value), focused differentiation (premium for a niche), and the danger zones of raised prices without added value — which lose customers fast. The Ansoff matrix maps strategic direction by product and market: market penetration (existing/existing — lowest risk: promotion, loyalty, share gains), product development (new/existing — leverage brand loyalty, R&D risk), market development (existing/new — exporting, new segments, unfamiliar-competitor risk), diversification (new/new — highest risk, spreads risk across markets; related safer than conglomerate). Evaluation: risk rises as the firm moves from what it knows, but a 'safe' penetration strategy in a declining or saturated market can be the worst choice — risk must be weighed against reward, market conditions and the firm's core competences: the strongest direction exploits what the firm is genuinely best at (VRIN competences) in markets with attractive five-forces profiles. A decision tree quantifies risky choices: squares mark decisions, circles mark chance outcomes, and each outcome carries a probability and financial value. Method: multiply each outcome by its probability, sum to get the expected value (EV) of each chance node, then compare EVs — for a launch-with-cost option, subtract the launch cost from the EV. Full worked example: a firm must launch a product (cost £50,000) or not. If launched: high demand (probability 0.6) yields £120,000; low demand (0.4) yields £10,000. EV of high demand branch: 0.6 × 120,000 = £72,000. EV of low demand branch: 0.4 × 10,000 = £4,000. EV of launching = 72,000 + 4,000 = £76,000. Net gain of launching = 76,000 − 50,000 = £26,000 — positive, so launch; not launching yields £0. Uses: quantifies risk, forces explicit probabilities and options, and shows which outcomes drive the decision. Limitations to evaluate: probabilities are subjective estimates (garbage in, garbage out); EV is an average — it can hide a catastrophic low-demand outcome that a risk-averse firm cannot survive; it ignores qualitative factors (brand, staff, strategy fit) and non-financial objectives. A* answers state the net gain, then judge: the EV supports launching, but the £10,000 downside must be survivable and the 0.6 probability must be well-evidenced (market research). Investment appraisal (full step-by-step workings in the Finance topic — recap here for strategy use): Payback — time to recover the outlay: £100,000 at £30,000 a year = 3.33 years; favours liquidity, ignores post-payback flows and time value. ARR — average annual profit ÷ average investment × 100; comparable percentages, forecast-based, ignores timing. NPV — discount future cash flows (10% factors 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621): £100,000 outlay returning £30,000 a year for 5 years → 30,000 × 3.790 = £113,700 − 100,000 = +£13,700 ; positive NPV beats the cost of capital. Evaluation: NPV is theoretically superior; payback suits liquidity-constrained firms; decision trees add probability structure that appraisal lacks. All depend on forecast accuracy, and none captures strategy fit — a positive-NPV project that dilutes the brand or over-stretches management may still be wrong. The strongest strategic answers combine quantitative tools (decision trees, NPV) with qualitative analysis (five forces, SWOT, core competences) and reach a conditional judgement. Change is driven internally (new leadership, restructuring, culture programmes) and externally (PESTEL shifts, technology, competition). Lewin's model — unfreeze (create the case for change, challenge current behaviour), change (implement the new way), refreeze (embed and stabilise). His force-field analysis lists driving forces for change (competition, technology, leadership vision, financial pressure) against restraining forces (staff habits, fear, cost, culture); successful change strengthens drivers and — more effectively — weakens restraints. Kotter's eight steps operationalise it: create urgency ; build a guiding coalition ; form a strategic vision ; communicate the vision; empower employees to act; generate short-term wins ; consolidate gains and push further; anchor changes in culture. The steps matter for analysis: change fails most often at the start (no urgency, weak coalition) — which is why Kotter front-loads them. Kotter and Schlesinger's reasons for resistance: self-interest (fear of losing status, pay or job), misunderstanding (poor communication, lack of trust), low tolerance for change (feeling overwhelmed), and different assessments (staff genuinely disagree that change is needed). Methods to overcome resistance — matched to cause: education and communication (misunderstanding); participation and involvement (different assessments — co-ownership builds commitment); facilitation and support (low tolerance — training, counselling); negotiation and agreement (self-interest — e.g. enhanced redundancy terms); manipulation and co-option (fast but ethically dubious — destroys trust if exposed); explicit/implicit coercion (fastest, but breeds resentment and sabotage — a last resort). Organisational culture (Handy) — power, role, task, person — explains why change is hard: routines and values that delivered past success resist new ways; culture change (Kotter's anchor step) is slow, which is why quick structural change without cultural change usually reverts. Strategic drift (Johnson): gradual divergence between strategy and a changing environment — incremental change lags accelerating external change until a crisis forces transformational change (or the business fails): Kodak clung to film as digital matured; BlackBerry clung to keyboards. Leading and evaluating change: communicate the vision relentlessly, resource the change, celebrate early wins, and monitor KPIs (productivity, turnover, customer satisfaction, financial performance) to confirm the change delivers. Evaluation: the success of change management depends on the cause and depth of resistance (participation works for disagreement, not for self-interest), the speed demanded (coercion is fast but toxic), and the culture — the strongest answers judge change methods against context and stress that embedding change in culture is what makes it last.

topics.searchText: politics Politics The UK Constitution Describe the nature of the UK constitution — uncodified, unentrenched, unitary — and explain parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law (AQA 3.1.1.1; Edexcel P2 1.1) Identify the five sources of the constitution and illustrate each with statutes, cases or conventions (AO1) Analyse the constitutional reforms of 1997–2010 and 2010 to the present, assessing their significance (AQA 3.1.1.2; Edexcel P2 1.2) Explain the role and powers of the Scottish Parliament, Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly (AQA 3.1.1.3; Edexcel P2 1.3) Evaluate the impact of devolution on the UK, including the West Lothian Question and quasi-federalism (AO2/AO3) Construct balanced arguments for and against codification and further reform (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel P2 1.4) Uncodified + unentrenched = flexible: any constitutional rule can be amended by a simple parliamentary majority. Five sources: statute law, common law, conventions, works of authority, treaties. Labour 1997–2010: devolution, HRA 1998, Lords Act 1999, FOI Act 2000, Constitutional Reform Act 2005 (Supreme Court 2009). 2010 onwards: FTPA 2011 (repealed 2022), Scotland Acts 2012/2016, EU Withdrawal Acts 2018/2020, DCPA 2022. Miller II (2019): prorogation unlawful — courts willing to police the executive inside an uncodified constitution. Devolution is asymmetric (Scotland strongest); England has no parliament — quasi-federal, not federal. Uncodified constitution A constitution not contained in a single authoritative written document; its rules come from multiple sources, some written (statutes, cases) and some unwritten (conventions). Entrenchment Special legal protection making a constitutional rule hard to amend or repeal; the UK constitution is unentrenched, so Parliament can change it by simple majority. Parliamentary sovereignty The principle that Parliament is the supreme law-making body: it can legislate on any matter, cannot bind its successors and no court can strike down an Act (A V Dicey). Rule of law Dicey's principle that no one may be punished without a fair trial, all are equal before the law, and rights result from the ordinary law rather than a written constitution. Unitary state A state in which legal sovereignty rests with one central parliament; devolved bodies exercise delegated, not sovereign, power. Statute law Law made by Parliament in Acts; the most important source of the constitution (e.g. Human Rights Act 1998, Scotland Act 1998). Common law Judge-made law developed through precedent, including the royal prerogative and fundamental rights (e.g. Entick v Carrington 1765). Constitutional conventions Unwritten rules of behaviour regarded as binding but not legally enforceable — e.g. royal assent is always granted and the prime minister must sit in the Commons. Works of authority Respected scholarly texts that clarify constitutional practice — Dicey's Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution, Bagehot's The English Constitution, Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice. Devolution The transfer of powers from central government to subordinate elected bodies (Holyrood, Senedd, NI Assembly) without transferring sovereignty. Quasi-federalism A unitary state that in practice operates with federal-style features — powerful, asymmetrical devolved legislatures alongside a sovereign Westminster. West Lothian Question The anomaly that Scottish MPs at Westminster can vote on English matters while English MPs cannot vote on devolved Scottish matters. The UK constitution is uncodified : there is no single, authoritative document setting out the rules of the political system. Its rules are scattered across statutes, court judgments, conventions and works of authority. It is also unentrenched — no rule enjoys special legal protection, so any element can be amended or repealed by a simple parliamentary majority. This makes the constitution flexible : major changes (devolution, the Human Rights Act) were enacted without special procedures, in contrast to the cumbersome amendment processes of codified constitutions. Three principles anchor the system. Parliamentary sovereignty (A V Dicey): Parliament is the supreme legal authority — it can make or unmake any law, cannot bind its successors, and no court may strike down an Act of Parliament. The rule of law : no one may be punished without a fair trial, everyone is equally subject to the law, and rights arise from the ordinary law. The unitary state : legal sovereignty rests at Westminster; devolution (1998 onwards) delegated power to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland without sharing sovereignty — although in practice the UK now displays quasi-federal features. The contrast with codified constitutions is a favourite examiner's line. In the USA the constitution is entrenched : amendment needs supermajorities and the Supreme Court can strike down Acts of Congress as unconstitutional. In the UK, sovereignty means judges can interpret Acts and declare incompatibility but cannot invalidate primary legislation — so constitutional change is political, not judicial. Note too that much of the UK constitution is written: the HRA 1998, the Scotland Act 1998 and the Ministerial Code are all textual. What is missing is a single hierarchy of rules with higher-law status. Source What it is Key examples Statute law Acts of Parliament — the most important source because of sovereignty Human Rights Act 1998; Scotland Act 1998; Constitutional Reform Act 2005; EU Withdrawal Act 2018 Common law Judge-made law from precedent, including the royal prerogative and fundamental rights Entick v Carrington (1765) — state power requires legal authority; A and others v Jackson (2005) on the Parliament Acts; R (Miller) v The Prime Minister (2019) Conventions Unwritten, non-enforceable rules regarded as binding Royal assent always granted; the PM sits in the Commons; the Salisbury Convention; collective responsibility Works of authority Respected scholarly texts clarifying practice Dicey (1885); Bagehot (1867); Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice Treaties International agreements binding in international law Treaty of Accession 1972 / EU membership 1973–2020; ECHR (incorporated domestically via the HRA 1998) Why conventions matter in essays Conventions show both the constitution's flexibility and its fragility. Because they are not legally enforceable they can be broken — as Johnson attempted with prorogation in 2019, when the Supreme Court ruled the advice to the monarch unlawful (Miller II), and as the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 demonstrated by reversing the statutory fixed-term rules. Use conventions to evaluate whether an uncodified constitution adequately constrains the executive. Labour entered office in 1997 with a programme of democratic renewal . The reforms devolved power, strengthened rights protection and separated the judiciary from the executive — but they were piecemeal rather than codifying. Devolution (Scotland Act 1998, Government of Wales Act 1998, Northern Ireland Act 1998 alongside the Good Friday Agreement): created elected bodies in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast with legislative and (in Scotland) tax-varying powers — the most transformative reform. Human Rights Act 1998 : incorporated the ECHR into UK law. Judges must interpret legislation compatibly with convention rights (s3); where that is impossible, courts may issue a declaration of incompatibility (s4), to which Parliament may respond — rights protection without overriding sovereignty. Public authorities are bound to act compatibly (s6). House of Lords Act 1999 : removed all but 92 hereditary peers, modernising the second chamber's composition. Freedom of Information Act 2000 : gave citizens a qualified right of access to information held by public bodies. Constitutional Reform Act 2005 : replaced the Law Lords with a UK Supreme Court (opened 2009) in a separate building, created an independent Judicial Appointments Commission and redefined the Lord Chancellor's role — a fuller separation of powers. Evaluation: the reforms fragmented executive power and made rights justiciable in UK courts, but stopped short of codification, left Lords reform unfinished (the Wakeham Royal Commission 2000 proposed a largely appointed chamber; nothing was enacted) and made the constitution more complex and more litigious. Whether they strengthened democracy depends on the benchmark chosen: devolution clearly did; the HRA's reliance on parliamentary goodwill did not fully. The courts' use of the HRA is instructive: declarations of incompatibility in the Belmarsh case (A and others v SSHD, 2004) and Bellinger v Bellinger (2004) prompted legislative change, and Parliament responded in each — rights protection working as designed, if indirectly. Impact detail: the reforms reshaped party politics too — the SNP's rise in Scotland, a distinctive Welsh Labour government, and power-sharing in Belfast. The Freedom of Information Act changed accountability culture: the MPs' expenses scandal (2009) was exposed through FOI requests. These effects make the Labour reforms a strong case study in 'most significant reform' questions — but they also show the constitution becoming more litigious, with the courts' role expanding. The 2010–15 coalition produced the first statutory change to the electoral timetable: the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 (FTPA), setting five-year terms and replacing the PM's dissolution prerogative with a two-thirds Commons vote or a loss of confidence. It was used once — the 2017 early election — and tested unsuccessfully in 2019, when May's third attempt at an early election required the separate Early Parliamentary General Election Act 2019 instead; its repeal in 2022 restored the prime minister's traditional advantage over dissolution timing. The EU Act 2011 required a referendum for any further transfer of power to the EU. Devolution deepened: the Scotland Act 2012 and Wales Act 2014 devolved significant tax powers. From 2015 Conservative governments continued reshaping the constitution: the Recall of MPs Act 2015 allowed constituents to trigger a recall petition — and a by-election — for MPs sentenced to prison or suspended from the House; the Scotland Act 2016 devolved income tax rates and bands and declared Holyrood's permanence; the European Union Withdrawal Act 2018 and EU (Withdrawal Agreement) Act 2020 ended the supremacy of EU law in the UK, returning competences to Westminster and the devolved legislatures. Ministers relied on wide delegated powers ('Henry VIII clauses') to amend retained EU law without full parliamentary scrutiny — a standard criticism linking the constitution to executive power. In 2022 the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed the FTPA and restored the prerogative — a reversal illustrating the constitution's flexibility in both directions. Judicial–executive friction sharpened during Brexit. In R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the EU (Miller I, 2017) the Supreme Court held that triggering Article 50 required parliamentary authorisation; in R (Miller) v The Prime Minister (Miller II, 2019) it ruled the 2019 prorogation unlawful because it had the effect of frustrating Parliament's ability to carry out its constitutional functions without reasonable justification. These cases show judges policing the boundary between prerogative and sovereignty — key evidence in debates on whether an uncodified constitution still protects against executive overreach. Plans to replace the HRA with a British Bill of Rights were announced and then abandoned in 2023, leaving the reform agenda unfinished. Scotland: the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood (129 MSPs elected by the Additional Member System) holds primary legislative competence over devolved matters — health, education, justice, the environment, transport — under a reserved matters model: everything not reserved to Westminster is devolved. Since the Scotland Acts 2012 and 2016 it sets Scottish income tax rates and bands and controls land and transaction taxes. The 2014 independence referendum (55%–45%) tested the settlement, and the Scotland Act 2016 declared the parliament permanent — though s28(7) of the 1998 Act explicitly preserves Westminster's sovereignty. Wales: the Senedd (renamed from the National Assembly in 2020) began in 1999 with only secondary, delegated powers; a 2011 referendum and the Wales Acts 2014/2017 converted it into a primary legislature with income tax powers. It expanded from 60 to 96 members from the 2026 election. Northern Ireland: the Assembly is a consociational power-sharing body — key decisions require cross-community consent, reflecting the Good Friday Agreement 1998. It has twice collapsed (2017–2020 and 2022–2024), showing devolution's dependence on local consent. England: has no parliament of its own. English Votes for English Laws (EVEL) (2015) gave English MPs a veto stage over English-only bills; it was abolished in 2021 as complex and largely ineffective. Instead, England is devolved functionally: a directly elected London Mayor (from 2000) and metro mayors with combined authorities (Greater Manchester, West Midlands) control transport, skills and some budgets. Further county-level deals and a devolution framework continue to extend this model, and the Barnett formula still distributes much devolved funding by population — a further sign the settlement is pragmatic rather than principled. Impact: devolution has produced policy divergence (free tuition and personal care in Scotland; a differently organised NHS in Wales), built a quasi-federal pattern of asymmetrical power, and raised the West Lothian Question . It has arguably strengthened the union by giving the nations legitimate democratic outlets — but it has also created rival centres of legitimacy and kept constitutional pressure alive (the 2014 referendum, demands for indyref2). Whether devolution strengthens or weakens the union is the classic essay judgement: mark schemes reward both sides plus a supported verdict. Codification is the central debate. Arguments for : a codified constitution would clarify the rules (citizens and courts could find them in one authoritative place); strengthen rights protection (rights could not be repealed by ordinary statute); limit executive power (courts could strike down unconstitutional acts, as in the USA); and deepen civic understanding. Arguments against : flexibility allows rapid responses to crises and changing values; parliamentary sovereignty would remain, so Parliament could override judicial rulings anyway; codification would transfer power to unelected judges and invite judicial activism; and the current system has demonstrably adapted — devolution, the HRA and EU exit show an evolving constitution. Consider also partial codification — the route the UK has effectively taken: a written rights charter (the HRA), a statute-protected devolution settlement, and a codified procedure for treaties (Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010) — without a single higher-law document. Essays can argue the UK is drifting towards codification piecemeal, or that these are exceptions proving the flexibility rule. Other live debates for evaluation: House of Lords reform : should the second chamber be fully elected? Legitimacy versus expertise; the hereditary by-elections and crony peerage criticisms (see the Parliament topic). HRA vs a British Bill of Rights : would a domestic bill of rights protect rights better, or weaken protection and damage the UK's relationship with the ECHR? English devolution : a federal UK with an English parliament, or deeper metro-mayor devolution? Electoral reform : FPTP versus PR (the 2011 AV referendum rejected change) — link to representation and legitimacy. The voting age : lowering it to 16 (already used in Scottish and Welsh devolved elections; proposed for UK-wide elections in 2025) links the constitution to democracy and participation. Parliamentary terms : the FTPA's repeal in 2022 reopened the debate on dissolutions and prime ministerial advantage. Essay logic: high-mark answers weigh clarity against flexibility, protection against sovereignty, and constitutional stability against democratic renewal — then commit to a judgement with evidence (the Miller cases, the devolution record, the FTPA's rise and fall).

topics.searchText: politics Politics Parliament Describe the structure and composition of the Commons and Lords, and explain Commons primacy (AQA 3.1.2.1; Edexcel P2 2.1) Explain the functions of Parliament: legislation, scrutiny, representation, recruitment, deliberation and legitimacy (AQA 3.1.2.2; Edexcel P2 2.2) Outline the stages of the legislative process and analyse how government and backbenchers shape bills (AQA 3.1.2.3; Edexcel P2 2.3) Analyse the mechanisms of scrutiny — questions, select committees, debates and votes — and assess their effectiveness (AQA 3.1.2.2/3; Edexcel P2 2.4) Evaluate how effectively Parliament holds the executive to account (AO2/AO3) Evaluate arguments for and against a fully elected House of Lords (AO2/AO3) Commons primacy: democratic mandate + Parliament Acts 1911/1949 — the Lords can delay and amend but not defeat (with rare exceptions). Salisbury Convention: the Lords does not veto manifesto bills (tested by the Brexit amendments, 2017–19). Functions: legislation, scrutiny, representation, recruitment of ministers, deliberation, legitimacy. Scrutiny tools: PMQs, ministerial and urgent questions, departmental select committees (chairs elected since 2010), the Liaison Committee. 2019: May's record Commons defeats (three rejections of her Brexit deal) — the strongest modern evidence of Commons power. Royal assent is a formality — last refused 1708; the Lords' veto was curtailed by the Parliament Acts. Bicameral parliament A legislature with two chambers; the UK has the elected House of Commons and the unelected House of Lords. Confidence and supply A minimal governing arrangement in which a minority government wins confidence votes in return for support on budgets (supply) — e.g. the Conservative–DUP deal, 2017–19. Royal assent The monarch's formal approval of a bill, converting it into an Act; by convention assent is always granted — last refused by Queen Anne in 1708. Salisbury Convention The convention that the Lords does not block at second reading, or wreck, government bills enacting manifesto commitments. Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 Statutes limiting the Lords: money bills can be enacted without Lords consent after a month; other bills after two sessions and a one-year delay, with the Commons able to override. Select committee A small cross-party committee (usually 11–15 members) conducting in-depth inquiries into a department's spending, policy and administration; chairs elected since 2010. Public bill committee A legislative committee that examines a government bill line by line after second reading; its membership reflects the Commons party balance, so government majorities usually prevail. Private Members' Bill A bill introduced by a backbencher (via ballot, presentation or the ten-minute rule); rarely passes without government time, but can be landmark — e.g. the Abortion Act 1967. Whip An MP or peer responsible for party discipline — ensuring attendance and voting with the party; a three-line whip marks a compulsory vote. Backbencher An MP or peer holding no ministerial or shadow office; the source of private members' bills, committee work and backbench rebellions. Parliamentary privilege Freedom from legal liability for words spoken in Parliament (Article 9, Bill of Rights 1689), protecting frank debate and witnesses. Second reading The stage at which a chamber debates the general principles of a bill and votes on whether it proceeds. Parliament is bicameral : an elected House of Commons (650 MPs, one per constituency, elected by FPTP) and an unelected House of Lords (around 800 members). The Commons supplies the government and holds primacy: ministers are overwhelmingly drawn from it (the prime minister must, by convention, sit in the Commons), it alone approves taxation and it alone can remove a government through confidence. The Lords' powers were curtailed by the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 . House of Commons House of Lords Members 650 MPs elected by FPTP c. 800: life peers (independent commission plus PM patronage), 92 hereditary peers (internal by-elections under the House of Lords Act 1999), 26 bishops (the Lords Spiritual) Mandate Democratic — elected None — appointed, inherited or clerical Legislative power Full; approves money bills; can override the Lords via the Parliament Acts Delay (one year) and amendment; cannot block money bills or manifesto commitments (Salisbury Convention) Government role Supplies the PM and most ministers; confidence role Contains a few ministers (e.g. the Lords' Leader); no confidence role The Commons' work is organised around the Speaker (elected by MPs, expected to act impartially and holding a casting vote), the chamber's daily business, and constituency work — MPs spend much of the week on casework. The Lords' strengths are expertise and independence : peers face no re-election, so crossbenchers and former judges, medics and officials revise legislation with specialist knowledge. Its weaknesses are legitimacy (no mandate) and size. The hereditary element survived the 1999 Act by political compromise — a standing criticism in Lords reform essays. Reform history matters here: the Parliament Act 1911 followed the Lords' rejection of the 1909 People's Budget, establishing Commons financial primacy; the 1949 Act shortened the delay from two years to one; the House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers. Composition and power have shifted together — a useful analytical thread in essays. Parliament performs six overlapping functions: Legislation : passing, amending and debating bills — the core law-making role (see the legislative process below). Scrutiny and accountability : questioning ministers, committee inquiries, debates and votes that hold the executive to account. Representation : MPs represent constituencies and interests. The classic debate is trustee vs delegate (Burke): MPs exercise judgement, or follow constituents' views. Descriptive representation — how far Parliament mirrors society — has improved (the 2024 Commons contains record gender and ethnic diversity, with over 40% women) but still lags the population. Recruitment of ministers : government is formed from Parliament, giving MPs a route to office and ministers a parliamentary base — a fusion of executive and legislature that also defines the UK's weak separation of powers. Deliberation : debating the major issues of the day — opposition days, emergency debates (e.g. the 2019 Brexit debates) and backbench business committee time. Legitimacy : by consenting to taxation and legislation, the elected chamber confers democratic authority on government — the deepest source of Commons primacy. Financial control : the Commons alone grants supply (taxation and spending); the Public Accounts Committee examines audited departmental spending — though the executive's Budget proposals are rarely amended, a historic vestige of Crown control of finance. Evaluation point: the functions sometimes conflict. Effective scrutiny can slow legislation; representation can clash with party discipline (the whips). A strong essay weighs these tensions rather than listing functions — and notes that some functions (scrutiny) are stronger than others (initiating legislation). Financial control is real in form but weak in practice — the Budget is almost never amended, so the Commons' 'power of the purse' is largely retrospective scrutiny through the PAC. A government bill passes through: first reading (formal introduction), second reading (debate and vote on principles), committee stage (a public bill committee examines it line by line), report stage (further amendments), third reading (final approval), then the same stages in the Lords, ping-pong (exchanging amendments between the chambers) and royal assent . In practice the executive usually controls the process. Whips enforce discipline; programme motions (timetabling, used since 1998) can limit debate; public bill committees reflect the government's majority; and the Salisbury Convention stops the Lords vetoing manifesto bills. Yet Parliament does influence legislation: Amendments : governments concede changes to avoid defeat; the Lords routinely amends bills — the Brexit bills (2017–19) suffered 14+ Lords defeats on Article 50 and withdrawal terms, most later accepted or reversed. Government defeats : May's government suffered record Commons defeats in 2019 (her withdrawal deal was rejected three times), forcing delay and reshaping Brexit — the strongest modern evidence of Commons power. Johnson's large 2019 majority made defeats rare again — showing arithmetic determines parliamentary influence. Historic defeats — the Maastricht rebellions under Major (1992–93), which forced a confidence vote — show the same pattern: small majorities empower Parliament. Private Members' Bills : backbenchers in the ballot occasionally pass landmark laws — the Abortion Act 1967 and the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 — though most fail without government time. Since 2010 the Backbench Business Committee (the Wright Committee reforms) gives backbenchers control of some debating time. Urgent questions and emergency debates : the Speaker's discretion forces ministerial statements (used aggressively by Bercow, 2009–19). Evaluation: parliamentary influence is real but conditional — greatest when the government's majority is small, the governing party is divided, or the Lords is united. Government dominance of the timetable is the structural limit; the 2019 Brexit session, when the Commons seized control of the order paper, is the exception that proves the rule. PMQs (Wednesdays): the flagship scrutiny event — adversarial and theatrical, rewarding soundbites; critics doubt its substance, but it forces the PM to answer weekly and sets the political agenda. Ministerial and urgent questions : written and oral questions to departments; the Speaker can grant urgent questions for immediate answers — an effective modern innovation. Departmental select committees (since 1979; reformed by the Wright Committee, 2010, which introduced elections for chairs and members): around 11–15 cross-party MPs inquire into spending, policy and administration; they publish reports, summon witnesses and can embarrass government — e.g. the Treasury Committee's scrutiny of the 2022 mini-budget. The Liaison Committee questions the PM several times a year. Their power is influence, not compulsion : government may ignore recommendations but rarely escapes the publicity. Legislative vs select committees : public bill committees examine bills; select committees examine the government — keep this distinction crisp in exams. Votes : the ultimate check — opposition days, motions, and the confidence mechanism. Callaghan lost confidence by one vote in 1979; the FTPA's two-thirds rule (2011) was repealed in 2022, restoring simple-majority confidence votes. Overall assessment: scrutiny is stronger at the margins (committees, urgent questions) and weaker at the centre (PMQs, whipped votes). The strongest answers balance this and reach a supported judgement — Parliament holds ministers to account effectively when publicity and expertise combine, less effectively when party loyalty dominates. Strengths: committees influence policy and administration; amendments are frequently passed; the Lords' expertise produces detailed revision; Parliament asserted itself over Brexit (the 2019 defeats; the Benn Act 2019, which forced an extension request); e-petitions and backbench time broaden engagement. Weaknesses: executive dominance remains the structural problem — fusion of powers, whips, timetabling control and majorities usually deliver the government's programme; PMQs is theatre; Lords reform is incomplete (hereditary by-elections, crony peerage criticism, an ever-larger chamber); governments can ignore committee reports. Reform debates: A fully elected Lords : for — democratic legitimacy and no patronage; against — risks rival legitimacy with the Commons (deadlock), loses crossbench expertise, and would fill the chamber with party loyalists. The 2012 House of Lords Reform Bill was abandoned amid coalition tensions — evidence of political difficulty. Removing the hereditaries : the 2024 Labour government introduced legislation (the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Bill) to abolish the by-elections and remove the remaining hereditaries — partial reform, not full election. Strengthening the Commons : committee elections, more backbench time, reforming the PMQs format. Essay logic: weigh structural executive dominance against Parliament's expanded scrutiny toolbox; use the 2019 Brexit session, committee evidence and Lords amendments as proof points; finish with a judgement on whether reform has made Parliament more effective — and whether an elected Lords would strengthen or complicate scrutiny.

topics.name: The Prime Minister and Cabinet
topics.subject: politics
topics.searchText: politics Politics The Prime Minister and Cabinet Describe the roles and powers of the Prime Minister and of the Cabinet, using key concepts — core executive, primus inter pares, inner cabinet, cabinet committees (AQA 3.1.1.3; Edexcel P2 Topic 3) Explain the difference between individual and collective ministerial responsibility, supported by named examples such as Crichel Down (1954) and Iain Duncan Smith (2016) (AO1/AO2) Analyse the factors that shape the relationship between the Prime Minister and the Cabinet: majority size, party unity, cabinet management style and events (AO2) Deploy case studies of prime ministerial power — one from 1945–1997 (e.g. the poll tax, 1990) and one from 1997 to the present (e.g. the invasion of Iraq, 2003) — as the AQA specification requires (AO1) Evaluate the 'presidentialism' debate (Foley) using evidence for and against prime ministerial dominance (AO3) Link prime ministerial power to the other branches — Parliament, the judiciary (Miller II) and devolution — for synoptic credit (AO2/AO3) AQA 3.1.1.3 requires two examples of the PM and Cabinet dictating events: one from 1945–1997 (e.g. poll tax, 1990) and one from 1997–present (e.g. Iraq, 2003). Collective responsibility has agreed exceptions — the 1975 EEC referendum and the 2016 Brexit referendum allowed Cabinet free votes. Power depends on circumstance: an 80-seat majority (Johnson 2019) empowers; a hung parliament (May 2017) weakens. Miller II (2019) struck down prorogation — judicial constraint on the prerogative is now essential evidence in essays. The 2022 mass ministerial resignations that ended Johnson's premiership show party, not Parliament, is the PM's real check. Core executive The network of bodies at the apex of government — the Prime Minister, Cabinet, Cabinet committees and the Treasury — where power over policy and resources is contested and negotiated (Hennessy). Primus inter pares 'First among equals': the constitutional position of the Prime Minister as the most senior but nominally equal member of the Cabinet. Inner cabinet The small group of the most senior ministers (e.g. Prime Minister, Chancellor, Foreign Secretary, Home Secretary) who take the biggest decisions, often outside full Cabinet. Cabinet committee A sub-group of ministers, chaired usually by a senior minister or the Prime Minister, that settles policy in a defined area before it reaches full Cabinet — a key mechanism of delegation. Patronage The Prime Minister's power to appoint and dismiss ministers and to distribute other offices; it compels loyalty because careers depend on the Prime Minister's favour. Royal prerogative Residual powers now exercised in practice by ministers without parliamentary approval, including deploying the armed forces, treaty-making, granting honours and, since the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022, calling general elections. Collective responsibility The convention that Cabinet decisions are binding on all ministers, who must defend them publicly and resign or be dismissed if they cannot support them; includes confidentiality of Cabinet proceedings. Individual responsibility The convention that each minister is answerable to Parliament for their personal conduct and the errors and policy failures of their department, traditionally resigning for serious failures. Ministerial Code The rulebook for ministerial conduct, built on the seven Nolan principles; breaches are investigated by the independent adviser on ministers' interests — revised in 2022 under Johnson, softening the expectation that ministers resign for breaches. Presidentialism Michael Foley's thesis (2000) that UK prime ministers increasingly resemble presidents: spatial leadership, a personalised mandate and direct media appeals to the people over the party. Sofa government The Blair-era style of decision-making through informal chats with advisers and favoured ministers in the Prime Minister's study rather than through the formal Cabinet system (identified by the Butler Review, 2004). Vote of no confidence A Commons motion that, if lost by the government, triggers resignation or a general election; the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 codified this and its 2022 repeal restored the convention. The Prime Minister combines several roles: head of the executive and chair of Cabinet, leader of the largest party (giving a personal mandate after an election win), chief foreign-policy spokesman on the world stage (G7, NATO and summit diplomacy), the public face of government through weekly PMQs, and patron-in-chief. Patronage is the foundation of power: the PM appoints and dismisses around 100 paid ministerial posts — the Cabinet, junior ministers and whips — so careers depend on the PM's favour. Thatcher promoted loyalists in 1983; Sunak's 2022 and 2024 reshuffles rewarded unity. Patronage can also fail: ministers with independent power bases (a faction, a media profile, a big department) are hard to move. Ministers also exercise royal prerogative powers in the PM's name: deploying the armed forces (Blair committed troops to Iraq in 2003 without a binding vote before the conflict), negotiating treaties (the Brexit Withdrawal Agreement, 2019–20), granting honours (resignation honours lists) and — since the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 repealed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 — choosing the date of general elections. Prerogative power is not unlimited: Miller II (2019) made a five-week prorogation unlawful, and statute can override prerogative ( Miller I , 2017 — Article 50 required an Act of Parliament). Conceptually, the PM sits within the core executive (Hennessy): a network — PM, Cabinet, Cabinet committees, the Treasury and senior advisers — in which resources and policy are negotiated, not commanded. The inner cabinet (PM, Chancellor, Foreign and Home Secretaries) takes the biggest decisions, and cabinet committees settle most business before full Cabinet. This supports the view that the PM is primus inter pares — first among equals — rather than a president. Yet prime ministerial resources have grown: the Cabinet Office and No.10 policy units, the pool of special advisers, and control of the government's media narrative all give the modern PM levers Attlee lacked. Collective responsibility has three strands: unanimity (Cabinet decisions bind every minister, who must defend them publicly), confidentiality (internal argument stays private, protected even from select committees) and confidence (the government resigns or seeks a dissolution if it loses a confidence vote). Enforcement is by resignation or sacking: Robin Cook (2003) and Clare Short (2003) resigned over Iraq; Iain Duncan Smith (2016) resigned over welfare reform cuts — both AQA-cited examples. The convention bends when agreed: Wilson allowed a free campaign in the 1975 EEC referendum, and Cameron suspended collective responsibility for the 2016 Brexit referendum — letting Johnson, Gove and Leadsom campaign Leave from the Cabinet table. It can also be weakened in effect: Johnson's 2022 revision of the Ministerial Code relaxed the expectation that ministers resign for breaches, before party revolt forced him out anyway. Individual responsibility makes each minister answerable to Parliament — through oral and written questions, statements and departmental select committees — and responsible for departmental failure and personal conduct. The classic precedent is Crichel Down (1954) : Sir Thomas Dugdale resigned even though officials, not the minister, were at fault. Modern examples split into departmental failure (Lord Carrington after the Falklands invasion, 1982; Estelle Morris, 2002; Amber Rudd over the Windrush scandal, 2018) and personal misconduct (Priti Patel's 2020 bullying findings, which Johnson defended; Gavin Williamson's 2021 sacking over leaks; Suella Braverman's two resignations, 2022 and 2023, over security breaches and inflammatory comments). Whether ministers must resign is contested — the Ministerial Code has no automatic sanction — so strong Edexcel answers argue accountability now depends more on the PM's political judgement than on convention. Convention Definition Enforcement example Collective responsibility Ministers defend Cabinet decisions or leave Robin Cook, Iraq (2003) Individual responsibility Ministers answer for their department and conduct Amber Rudd, Windrush (2018) Confidentiality Cabinet discussion stays private Leak inquiries into Williamson (2021) The relationship between the Prime Minister and Cabinet is not fixed; it varies with four main factors. 1. Size of the majority. Landslide majorities make the Commons near-irrelevant and the PM unchallengeable in Cabinet — Thatcher after 1983 (144) and Blair after 1997 (179) could govern by decree. Minority or small majorities shift power to Parliament and to recalcitrant ministers: May's 2017 loss of her majority made the DUP and Cabinet Brexit factions decisive — Davis and Johnson both resigned over the Chequers plan. 2. Party unity. A united party lets the PM dominate; a divided one paralyses them. Europe destroyed Thatcher (Howe's 1990 resignation speech triggered Heseltine's challenge) and May (repeated Commons defeats); the 2022 resignations — Sunak and Javid first, then 50+ ministers — destroyed Johnson. 3. Cabinet management style. Thatcher was domineering but initially let ministers run their departments; Blair bypassed Cabinet through sofa government with advisers and a few trusted colleagues (Butler Review, 2004); May was inclusive but indecisive; Truss excluded the Treasury and cabinet committees from the mini-budget — with catastrophic results. 4. Events and circumstances. War and crisis centralise power in No.10: the Falklands (1982) and Ukraine (2022) boosted incumbent PMs; COVID-19 gave Johnson emergency control of the timetable — but also exposed weak cabinet management (Cummings's account of chaotic decision-making). Economic crises constrain: Truss's mini-budget (September 2022) was reversed by markets, the Bank of England and her own MPs within weeks — the starkest modern proof that 'events, dear boy' (Macmillan) govern premierships. 5. Media and public standing. Blair's media mastery and Johnson's press celebrity sustained them through crises that would have felled others; Sunak's poor poll ratings weakened his authority from 2023. The presidentialism debate (Foley, 2000) synthesises these factors: spatial leadership (the PM as a brand apart — 'Blair's Britain'), a personalised mandate (leader-centred campaigns, televised debates) and plebiscitary devices (referendums, direct appeals over the party's head). The counter-case: Brown, May, Truss and Sunak all reached No.10 without winning a general election as leader; collective Cabinet proved indispensable in COVID COBRA meetings; and Parliament humiliated May and Johnson alike. The A* judgement: prime ministerial power is contingent — patronage, media and majority explain dominance; party division, events and, since Miller II, the courts explain subordination. The AQA specification requires one example of the PM and Cabinet dictating events from 1945–1997 and one from 1997 to the present . The safest pair: the poll tax (1990) and the invasion of Iraq (2003) . Poll tax (Thatcher). Thatcher imposed the community charge against Cabinet and Treasury warnings, using her 1987 majority and patronage to overrule dissent. Riots (Trafalgar Square, 1990), mass non-payment and Conservative MPs' panic forced Heseltine's challenge; Howe's resignation speech sealed her fall. It shows a PM dictating policy — and the limits when policy fails. Iraq (Blair). Blair committed Britain to the 2003 invasion through sofa government and close alignment with George W. Bush, with Cabinet discussion minimal and Parliament voting after the decision was effectively taken. The Butler Review (2004) criticised the use of intelligence. 139 Labour MPs rebelled — the largest revolt on a major issue since 1945 — and the fallout defined his legacy. Supporting case studies round out the comparison: PM Dates Evidence of power Limits exposed Thatcher 1979–90 Three election wins; dominated Cabinet; poll tax imposed Party revolt ended her — Europe, poll tax Blair 1997–2007 179-seat majority; sofa government; Iraq Backbench revolt; Butler Review criticism Brown 2007–10 Crisis management of the 2008 banking rescue No personal mandate; 2010 hung parliament Cameron 2010–16 Coalition control; AV referendum (2011); EU referendum called on his authority Referendum backfired; resigned 2016 May 2016–19 Set the Brexit agenda; controlled the timetable Lost majority 2017; defeated 432–202 on her deal; prorogation ruled unlawful Johnson 2019–22 80-seat majority; centralised COVID decisions Partygate; Miller II; 2022 mass resignations Truss 2022 Imposed the mini-budget on a cabinet kept in the dark Markets and MPs forced U-turns; 49 days Starmer 2024– 412-seat landslide; disciplined patronage Early controversies tested backbench loyalty For Edexcel, these cases feed the Topic 3 question of whether the PM and executive dominate Parliament: strong-majority PMs (Thatcher, Blair, Johnson in 2019) largely do; minority PMs (May) are dominated by it. Most questions on this topic are 'evaluate the view' essays (AQA 25 marks; Edexcel 30 marks) — typically presidentialism, PM-Cabinet power or ministerial accountability. Structure for the top band: Thesis in the introduction: state a qualified judgement up front, e.g. 'Prime ministers are presidents in presentation only — power depends on majority, party unity and events, as Thatcher's fall and Truss's 49 days show.' Three analytical paragraphs for the view (patronage; media and spatial leadership; majority control of Parliament), each with a named example. Three against: core executive negotiation (Hennessy); collective Cabinet in crises (COVID COBRA); constraints from party revolt (2022 resignations), Parliament (May's 432–202 defeat) and the courts (Miller II). A judgement that answers the question: not 'it depends' but what it depends on — the variables above. Synoptic links for the top band: Parliament (select committees and the Liaison Committee questioning the PM); the judiciary (Miller II on prorogation; Miller I on the prerogative-statute boundary); devolution (COVID showed No.10 cannot dictate to Holyrood and Cardiff — four-nations divergence); and the location of sovereignty (prerogative now bounded by both statute and judicial review). Common traps: narrating premierships without analysis; using only pre-2016 examples (Truss, Sunak and the 2022 resignations are fresh, examiner-friendly evidence); ignoring the counter-case that weak-mandate PMs (Brown, May, Truss, Sunak) disprove the presidential thesis as decisively as Thatcher and Blair support it.

topics.name: The Judiciary and Civil Liberties
topics.subject: politics
topics.searchText: politics Politics The Judiciary and Civil Liberties Describe the composition of the judiciary and the appointments process — the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the Supreme Court (2009) and the Judicial Appointments Commission (AQA 3.1.1.4; Edexcel P2 Topic 4) Distinguish judicial independence from judicial impartiality (neutrality) and evaluate how each is protected or threatened (AO1/AO2) Explain the role and powers of the Supreme Court: judicial review, ultra vires, statutory interpretation under HRA ss.3 and 4 (AO1/AO2) Evaluate the impact of Miller I (2017) and Miller II (2019) on the executive, legislature and the policy process (AO2/AO3) Assess how far the Human Rights Act 1998 protects civil liberties, using cases such as A v SSHD (2004) and PJS v News UK (2016) (AO2/AO3) Construct balanced judgements on the politicisation of the judiciary and on further reform, linking to the location of sovereignty (AO3) Miller I (2017, 8–3): triggering Article 50 required an Act of Parliament — the prerogative cannot override statute. Miller II (2019, 11–0): the five-week prorogation was unlawful, 'void and of no effect' — a direct check on the executive. A v SSHD (2004, Belmarsh): detention of foreign terror suspects was incompatible with ECHR Arts 5 and 14 — a s.4 declaration that forced the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005. Declarations of incompatibility do not strike down Acts — parliamentary sovereignty survives Miller I/II. The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 limited quashing orders and abolished Cart judicial reviews — executive push-back against judicial power. Judicial independence The principle that judges decide cases free from pressure by the executive, Parliament, parties or the media — protected by security of tenure, paid salaries from the Consolidated Fund, sub judice rules and a ban on political activity. Judicial impartiality The principle (AQA's term; also 'neutrality') that judges apply the law without personal bias or political sympathy — assessed through the judiciary's social composition and case outcomes. Separation of powers Montesquieu's principle that legislative, executive and judicial power should be held by different bodies; the Constitutional Reform Act 2005 moved the UK closer to it by separating the judiciary from the Lord Chancellor and the Lords. Ultra vires 'Beyond the powers': the doctrine that public bodies acting outside the powers given to them by Parliament (or natural justice) can be struck down by the courts. Judicial review The process by which the High Court and Supreme Court review the lawfulness of executive action and delegated legislation — a check on the executive, not on Acts of Parliament. Declaration of incompatibility Under s.4 of the Human Rights Act 1998, a court statement that legislation is incompatible with the ECHR; it does not strike the law down — Parliament chooses whether to respond, preserving parliamentary sovereignty. Human Rights Act 1998 The Act that incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law: s.3 requires compatible interpretation of statutes where possible, s.4 allows declarations of incompatibility, s.6 makes it unlawful for public authorities to act incompatibly. European Convention on Human Rights The Council of Europe treaty (1950) whose rights — life (Art 2), liberty (Art 5), fair trial (Art 6), privacy (Art 8), expression (Art 10) — are enforced in UK courts through the HRA, not by EU membership. Constitutional Reform Act 2005 The Act that ended the Law Lords' seat in the House of Lords, created the Supreme Court (opened 2009), curtailed the Lord Chancellor's combined role and created the Judicial Appointments Commission. Judicial Appointments Commission The independent commission (est. 2006) that selects judges through open competition on merit, replacing the Lord Chancellor's secretive 'secret soundings' of candidates. Sub judice The rule that MPs and peers may not debate cases active before the courts — one safeguard of judicial independence from Parliament. Residual liberties Dicey's view of UK rights: everything is permitted unless the law forbids it, and rights result from ordinary law and court judgments rather than a written charter — contrasted with the positive, listed rights of the HRA. Before 2005 the most senior judges sat as Law Lords in the House of Lords — legislators and judges — while the Lord Chancellor combined executive, legislative and judicial roles in one office. The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 unpicked this: it created the Supreme Court (opened October 2009 in the Middlesex Guildhall, Parliament Square), ended the Lord Chancellor's headship of the judiciary (transferred to the Lord Chief Justice) and established the Judicial Appointments Commission (2006), which selects judges through open competition on merit rather than the 'secret soundings' by which past Lord Chancellors picked judges who shared the government's politics. Security of tenure (judges cannot be removed for their rulings, under the Act of Settlement 1701), salaries paid from the Consolidated Fund, the sub judice rule and a bar on judges' political activity all protect judicial independence — the absence of pressure from the executive, Parliament, parties or media. Impartiality (neutrality) is harder to guarantee by design because it depends on who the judges are. Critics point to the composition of the senior judiciary: most Supreme Court justices were educated at Oxford or Cambridge, many privately schooled, and the bench has historically been dominated by white men — Lady Hale became the first female President of the Supreme Court only in 2017, and ethnic-minority and state-school representation at the top remains thin, though women now make up around a third of judges overall and diversity below the top has improved. Defenders reply that judicial diversity has increased, that appointments are merit-based and transparent since the JAC, and that judgments themselves (unanimous 11–0 rulings, decisions against governments of both parties) demonstrate impartiality in practice. For essays, keep the two concepts distinct: independence = freedom from pressure (institutional), impartiality = absence of bias (compositional and behavioural). The Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for all UK civil cases and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and it hears devolution disputes. It only decides points of law of general public importance — typically 60–80 appeals a year — but its impact on government, the legislature and the policy process is disproportionate (AQA 3.1.1.4). Its main weapons: Judicial review of executive action. Under the doctrine of ultra vires , ministers and public bodies acting beyond the powers Parliament gave them — or contrary to natural justice — can be struck down. R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor (2017) quashed employment tribunal fees: the Court held that access to justice is a constitutional right, not a commodity, forcing the government to repay £27m+ in fees. Statutory interpretation under the HRA. Section 3 requires statutes to be read compatibly with the ECHR where possible (Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza, 2004); where impossible, s.4 permits a declaration of incompatibility — which does not strike the law down. Parliament usually responds: after A v SSHD (2004) — the Belmarsh case, where detaining foreign terror suspects without trial was held incompatible with ECHR Arts 5 and 14 — the government replaced detention with control orders (Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005). Constraining the prerogative. Miller I and Miller II (below) proved that even the executive's most traditional prerogative powers are reviewable — a shift in the location of sovereignty in all but name. Note the limit: the Court cannot strike down Acts of Parliament. Miller I (2017, 8–3) held that triggering Article 50 required an Act of Parliament because the prerogative cannot override statute; it also confirmed the Sewel convention (no legislation on devolved matters without consent) is political, not justiciable. The Court polices the boundary between prerogative and statute — it does not overrule Westminster. Miller I — R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union (2017). The government argued its prerogative powers over treaty-making let it trigger Article 50 without Parliament. The Supreme Court disagreed, 8–3: ministers cannot use prerogative powers to remove rights established by Parliament (the European Communities Act 1972) — primary legislation was required, and the European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017 followed. Significance: the Court reasserted parliamentary sovereignty at the moment of the biggest constitutional change since 1945, and MPs were given a vote ministers wanted to avoid. The press reaction mattered as much as the ruling: the Daily Mail 's 'Enemies of the people' front page (November 2016, after the High Court stage) crystallised the accusation that judges had entered politics. Miller II — R (Miller) v The Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General for Scotland (2019). Boris Johnson prorogued Parliament for five weeks in September 2019 — the longest prorogation in recent history, in the final stages of the Brexit deadline. All 11 justices ruled the prorogation unlawful, void and of no effect : a decision with 'such an extreme effect' on the fundamentals of parliamentary democracy is not beyond judicial review. Parliament resumed within days; the Brexit deadline was then extended by the Benn Act. Significance: a unanimous Court set a justiciable limit on even the prerogative of prorogation — the strongest modern assertion that no minister is above the law. The executive responded by legislating: the Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act 2022 restored full prerogative control of dissolution, and the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 limited quashing orders and abolished Cart judicial reviews — evidence for essays that executive push-back against judicial power is itself a live constitutional issue. For A* evaluation: Miller I and II show the Court shaping the policy process (forcing Acts, voiding executive action) without acquiring American-style power — the sovereignty of Parliament survived intact because declarations and procedural rulings leave the last word to Westminster. Compare AQA's alternative phrasing: the Supreme Court 'interacts with and influences' the legislative process rather than controlling it. The HRA 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law, converting Dicey's residual liberties (everything legal unless forbidden) into positive rights that public authorities must actively respect (s.6). Rights with heavy exam use: liberty of the person (Art 5), fair trial (Art 6), privacy (Art 8), freedom of expression (Art 10). The Act works through courts, not repeal: s.3 interpretation: courts read legislation compatibly wherever possible — Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza (2004) read 'surviving spouse' to include same-sex partners without amending the statute. s.4 declarations of incompatibility: A v SSHD (2004) — Belmarsh — held detention of foreign terrorism suspects incompatible with Arts 5 and 14; Parliament replaced the regime with control orders. Hirst v UK (2005) ruled the blanket ban on prisoner voting unlawful; Parliament, defying the judgment, kept the ban — proof that incompatibility judgments are advisory pressure, not commands. Arts 8 v 10 conflicts: PJS v News Group Newspapers (2016) upheld a privacy injunction against tabloid reporting of an extramarital affair — the Court prioritised privacy, though the story spread online, showing the limits of court orders in the internet age. Evaluation for essays: the HRA is the most consequential rights reform since 1997 — ordinary citizens can enforce rights in UK courts without going to Strasbourg, and the courts have checked counter-terror legislation (Belmarsh), Home Office policy (Windrush-era disputes) and press power. Against: rights remain under parliamentary sovereignty — incompatibility can be ignored (Hirst), recent governments have sought repeal or replacement (the Conservative Bill of Rights Bill 2022, introduced then abandoned), and the government elected in 2024 pledged to keep the HRA while reforming its operation. The civil-liberties verdict is therefore conditional: the HRA protects rights through parliamentary sovereignty, and its protection is only as strong as Parliament's willingness to respond. Judicial independence survives in structure, but its perception has been battered. After Miller I, tabloids branded judges 'Enemies of the people'; after Miller II, ministers and commentators attacked a ' politicised' court; Home Secretaries and Justice Secretaries have publicly criticised rulings and sentencing, and the Johnson-era Ministerial Code changes and Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 showed executive willingness to trim judicial power. Structural rebuttals for essays: judges cannot be sacked for their rulings (Act of Settlement 1701); appointments are independent of ministers since the JAC (2006); the Court rules against governments of both parties (UNISON 2017 against the Conservative fee regime; Miller I/II; A v SSHD against Labour); and unanimity (11–0 in Miller II) signals law, not politics. The scholarly case that composition undermines impartiality — elite education, under-representation of women and ethnic minorities at senior levels — is best used to concede neutrality concerns while distinguishing them from independence. Reform debates for evaluation: (1) Should the Supreme Court have power to strike down legislation, as in the USA? Against: it would end parliamentary sovereignty and politicise appointments still further; for: s.4 declarations are weak pressure when Parliament ignores them (Hirst). (2) Should judicial review be restricted? The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 did restrict it (suspended quashing orders, abolition of Cart reviews) — weigh government efficiency and the separation of powers against access to justice (UNISON). (3) Should appointments include ministers again, or diversify further? JAC merit-based appointment v the old secret soundings; diversity v judicial neutrality debates. Synoptic links: the location of sovereignty (Parliament still supreme — s.4; but prerogative now judicially bounded); devolution (the Court resolves devolution disputes, making it a quasi-constitutional arbiter); the constitution topic (Miller I/II as key evidence for codification and entrenchment arguments); and the executive topic (prerogative constraints on the PM). A top-band judgement: the judiciary has grown from the least to a leading branch since 2005 — Miller I and II made it a genuine check on the executive — yet it remains deliberately powerless against Acts of Parliament, by design.

topics.name: Democracy and Participation
topics.subject: politics
topics.searchText: politics Politics Democracy and Participation Distinguish direct from representative democracy and assess the advantages of each with UK examples (AQA 3.1.2.1; Edexcel P1 Topic 1) Evaluate claims that the UK suffers a participation crisis, using turnout, party membership and partisan dealignment data (AO2/AO3) Trace the development of the franchise from the Great Reform Act (1832) to the present, with the roles of the Chartists, Suffragists and Suffragettes (AO1) Analyse the influence of pressure groups, think tanks, lobbyists and corporations on government and Parliament (AQA 3.1.2.4; Edexcel P1 Topic 1.4) Evaluate democratic reforms since 1997 — devolution, the HRA, referendums, Lords reform, recall — and remaining deficits (AO2/AO3) Construct top-band judgements on franchise extension, compulsory voting and the health of UK democracy (AO3) Turnout collapsed to 59.4% in 2001 but recovered to 67.3% (2019) — the participation crisis is contested, not settled. 2016 EU referendum: 72% turnout, 52–48 — the biggest act of direct democracy in UK history. Franchise milestones: 1832 → 1867 → 1884 → 1918 → 1928 → 1969 (age 18); Chartists, Suffragists, Suffragettes drove change. Recall of MPs Act 2015 triggered two by-elections (Onasanya and Davies, both 2019) — first successful recalls in UK history. Other influences named in both specs: think tanks (Policy Exchange, IPPR), lobbyists (Transparency of Lobbying Act 2014), corporations (CBI) and the media. Direct democracy Citizens make decisions themselves without intermediaries — through referendums, initiatives and e-petitions; used sparingly in the UK (1975 EEC, 2011 AV, 2016 EU referendums). Representative democracy Citizens elect representatives (MPs, peers, councillors) who take decisions on their behalf — Burkean trustees rather than delegates — and are accountable at elections. Democratic deficit The gap between democratic ideals and practice: low turnout, unaccountable institutions (the Lords), safe seats and executive dominance reduce the legitimacy of decisions. Participation crisis The claim that declining turnout, collapsing party membership and partisan dealignment show citizens disengaging from formal politics — contested by evidence of referendum turnout and online activism. Suffrage / franchise The right to vote in public elections; extended from roughly one adult male in seven in 1832 to universal adult suffrage at 18 by 1969. Universal suffrage The franchise held by all adult citizens regardless of property, gender or class — achieved in stages: 1918 (all men, women over 30), 1928 (equal franchise), 1969 (age 18). Partisan dealignment The long-term decline in stable class-based party loyalty, making voters floating and elections more volatile — a key indicator used in participation-crisis arguments. Pluralist democracy A system in which power is dispersed among competing groups — parties, pressure groups, media — whose competition approximates the public interest (AQA 3.1.2.4's 'pluralism'). Insider pressure group A group with regular access to government decision-making (e.g. the BMA, NFU, CBI); effective but dependent on political favour. Outsider pressure group A group without access to government that campaigns externally through media and direct action (e.g. Just Stop Oil, Fathers 4 Justice); attention-grabbing but rarely consulted. Think tank A research body generating policy ideas outside parties and government (e.g. IPPR, Demos, Policy Exchange, IEA) — an 'other influence' on government named in both specs. Recall election Under the Recall of MPs Act 2015, an MP convicted of an offence or suspended for at least 10 sitting days faces a by-election if 10% of constituents sign a recall petition. Direct democracy means citizens decide issues themselves. UK use: UK-wide referendums on EEC membership (1975, 67% Yes), the Alternative Vote (2011, 68% No on a 42% turnout) and EU membership (2016, 52–48 on a 72% turnout — the largest act of direct democracy in UK history); devolved referendums (Scottish independence 2014, 55–45 on an 84.6% turnout — the highest for any UK vote since universal suffrage); and e-petitions, where 100,000 signatures make a petition eligible for consideration for debate — the 2019 'revoke Article 50' petition reached 6.1m signatures, the largest ever, and was debated but not acted on. Representative democracy means electing intermediaries: MPs, devolved and local representatives, under Burkean trustee rather than delegate logic. Advantages of representation: expertise, protection of minorities from majority tyranny, feasibility for complex government, and stable accountable government; advantages of direct democracy: legitimacy for constitutional questions, engagement, and decisions immune to party spin. A* answers use both : direct democracy suits issues of principle (Brexit, Scottish independence), representation suits technical governance — few voters can audit a budget. The participation crisis debate is the topic's core evaluation. Evidence for: general election turnout collapsed from ~84% (1950) to 59.4% (2001) and fell again to 59.7% (2024); party membership fell from millions in the 1950s (when around one in ten adults belonged) to under 500,000 combined today; partisan dealignment has made class voting unreliable and elections volatile; the 2009 expenses scandal damaged trust; and the majority of constituencies are safe seats where individual votes rarely matter. Evidence against: 2016 (72%) and 2017 (68.8%) turnout spikes; the Scottish referendum's 84.6%; surging online participation — 38 Degrees, Change.org, #MeToo and Black Lives Matter; and pressure-group membership that dwarfs party membership (the National Trust and RSPB each claim more members than all UK parties combined). The judgement that scores: 'crisis' overstates engagement collapse — participation has migrated from parties and elections to causes, campaigns and referendums. Both specs require analysis of participation beyond voting and parties. Pressure groups divide by access and motive. Insider groups hold regular access to government: the BMA shaped NHS policy and its 2023–24 strike ballot moved ministers; the NFU and CBI (a business group) are consulted routinely. Outsider groups campaign externally: Just Stop Oil (road blockages, 2022–23) and Insulate Britain generated headlines and pushed energy policy up the agenda but achieved little direct policy change; Snowdrop (after Dunblane, 1996–97) won the firearms ban — proof outsider groups can succeed when public sympathy is overwhelming. Promotional groups campaign for a cause (Liberty, Amnesty); interest groups defend members (unions, professional bodies). Success factors: resources and organisation, government sympathy, opposition status, public opinion and method fit. Think tanks generate the policy ideas parties borrow: New Labour drew on IPPR and Demos; Cameron's modernisation on Policy Exchange; Truss's 2022 mini-budget drew heavily on the Institute of Economic Affairs' free-market agenda — influence that can outlast any one government.
