Coasts are open systems : inputs of marine energy (waves, tides, currents) and sediment (cliff erosion, river load, offshore deposits, wind-blown sand), stores (beaches, dunes, salt marshes, bars) and outputs (sediment moved offshore or along-drift out of the cell). Dynamic equilibrium exists when inputs and outputs balance; disturbances (storm, human interference such as a groyne field) shift the system toward a new equilibrium. Energy derives from wind - fetch (distance of open water over which wind blows) controls wave size; wave height grows with wind speed, duration and fetch. Wave types: constructive waves (low height, long wavelength ~100 m, strong swash, weak backwash, low frequency 6-8/min) build beaches; destructive waves (high, steep, strong backwash, high frequency 10-14/min) erode. Beach morphology feeds back: a steep storm beach encourages plunging destructive waves; a gentle, wide dissipative beach absorbs energy. Sediment cells (littoral cells): England/Wales divided into 11 major cells; each has sources (rivers ~major supplier, cliff erosion e.g. Holderness supplying ~30% of cell sediment, offshore sandbanks), transfer zones (longshore drift, tidal currents) and sinks (spits, mudflats, dunes). Cells are treated as closed sub-systems for planning, but boundaries leak - sediment crosses cell edges, so schemes in one cell (e.g. groynes at Mappleton) starve downdrift areas. This is the systems-concept link examiners reward: management interventions are disturbances whose effects propagate along the cell. Wave refraction concentrates energy on protruding headlands (deeper water slows less, so waves bend and focus) and dissipates it in bays - explaining why headlands erode into caves/arches while bays accumulate beaches. Coastal energy is unevenly distributed: high-energy coasts (exposed, large fetch, e.g. Atlantic-facing Cornwall, North Sea Holderness) are drift- or swash-aligned with cliffs and storm beaches; low-energy coasts (sheltered estuaries, e.g. Humber, Solent) are dominated by deposition and mudflat/salt-marsh development. In 20-mark answers, use morphology-energy feedback explicitly: as a beach grows wider and gentler, it absorbs more wave energy, so deposition is self-limiting ; as a cliff recedes, the widening platform trips approaching waves, so erosion is self-limiting - both are negative feedbacks producing equilibrium profiles. Marine erosion: hydraulic action (water and compressed air forced into cracks - dominant on jointed rocks), abrasion/corrasion (sediment hurled at cliffs wears them down), attrition (clasts collide, becoming smaller and rounder), corrosion/solution (dissolving of calcareous rock - carbonic acid attacking chalk/limestone). Erosion rates vary with rock lithology (resistant chalk/granite vs weak boulder clay) and structure (dip, joints, faults). Marine transport and deposition: longshore drift (swash oblique, backwash perpendicular) moves sediment along drift-aligned coasts; traction, saltation, suspension and solution move material in the water column. Deposition occurs when energy falls - in sheltered bays, behind spits, at estuaries - governed by gravity settling and flocculation of clay particles in brackish water. Sub-aerial processes prepare and deliver cliff material to the sea: weathering - freeze-thaw, salt crystallisation, wetting/drying (mechanical); carbonation and hydrolysis (chemical, on limestone/chalk); biological (root growth, burrowing). Mass movement - rockfall on steep hard-rock cliffs; rotational slumping on saturated weak clays (slump scars, terraced cliff profiles - classic on Holderness boulder clay); mudflows and landslides (e.g. Holbeck Hall, Scarborough, 1993 - hotel lost as ~1 million tonnes of land slipped). The interplay matters: marine erosion undercuts the cliff foot, steepening the profile, while sub-aerial processes weaken and lower the top - cliffs retreat by combined marine and sub-aerial action, not waves alone. Erosional landforms develop where erosion is concentrated on weaknesses. Cliffs and wave-cut platforms: waves attack the base between high and low tide, cutting a wave-cut notch; the unsupported cliff retreats by mass movement, leaving a gently sloping wave-cut platform (typically ~1°-4° slope, hundreds of metres wide, exposed at low tide). Example: the platforms beneath the chalk cliffs at Flamborough Head. Caves, arches, stacks, stumps: on headlands with joints/faults, hydraulic action and abrasion deepen a cave; caves on opposite sides meet to form an arch (Durdle Door, Dorset); the arch roof collapses to leave a stack (Old Harry Rocks - the chalk stack formed when its arch collapsed; the Pinnacles are its stump stage). Sequence + named example + process attribution = full AO1/AO2 credit. Depositional landforms: spits - longshore drift deposits sand/shingle across a bay where the coastline changes direction, often with a hooked/recurved end (Spurn Head, Holderness; Orford Ness); bars - a spit growing across a bay encloses a lagoon (Slapton Ley); tombolos - ridge linking mainland to island (Chesil Beach to Portland, ~18 km of graded shingle); cuspate forelands (Dungeness) form where drift meets from two directions; salt marshes develop in sheltered estuaries as flocculated clay settles, with a vegetation succession from pioneer samphire to upper-marsh scrub. Emphasise interaction : spit growth alters wave patterns, causing erosion downdrift - landforms are part of the system, not static features. Named-example bank for landform questions: Flamborough Head (chalk cliffs, headland erosion, Old Harry stack), Durdle Door (limestone arch), Lulworth Cove (concordant coast, differential erosion of Purbeck/Portland beds), Chesil Beach (tombolo/bar with graded shingle, finest at the Portland end), Spurn Head (spit with recurved end at the Humber mouth), Dungeness (cuspate foreland), Slapton Ley (bar enclosing freshwater lagoon). For each, always attribute the process (longshore drift, wave refraction, differential erosion) and, where relevant, the factor (lithology - resistant vs weak rock; structure - concordant vs discordant coastline; vegetation - marsh succession). A* answers link two landforms in one causal chain, e.g. spit growth at Spurn Head alters tidal flow into the Humber, encouraging mudflat deposition - showing the landforms interact within the cell. Eustatic change is global: at the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 yr BP) sea level stood ~120 m lower (water locked in ice sheets); post-glacial warming and current thermal expansion (plus meltwater) raise it - global mean sea level rose ~1.7 mm/yr over the 20th century and ~3.3-3.7 mm/yr since the 1990s. Isostatic change is local land movement: Scotland is still rebounding (~1 mm/yr uplift) after ice-sheet unloading, while south-east England subsides (~1 mm/yr, forebulge collapse plus sediment compaction) - so relative sea level is falling in the north, rising in the south. Landforms of emergence and submergence: emergence leaves raised beaches and relict cliffs (e.g. Isle of Arran, west Scotland; Portland, Dorset); submergence leaves rias (drowned river valleys - Kingsbridge Estuary, Devon), fjords (glacially carved drowned valleys - Scottish lochs), Dalmatian coasts (drowned fold-aligned valleys, Croatia) and submerged forests (e.g. at Borth, Wales). Coastal flooding: risk concentrates on low-lying depositional coasts (east England estuaries, fens, Thames Gateway) where relative sea-level rise, storm surges (1953 surge killed ~300 in England; 2013 surge tested defences), high tides and fluvial inputs combine; human factors (development on floodplains, drained marshland subsidence) magnify exposure. Britain's coasts respond to eustatic fall/rise cycles - learn the paired processes: isostatic uplift + emergence vs subsidence + submergence, each with landform evidence. UK flooding case details worth quoting: the 1953 North Sea surge (~3 m above predicted tide; ~300 deaths in England, ~1,800 in the Netherlands) triggered the Thames Barrier and coastal defence investment; the 2013 surge (~0.5 m higher than 1953 in places) caused far less loss, showing the value of post-1953 defences. The Thames Barrier is now closed ~2x/yr for tidal flood threat versus rare closures in the 1980s - evidence that relative sea-level rise is increasing flood frequency in south-east England, where isostatic subsidence adds to the eustatic trend. Holderness (Flamborough Head to Spurn Head, ~61 km): one of Europe's fastest-eroding coasts - average 1-2 m/yr , locally up to 10 m/yr in storm years; cliffs of weak glacial boulder clay (till) fail by rotational slumping when saturated; destructive North Sea waves attack the base; narrow beaches give little protection, and longshore drift (north to south) removes sediment. Losses: ~30 villages since Roman times; ~2 m/yr at Hornsea and Mappleton; Easington gas terminal and villages (Mappleton, Withernsea) sit at risk. Defences and their consequences: Mappleton - two rock groynes (~£2 m, 1991) trapped beach sediment, halted local erosion, but terminal scour downdrift accelerated cliff retreat (Great Cowden losing ~10 m/yr); Hornsea - groynes + sea wall protect the town but starve beaches south; Withernsea - sea wall + rock armour; Spurn Head - held by 'holding the line' historically, repeatedly breached. Classic evidence for 'management shifts the problem along the cell'. Hard engineering: sea walls (£5,000-10,000/m, effective but reflective scour and maintenance burden), groynes (£150,000-200,000 each; interrupt drift, downdrift starvation), gabions (cheap wire cages, ~£100/m scale, but corrode in 10-20 years and unsightly), rock armour/riprap (absorb energy, durable). Soft engineering: beach nourishment (e.g. ~£5/m3, needs repeated recharge), cliff regrading and drainage, dune stabilisation, and managed realignment - breaching defences to restore salt marsh that absorbs wave energy and stores carbon (Medmerry, Sussex, 2011-13, ~£28 m, protecting ~350 properties and reducing flood risk where a £20 m/yr sea-wall renewal would have been needed; Wallasea Island, Essex). Do-nothing is also an explicit policy where protection costs exceed benefits. SMPs and ICZM: SMPs set one of four policies per management unit over 0-20, 20-50 and 50-100 years: Hold the Line (Mappleton, Hornsea, Withernsea, Easington), Managed Realignment (increasingly for undefended low-value farmland), No Active Intervention (most of Holderness farmland), Advance the Line (rare). Strengths: cell-based, cost-benefit tested (DEFRA/FEMA-style benefit-cost ratios), forward-looking. Weaknesses: non-statutory, relies on local authority budgets, contentious for communities losing protection. ICZM is the wider ideal: whole coastal zone, all sectors and stakeholders, cross-boundary cooperation - sustainable but hard to coordinate; SMPs are its practical UK expression. Evaluation line for essays: sustainability now favours strategic realignment over blanket holding the line as sea-level rise accelerates costs. ICZM detail for evaluation: ICZM principles (EU Recommendation 2002) include working with natural processes, whole-cell management, stakeholder participation, adaptive management and cross-boundary cooperation between sectors (tourism, ports, conservation, flood risk). In essays, contrast ICZM's holistic ideal with practical fragmentation: SMPs are non-statutory, funded through Environment Agency/local authority budgets, and community objections (e.g. Fairbourne, Wales - designated for eventual realignment) show the political limits of strategic retreat. This tension - sustainable cell-wide planning versus local democracy and property values - is the strongest AO3 angle for management questions.

topics.name: Hazards
topics.subject: geography
topics.searchText: geography Geography Hazards Explain plate movement mechanisms (slab pull, ridge push, convection) and describe the hazards and landforms of constructive, destructive, conservative and collision boundaries (AQA 3.1.5.1; Edexcel 2A.1; OCR 1.1.a) Explain volcanic hazards - pyroclastic flows, lahars, ashfall, gases, lava - and evaluate monitoring and prediction using the VEI and Mount Pinatubo 1991 (AQA 3.1.5.2; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.a) Describe earthquake waves and compare the Richter, moment magnitude and Mercalli scales; explain liquefaction and secondary hazards (AQA 3.1.5.3; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.a) Explain tsunami formation, characteristics and warning systems, using the 2004 Indian Ocean and 2011 Tohoku tsunamis (AQA 3.1.5.4; Edexcel 2A.3; OCR 1.2.b) Explain tropical storm formation and structure, apply the Saffir-Simpson scale, and assess wildfire causes, conditions and impacts (AQA 3.1.5.5-3.1.5.6; Edexcel 2A.2; OCR 1.2.c) Apply hazard perception and the Park model, and evaluate a multi-hazard environment (Philippines) plus local, national and international responses using Nepal 2015 (AQA 3.1.5.1, 3.1.5.7; Edexcel 2A.4-2A.6; OCR 1.3.a) Focus (hypocentre) The point within the crust where an earthquake's energy is released; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest. Moment magnitude scale (Mw) Logarithmic scale measuring total energy released, calculated from fault rupture area x slip x rock rigidity; does not saturate, so it is the standard for great earthquakes (Nepal 2015 = Mw 7.8). Pyroclastic flow (nuee ardente) A superheated (300-800 degrees C), fast-moving (100-300 km/h) avalanche of gas, ash and volcanic rock flowing down a volcano's flanks; usually the deadliest volcanic hazard (Montserrat 1997, Pompeii AD 79). Lahar A volcanic mudflow formed when ash and tephra mix with water (rainfall or melted snow/ice), flowing tens of kilometres at 30-60 km/h before setting concrete-hard (Nevado del Ruiz 1985 buried Armero, ~23,000 killed). Liquefaction Loss of shear strength in water-saturated fine sediments (reclaimed land, river deltas, valley fills) when shaken, so the ground behaves as a liquid and buildings tilt or sink (Christchurch 2011; Kathmandu 2015). Tsunami A series of long-wavelength ocean waves generated mainly by undersea earthquakes of Mw 7+ with vertical seabed displacement (also volcanic flank collapse, landslides); open-ocean speed ~700-800 km/h, growing to 10-30+ m near shore. Storm surge A rise in sea level at the coast driven by strong onshore winds and low pressure beneath a tropical storm, flooding low-lying land; usually the deadliest tropical-storm hazard (Haiyan 2013; 1953 North Sea surge). Saffir-Simpson scale A 1-5 category scale rating tropical storm (hurricane) intensity by sustained wind speed: Category 1 at 119 km/h or more; Category 5 at 252 km/h or more. Park model (disaster response curve) A curve plotting quality of life against time through a disaster: pre-disaster, disruption (sharp fall), relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction. Steepness of the fall indicates impact severity; gradient and length of recovery indicate level of development. Hazard perception How people judge the risk a hazard poses to them, shaped by experience, wealth, education and personality/worldview; perception determines whether households mitigate, insure, evacuate or remain fatalistic. Plate movement: the lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle) is broken into plates riding the semi-molten asthenosphere at 1-10 cm/yr. Driving forces: slab pull (dense oceanic lithosphere sinking at subduction zones - the dominant force), ridge push (gravity sliding off elevated ridges) and mantle convection. Evidence for seafloor spreading: symmetrical palaeomagnetic stripes either side of ridges and sea-floor age increasing with distance from ridges. Boundary types and their hazards: Boundary Motion / process Named example Typical hazards Constructive (divergent) Plates separate; magma upwells, new basaltic crust, sea-floor spreading Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Iceland); East African Rift Effusive lava, shield volcanoes, shallow low-magnitude quakes; Eyjafjallajokull 2010 ash cloud closed European airspace ~6 days Destructive (oceanic-continental) Denser oceanic plate subducts beneath continental plate along a Benioff zone, partially melting to viscous andesitic magma Nazca plate under South America (Andes) Explosive composite volcanoes (Pinatubo), deep to shallow quakes - some of the largest recorded (Chile 1960, Mw 9.5) Destructive (oceanic-oceanic) Denser plate subducts, forming volcanic island arcs Philippine Sea plate subduction; Japan trench Island-arc volcanoes, frequent shallow quakes, undersea quakes generating tsunami (Tohoku 2011) Conservative (transform) Plates slide past each other, grinding and locking - no crust created or destroyed San Andreas Fault (California) Shallow-focus, powerful earthquakes; no volcanism (San Francisco 1906) Collision Two continental plates converge; neither subducts - crust folds and thickens into mountain belts Indian plate meeting Eurasian plate - Himalayas Shallow-focus but high-magnitude earthquakes on thrust faults (Nepal 2015) Volcano types: lava viscosity depends on silica content - basaltic lava (~50% silica) is runny and degasses easily, giving effusive shield volcanoes (Mauna Loa, Hawaii) that rarely kill; viscous, gas-trapping andesitic/rhyolitic magma gives explosive Plinian eruptions and composite volcanoes (Pinatubo, Fuji) with pyroclastic flows. The silica-viscosity-explosivity chain is the AO2 link examiners reward: it explains why subduction zones (andesitic) kill far more people than hotspots (basaltic). Primary hazards: pyroclastic flows (nuees ardentes) - superheated (300-800 degrees C) mixtures of gas, ash and rock collapsing down valleys at 100-300 km/h; the deadliest volcanic hazard (Montserrat 1997 - Plymouth abandoned; Pompeii AD 79). Tephra and ashfall - collapses roofs (especially wet ash), contaminates water, destroys crops and halts aviation (Eyjafjallajokull 2010). Lava flows - destroy property and farmland but usually advance slowly enough to evacuate. Volcanic gases - SO2 converts to sulphuric aerosols that reflect sunlight: Pinatubo injected ~20 million tonnes of SO2, cooling global temperatures ~0.5 degrees C for over a year; gases can pool lethally (Lake Nyos 1986 CO2 cloud, ~1,700 killed). Lahars - volcanic mudflows wherever ash meets water: monsoon rain (Pinatubo's lahars buried towns for years after 1991) or flash-melted snow (Nevado del Ruiz 1985 - Armero buried, ~23,000 killed, despite warnings never acted on). Secondary hazards: tsunami (Krakatoa 1883, ~36,000 deaths), landslides and flank collapse, post-eruption famine and displacement. Monitoring and prediction: unlike earthquakes, volcanoes give precursors days-weeks ahead, so monitoring works where agencies are funded. Methods: seismometers detecting shallow harmonic tremor and magma-rise quake swarms; tiltmeters/GPS measuring summit inflation; gas spectrometry tracking rising SO2; thermal imaging and satellite radar detecting dome growth - all feeding hazard maps, alert levels and evacuation zones. The VEI (Volcanic Explosivity Index) rates eruptions 0-8 logarithmically by ejected tephra volume - Pinatubo 1991 was VEI 6; it describes size, not impact, so pair it with casualty data in answers. Case detail: Mount Pinatubo, Philippines 1991 (VEI 6) June 1991, after ~600 years dormant: PHIVOLCS and USGS combined monitoring (tremor, inflation, SO2) to forecast the climax eruption, evacuating ~200,000 people before 15 June - credited with saving thousands of lives. The eruption ejected ~10 km3 of tephra and ~20 Mt SO2 (global cooling ~0.5 degrees C); Typhoon Yunya's rain plus ashfall collapsed roofs, and lahars destroyed farmland and infrastructure for years, displacing hundreds of thousands. Classic synthesis evidence: prediction cut primary deaths, yet secondary hazards still devastated livelihoods. Cause and waves: stress accumulates along locked faults until rock fails - elastic rebound releases stored energy as seismic waves from the focus . P-waves : fastest (~6-8 km/s), compressional (push-pull), travel through solids and liquids, arrive first, weakest shaking. S-waves : ~half P speed, shear (side-to-side), solids only, stronger shaking - cannot cross the outer core, creating the shadow zone. Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh): slowest but most destructive - rolling and sideways ground motion. Shaking is strongest near the epicentre and from shallow foci, amplified by soft sediment - valley cities suffer more than rock foundations. Measurement - three scales, one comparison point: Richter - logarithmic amplitude-based scale (each whole number = 10x amplitude, ~31x energy), but saturates above ~M7, under-rating great quakes. Moment magnitude (Mw) - from fault area x slip x rigidity; measures total energy, does not saturate; the modern standard (Nepal 2015 = Mw 7.8; Tohoku 2011 = Mw 9.0). Mercalli (I-XII) - subjective observed effects; varies with distance, geology and building quality - maps damage patterns but cannot compare quakes objectively. In essays: magnitude measures energy; impact depends on depth, distance, time of day, geology and - above all - development and preparedness. Liquefaction and secondary hazards: shaking turns water-saturated fine sediments into a fluid - buildings tilt and sink, buried pipes float up (Christchurch 2011 on reclaimed land; Kathmandu valley sediments in 2015). Other secondary hazards: landslides and avalanches in steep relief (Nepal 2015; Everest Base Camp), fires from fractured gas mains (San Francisco 1906), disease from broken sewers, and tsunami. Tsunami: generated mainly by undersea quakes of Mw 7+ with vertical seabed displacement (also volcanic flank collapse, large landslides), moving the whole water column. Open ocean: wavelength up to ~200 km, amplitude under 1 m, speed ~700-800 km/h. At shore: friction slows the wave, wavelength shortens, energy concentrates - amplitude grows to 10-30+ m, often as several waves with a strong backwash. Detection: seismic alert networks, DART deep-ocean pressure buoys and tide gauges (Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre). The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (Sumatra-Andaman, Mw 9.1; ~230,000 deaths across 14 countries) struck coastlines with no regional warning system - one was established after; the 2011 Tohoku tsunami (Mw 9.0, run-up up to ~40 m) overtopped Japan's sea walls, killed ~18,000 and caused the Fukushima nuclear accident - evidence that protection alone is insufficient without evacuation. Case study: Nepal (Gorkha) earthquake, 25 April 2015 - Mw 7.8 Cause: collision-boundary earthquake on the Main Himalayan Thrust (India subducting beneath Eurasia), shallow focus (~8-15 km), epicentre near Gorkha, ~80 km northwest of Kathmandu. Impacts: ~ 9,000 deaths and ~22,000 injured; ~8 million people affected; ~600,000 homes destroyed and a similar number damaged; ~2.8 million displaced. Unreinforced brick masonry in Kathmandu collapsed en masse and soft valley sediments amplified shaking (liquefaction and resonance); Langtang village was buried by a co-seismic avalanche; the Everest Base Camp avalanche killed 22; the Mw 7.3 aftershock (12 May) added deaths and hindered rescue. Economic loss ~US$7 billion - roughly a third of GDP - with heritage sites (Dharahara Tower) destroyed. Landlocked, so no tsunami; instead steep-relief landslides dammed valleys and cut off villages during the approaching monsoon. Responses: local communities dug survivors out before services arrived; national government declared a state of emergency and deployed the army; international aid flowed (India and China first responders; UN and NGO coordination; UK Disasters Emergency Committee appeal raised ~£33 million). Reconstruction was slow: hundreds of thousands remained in temporary shelter years later and earthquake-resistant building codes were enforced weakly - evidence for Park-model arguments about development and recovery speed. Tropical storm formation: they develop over oceans warmer than 26.5 degrees C (to ~50 m depth), between 5-20 degrees latitude (Coriolis force is too weak at the equator to organise rotation), with low vertical wind shear, high humidity and a pre-existing disturbance. Rising moist air condenses, releasing latent heat that fuels further uplift - a self-sustaining heat engine; pressure falls below ~950 mb. Structure: calm, cloud-free eye ; eyewall with the strongest winds and rain; spiral rain bands. The Saffir-Simpson scale rates intensity 1-5 by sustained wind speed (Cat 1: 119+ km/h; Cat 5: 252+ km/h) - a hazard-profile tool, not an impact scale. Deadliest impacts come from storm surge plus intense rainfall: Typhoon Haiyan (Philippines, November 2013, Cat 5, gusts ~315 km/h) killed ~6,300 and displaced ~4 million, with 5-7 m surge in Leyte Gulf; surges also dominate mid-latitude floods (1953 North Sea surge, ~300 deaths in England). AO3 point: warmer seas mean higher-intensity storms and possible poleward shifts - intensity trends, not frequency trends, are the climate signal. Wildfire: ignited by lightning or by people (arson, sparks, slash-and-burn clearance). Conditions: abundant dry fuel (worsened where fire suppression lets it accumulate), drought (ENSO-linked in Australia/Indonesia), low humidity, strong wind. Impacts: deaths, property loss, smoke pollution - the 2019-20 Australian 'Black Summer' burnt ~24 million hectares and killed or displaced ~3 billion animals. Some ecosystems are fire-adapted (serotinous cones need heat to open). Management: satellite hot-spot monitoring, prescribed burns, firebreaks, ember-resistant building codes. Hazard perception: how people judge risk - shaped by experience, wealth, education and personality/worldview. Perception drives response: poor hazard-prone communities often show fatalism and informal adaptation; wealthy ones fund prediction, zoning and building codes - the perception-development link is a high-value synthesis thread in 20-mark answers. Park model (disaster response curve): plots quality of life against time through pre-disaster, disruption (sharp fall), relief (immediate rescue, often externally aided), rehabilitation (temporary shelter, partial services) and reconstruction . Read comparatively: fall depth = impact magnitude; recovery gradient and duration = development and preparedness - Japan recovered within years after Tohoku (2011), Nepal's stretched over many; repeated hazards can lower the baseline itself. Multi-hazard environment - Philippines: typhoon belt (~20 typhoons enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility yearly) plus the Pacific 'Ring of Fire' (Philippine Sea plate subduction: ~20+ active volcanoes, frequent shallow quakes) plus monsoons. Hazards compound: Typhoon Yunya's rain met Pinatubo's ash to trigger lahars (1991); Haiyan (2013) was followed by further typhoons and quakes interrupting recovery. Repeated losses erode development gains - the classic AO3 link between multi-hazard incidence and persistent underdevelopment. Responses at three levels: local - community preparedness, evacuation drills and warnings (Philippine NDRRMC), hazard maps, hazard-resistant traditional building, community search-and-rescue (Nepal's spontaneous rescue saved most lives). national - monitoring agencies (PHIVOLCS, USGS, JMA), building codes and land-use zoning (Nepal's post-2015 code push), stockpiles, reconstruction programmes. international - UN OCHA coordination, NGOs (Red Cross/Red Crescent), bilateral aid (India and China to Nepal, 2015), the Sendai Framework 2015-2030 (reduced mortality and damage). Effective management runs mitigation-preparedness-response-recovery, matched to perceived risk and development capacity.

topics.searchText: geography Geography Global Systems and Governance Explain globalisation as the widening, deepening and speeding-up of worldwide interconnectedness, describe its economic, political, social and environmental dimensions, and account for the factors accelerating it - transport, communications, finance, management/information systems, security, trade agreements and global marketing (AQA 3.2.1.1) Describe and explain unequal flows of people, money, ideas and technology, and analyse the asymmetries (capital concentration, brain drain, terms of trade) that make globalisation winners and losers (AQA 3.2.1.1) Describe global trade flows and patterns, explain commodity chains and market access, and assess how unequal power relations are reproduced through the IMF, World Bank, WTO, structural adjustment and trade blocs (AQA 3.2.1.2-3.2.1.3) Explain the spatial organisation of TNCs - global production networks, outsourcing, FDI, transfer pricing - using Apple/Foxconn, and evaluate TNC power relative to states (AQA 3.2.1.2) Explain the concept of the global commons and describe the Antarctic Treaty system (1959 Treaty, Madrid Protocol 1991, CCAMLR, MPAs), threats to Antarctica, and the role of NGOs and international law (AQA 3.2.1.4) Evaluate the effectiveness of global governance of Antarctica and discuss sovereignty versus interdependence in a globalised world (AQA 3.2.1.4) Globalisation The widening, deepening and speeding-up of worldwide interconnectedness: the process by which decisions, events and activities in one region come to have significant consequences for people and places elsewhere, across economic, political, social and environmental dimensions. Glocalisation The adaptation of global products, brands or services to local markets and cultures - global reach with local tailoring (McDonald's vegetarian McAloo Tikki in India; Coca-Cola's localised campaigns). Global commons Resource domains that lie outside national jurisdiction and are shared by all - the high seas, the atmosphere, Antarctica and outer space; no state can exclude others from them, and overuse by some diminishes them for all. TNC (transnational corporation) A firm that owns or controls production or service facilities in more than one country, coordinating a global production network - locating design, manufacture, assembly and marketing in different places to maximise profit (Apple, Foxconn, Shell). FDI (foreign direct investment) Investment by a firm or government in productive assets (factories, offices, land, mergers) in another country, giving a lasting interest and control; the main channel through which TNCs transfer capital and technology (global FDI roughly $1.3 trillion in 2023). Structural adjustment IMF/World Bank conditionality attached to loans: privatisation of state assets, trade liberalisation, subsidy removal, currency devaluation and public-spending cuts - criticised for deepening recessions and opening economies to foreign competition (Jamaica from 1977; Greece 2010-15). Transfer pricing The pricing of transactions between branches of the same TNC in different countries, used to shift taxable profits to low-tax jurisdictions and minimise the tax paid where profits are actually earned (Apple ordered in 2016 to repay ~13 billion euros to Ireland). Antarctic Treaty (1959) The agreement signed on 1 December 1959 by the 12 states active in the International Geophysical Year, in force since 1961: Antarctica used for peaceful purposes only, territorial claims frozen (Article IV), military activity and nuclear explosions banned, freedom of scientific investigation guaranteed, decisions taken by consensus of consultative parties. Definition and dimensions: globalisation is the widening, deepening and speeding-up of worldwide interconnectedness - the process by which decisions and events in one place increasingly shape lives and livelihoods elsewhere. It operates across four interlocking dimensions: economic (the growth of TNCs, FDI and global production networks; 24-hour financial markets), political (the growth of IGOs and trading blocs; the diffusion of liberal-democratic norms), social and cultural (migration and diasporas, global media and consumer culture, English as a lingua franca) and environmental (shared atmosphere and oceans; cross-border problems such as climate change, ozone depletion and plastic waste). Synoptic framing: the dimensions are mutually reinforcing - cheap communications enable offshoring, offshoring generates migration flows, migration spreads cultural traits - so high-bandwidth answers chain the dimensions rather than listing them. Historical depth earns AO1: earlier waves of globalisation existed (the Silk Road; colonial trade empires), but the current phase, beginning around 1950 and accelerating sharply after 1990 (the end of the Cold War, China's open-door policy and its WTO accession in 2001), is unprecedented in speed, scale and reach because of the transport, communications and financial revolutions set out below. Global flows and their asymmetries: globalisation is made visible by flows of capital, labour, products and services, information and ideas - and the flows are deeply unequal. Flow Scale and named example Dominant direction Pattern Capital (FDI) ~$1.3 trillion (2023); USA, China and the EU dominate recipients Into ACs and EMEs; AC-to-AC mergers Highly concentrated and volatile Labour 281 million international migrants (IOM 2024); remittances ~$860 billion a year LIDC to EME to AC ('stepwise' migration) Networked by diasporas; gendered (construction; care work) Goods Container shipping carries ~80% of merchandise trade by volume; China exports ~$3.4 trillion Asia to AC consumer markets; LIDC primary exports outward Just-in-time supply chains; hub-and-spoke ports Information and ideas ~5.4 billion internet users; 2.6 billion offline (digital divide) Diffuse but platform-controlled (US and Chinese platforms) Instant; shaped by algorithms and technical standards The asymmetries: capital and technology are concentrated in a triad of North America, Europe and East Asia; many LIDCs export low-value primary commodities (fuel, ores, coffee, cotton) while importing high-value manufactures, so their terms of trade deteriorate; and the poorest states lose skilled workers - a large share of doctors and nurses trained in sub-Saharan Africa work in ACs - producing brain drain for the origin and brain gain for the destination, only partly offset by remittances and diaspora investment. Flows of services are also unequal but new: outsourcing of back-office and call-centre work to India (Bengalore and Hyderabad; the Indian IT/business-process sector employs roughly 5 million) exploits time-zone arbitrage, while medical tourism and digital work redistribute income in the opposite direction - first-class AO2 evidence that flows are multi-directional and changing. Accelerating factors: the current phase was unlocked by a cluster of interdependent factors that AQA 3.2.1.1 names explicitly. Transport : containerisation from Malcom McLean's 1956 voyage - standardised 20-foot TEUs collapsed loading costs and port time, slashing the cost of moving goods across oceans; modern vessels of 18,000+ TEU (Maersk's Triple-E class) exploit economies of scale; air freight carries high-value, time-sensitive goods (electronics, flowers, pharmaceuticals). Communications : fibre-optic cables carry around 99% of intercontinental data; mobile platforms enable instant transactions and banking (M-Pesa in Kenya), and social media marketing reaches billions at negligible marginal cost. Finance : deregulation such as London's 1986 'Big Bang', computerised 24-hour trading across time zones and global credit markets. Management and information systems : just-in-time supply chains (the Toyota model) with RFID and satellite tracking allow components to cross borders several times before final assembly. Security : post-9/11 securitisation shapes the flows of people, goods and data (border screening, export controls on strategic technology). Trade agreements : successive WTO rounds plus regional blocs cut tariffs and standardise rules. Global marketing : global brands adapt to local markets - glocalisation : McDonald's sells the vegetarian McAloo Tikki in India, Coca-Cola localises campaigns and even product names, Apple maintains a uniform product identity while tailoring advertising to local cultures. Case detail: Bangladesh and the global garment trade Bangladesh shows an EME embedded in global supply chains: ready-made garments are roughly 84% of export earnings (about $47 billion in 2022-23), supplied to brands such as H&M, Primark and Zara on the strength of among the world's lowest wage costs (the minimum wage was raised to about $113 a month in 2023 only after mass strikes). The Rana Plaza factory collapse (24 April 2013) killed 1,134 workers, exposing the human cost of cost-driven outsourcing and prompting the Accord on Fire and Building Safety, signed by more than 200 brands. Assessment points: participation in global flows has delivered growth of around 6% a year, mass female employment and rising human development, yet the country remains dependent on a single low-margin industry vulnerable to buyer power, automation and order-cancellation shocks - the classic interdependence-with-vulnerability argument for 20-mark essays. Interdependence, complexity and vulnerability: global systems create mutual reliance, so local events now have global consequences: the Ever Given grounded in the Suez Canal in March 2021 closed it for six days, holding up roughly $9.6 billion of trade a day; the 2020-22 semiconductor shortage idled car plants on three continents; Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine spiked global wheat, fertiliser and energy prices and pushed food inflation worldwide. Interdependence therefore delivers efficiency and growth, but also contagion risk - the 2008 financial crisis spread through linked banking systems within weeks - and it concentrates power in the actors that control the 'switches' of the global network: chokepoints (Suez, Malacca, Hormuz), technical standards, financial centres and digital platforms. The gains, too, are unevenly shared: the richest 1% of adults hold close to half of global wealth, while the same globalisation has lifted more than a billion people out of extreme poverty since 1990, mostly in China. This unequal distribution of both gains and control is the conceptual bridge into Sections 2 and 3: who owns the switches decides whom the rules serve. Measuring globalisation (AO3): composite indices quantify the unevenness: the KOF Globalisation Index combines economic (trade and FDI), social (contact and information flows) and political (embassies, treaties, peacekeeping) sub-indices - Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium rank highest; the AT Kearney/Foreign Policy index is comparable. Use indices for three AO3 judgements: globalisation is uneven in degree (some states remain barely integrated); it is uneven in nature (integration is not the same as westernisation - East Asian and Gulf globalisation follow different cultural paths); and its costs and benefits are distributed unequally - the core evaluation in essays asking whether globalisation benefits everyone. Flows of people in detail: migration theory earns AO1: Lee's push-pull model (push factors: poverty, conflict, drought; pull factors: wages, safety, opportunity; intervening obstacles: borders, distance, cost) explains why movement is 'stepwise' - LIDC to EME to AC - and why flows follow diaspora networks (chain migration lowers the costs and risks for the next migrant). Scale and consequence: refugees and people in refugee-like situations number over 40 million (UNHCR), concentrated in LIDC host states that can least afford them; remittances reach a quarter of GDP in Nepal and around 9% in the Philippines, exceeding aid several-fold. Migration is gendered (construction corridors for men; domestic and care work for women) and increasingly urban-ward. AO2: migration makes places as well as economies - diasporas transplant culture (food, faith, festivals) and transfer ideas as well as money, the direct link from this section into Changing Places (AQA 3.2.2). Cultural globalisation and resistance: cultural flows now travel at media speed: Netflix operates in over 190 countries, the Premier League is broadcast to 200+ territories, and English functions as the lingua franca of business, science and aviation. The exam debate is homogenisation versus heterogenisation : one view sees a 'McWorld' of converging consumer culture eroding local identity (placelessness); the other stresses that globalisation also distributes culture outwards - K-pop, Bollywood and Nollywood have global audiences - and provokes resistance: glocalisation as adaptation, and political backlash from populism and nationalism (the Brexit vote in 2016; 'China dream' discourse). AO3: globalisation produces convergence in consumption but divergence in politics - the judicious line in essays asking whether globalisation creates a uniform, borderless world. Global systems and trade flows: a global system is a set of interconnected flows and nodes - inputs, transactions, outputs - linking production and consumption worldwide; trade is its most visible flow. World merchandise trade is roughly $24 trillion a year, dominated by the US-EU-East Asia triad plus China (exports of about $3.4 trillion). World trade has grown roughly 400-fold since 1950 - far faster than output - because tariffs fell under GATT/WTO rounds and transport and communications costs collapsed. The historic pattern - ACs exporting manufactures, LIDCs exporting raw materials - was reshaped by global shift : manufacturing migrating to low-cost EMEs from the 1970s (Japan, then the Asian Tigers, then China after WTO accession in 2001, now Vietnam, Bangladesh and Ethiopia), leaving deindustrialisation and rust belts in ACs (Detroit, north-east England) - a process whose social legacy is examined in Changing Places (AQA 3.2.2). Commodity chains reveal where value is captured: in the coffee chain, producing countries receive well under 10% of final retail value, with roasting, branding and retail concentrated in ACs; dependence on a narrow commodity base exposes states to price crashes - oil is roughly 80-90% of Nigeria's export earnings, and the 2014-16 oil price collapse cut government revenue by more than a third (the resource curse ). Access to markets and unequal power relations: market access is structurally unequal. Barriers facing LIDC exporters include tariffs and tariff escalation (processed goods face higher duties than raw materials, discouraging industrialisation); rich-world agricultural subsidies - the EU's Common Agricultural Policy and US farm subsidies depress world prices and undercut developing-country farmers, the core complaint behind the stalled Doha Development Round (launched 2001, effectively dead since 2008); technical and sanitary standards whose certification costs small producers cannot meet; and geographical disadvantage - landlocked states (Chad, Uganda) pay high transport costs and depend on neighbours' ports. Protectionism has returned with the US-China trade war (2018-19 tariffs on roughly $450 billion of bilateral trade), 'buy national' procurement rules and export controls on strategic technologies (advanced semiconductors). AO2: these barriers are not accidental - they reflect unequal power, because the states that write trade rules protect their own sectors while requiring others to liberalise. IGOs governing trade and finance: three institutions set the rules of the system - and their power is unequal: IGO Role Named example Unequal-power critique WTO (1995; 166 members) Liberalises trade (most-favoured-nation principle), hosts negotiation rounds, settles disputes between members US-EU banana dispute (1999-2012); Doha Round stalled since 2008; Appellate Body paralysed since 2019 by US blocking appointments De facto power sits with large markets; disputes drag on for years; agenda set by ACs and big emerging economies IMF (1944; 190 members) Balance-of-payments lending, macroeconomic surveillance, technical assistance Greece bailouts 2010-15 (~289 billion euros with the EU); Jamaica 1977-85 austerity programmes Voting weighted by quota (US ~16% = effective veto); conditionality (privatisation, spending cuts) criticised for deepening recessions World Bank (1944) Development finance - IBRD loans, IDA concessional credit, infrastructure and human-capital projects Rural electrification and railway lending in India; social-protection systems worldwide President traditionally nominated by the USA; earlier top-down mega-projects displaced communities without consultation Structural adjustment and its critics: both Bretton Woods institutions were created in 1944 and remain dominated by AC capital, so LIDCs borrow on terms set by others. Structural adjustment programmes condition IMF lending on privatisation, trade liberalisation, subsidy removal and public-spending cuts: Jamaica's programmes from 1977 (documented in the film Life and Debt , 2001) opened its markets to subsidised US imports and cut public services while local farmers could not compete - the classic 9-mark example of governance producing unequal outcomes. Greece's bailouts (2010-15) attached austerity that deepened the recession - evidence that conditionality bites ACs too, but under very different power relations. Reform pressure now comes from the BRICS' New Development Bank and China's Belt and Road Initiative (about 150 countries signed up; lending of the order of $1 trillion) - an alternative, China-centred financing system, though BRI debt sustainability is contested (Sri Lanka's Hambantota port leased to China Merchants for 99 years in 2017). Trade blocs: preferential groupings deepen integration - and divert as well as create trade. The EU single market (27 members; free movement of goods, services, capital and people); USMCA (US, Mexico, Canada; replaced NAFTA in 2020 with tightened automotive rules of origin); ASEAN (10 members; a global manufacturing hub); and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA, trading from 2021; 54 signatories) which aims to raise intra-African trade from roughly 15% of the continent's trade and lift tens of millions out of poverty. AO2: blocs raise members' collective bargaining power against outsiders (the EU negotiates as one bloc) but discriminate against excluded exporters; and within blocs, poorer members absorb asymmetric shocks (Greece within the eurozone; Lesotho within the Southern African Customs Union) - unequal power operates inside blocs as well as between them. TNCs: the operating units of global systems: TNCs coordinate production across borders and are the principal system-builders of globalisation. Their global production networks locate each function where it is most profitable: R&D and design in AC agglomerations; component manufacture in specialised clusters; final assembly in low-wage zones; marketing and after-sales in consumer markets. Apple is the archetype: design in Cupertino, California; chips fabricated by TSMC in Taiwan, memory from Samsung (Korea) and Sony (Japan); final assembly by Foxconn in Zhengzhou - 'iPhone City', employing 200,000-350,000 workers at peak, whose dormitories, 2010-12 suicides and strikes drew global scrutiny; and global logistics delivering millions of units within days of launch. Apple's revenues (about $383 billion in 2023) exceed the GDP of most UN member states - TNC power is comparable to state power. TNC behaviour creates flows and inequalities simultaneously: FDI transfers capital, technology and training (Foxconn-linked investment helped raise inland Chinese wages), but transfer pricing and profit-shifting move taxable profits to low-tax jurisdictions (Apple was ordered in 2016 to repay about 13 billion euros to Ireland in the EU state-aid case, upheld in 2024), and buyer power squeezes suppliers (Rana Plaza, Section 1). Offshoring is now partially reversing - reshoring and 'friend-shoring' of semiconductors (the US CHIPS Act, 2022, ~$52 billion of subsidies) show geopolitics re-sorting the map of production: a first-class AO3 point that globalisation is not a one-way process. Case detail: Shell in the Niger Delta - TNC power and the environment Royal Dutch Shell has pumped oil in the Niger Delta since 1958. The UN Environment Programme assessment of Ogoniland (2011) found oil contamination of soil and groundwater up to 900 times guideline levels and estimated clean-up could take 25-30 years; Shell has paid settlements (15.5 million dollars over the 1995 execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa's campaign was settled out of court in 2009; a UK Supreme Court ruling in 2021 allowed Nigerian claims against Shell's parent company to proceed). Use for AO2/AO3: a TNC operating with weak host-state regulation externalises environmental costs onto communities - unequal power in a global system extends beyond trade and finance to the environment, and links forward to global-commons governance (Section 3). Liberalisation in historical perspective: GATT (1947) held eight negotiating rounds, cutting average industrial tariffs from about 22% in 1947 to under 3% today; the Uruguay Round (1986-94) created the WTO (1995) and extended the rules to services (GATS) and intellectual property (TRIPS). TRIPS is itself an unequal-power case: patent rules protect AC pharmaceutical firms while restricting access to generic medicines - the 2001 Doha Declaration on TRIPS and public health allowed compulsory licensing for health emergencies only after the South African HIV-drug controversy. AO2: liberalisation benefits efficient exporters, but the extension of the rules reflects AC interests - unequal power operates inside the institutions that claim to be neutral. The new trade geography: the map of trade is being re-sorted by geopolitics: RCEP (signed 2020; 15 Asia-Pacific members; roughly 30% of world GDP) is the largest bloc by population and excludes the USA; BRICS expanded in 2024 (Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE joining) with its own New Development Bank; Mexico overtook China as the USA's largest goods trading partner in 2023 as firms nearshore under USMCA. AO3: these shifts are first-class counterpoint evidence in essays arguing that globalisation is not irreversible or one-directional - integration patterns respond to politics, security and power, not just to efficiency. The global commons: parts of the planet outside national jurisdiction - the high seas, the atmosphere, Antarctica, outer space - are global commons : shared resource domains that no state owns, from which none can be excluded, and whose overuse by some diminishes them for all. Hardin's 'tragedy of the commons' (1968) predicts over-exploitation where users act individually and rationally; Elinor Ostrom's work showed commons can be governed successfully where users build rules, monitoring and sanctions together. Governing them requires international law, norms and institutions rather than sovereignty - and Antarctica (AQA 3.2.1.4) is the set-text example of governing a global common. Antarctica: the resource and the claims: 14 million km2 (roughly 1.4 times the USA), holding about 90% of Earth's ice and roughly 70% of its fresh water - enough to raise global sea level by tens of metres if fully melted. It has no indigenous population and no permanent residents: about 1,000 people overwinter and roughly 4,000-5,000 scientists and support staff occupy seasonal and year-round stations. Seven states claim sectors (Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the UK - the Argentine, Chilean and British claims overlap), most states recognise none, and the USA and Russia reserve the right to make claims. Resources at stake: minerals and hydrocarbons (suspected offshore oil); the krill fishery (krill is the base of the Southern Ocean food web; the precautionary quota is about 5.6 million tonnes a year, actual catches around 400,000 tonnes); finfish including Patagonian toothfish (high-value and IUU-poached); tourism (~74,000 visitors in 2019-20, IAATO-supervised); fresh water (icebergs); and bioprospecting - genetic resources from cold-adapted organisms for pharmaceuticals and industrial enzymes, which no treaty yet regulates. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) and its system: signed on 1 December 1959 by the 12 states active in the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Chile, France, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, South Africa, the USSR, the UK and the USA), in force since 1961, now with 57 parties of which 29 are consultative (decision-making) parties. Key provisions: Article IV freezes territorial claims - no new claims, no enlargement of existing ones and no recognition of others' claims (a diplomatic fudge that made agreement possible and holds to this day); Antarctica to be used for peaceful purposes only - military activity, nuclear tests and radioactive waste disposal are banned ; freedom of scientific investigation with exchange of personnel, data and plans; and decisions by consensus of consultative parties. The treaty grew into a governance system : Instrument Date Key provision Named example Agreed Measures / environmental rules 1964; Madrid Protocol 1991 Wildlife protection; then Article 7 of the Protocol bans all mineral resource activities indefinitely, designating Antarctica a 'natural reserve, devoted to peace and science'; EIA and waste management required; review possible only after 50 years (from 2048) by three-quarters of consultative parties Madrid Protocol - the reason there is no mining in Antarctica CCAMLR 1982 Conserves Southern Ocean marine life; sets precautionary fishery quotas and marine protected areas Ross Sea MPA 2017 - 2 million km2, the world's largest at designation Montreal Protocol 1987 Banned ozone-depleting substances; the Antarctic ozone hole is projected to recover by about 2066 The clearest success of global environmental governance UNCLOS / IMO Polar Code 1982; Polar Code 2017 Law of the sea governing Southern Ocean shipping; mandatory safety and pollution standards for polar shipping Polar Code applies to the growing tourist and resupply fleet ICRW whaling moratorium 1982 Commercial whaling paused; Japan left the IWC in 2019 but resumed whaling only in its own EEZ, not Antarctic waters Enforcement limits revealed by withdrawal Case detail: Ross Sea Marine Protected Area (2017) After five years of negotiation, CCAMLR members - including Russia and China, whose fleets fish krill and toothfish - agreed a 2 million km2 marine protected area in the Ross Sea, the world's largest at designation, with 1.12 million km2 fully closed to fishing and a review scheduled after 35 years (2052). Significance: the largest act of cooperative ocean protection in history, agreed after progress stalled repeatedly (a Chinese vessel fire in 2015 pushed the parties to cooperate) - evidence that governance works when science (penguin and krill population data) and diplomacy combine. But the 35-year sunset clause and reliance on voluntary compliance show its fragility. NGOs - the Antarctic and Southern Ocean Coalition (ASOC), WWF and Greenpeace - campaigned throughout: the standard AO2 evidence for NGO influence in global governance. NGOs, international law and non-state governance: NGOs watchdog the commons: ASOC holds standing at Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings; Greenpeace built the first non-governmental Antarctic base (World Park Base, 1987-92) to lobby for a 'World Park' and against mining; WWF tracks krill fisheries and pushes for MPAs. Their leverage is agenda-setting, science and publicity rather than legal power - contrast with states' enforcement power: treaty inspection teams may inspect any station or vessel without notice. International law supplies the framework, but enforcement depends on consent: there is no Antarctic police force; compliance rests on transparency, peer inspection and reputational cost. This is the general condition of global-commons governance - law without sovereign enforcement. Threats and the effectiveness of governance (AO2/AO3): pressures on Antarctica include: climate change (the Antarctic Peninsula has warmed by roughly 3 degrees C since 1950; West Antarctic ice-sheet thinning - the Thwaites 'doomsday glacier' alone could eventually add tens of centimetres to sea level); recovering whale and fish stocks inviting commercial expansion; tourism growth (quadrupled since the 1990s; ever-larger vessels raise oil-spill risk - the cruise ship Explorer sank in 2007, fortunately with no casualties); bioprospecting outside any regulatory regime; and, beyond the 2048 review window, potential pressure to revisit the mining ban as global mineral demand rises. Assessment: governance of Antarctica is widely judged the most successful global-commons regime - territorial claims frozen for over 65 years, mining banned, science open to all 57 parties, disputes settled by consensus and prevented from escalating (no war has been fought there), the ozone hole healing under the Montreal Protocol. But its weaknesses are structural: consensus means any consultative party can veto (Russia and China have blocked successive MPA proposals); climate impacts on Antarctica are governed by a separate regime (the UNFCCC) that Antarctica's ecosystems cannot participate in; and enforcement is consensual rather than coercive. Strong 20-mark answers weigh institutional success (longevity, environmental protection, conflict prevention) against fragility (compliance, external pressure, climate change) and conclude conditionally. Sovereignty vs interdependence (synoptic close): Antarctica crystallises the tension at the heart of globalisation: claimant states assert sovereignty; the treaty system pools it - sovereignty is frozen in exchange for shared scientific access, peace and environmental protection. More broadly, global governance trades absolute sovereignty for the benefits of interdependence: states accept treaty constraints (WTO rules, UNCLOS, the Madrid Protocol) because the gains from cooperation exceed the gains from autonomy - yet unequal power means the rules are written largely by the powerful (Section 2), and IGO membership itself redistributes sovereignty asymmetrically (the US quota-veto at the IMF; consultative vs non-consultative status in Antarctica). The AO3 judgement: sovereignty is not lost but shared and reconfigured - and where governance fails or is absent (climate, bioprospecting), even the most isolated continent shows that interdependence is unavoidable. Governance machinery in practice: the system runs through annual Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings (ATCMs) and the Committee for Environmental Protection (CEP, since 1998), which reviews environmental impact assessments, waste plans and site guidelines; mutual inspections - any party may visit any station or vessel without notice - have operated since 1961; and disputes can go to the International Court of Justice where parties accept its jurisdiction. Tourism is regulated largely through self -regulation: IAATO operators follow site guidelines, landing-size limits and biosecurity protocols - a distinctive AO2 example of non-state governance working, though critics note it is voluntary and unaccountable. Claimant states enforce their law only over their own nationals in their own sectors; no state enforces law over another's nationals - sovereignty in Antarctica is territorial claim without territorial jurisdiction, the sharpest illustration of the sovereignty-interdependence trade-off. Why Antarctica matters for the synoptic essay: the topic links across the specification: to water and carbon cycles (ice sheets and albedo; the Southern Ocean absorbs a large share of anthropogenic CO2, and its weakening would accelerate warming), to hazards (sea-level rise from ice-sheet loss), and to global systems (krill quotas as resource governance; tourism as a global flow). 20-mark essays on governance reach Level 4 by weighing named instruments against named failures - Treaty and Madrid Protocol against consensus vetoes and IWC withdrawal - and by concluding conditionally: success in conflict prevention and mining prohibition, fragility in climate response and voluntary compliance.

topics.subject: geography
topics.searchText: geography Geography Changing Places Define place through location, locale and sense of place, explain placelessness (Relph 1976) and non-places (Auge 1992), and distinguish insider and outsider perspectives on place (AQA 3.2.2.1) Categorise endogenous factors (location, topography, physical geography, land use, built environment, infrastructure, demographic and economic characteristics) and exogenous factors (flows of people, capital, resources and ideas) and analyse how they interact to shape place character (AQA 3.2.2.1) Explain how shifting flows of people, resources, money and investment reshape the demographic, cultural and economic character of places, using deindustrialisation and the Detroit case study (AQA 3.2.2.2) Describe and evaluate rebranding and regeneration strategies - flagship, market-led and heritage/legacy approaches - and assess their effectiveness in Detroit (AQA 3.2.2.2; Edexcel Regenerating Places) Plan and evaluate a local place study using quantitative sources (census, Index of Multiple Deprivation), qualitative sources (interviews, media, photographs) and GIS, and discuss how places are represented (AQA 3.2.2.3; OCR Changing Spaces; Making Places) Place A location invested with meaning and identity, combining Agnew's (1987) three fundamental aspects: location (where it is), locale (the material setting for social relations) and sense of place (subjective emotional attachment). Sense of place The subjective meanings, emotions and attachments that people and groups give to a place; strongest at home (Relph's existential insider) and constructed differently by outsiders such as tourists, planners and census analysts. Placelessness Relph's (1976) term for the erosion of distinctive, authentic places by standardised, place-independent landscapes - clone high streets, retail parks, airports, motorway services - produced by the 'inauthentic' attitudes of planners, developers and corporations; Augé's (1992) 'non-places' (transit spaces with no history or community) are the extreme case. Endogenous factors Internal characteristics that shape a place's character from within: location, topography, physical geography, land use, built environment, infrastructure, and its demographic and economic features. Exogenous factors External influences on place character arising from relationships and connections with other places: shifting flows of people (migration), capital and investment, resources, and ideas and technology, mediated by globalisation, TNC decisions and government policy. Rebranding How a place is re-presented to overcome a negative image: new logotypes, media campaigns, flagship developments and events designed to change external perceptions and attract people and investment. Regeneration The physical, economic and social renewal of a declining area - property-led and flagship schemes (Detroit's RiverWalk, Little Caesars Arena), heritage-led reuse (Michigan Central Station) and community-level programmes. Gentrification The influx of middle-class residents and investment into historically working-class neighbourhoods, refurbishing housing but displacing original residents - visible in Detroit's Midtown and Corktown. What is place? Open with Agnew's (1987) three fundamental aspects: location - the objective 'where of place', fixable by grid coordinates; locale - the material setting for social relations, the physical and built environment staging everyday life; and sense of place - the subjective, emotional attachment to a place, its meanings and identity. Tuan (1974) called positive attachment topophilia ('love of place'); the examiner-recognised step is that space becomes place only when invested with meaning. High-band answers add that places are multi-layered: residents, commuters, tourists and planners read the same locale differently, so one place can hold multiple, even conflicting, senses of place. Placelessness and authenticity: Relph (1976, Place and Placelessness ) argued that modernity produces placelessness - standardised, serialised landscapes lacking genuine place identity: chain stores and clone high streets, motorway services, airport terminals, retail parks, international hotels, anonymous suburbs. It stems from the 'inauthentic' attitudes of planners and corporations imposing place-independent design; Augé (1992) extended this with non-places - transit and consumption spaces where people coexist without community, history or identity, negotiated through signs and tickets rather than relationships. Relph's perspectives earn AO2: existential insider (belongs, place as home), empathetic outsider (strives to understand), objective outsider (detached study, as census analysts do), ideological outsider (imports media preconceptions - risks stereotyping). Massey (1991, 'A Global Sense of Place') counters: places are not sealed containers but bundles of social relations and flows (Kilburn in London: multi-ethnic, globally connected), so identity should be progressive - outward-looking - not reactionary localism; Harvey (1996) adds that places are socially constructed and can exclude (gated communities). Endogenous and exogenous factors: endogenous factors act from within; exogenous factors reach the place through relationships and connections with other places. Both must be chained to a case study - lists score level 1. Factor set Components Detroit example Endogenous Location, topography, physical geography River-and-lakes site on the Detroit River; flat land; border to Canada Endogenous Land use, built environment, infrastructure Industrial waterfront, residential grids, about 40 sq miles vacant; Ambassador Bridge (1929), QLine (2017) Endogenous Demographic, economic characteristics 639,111 (2020), majority-black; automotive then low-wage services Exogenous Flows of people Immigrant labour and Great Migration in; white flight after 1967 Exogenous Flows of capital, investment, resources Auto investment and Great Lakes ore in; offshoring and the 2008 crisis out Exogenous Flows of ideas, decisions Assembly line (1913), automation, Japanese competition post-1973, bankruptcy decision (2013) The two interact: exogenous flows are filtered through endogenous qualities. Detroit's river-and-lakes location drew the automobile industry; globalisation - the same force - later stripped it away. This double edge of connectivity is the synoptic heart of the topic and the pivot for most 20-mark judgements. Examiner tip: framing endogenous/exogenous in essays Trace one chain, not a list: endogenous location draws exogenous investment; exogenous change rewrites the endogenous base (jobs, demographics, land use); the new base attracts new flows. Chains reach level 3. Shifting flows remake place character: a place's demographic, cultural and economic character is continuously rewritten by relationships and connections - shifting flows of people, resources, money and investment. Demographic change: migration rewrites age structure and ethnic mix (2021 census: England and Wales 81.7% White, one in six residents born abroad; rapid EU migration reshaped towns such as Boston, Lincolnshire). Cultural change: language, food, religion and festivals follow migrants and global media. Economic change: employment shifts from primary to secondary to tertiary and quaternary, and deindustrialisation - the collapse of manufacturing employment in ACs - is the topic's dominant theme. Detroit is the set-text example of place both made and unmade by exogenous flows. Detroit: made by the car, unmade by deindustrialisation. Made: Detroit's location on the Detroit River - the link between Lakes Erie and Huron, a border crossing to Canada (Ambassador Bridge 1929, Windsor Tunnel 1930) - plus cheap land and Great Lakes access to iron ore and coal drew manufacturing. Ford's moving assembly line (1913, Highland Park) and the River Rouge complex (from 1918, about 100,000 workers at peak) made it the 'Motor City': the Big Three dominated, wartime output earned 'Arsenal of Democracy', population peaked at 1.85 million (1950) - then among the richest US cities per head - and Motown Records (1959) gave it a global cultural brand. Unmade: automation and offshoring cut manufacturing from about 296,000 jobs (1950, roughly half of city employment) to under 20,000; Japanese competition after the 1973 oil crisis closed Big Three plants; the 1967 uprising (43 deaths, about 2,000 buildings burned) accelerated white flight to the suburbs; and the 2008 financial crisis pushed GM and Chrysler into Chapter 11 (2009) and caused about 65,000 foreclosures (2005-15). Population fell about 65% to 639,111 (2020); a third of the city's 139 square miles became vacant; unemployment peaked near 25% (2009); and in 2013 Detroit filed the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history (about 18 billion dollars of debt), exiting in 2014 through the 'grand bargain' that shed about 7 billion dollars. Rebranding and regeneration: the comeback city? The two work together: regeneration (physical-economic renewal) and rebranding (re-presentation to change perceptions). The Detroit Riverfront Conservancy (founded 2003) converted derelict docks into the RiverWalk - over three miles including the Renaissance Center (GM headquarters, 1996), Atwater Beach and Cullen Plaza (2016) - drawing three million-plus visits a year. Rocket Mortgage moved its headquarters downtown (2010); Dan Gilbert refurbished over 100 buildings (about 5.6 billion dollars); the QLine streetcar (2017, 137 million dollars) relinked Woodward Avenue; Little Caesars Arena (2017, 863 million dollars) anchored the District Detroit quarter; Shinola (2011) rebuilt a heritage brand ('Built in Detroit'); and Ford spent about 950 million dollars restoring Michigan Central Station (derelict from 1988, reopened 2024) as a mobility-innovation campus - beside the 'America's Great Comeback City' rebrand. AO3 evaluation: the projects are flagship-concentrated downtown and in Midtown (a 'comeback island') while outer neighbourhoods lose population, housing and services; the economy stays narrower than before; and rebranding attracts visitors and graduates faster than it restores manufacturing jobs - so regeneration changed the place image but only partly reversed the deindustrialisation that caused decline. Quantitative sources: the local place study (AQA 3.2.2.3; OCR 'Changing Spaces; Making Places'; Edexcel 'Diverse Places') is built from citable data. The ONS Census (2021, England and Wales) gives decennial counts of population, age, ethnicity, country of birth, tenure, qualifications, occupation and car availability down to output-area level, enabling change-over-time comparison with the 2001 and 2011 tables. The Index of Multiple Deprivation (England: IMD 2019) ranks every LSOA on seven weighted domains - income (22.5%), employment (22.5%), education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, living environment - and is designed for choropleth mapping of deprivation hot and cold spots. Add claimant-count unemployment, Land Registry house-price series and environmental quality surveys (bipolar scoring of litter, noise, greenery) collected along transects. Qualitative sources and representations: quantitative data describe who and how many; qualitative data recover meaning and sense of place. Interviews (structured through unstructured) and open-question surveys capture insider testimony - why residents value or fear change - but samples are small and answers can be performative. Participant observation (walking the place as an 'empathetic outsider'), field sketches and photography (your own images versus archive photographs) document lived experience. Media representations - newspapers, TV, film, tourism brochures, property marketing, art, literature - are curated constructions that rebrand places selectively: compare a council's investment prospectus with residents' interviews or national press coverage, and the gap between representation and lived reality is itself AO3 evidence. Every source is a representation: the census's categories, the media's angles and your own photographs all involve choices. GIS: QGIS or ArcGIS layers sources spatially: choropleth maps of IMD deciles or census ethnicity by output area; buffers around regeneration sites; heat maps of geotagged photographs or social-media posts to compare an outsider's digital image of a place with residents' priorities. Strengths for AO3: rapid multi-layer comparison, pattern detection, change-over-time mapping. Limitations: the census is a decade old the day it is published; data are aggregated (ecological fallacy - LSOA averages hide individual experience); digital sources under-represent elderly and low-income groups. Synthesis: a strong study triangulates - a quantitative skeleton (census, IMD), qualitative flesh (interviews, observation, media analysis) and GIS to integrate both - and reflects explicitly on insider versus outsider perspectives (Relph's four-fold framework) so the place profile distinguishes lived meaning from external representation. Examiner tip: the 9-mark source-evaluation answer Judge each source on purpose (why was it produced?), date, scale (national dataset or one street's sample?), curation (whose view is absent?) and fitness for the question. Conclude with a judgement: census data are authoritative but static; interviews are current but small-sample; media sources are vivid but curated - so triangulate.

topics.name: Arguments for the Existence of God
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Arguments for the Existence of God Set out Anselm's Proslogion 2-3 argument and Descartes' version, then evaluate Gaunilo's perfect-island parody and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' reply (AO1/AO2) Reproduce Paley's watchmaker analogy and Aquinas' Fifth Way, distinguishing regularity from purpose (AO1) Explain modern design arguments: Tennant's anthropic principle, aesthetic argument and Swinburne's probability reasoning (AO1) Recite Hume's five Dialogues critiques and Mill's objection from nature's cruelty, and weigh them against the anthropic counter (AO2) Outline Aquinas' First, Second and Third Ways for WJEC/CCEA coverage, including infinite regress and contingency (AO1) Distinguish a priori, a posteriori and abductive reasoning and classify each argument correctly (AO1) Plan an evaluative essay with a structured argument, scholarly support and a justified verdict rather than a summary (AO2/AO3) Ontological: a priori, from definition; Anselm (Proslogion 2-3) vs Gaunilo and Kant. Design: a posteriori, from order; Paley's watchmaker vs Hume's five critiques and Dawkins. Modern design: Tennant's anthropic principle; Swinburne's probabilistic cumulative case. Cosmological (WJEC/CCEA): Aquinas' First, Second and Third Ways; contingency and regress. a priori Reasoning independent of sense experience; based on analysis of concepts or definitions alone (the ontological argument). a posteriori Reasoning from observed evidence about the world to a conclusion beyond it (design and cosmological arguments). contingent existence Existence that depends on something else and could fail to exist; anything whose non-existence is conceivable. necessary existence Existence that cannot fail to be and does not depend on anything else; Anselm holds it belongs uniquely to God (Proslogion 3). predicate A property asserted of a subject; Kant argues existence is not a real predicate because it adds no property, only asserts instantiation. reductio ad absurdum Argument that refutes a position by deriving a contradiction from it; Anselm's method in Proslogion 2-3. teleological argument A posteriori argument inferring a designer from order, regularity or purpose in the universe (Greek telos = end/purpose); also called the design argument. anthropic principle Tennant's claim that the universe is finely tuned for intelligent, moral life; the conditions of the cosmos point to design rather than chance. infinite regress An endless chain of explanations; Aquinas rules it out for causes and motion, since then no first cause would exist to start the series. epicurean hypothesis Hume's alternative: particles in chaos, given infinite time, randomly settle into stable, ordered configurations with no designer. principle of sufficient reason Leibniz's claim that every contingent fact needs an explanation; even an infinite series of causes needs a reason outside the series. Classification: a priori - it rests on analysis of the concept of God rather than observation. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.1.1.2; OCR H573/01. Anselm (Proslogion 2): God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'. Even the fool who denies God (Psalm 14:1) understands this definition, so it exists in the understanding ( in intellectu ). Existence in reality ( in re ) is greater than existence in the mind alone. If the greatest conceivable being existed only in the mind, a greater being could be conceived - one existing in reality - which is a contradiction. Therefore God exists in reality. The argument proceeds by reductio ad absurdum : assume God exists only in the understanding, derive a contradiction, conclude he exists. Anselm (Proslogion 3): the greatest conceivable being cannot be conceived not to exist. A being that cannot be thought of as non-existent is greater than one that can; God is the former; therefore God exists necessarily - his existence is not contingent on anything, including whether anyone happens to think of him. Distinguish this from merely existing forever. Gaunilo ('On Behalf of the Fool'): parody argument - by the same logic a 'perfect island' existing in the understanding must exist in reality, since reality makes it greater. The satire targets the move from definition to existence. Anselm's reply: the parody only works for contingent, surpassable things. There is no coherent 'greatest possible island' (an island could always be bigger and better), but the concept of a uniquely supreme necessary being is coherent; the reductio applies only where necessary existence is part of the concept. Descartes (Meditation V): existence belongs to God's essence just as three angles belong to a triangle's essence; existence is a perfection, so the supremely perfect being cannot lack it. God's existence is as self-evident, once the concept is grasped, as a triangle's angle-sum of two right angles. Kant's critique (Critique of Pure Reason): existence is not a real predicate - saying something exists adds no property to it, it only asserts that the concept is instantiated. 'A hundred real thalers do not contain the least bit more than a hundred possible ones.' So treating existence as a perfection is a mistake, 'necessary existence' is incoherent, and the argument collapses. Malcolm's defence: an unlimited being cannot exist contingently, so God's existence is either impossible or necessary; since Anselm shows it is conceivable, it is necessary. Critics reply that Malcolm establishes coherence, not actual instantiation - the very gap Kant identified remains open. Classification: a posteriori, inductive; it infers a designer from order, regularity and apparent purpose. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.1.1.1; OCR H573/01. Aquinas (Fifth Way, Summa Theologiae I.2.3): natural bodies lacking intelligence act for an end - they achieve the best result 'always or for the most part' (arrows fly, seeds grow predictably). Nothing that lacks knowledge can act for an end unless directed by a being with knowledge, as the arrow is directed by the archer. Therefore an intelligent being (God) orders all natural things to their end. Note: this is an argument from regularity , not from complexity - a common exam confusion with Paley.
