Paley (Natural Theology, 1802): the watch on the heath - its intricate mechanism, the precise fitting of parts for the purpose of telling time, would compel the inference to a watchmaker even for someone who had never seen a watch made. The eye and the universe are vastly more intricate and purposeful, so they compel the inference to a vastly more capable designer. Paley's supporting points: even an imperfect watch still implies a maker; the inference survives ignorance of how the mechanism works; the parts are assembled for a purpose, not found that way by chance. Argument Basis Key scholars Classic critique Ontological Definition of God (a priori) Anselm, Descartes, Malcolm Kant: existence not a predicate; Gaunilo parody Design from purpose Adaptation of means to ends Aquinas (Fifth Way), Paley Hume: weak analogy, alternative causes Design from regularity Laws and fine-tuning Tennant, Swinburne Multiverse; chance over infinite time; Darwin Tennant (Philosophical Theology, 1930): the anthropic principle - the universe is uniquely adapted to intelligent, moral, religious life (stable physical constants, life-permitting conditions); the aesthetic argument - beauty in nature exceeds any survival need, suggesting a mind behind nature; a cumulative case combining many strands is stronger than a single analogy. Swinburne (The Existence of God, 1979): regularities of succession (temporal order, the persistence of laws) are too fundamental for science to explain - science explains one regularity by another; God is the simplest possible explanation of the universe's order. The argument is probabilistic, not demonstrative: the evidence raises the probability of God's existence, giving rational grounds for belief without proof. Later challenge - Dawkins (The Blind Watchmaker, 1986): cumulative natural selection explains apparent design with no designer: small heritable variations, sifted over deep time, produce complexity. Reply: evolution presupposes a lawful, life-permitting universe in which selection can operate, and selection cannot explain the origin of those laws - the anthropic question remains open (Tennant's counter). Hume (Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, published 1779): the character Philo presses five objections - written before Paley but almost always examined against him, which examiners reward. Weak analogy: the universe is unique - there is only one, so we cannot compare it with familiar artefacts whose origins we know. It may be more like a vegetable or animal (growing, reproducing) than a machine, in which case the inference is to generation, not design. Alternative causes: given infinite time, random matter under the epicurean hypothesis could settle into stable, ordered configurations; order does not require a designer, only time and chance. Multiple designers: a great effect may have many causes - machines are made by teams; from the universe one might infer many gods, a cosmic infant or a clumsy deity rather than one perfect God. Finite or flawed maker: the defects of the world (disease, earthquakes, waste) suggest a finite, imperfect or careless architect, not the omnipotent, omnibenevolent God of classical theism. Problem of evil: a world full of suffering suggests an indifferent or malevolent maker; the design argument undermines the very God it is meant to prove. Mill (Three Essays on Religion, 1874, posthumous): 'nearly all the things which men are hanged or imprisoned for doing to one another are nature's every-day performances'; nature is wasteful and cruel, so its Designer cannot be both omnipotent and perfectly good. Mill accepts at most a limited designer. Kant (Critique of Pure Reason): even if the design argument worked, it would establish only a world-architect within the realm of possible experience, not the transcendent, necessary being of theism; and to reach necessary existence it must borrow from the ontological argument, inheriting its failure. For Kant both arguments fail as proof, though the concept of God remains a regulative ideal of reason. Mackie (The Miracle of Theism, 1982): order arises from the evolution of chaos plus selection-like processes; the theistic reply that fine-tuning is astronomically improbable on chance keeps the anthropic debate alive, but Mackie insists that multiplying weak arguments does not make them strong. Weighing point: Hume's objections anticipate Paley, but the anthropic principle and fine-tuning claims postdate him - a modern design argument is not refuted by the vegetable analogy alone. A* essays stage this as a conversation: Hume versus Paley, Darwin versus Paley, Tennant/Swinburne versus Hume. Aquinas' First Way (motion/change): some things are in the process of change; whatever changes is changed by another; an infinite regress of changers is impossible, since then there would be no first changer and no subsequent change; therefore there is a first unmoved changer - God. Second Way (efficient causation): everything that comes into existence has a cause; an infinite regress of causes is impossible; therefore there is a first efficient cause - God. Third Way (contingency): things exist contingently (they could fail to exist, so at some time nothing existed); if nothing ever existed nothing could exist now; therefore there must exist a necessary being - God. Hume's critiques: the causal principle (everything has a cause) is not self-evident - we can conceive of things beginning uncaused; the universe as a whole need not have a cause even if everything in it does (fallacy of composition); 'a necessary being' may be an empty phrase - anything conceived to exist could be conceived not to exist. Kant: the cosmological argument covertly relies on the ontological argument to identify the first cause as a necessary being, so it fails with it. Copleston vs Russell (BBC radio debate, 1948): Copleston defends Aquinas - the question 'why is there anything at all?' demands an answer; Russell: the universe is 'just there, and that's all', and 'the whole concept of cause is not applicable to the total'. This exchange is the standard AO2 currency for WJEC/CCEA essays. Leibniz (principle of sufficient reason): contingent facts need sufficient reasons; even an infinite series of contingent causes needs an explanation outside the series - a necessary substance (God). Differs from Aquinas: God is needed to explain the series as a whole, not merely to start it. Conceptual vs existential: a priori arguments at best establish coherence (that God's existence is conceivable), not that God exists - Kant's instantiation point is the sharpest critique and A* essays must lead with it rather than resting on Gaunilo. Inference to the best explanation: design arguments are abductive - they compete with natural selection, the epicurean hypothesis and multiverse reasoning. Strong answers weigh relative explanatory power (Swinburne: God is the simplest explanation; simplicity is a theoretical virtue) rather than demanding proof. A* structure: state the argument's premises, give the strongest critique, give the theistic reply, weigh, then verdict. Cumulative case: Tennant and Swinburne argue that single analogies are weak but convergence - cosmological plus design plus religious experience - raises the probability of theism. Mackie's reply: weak arguments multiplied remain weak. Assess whether accumulation genuinely strengthens inference or merely stacks speculation. Religious perspectives: Barth - natural theology overreaches: God is known through revelation alone, and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding' begins from belief rather than neutral reason, so the argument is best read as theology's self-reflection. Against this, Catholic tradition (Vatican I) teaches that God's existence can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason - the arguments retain apologetic value. Exam technique: AQA 7062 Paper 1 Section A: each question is worth 25 marks - a 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' part followed by a 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...' essay; answer both parts of two questions. OCR H573/01: 2-hour paper; extended 'Critically discuss' essays reward a justified line of argument rather than balanced description. WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA similarly combine AO1 exposition with AO2 evaluation, and CCEA also expects the cosmological argument. Command words: 'Explain' = accurate, developed AO1 with scholarship; 'Critically discuss' = sustained argument ending in a justified verdict, not a summary. Pitfalls: mislabelling the ontological argument as a posteriori; conflating Paley's purpose-based argument with Aquinas' regularity-based Fifth Way; presenting Gaunilo as refuting Anselm (the parody only targets contingent things); quoting Dawkins without engaging the anthropic counter; listing critiques without weighing them. Examiner tips: memorise the key phrases ('that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; 'existence is not a real predicate'; 'just there, and that's all'); signpost premises with 'firstly... therefore'; name the scholars and texts (Proslogion, Natural Theology, Dialogues); reserve your final paragraph for a reasoned verdict.

topics.name: The Problem of Evil
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies The Problem of Evil State the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad) and the free will defence response, and evaluate both (AO1/AO2) Explain the evidential problem, including Rowe's fawn and pointless suffering (AO1) Set out Augustine's theodicy: privatio boni, the Fall, original sin - and its standard critiques (AO1/AO2) Set out Irenaeus' theodicy as developed by Hick: epistemic distance, soul-making, eschatological justification - and its critiques (AO1/AO2) Distinguish moral from natural evil and explain why the distinction matters for each theodicy (AO1) Apply D.Z. Phillips' protest that theodicies can be morally obscene and weigh it in a verdict (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified conclusion (AO2/AO3) problem of evil The apparent incompatibility between the existence of an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God and the existence of evil and suffering. logical problem of evil Mackie's claim that God's omnipotence, complete goodness and the existence of evil are mutually inconsistent - it is logically impossible for all three to be true. evidential problem of evil Even if logically possible, the sheer amount and distribution of pointless evil makes God's existence improbable (Rowe, Hume). inconsistent triad Mackie's triangle of three claims: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, evil exists - any two can be held but not all three. free will defence Plantinga's response: genuine freedom requires the possibility of evil; God cannot guarantee free creatures always choose good without removing their freedom, so evil is not evidence against God. theodicy A defence of God's goodness and power in the face of evil that also explains why God permits it (Augustine, Irenaeus, Hick). privatio boni Augustine's doctrine that evil is a privation - an absence or corruption of good, not a created substance; God therefore created no evil. original sin The inherited sinful nature and guilt all humans share since the Fall, which explains (for Augustine) why natural evil and punishment are deserved. Mackie (Evil and Omnipotence, 1955): the inconsistent triad - (1) God is omnipotent, (2) God is wholly good, (3) evil exists. A good being eliminates evil as far as it can; an omnipotent being can eliminate all evil; therefore a good omnipotent God would eliminate all evil - but evil exists, so at least one claim fails. Mackie adds the paradoxes: why did God not create a world without evil, and why does he not remove at least some evil (the most extreme) if he can remove any? Epicurus' formulation: 'Is he willing but not able? Then he is impotent. Is he able but not willing? Then he is malevolent. Is he both able and willing? Whence then is evil?' Hume reproduces this in the Dialogues. Plantinga's free will defence: God values genuine freedom; a world containing free agents who sometimes do wrong is more valuable than a world of programmed goodness. God cannot guarantee that free creatures never sin while remaining free - so the existence of evil is logically possible alongside God, and the triad is broken. Plantinga adds the possibility that natural evil stems from fallen angels (the free will defence extends to demonic freedom). Standard critique: Mackie's rejoinder - an omnipotent God could create beings who freely always choose good (as the blessed in heaven are often said to do); Plantinga replies that we cannot know this is feasible and it may be logically impossible. The debate turns on what omnipotence can do with freedom - A* essays weigh this carefully. Plantinga's refinement - transworld depravity: it is possible that every essence suffers from transworld depravity - in any feasible world it would do at least some wrong; so it may not be feasible for God to create free creatures who always do good. This is the technical core of Plantinga's defence of the possibility of God and evil co-existing. Defence vs theodicy: the free will defence claims only logical compatibility, not that we know God's reasons - a theodicy (Augustine, Hick) goes further and explains why God permits evil. Keep the distinction explicit in essays. Rowe (The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism, 1979): even if God and evil are logically compatible, the existence of pointless evil makes God improbable. The fawn: a fawn suffers and dies in a forest fire with no witness, no moral lesson and no redeeming outcome - there appears to be no greater good that justified its suffering. Rowe's inference: an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God would prevent pointless evil; pointless evil exists; therefore probably no such God exists. Hume (Dialogues): the quantity and intensity of suffering, its distribution (the innocent suffer alongside the guilty) and the waste of animal suffering all count as evidence against a perfectly good designer. Is-ought aside, Hume's evidential case is cumulative. Skeptical theism (Wykstra): we are not in a position to know that any given evil is pointless - cognitive limitation means 'we can't see a reason' does not imply 'there is no reason'; the 'noseeum' inference is weak because the gap between our minds and God's is vast. Reply: if reasons are always beyond our ken, moral action itself becomes problematic, and the theodicy position collapses into inscrutability. Distinction - moral vs natural evil: moral evil (suffering caused by free human choices: war, murder, cruelty) is handled by the free will defence; natural evil (earthquakes, disease, animal suffering) is not caused by human choice, so the free will defence alone cannot cover it - Augustine blames fallen angels, Hick uses it as soul-making stimulus, Rowe uses it as his strongest case. Dostoevsky (The Brothers Karamazov, 'Rebellion'): Ivan refuses all theodicy - the suffering of one innocent child cannot be justified by any future harmony: 'if the sufferings of children go to make up the sum of sufferings needed to buy truth, then I protest that the truth is not worth such a price'. Ivan's protest is the literary form of the evidential and moral problem and pairs naturally with Phillips. Swinburne (Providence and the Problem of Evil, 1998): a defence extending free will - God gives humans responsibility through epistemic limitations: if we always knew the consequences, our choices would not be free or responsible; a world with ignorance and risk is necessary for genuine agency. Critique: like Hick, Swinburne must still explain why responsibility requires this much suffering. Augustine (Confessions; City of God): God is perfect and created a world 'all good'; evil is privatio boni - a privation or corruption of good, not a substance God made (so God created no evil); evil arises from the misuse of free will by angels and humans (the Fall); the resultant disharmony of nature is natural evil; since all humanity was seminally present in Adam ( in Adamo ), all share the guilt and deserved punishment of original sin; God's goodness is shown in the redemption through Christ. Theodicy structure: creation good - fall - redemption. Schleiermacher's objections: a perfect creation cannot go wrong - if evil emerged from a perfectly good world, either evil existed already or perfection was an illusion; and it is incoherent to say free creatures in a perfect environment freely fell. Heaven problem: if the blessed in heaven freely never sin, free will without sin is possible - so why did the original creation not secure it? In Adamo: the claim that all were seminally present in Adam is biologically untenable (Augustine assumed traducianism) and morally objectionable - guilt for a pre-existent act is unjust. Natural evil: blaming fallen angels for earthquakes and disease is ad hoc and unsupported by evidence. Strengths: preserves God's omnipotence (evil is not a created thing) and takes original sin seriously; biblical roots; explains why moral evil and punishment are universal. It is a theodicy for a Christian framework rather than a secular proof. Modern Catholic restatement: the Catechism of the Catholic Church maintains the creation-fall-redemption structure: evil is permitted by God who brings good from it (the felix culpa tradition - 'O happy fault'); original sin is transmitted, not by imitation, by propagation. Weighing: Augustine preserves God's omnipotence better than any alternative (evil is not a thing God made) but at the cost of the Schleiermacher objections; A* essays should grant its coherence within a Christian framework while pressing its biologically and morally problematic claims. Irenaeus (Adversus Haereses): humans are created in the image of God but immature; they must grow into the likeness of God through free response to challenge and suffering; evil is the necessary environment for moral and spiritual development; the world is a 'vale of soul-making'. Hick (Evil and the God of Love, 1966; Philosophy of Religion): develops Irenaeus into a modern theodicy. Epistemic distance: God created humanity at a distance from himself, in an imperfect world, so that faith and moral choice are genuinely free - a world of unmediated divine presence would coerce belief and obedience. Soul-making: virtues (courage, compassion, forgiveness) are formed through responding to evil; hardship and natural laws provide the challenge; a paradise without evil would produce no moral growth. Eschatological justification: universal salvation - eventually all will be perfected, and God will justify the suffering by the end-state; the process is incomplete now, so evil appears unjustified from within history. Disproportionate evil: the theodicy may explain some challenge, but not the excessive, degrading suffering of children, the Holocaust or animal pain - no moral growth plausibly requires this much evil (Mackie's rejoinder; D.Z. Phillips' protest). D.Z. Phillips (The Problem of Evil and the Problem of God, 2004): it is morally obscene to treat the torture of a child as a 'means to an end' of soul-making - theodicies rationalise suffering in ways victims could not accept; suffering has no divine purpose, it is simply evil. Universalism: eschatological justification undermines human moral responsibility (everyone is saved regardless) and sits uneasily with traditions holding real judgement and hell. Strengths: avoids Augustine's incoherent perfect-creation problem; fits evolutionary biology (immaturity precedes maturity); epistemic distance is philosophically robust; preserves free will; treats evil as part of a developing world rather than a punishment. Weighing point: Hick's theodicy is the more philosophically coherent of the two, but Phillips' protest is the sharpest objection to both - A* essays stage Augustine vs Hick on coherence, then Phillips against both on morality. Hick's epistemic distance in full: a world of unmediated divine presence would be a 'divine theme park' - awe and obedience would be coerced, not free; imperfection, doubt and the possibility of atheism are the conditions of genuine faith. Weighing: the epistemic distance argument is the most philosophically robust element of the Irenaean tradition - it survives Mackie's quantitative objections better than the soul-making claim itself, and A* essays should separate the two strands: distance answers the challenge of a coercive paradise; soul-making answers the challenge of gratuitous evil - and only the first succeeds fully. Spec coverage: AQA 7062/1A section 3.1.2 (Evil and suffering) - the challenge of evil and suffering for belief in God, the logical and evidential problems, free will defence, Augustine and Irenaeus/Hick. OCR H573/01 (problem of evil) - logical, evidential, Augustinian, Irenaean, Hick, plus the relation to God's omnipotence and goodness. WJEC/Eduqas Component 1 and CCEA include similar theodicy content. Comparative judgement: the strongest A* essays argue - e.g. Hick's soul-making is more coherent than Augustine's fall-based account (Schleiermacher's objection disposes of Augustine), but both fail before Phillips' protest and Rowe's fawn; or the free will defence handles moral evil but cannot extend to natural evil without ad hoc moves; or skeptical theism insulates God but at the cost of moral inscrutability. Command words and structure: AQA Paper 1 Section A: 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'. OCR: extended essays with a justified line of argument. Plan: (1) define evil, moral vs natural; (2) set out the problem (logical, evidential); (3) theodicy 1 with critique; (4) theodicy 2 with critique; (5) weigh and conclude. Pitfalls: conflating the logical and evidential problems (they are distinct challenges); presenting the free will defence as a theodicy (it is a defence - it explains compatibility, not God's reasons); ignoring natural evil when using the free will defence; asserting 'evil is a test from God' without naming a scholar (unexamined assertion); summarising Augustine and Hick without comparative evaluation. Examiner tips: quote Mackie's triad in full; name the fawn (Rowe) and the Holocaust (Phillips) as concrete anchors; distinguish 'defence' from 'theodicy' explicitly; use Schleiermacher's objection as the hinge between Augustine and Hick; finish with a justified verdict, not 'both sides have points'.

topics.name: Religious Experience and Miracles
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Religious Experience and Miracles Classify types of religious experience (visions, voices, numinous, mystical, corporate) with James' four qualities and Stace's distinction (AO1) Explain Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony as the main argument from experience to God (AO1) Set out the challenges from Freud (wish-fulfilment), Jung (collective unconscious) and Feuerbach (projection) (AO1/AO2) Reproduce Hume's definition of miracles and his four a posteriori arguments, and Wiles' objection (AO1) Evaluate whether religious experience and miracles justify belief in God, using conversion evidence (Lourdes, Alister Hardy) (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) religious experience An experience in which the subject apprehends or feels touched by a divine or transcendent reality, directly or indirectly. mystical experience An experience of unity with or apprehension of the divine (Stace: extrovertive - unity in the world; introvertive - unity beyond all sense content). numinous experience Rudolf Otto's category: encounter with the 'wholly other' divine as mysterium tremendum et fascinans - awe-inspiring and attractive at once. ineffability James' first quality of mysticism: the experience defies adequate expression in language. noetic quality James' quality of mysticism: the experience yields insight or knowledge felt to be of objective truth, not mere feeling. transiency James' quality of mysticism: the experience is brief (minutes or hours) though its effects persist. passivity James' quality of mysticism: the subject feels received or seized by a power beyond the will (e.g. automatic writing, prophetic speech). principle of credulity Swinburne: if it seems to a subject that X is present, then probably X is present - appearances should be trusted unless there is special reason to doubt. principle of testimony Swinburne: other people's reports of experiences should be believed absent special reasons to doubt them. wish-fulfilment Freud's psychological explanation: religious experiences are projections of deep human desires for a father-figure and protection, not perceptions of God. collective unconscious Jung's concept: religious experience arises from universal archetypes shared by humanity - explaining religion psychologically without denying its value. miracle (Hume) A transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity or by the interposition of some invisible agent. Classification: direct experiences (visions, voices, the numinous - God encountered immediately) vs indirect experiences (seeing God through the natural world, beauty, conscience). Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.1.3; OCR H573/01. William James (The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902): studies mysticism empirically, from its fruits not its origins. Four qualities of the mystical state: ineffability (defies expression), noetic quality (yields insight felt as objective truth), transiency (brief, with lasting effects), passivity (the subject is received or seized). James' pragmatic conclusion: by their fruits (saintliness, moral transformation) mystical experiences have value and are worth taking seriously - 'the truth of the experience is tested by its fruits'. Stace (Mysticism and Philosophy, 1960): distinguishes extrovertive mysticism (unity perceived in the world - all things as one) and introvertive mysticism (unity beyond all multiplicity and sense content); both share a common core, which Stace takes as evidence that mystics apprehend a single reality. Otto (The Idea of the Holy, 1917): the numinous - the divine as mysterium tremendum et fascinans : wholly other, awe-inspiring (tremendum) and fascinating (fascinans); the experience is non-rational and pre-conceptual. Corporate experiences: Toronto Blessing (1994) and Pentecostal revivalism, Marian apparitions at Lourdes (1858, Bernadette Soubirous) - communal experiences resist the 'private delusion' charge but raise crowd-psychology worries. Visions classified (Teresa of Avila): corporeal visions (sensed with the eyes - Bernadette at Lourdes), imaginative visions (seen in the mind's eye), and intellectual visions (apprehended without images - Teresa's own account of Christ's presence); voices are similarly graded. Conversion experiences: James' examples - Paul on the Damascus road, Augustine's garden conversion ('tolle lege') - sudden vs gradual conversion; James: conversion is the process by which a self 'divided and consciously wrong, inferior and unhappy, becomes unified and consciously right, superior and happy' - the most empirically tractable class of religious experience. Swinburne (The Existence of God, 1979): religious experience is evidence for God. Principle of credulity: if it seems to a subject that X is present, then probably X is present - we should trust appearances (of tables, people, God) unless there is special reason to doubt: the subject was drunk, known to be unreliable, or conditions were abnormal. Principle of testimony: others' reports of their experiences should be believed absent special reasons to doubt. Since millions report experiences of God and no special reason undermines them all, religious experience is substantial evidence; combined with the design argument it makes theism more probable than not. Response 1: religious experience lacks the public checkability of sense experience - two people can see the same table; only one receives the vision. Swinburne's reply: private experience still counts; many everyday judgements (pain, memories) rest on private data. Response 2: the experience is interpreted differently across traditions - a Buddhist, a Christian and a Hindu report incompatible objects. Hick's response: this is the ambiguous data problem - experiences are shaped by concepts, but so are all perceptions; the ambiguity does not defeat them all. Conversion evidence: Alister Hardy's Religious Experience Research Unit collected thousands of first-hand accounts; documented conversions (e.g. James' examples) produce lasting moral fruit - James' 'fruits not roots' argument: even if experiences have psychological origins, their effects support their value. Alston's perceptual model (Perceiving God, 1991): Christian mystical practice is a socially established doxastic practice in which God is experienced as an external object, analogically to sense perception; since the practice is socially established, coherent, self-supportive and productive of fruit, its beliefs are prima facie justified. Reply: rival practices (Buddhist, Hindu) are equally established, so Alston's epistemic conservatism limits the inference to one God - the ambiguity-of-object objection again. Hick's resolution: the experiences are all veridical responses to the same Reality, differently conceptualised - but this is Hick's pluralism, which itself flattens doctrinal differences. Freud (The Future of an Illusion, 1927): religion is an illusion - a projection of infantile wishes for an all-powerful father-figure, protection from danger and cosmic justice; religious experiences are wish-fulfilments, not perceptions. Reply: Freud commits the genetic fallacy - explaining the origin of a belief does not show it is false; the desire for a father-figure could itself be explained by a real God who created beings oriented to him (the theistic rejoinder). Jung (Psychology and Religion, 1938): religious experience arises from the collective unconscious - universal archetypes (God, the Self) shared by all humanity; religion is psychologically valuable (individuation, mental health) but the archetypes need not correspond to an external God. Jung: 'I do not believe, I know' that the psyche contains God-images - but the inference from archetype to God remains disputed. Reply: Jung's account explains universality, which might equally suggest a common object of experience (Stace's common core argument). Feuerbach (The Essence of Christianity, 1841): God is a projection of idealised human nature - theology is anthropology; religious experiences reflect human self-worship. Marx: religion is the 'opium of the people', an illusory consolation shaped by material conditions. Weighing point: projection theories explain universality and psychological function, but the genetic fallacy reply and the fruits-not-roots argument (James) keep the experience argument alive - A* essays must stage both sides. Verification angle (AQA/OCR language crossover): Ayer (Language, Truth and Logic, 1936) - religious experience reports are meaningless because they cannot be verified empirically; reply: the verification principle fails its own test and has been abandoned (Hick's eschatological verification gives religious claims a checkable structure). Marx (Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, 1843): religion is the 'opium of the people' - an illusory consolation shaped by material and economic conditions; religious experiences reflect class interests, not divine reality. Reply: the genetic fallacy again - and Marx's account explains why the oppressed find consolation but not why the experiences are false; James' fruits-not-roots argument survives all three projection theories at the level of value, though not at the level of veridicality. Hume (An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, 1748): a miracle is 'a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity'. Four a posteriori arguments against believing testimony of miracles: (1) no witness has enough experience of all laws of nature to be sure a law was transgressed; (2) human passion for the wonderful makes witnesses unreliable; (3) miracle testimony comes from ignorant, barbarous peoples and gains nothing from educated societies; (4) rival miracle claims in opposing religions cancel each other out - 'every miracle pretended on behalf of a false religion destroys the credit of the miracles of the true one'. Replies to Hume: the wise-man proportioning belief rule may still favour belief if the testimony is strong enough (a modern medical record of an inexplicable cure); Hume's 'ignorant and barbarous' claim is empirically false (educated witnesses report miracles today, e.g. Lourdes medical bureau cases); rival religions may report the same class of events, so the cancellation is overstated. Wiles (The Myth of God Incarnate contributor; Miracles essay): if God intervenes miraculously in some cases, his refusal to intervene in greater evils (Auschwitz) makes his action arbitrary and morally indefensible; therefore God acts uniformly (as creator) rather than occasionally - miracle reports are symbolic, not literal interventions. Reply: this sacrifices particular providence; believers hold that God's occasional action is consistent with a wider plan we cannot judge. Aquinas: defines miracles more carefully - events outside the order of created causes, done by God's power; they can have natural explanations at a lower level yet still be miraculous as divine signs (this survives Hume's first argument better than Hume's own definition). Hick: miracles are events with religious significance to the believer - an interpretive (non-realist-friendly) view that sidesteps law-transgression debates. Vatican II (Dei Verbum context): the Catholic tradition holds miracles as signs of revelation - events that authenticate divine speech; the Lourdes Medical Bureau documents 70 medically inexplicable cures among thousands of claims - the standard modern example for educated-witness replies to Hume. Weighing: Hume's critique of testimony is distinct from Wiles' critique of God's character - the first attacks whether reports should be believed, the second whether God would act selectively; A* essays must keep the two separate and assess each on its own terms. Spec coverage: AQA 7062/1A section 3.1.3 (Religious experience: visions, voices, the numinous, mystical and conversion experience; challenges from Freud and Jung) - and OCR H573/01 (religious experience; God as creator; miracles as challenges to God's existence and nature). WJEC/Eduqas Component 1 and CCEA include similar content. Judgement patterns for A*: (1) Swinburne's principles make experience prima facie evidence, but the ambiguity-of-object objection limits its evidential force; (2) James' fruits-not-roots answer survives the genetic fallacy but does not show the experiences are veridical; (3) projection theories explain universality but commit the genetic fallacy; (4) Hume's critique of miracles is a critique of testimony , not of God's ability to act - Wiles and Aquinas shift the debate; a strong essay keeps these distinct. Command words and structure: AQA Paper 1 Section A: 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'. OCR: extended 'Critically discuss' essays. Plan: (1) classify experience/miracle with a scholar; (2) strongest argument for veridicality; (3) strongest challenge; (4) reply and weigh; (5) verdict. Pitfalls: treating all religious experience as the same type (distinguish direct/indirect, numinous/mystical); presenting Freud as proving religion false (genetic fallacy); conflating Hume's four arguments into one; ignoring the ambiguity-of-object objection (examiners specifically reward it); assuming corporate experiences are more reliable without crowd-psychology analysis. Examiner tips: memorise James' four qualities by name; quote Swinburne's credulity condition ('absent special reason'); give one concrete example (Lourdes, Toronto Blessing, Rowe's fawn is evil - use Paul's Damascus road for vision); keep Hume's testimony critique separate from Wiles' moral critique; end with a justified verdict.

topics.name: Religious Language
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Religious Language Distinguish cognitive and non-cognitive uses of religious language (AO1) Reproduce the verification principle (Ayer) and Flew's falsification challenge, with Hare's bliks, Mitchell's partisan and Hick's eschatological verification as responses (AO1/AO2) Explain Aquinas' doctrine of analogy (attribution and proportion) and Ramsey's models and qualifiers (AO1) Set out Tillich's view of religious symbols (participation in the divine) and its critiques (AO1/AO2) Explain the via negativa (Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides) and its strengths and weaknesses (AO1/AO2) Explain Wittgenstein's language games and D.Z. Phillips' non-realism, and evaluate all approaches comparatively (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) cognitive language Language that asserts facts and can be true or false (realist religious language: 'God exists' reports a reality). non-cognitive language Language that expresses attitudes, commitments or ways of living rather than facts, so truth/falsity does not apply (Hare, Phillips, Wittgenstein). verification principle Ayer: a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable in principle; religious claims fail both tests and are meaningless. falsification principle Flew: a statement is meaningful only if some conceivable observation would count against it; religious believers allow nothing to count against 'God loves us', so the claim dies 'the death of a thousand qualifications'. eschatological verification Hick: religious claims are verifiable in principle - after death (if it occurs) the believer will 'see' God, so 'God exists' has a checkable condition, unlike Flew's examples. blik Hare's term for an unfalsifiable frame of mind or worldview (the paranoid student's blik); such bliks are not meaningless - they structure interpretation of evidence. analogy of attribution Aquinas: terms apply to God and creatures because God is the cause of creaturely perfections - 'God is good' because God causes goodness in creatures. analogy of proportion Aquinas: terms apply to God and creatures in proportion to their natures - God's goodness is infinite as God's nature is infinite, as a dog's health is proportionate to a dog. via negativa The apophatic way: God can only be described by what he is not, since positive language is anthropomorphic and inadequate (Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides). religious symbol Tillich: a symbol participates in the reality it points to, opens levels of reality otherwise closed, and cannot be replaced - unlike signs, which merely point. Cognitive vs non-cognitive: realists hold 'God loves us' asserts a fact that could be true or false; non-realists hold religious language expresses commitment, not facts. Spec: OCR H573/01; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1; CCEA AS. Ayer (Language, Truth and Logic, 1936): the verification principle - a statement is meaningful only if (1) analytic (true by definition) or (2) empirically verifiable at least in principle. 'God exists' and 'God loves us' pass neither test: they are not tautologies and no observation could verify them - so religious language is not false but meaningless. Standard critique: the principle fails its own test (it is neither analytic nor empirically verifiable); Ayer's strong version was abandoned, and even his revised weak version does not defeat all religious claims. Flew ('Theology and Falsification', 1950): the gardener parable - the explorer and the sceptic: the invisible, intangible, scentless gardener 'dies the death of a thousand qualifications'. God's love behaves exactly like non-love (childhood cancer, suffering), and believers qualify everything away ('God's love is not human love', 'his ways are higher'). Flew: if nothing could count against a claim, it asserts nothing. Replies: Hare: bliks - the paranoid student sees dons plotting murder; no evidence would change his blik, but the blik is not meaningless, it structures how all evidence is interpreted; religious commitment is a sane blik, not a false assertion. Critics: if bliks are not true or false, the realist question is dodged, not answered. Mitchell: the partisan - the resistance fighter meets a stranger who says 'trust me', then witnesses him aiding both sides and neither; he still trusts. Faith is trust held against evidence, not blind assertion; but Mitchell concedes the evidence genuinely counts against God - which Flew denies believers do. Hick: eschatological verification - 'God exists' is verifiable after death if it occurs; the claim has a checkable condition, unlike the gardener's qualifications. Critique: it verifies survival, not God, and depends on the afterlife being real. Verification and experience crossover: Ayer's principle would also render reports of religious experience meaningless - the standard link to the religious experience topic; Hick's eschatological verification restores checkability to both claims. Crombie's eschatological parables (New Essays in Philosophical Theology, 1955) - religious statements are meaningful as parables whose point is fully grasped only in the eschaton - a further structured reply to Flew. Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I.13): religious language is neither univocal (same meaning - God is 'good' as a person is good: anthropomorphism) nor equivocal (completely different meaning - then nothing is said of God). It is analogical . Analogy of attribution: terms apply to God as cause of creaturely perfections - 'God is good' because God causes goodness in creatures, as 'the food is healthy' because it causes health. Analogy of proportion: terms apply in proportion to each nature - God's goodness is infinite as God's nature is infinite, as a dog's health is proportionate to a dog's nature. Strengths: preserves meaningful talk of God without anthropomorphism; philosophically careful. Weaknesses: it is unclear how far the analogy stretches; critics say we still do not know what 'God is good' actually asserts. Ramsey (Religious Language, 1957): religious language uses models (positive terms like 'Father', 'good') and qualifiers ('infinitely', 'wholly') that stretch the model to divine scale; the qualifier prevents the anthropomorphic misreading. This is a modern restatement of proportion. Tillich (Dynamics of Faith, 1957): religious language is symbolic. A symbol (1) points to something beyond itself, (2) participates in the reality it symbolises (the flag participates in the nation's power), (3) opens levels of reality otherwise closed, (4) cannot be replaced by anything else, (5) grows and dies with the culture. 'God is our rock' participates in divine steadfastness. Standard critique: participation is mysterious - if symbols are non-cognitive, how can 'God is love' assert anything true? Tillich's own treatment of 'God is being-itself' edges toward saying something literal, which complicates his account. Via negativa (apophatic way): Pseudo-Dionysius (Mystical Theology) - God is beyond all affirmation; we ascend to him by negations, stripping away anthropomorphic terms; Maimonides (Guide for the Perplexed) - positive statements about God risk idolatry; 'God is not in space' tells us more reliably than 'God is spirit'. Strengths: avoids anthropomorphism; fits James' ineffability and Otto's wholly other; protects divine transcendence. Weaknesses: it may say nothing at all (negations without any positive content leave us with no concept of God); it conflicts with positive biblical language ('God is love', 'the Lord is my shepherd') and with worship and prayer, which address God positively; Brian Davies' critique - a negation is only informative against a background of positive understanding. Wittgenstein (Philosophical Investigations; Lectures on Religious Belief): language is a set of language games governed by forms of life - meaning is use within a practice; 'God exists' is meaningful within the religious language game, and its criteria of sense are internal to that game (not the scientific game). Religious statements do not function as hypotheses; they express pictures governing a way of life. D.Z. Phillips (non-realism): 'God exists' is not a report of an external being but expresses a form of life - prayer, worship, moral commitment; the realist question 'does God exist?' misfires. Standard critiques: (1) it makes religion immune from criticism - believers in any game are right by definition, which seems to license anything; (2) it conflicts with believers' own self-understanding - most believers take 'God exists' realistically; (3) if games are incommensurable, cross-game truth claims (mission, apologetics) become unintelligible. Comparative judgement: verificationism is decisively self-defeating; Flew's falsification challenge is the sharpest attack on realist religious language; analogy and via negativa preserve meaningful God-talk but may say too little; language games preserve meaningfulness but at the cost of immunity from critique. A* essays weigh these trade-offs and argue for a position. Spec coverage: OCR H573/01 (religious language: cognitive/non-cognitive, verification and falsification, via negativa, analogy, symbol, 20th-century perspectives); WJEC/Eduqas Component 1 (religious language); CCEA AS (religious language). AQA 7062 has no dedicated religious language topic, but verification/falsification arguments cross into the religious experience discussion. Command words and structure: OCR extended essays ('Critically discuss whether religious language is meaningful'); WJEC/Eduqas AO1/AO2 essay questions; CCEA structured questions. Plan: (1) frame cognitive vs non-cognitive; (2) sharpest challenge (verification or falsification); (3) the best reply (Hick, analogy or language games); (4) weigh trade-offs; (5) verdict. Pitfalls: saying Ayer's principle makes religion 'false' (it makes it meaningless - a different claim); confusing Hare's blik with Mitchell's partisan (blik = worldview; partisan = trust against evidence); presenting Tillich's symbols as merely signs; treating Wittgenstein as a realist; forgetting the verification principle is self-defeating - the single most rewarded critique; giving no verdict. Examiner tips: memorise the parables (gardener, dons, partisan) with their authors; quote 'dies the death of a thousand qualifications'; contrast univocal, equivocal, analogical explicitly; use Hick's eschatological verification as the structured reply; name Pseudo-Dionysius and Maimonides for via negativa; end with a justified verdict on which account best secures meaningful God-talk. Alston (Perceiving God, 1991): Christian mystical practice is a socially established doxastic practice - God is experienced as an external object, analogically to sense perception; beliefs formed in socially established, coherent, self-supportive practices are prima facie justified. Reply: rival practices (Buddhist, Hindu) are equally established, so Alston's epistemic conservatism limits the inference to one God; Alston concedes this and argues theism is better supported than rivals, not that rivals are meaningless. Crombie (in Flew and MacIntyre, New Essays in Philosophical Theology, 1955): religious statements are eschatological parables - meaningful as stories whose point is only fully grasped in the eschaton; like Hick, Crombie gives religious language a deferred but real sense. Cupitt (Taking Leave of God, 1980): non-realism - God is a spiritual ideal, not an objective being; religious language expresses human values and commitments ('God' = the sum of our spiritual ideals); the realist question 'does God exist?' is the wrong question. Critique: Cupitt's non-realism cannot account for prayer as petition to a real other, and most believers reject it as atheism in religious dress. Comparative verdicts for A*: (1) verificationism is self-defeating - it cannot be the standard; (2) Flew's falsification challenge is the sharpest attack on realist religious language, and Hick's eschatological verification plus Mitchell's partisan are the strongest structured replies; (3) analogy (Aquinas) is the strongest realist account of how God-talk is meaningful, but it may say too little; (4) language games and non-realism preserve meaningfulness by relocating it - at the cost of immunity from critique and conflict with believers' self-understanding; (5) weigh these trade-offs and argue for one position: e.g. religious language is meaningful analogically and non-cognitively in different uses, while verificationism fails on its own terms. Exam technique additions: OCR H573/01 also expects the connection between religious language and God's nature (omnipotence, omnibenelevance) - e.g. if 'God is good' is analogical, what does divine goodness mean for the problem of evil? AQA answers on religious experience should note the verification angle (Ayer) and Hick's eschatological verification as the crossover point. Final revision anchor: for OCR essays, pair one cognitive account (analogy or eschatological verification) with one non-cognitive account (language games or Tillich's symbols) in every answer - the mark scheme rewards coverage of both sides of the cognitive/non-cognitive divide.

topics.name: Utilitarianism
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Utilitarianism State Bentham's principle of utility and apply the seven criteria of the hedonic calculus to a case (AO1) Explain Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures, the harm principle and rule utilitarianism (AO1) Explain later developments: preference utilitarianism (Singer, Hare) and negative utilitarianism (Popper) (AO1) Evaluate the main strengths (impartiality, common sense, empirical) and weaknesses (tyranny of the majority, measurement, integrity) (AO2) Compare utilitarianism with religious ethics (natural law, situation ethics) and apply to euthanasia and business cases (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) principle of utility Bentham: the rightness of an action depends on its tendency to promote the greatest happiness (pleasure over pain) for the greatest number. hedonism The view that pleasure (and absence of pain) is the only intrinsic good; Bentham's foundational claim - 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure'. hedonic calculus Bentham's seven criteria for measuring pleasure: intensity, duration, certainty, remoteness, fecundity, purity, extent. act utilitarianism The view that each individual act should be assessed by the utility of its consequences - always perform the act with the greatest utility in that situation. rule utilitarianism The view that rules yielding the greatest utility should be established and followed; acts conforming to such rules are right even if a particular act breaches the rule for gain. higher and lower pleasures Mill: pleasures of the intellect, imagination and moral sense are qualitatively superior to bodily pleasures; 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'. harm principle Mill (On Liberty): liberty may only be restricted to prevent harm to others - the state and society may not coerce for the individual's own good. preference utilitarianism Singer: rightness depends on satisfying the greatest number of preferences, not pleasure; preferences are weighed impartially across all affected, including animals. negative utilitarianism Popper's variant: priority should be given to minimising suffering rather than maximising happiness. two-level utilitarianism Hare: intuitive rules for everyday decisions and critical utilitarian reasoning for hard cases or rule conflict. Bentham (An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, 1789): 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' Hedonism: pleasure is the only intrinsic good. Principle of utility: an action is right insofar as it promotes the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Bentham's psychology: humans seek pleasure and avoid pain, so utility grounds both description and prescription. Hedonic calculus - seven criteria for measuring pleasure: intensity (how strong), duration (how long), certainty (how likely), remoteness (how soon), fecundity (will it produce more pleasures), purity (unmixed with pain), extent (how many affected). Bentham: 'every man to count for one, nobody for more than one' - strict impartiality. Act utilitarianism: each act assessed individually by its consequences in that situation - no act is intrinsically wrong; the calculus decides. Application: lying is wrong only if it reduces utility in that instance; if lying saves five lives, the calculus requires it. Strengths: democratic and impartial; empirical (measures consequences, not intuitions); flexible - fits ordinary reasoning; simple single principle. Weaknesses: calculating is impractical in time-pressured decisions; pleasures may be incommensurable; individual rights can be overridden by majority benefit. Bentham's egalitarian extension: 'the question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?' - Bentham extends moral consideration to animals on the basis of sentience, anticipating Singer by two centuries; his penal reform (the Panopticon) applied utility to punishment: punishment is evil, justified only by preventing greater evil. Mill (Utilitarianism, 1861; On Liberty, 1859): accepts the principle of utility but distinguishes quality from quantity : pleasures of the intellect, imagination and moral sense are qualitatively superior to bodily pleasures - 'it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'. Mill's test: those who have experienced both prefer the higher pleasure; competent judges are the arbiters of quality. This answers the 'swine philosophy' charge against Bentham but complicates the calculus - qualities are not measurable on Bentham's scale. Harm principle (On Liberty): liberty may only be restricted to prevent harm to others; society may not coerce for a person's own good. This provides a rights-protection Mill derives from utility: long-run utility is maximised by protecting individual liberty, since free inquiry and self-development produce the higher pleasures and social progress. Critique: critics say the harm principle is not itself utilitarian - it protects rights regardless of utility in a given case, so Mill smuggles in deontology. Rule utilitarianism: rather than calculating per act, establish rules whose general observance maximises utility (no stealing, no lying); acts conforming to such rules are right even if a particular breach would gain utility. Strengths: protects rights and integrity; practical (rules are learnable); avoids the tyranny of the majority. Weaknesses: rule worship - if following the rule reduces utility in a case, the utilitarian principle itself demands breach; so rule utilitarianism either collapses into act utilitarianism or violates its own foundation. Mill's 'proof' of the principle of utility (Utilitarianism ch. 4): the only proof that something is desirable is that people actually desire it; happiness is desirable (each person's happiness is a good to that person); the general happiness is desirable to the aggregate of persons - a psychological premise plus an inferential step critics call the fallacy of composition (each person's happiness being good to them does not entail the general happiness is good to each); Mill's proof is contested but shows how he grounds the principle empirically rather than by intuition. Singer (Practical Ethics, 1979): preference utilitarianism - rightness depends on satisfying the greatest number of preferences , not producing pleasure; preferences are weighed impartially across all affected, including animals (speciesism - privileging human preferences without justification - is irrational). Singer's principle: give equal weight to like interests. Strengths: avoids the problem of hedonic measurement; respects autonomy and pluralism (people value different things); extends moral consideration to animals and future generations. Weaknesses: whose preferences count (informed, present, future?); 'offensive preferences' (racist or sadistic preferences) must be weighed too, or special reasons must exclude them - which reintroduces non-utilitarian judgment. Popper (The Open Society and Its Enemies, 1945): negative utilitarianism - priority to minimising suffering over maximising happiness; suffering is more urgent and more measurable than happiness. Standard critique: taken literally it implies painless extinction of all life would be ideal (the 'pinprick argument' variant) - so it needs the maximising side back. Hare (Moral Thinking, 1981): two-level utilitarianism - everyday decisions follow intuitive rules (do not lie, keep promises); hard cases and rule conflicts are resolved by critical utilitarian reasoning. This reconciles the practicality of rules with the authority of utility and answers the 'rule worship' charge by making rules defeasible. Ideal utilitarianism (Moore, Principia Ethica, 1903; Rashdall, 1907): goods other than pleasure - knowledge, friendship, beauty, virtue - are intrinsically good; rightness maximises the sum of ideal goods, not pleasure. This escapes hedonism but multiplies intrinsic goods, so the calculus loses its single measure - a standard AO2 point. Strengths: (1) impartial and democratic - every person counts for one, which fits modern equality; (2) empirical - outcomes can be observed, unlike appeals to intuition or divine command; (3) flexible - no act is intrinsically wrong, which fits dilemmas (euthanasia, whistle-blowing); (4) common sense - matches ordinary cost-benefit reasoning; (5) Singer's extension to animals and future generations fits contemporary concerns. Weaknesses: (1) tyranny of the majority - innocent minorities (rights, dignitary harms) may be sacrificed to aggregate benefit (the transplant case: kill one healthy patient to save five); (2) measurement - hedonic calculus is impractical and pleasures are incommensurable; (3) integrity and special relationships - impartiality makes partiality to family and friends irrational, which most people reject (Williams' integrity objection: Jim and the Indians - shooting one to save twenty makes Jim complicit in a way utilitarianism cannot capture); (4) consequences are uncertain - calculation rests on speculation; (5) it licenses acts most people deem monstrous (organised cruelty) if the numbers work. Religious comparison: natural law holds some acts intrinsically wrong regardless of outcome (contraception, euthanasia) - utilitarianism denies this; situation ethics (Fletcher) is a hybrid: one rule (agape) applied flexibly to each situation - it shares utilitarian flexibility but grounds the maxim in love of neighbour, not pleasure. AQA 7062 section 3.2.1.3 expects Bentham, Mill and comparison with religious ethics; OCR H573/02 expects Bentham, Mill, preference and applications (euthanasia, business, sexual ethics). Judgement for A*: act utilitarianism is the purest form but exposes rights; rule and two-level variants protect rights but risk collapsing back into act utilitarianism; the decisive questions are measurement and the sacrifice of the innocent - essays should weigh whether utilitarianism's impartiality is a strength or the source of its most serious failures. Singer's practical extension: the drowning child argument (Famine, Affluence and Morality, 1972) - if preventing suffering is in our power at small cost, we are morally required to act; distance is morally irrelevant; this radicalises utilitarian impartiality into a demanding global ethic - the standard application to famine and charitable duty. Religious comparison in full: Bentham's hedonism directly opposes natural law's telos (pleasure vs purpose); Mill's higher pleasures converge with Christian moral education; situation ethics (Fletcher) shares the per-situation method but grounds the maxim in agape; Aquinas would reject the calculus wholesale - some acts are intrinsically wrong regardless of outcome. AQA 7062 section 3.2.1.3 explicitly expects this comparison. Exam structure: AQA 7062 Paper 1 Section B: each question = 25 marks - 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'; two questions answered. OCR H573/02: extended 'Critically discuss' essays plus AO1 components. Plan for AO2: (1) state the theory's claim; (2) strongest supporting point with scholar; (3) strongest critique with scholar; (4) weigh; (5) justified verdict. Applications to have ready: euthanasia (Bentham: calculus per case; Mill: harm principle permits voluntary choice; Singer: preference of the dying patient; natural law: intrinsically wrong - contrast), business (utilitarian cost-benefit on pollution and wages vs Kantian dignity of workers), sexual ethics (utilitarian harm-based consent vs natural law telos). Name one case study per application. Pitfalls: confusing act and rule utilitarianism (per-act calculation vs rules); presenting Mill's harm principle as a separate non-utilitarian theory (it is Mill's own derivation); asserting 'greatest happiness' without the calculus criteria; missing Mill's quality/quantity distinction - the standard AO1 differentiator; forgetting Singer and preference utilitarianism in OCR answers; ignoring Williams' integrity objection; listing strengths and weaknesses without weighing. Examiner tips: memorise the seven calculus criteria in order (intensity, duration, certainty, remoteness, fecundity, purity, extent); quote 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied' and 'every man to count for one'; apply the calculus to one worked example (e.g. euthanasia case); state whether you defend act, rule or preference utilitarianism in your conclusion and say why. Further applications: whistle-blowing (utilitarian calculus vs Kantian duty); sexual ethics (harm-based consent vs NL telos); charity and famine (Singer's drowning child); punishment (Bentham: prevention of greater evil; Kant: retribution - punishment must fit the crime as an end in itself, opposing pure utility). A* essays pair utilitarianism with a contrasting theory per application. Spec note: OCR H573/02 also expects the link between utilitarianism and meta-ethics - the naturalistic fallacy (Moore): defining 'good' as pleasure commits it, so the theory's foundation is philosophically contested even before applications.

topics.name: Kantian Ethics
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Kantian Ethics Explain Kant's good will, duty and the distinction between hypothetical and categorical imperatives (AO1) State the first formulation of the categorical imperative (universalisability) and apply it to a case (AO1) State the second formulation (humanity as an end in itself) and apply it to euthanasia and business cases (AO1) Explain the third formulation (kingdom of ends), the summum bonum and Kant's postulates of freedom, God and immortality (AO1) Evaluate strengths (dignity, universalisability) and weaknesses (conflicts of duty, cold formalism, lying to the murderer) (AO2) Explain W.D. Ross' prima facie duties as a response to Kant's rigidity and weigh it in a verdict (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) good will Kant: the only thing good without qualification - a will that acts from duty out of respect for the moral law, not from inclination or consequence. duty The necessity of an action done from respect for the law; an action has moral worth only when done from duty, not merely in accordance with it. hypothetical imperative A conditional command: if you want X, do Y (instrumental reason); Kant - such commands bind only given a goal, so they are not moral law. categorical imperative Kant's unconditional moral command, binding on all rational agents: act only on maxims you can will as universal law. universalisability First formulation: act only according to a maxim you could rationally will everyone to follow; a maxim that cannot be universalised (e.g. lying) is wrong. humanity as an end in itself Second formulation: treat humanity, in yourself and others, always as an end and never merely as a means; persons have dignity, not price. kingdom of ends Third formulation: act as a law-making member of a community of rational agents who legislate universal laws for all. summum bonum The highest good: virtue rewarded with happiness; Kant argues morality demands it, which grounds his postulates of God and immortality. postulates of practical reason Kant: freedom, God and immortality must be assumed for morality to be coherent - freedom for duty, God/immortality for the summum bonum. prima facie duties W.D. Ross: conditional duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement) that can conflict; judgement decides which binds in a case. Kant (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785): the good will is the only thing good without qualification - 'it is impossible to conceive anything at all in the world... which can be taken as good without qualification, except a good will'. Talents, wealth and happiness can be used for evil; a good will cannot. Moral worth comes from acting from duty , not merely in accordance with it: the shopkeeper who is honest only for reputation acts in accordance with duty but not from it, so has no moral worth. Consequences are irrelevant to moral worth - outcomes are beyond our control; only the will is within it. Hypothetical vs categorical imperatives: a hypothetical imperative is conditional - 'if you want to pass, revise' - it binds only given a goal, and is merely instrumental. The moral law must be categorical: unconditional, binding on all rational agents regardless of desire. Kant offers three formulations, which he holds are the same law viewed from different angles. First formulation (universalisability): 'act only according to that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' Test for a maxim (e.g. 'I will make a false promise to get money'): (1) formulate the maxim; (2) universalise it; (3) check for contradiction. If everyone made false promises when convenient, promise-keeping itself would collapse - the maxim contradicts itself, so lying is wrong. Kant also uses perfect duties (never permissible: lying, suicide) vs imperfect duties (sometimes permissible: helping others, developing talents). Autonomy and the postulate of freedom: duty is possible only if the will is free; Kant's determinism problem - if actions are determined by natural causes, morality collapses; the postulate of freedom is a practical necessity, not a theoretical proof. O'Neill's refinement (Constructions of Reason, 1989): universalisability requires two tests - consistency in conception (the universalised maxim must be thinkable) and consistency in the will (it must be willed by all rational agents); this answers the 'absurd maxim' objection by tightening the test beyond mere contradiction. Second formulation (humanity as an end in itself): 'act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never merely as a means to an end but always at the same time as an end.' Persons have dignity (beyond price), not market value; objects have price. Application: lying to a person uses their rationality as a mere instrument - it is wrong for that reason as well as failing universalisability; business exploitation (misleading advertising, child labour) treats workers and consumers merely as means; voluntary euthanasia is complex - the patient may will their own end, but Kant still holds suicide is a perfect duty violation because it uses the person as a means to escape suffering. Third formulation (kingdom of ends): act as a law-making member of an ideal community of rational agents legislating universal laws for all - each member is both sovereign and subject. This unifies autonomy and law: moral agents give the law to themselves, so duty is not external coercion. Summum bonum and postulates: morality demands that virtue be rewarded with happiness - the summum bonum . Since we cannot guarantee this in this life, practical reason must postulate : freedom (for duty to be possible the will must be free), immortality (endless progress toward complete virtue), and God (who harmonises virtue and happiness). These are not proofs of God's existence but conditions of moral coherence - 'I have found it necessary to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.' Kant uses this to reject the moral argument as demonstration while retaining it as practical necessity. Strengths of duty: reason is universal - the moral law binds all rational agents regardless of culture or emotion; autonomy: each agent legislates the law for themselves, so morality is not imposed; dignity: persons are ends, which grounds human rights. Applying the second formulation further: sexual ethics - prostitution and deception use a person merely as a means; consenting adults who respect each other treat each other as ends (Kant's framework has limited but real application to sexual ethics); business ethics - CSR grounded in dignity: workers are never merely labour costs; the murderer at the door revisited: Kant's own essay (On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy, 1797) insists on truth-telling even here - 'to be truthful in all declarations is... a sacred and unconditionally commanding law of reason' - the standard AO2 exhibit for the rigidity objection. Strengths: (1) universalisability matches moral conviction - fairness and consistency are core to ethics; (2) dignity of persons grounds modern human rights and business ethics (workers as ends, not instruments); (3) motive matters - rewards and consequences cannot make an act moral, which fits moral intuition; (4) autonomy and reason make the law universal, not sectarian; (5) the postulates give a rational account of why morality seems to demand a moral universe. Weaknesses: (1) conflicts of duty - Kant holds perfect duties admit no exceptions, but cases exist where duties conflict (lying to the murderer at the door: truth-telling vs protecting life); Kant's own reply (tell the truth even then) is widely judged indefensible - if the murderer uses your truthful answer, you are implicated; (2) cold formalism - the theory ignores consequences and emotion; a rigid Kantian outcome (returning a weapon to a madman) is monstrous (Hegel: the theory is 'empty formalism'); (3) universalisability may be too permissive - absurd maxims ('everyone wear odd socks') universalise without contradiction, so the test needs extra conditions; (4) consequentialists (Bentham, Mill) argue ignoring outcomes is irrational - morality exists to make lives go better; (5) the summum bonum argument relies on dubious claims about what morality 'demands'. W.D. Ross (The Right and the Good, 1930): prima facie duties - conditional duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, self-improvement) that can conflict; in a case, judgement decides which duty binds. This is a deontological response to Kant's rigidity: duties are real but not exceptionless. Evaluation: Ross resolves conflicts of duty and fits moral experience, but 'judgement' is unexplained and risks intuitionism without criteria; A* essays use Ross to moderate Kant and weigh whether the price of rigidity is worth the security of exceptionless duties. Further evaluation: (6) the moral argument as postulate - Kant's summum bonum reasoning grounds God and immortality in practical necessity, which religious ethicists (Newman, C.S. Lewis' moral argument tradition) develop into a moral argument for God's existence: objective moral law points to a moral lawgiver; Kant himself denies this is demonstration - A* essays should distinguish Kant's use from the natural-law moral argument; (7) autonomy as strength - each agent legislates the law for themselves, so Kantian ethics avoids both divine command theory (morality is not arbitrary) and relativism (the law is universal) - the standard answer to 'is Kant's ethics religious?'. Spec coverage: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.1.4 (Kantian ethics: good will, duty, categorical imperative, summum bonum, postulates; comparison with religious ethics); OCR H573/02 (Kantian ethics: duty, categorical imperative, universalisability, humanity as an end, applications to euthanasia, business ethics, sexual ethics). Applications to have ready: euthanasia (Kant: suicide is a perfect duty violation; the patient's rationality may not be used to end their own life - contrast with Singer's preference utilitarianism), business ethics (workers and consumers as ends, not means - misleading advertising and exploitative wages are wrong regardless of profit; contrast with utilitarian cost-benefit), sexual ethics (using a person merely as a means is exploitation; but Kant's framework says little about marriage as an institution). Name one case per application. Exam structure: AQA Paper 1 Section B: each question = 25 marks - 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'; two questions answered. OCR H573/02: extended 'Critically discuss' essays plus AO1 components. Plan for AO2: (1) state the claim; (2) strongest support; (3) strongest critique; (4) reply and weigh (Ross as moderator); (5) justified verdict. Pitfalls: confusing hypothetical and categorical imperatives; treating consequences as irrelevant to the rightness of the maxim but asserting Kant ignores outcomes entirely (he holds outcomes are morally irrelevant to worth - the distinction matters); presenting the postulates as proofs of God's existence; missing the humanity-as-an-end formulation in applied answers (examiners expect it); asserting Kant's lying-to-the-murderer reply without stating his reasoning; ignoring Ross. Examiner tips: quote 'good without qualification' and 'never merely as a means'; work through the four-step universalisability test on one maxim in AO1; distinguish perfect and imperfect duties; name Hegel's 'empty formalism' and the murderer case in AO2; end with a justified verdict - e.g. Kantian ethics secures dignity and universalisability but Ross's prima facie duties better handle conflicts, so the second formulation survives better than the first. Comparison with natural law: both are deontological and rule-based; both hold some acts intrinsically wrong. But NL grounds precepts in human nature's telos (union with God) knowable by reason; Kant grounds the moral law in pure practical reason alone - the law is legislated by the rational will, not discovered in nature. Kant's universalisability is formal (any rational agent can test it); Aquinas' precepts are substantive (they depend on what human nature is for). Critique: Kant's formal test may be too thin to generate substantive duties (Hegel's 'empty formalism'); Aquinas' substantive precepts may be too thick for a secular age (the telos is contested). Comparison with Christian ethics: Kant's ethics is not divine command theory - morality is grounded in reason, not God's will; God is postulated only to secure the summum bonum. Christian ethics (agape - Fletcher; revelation - Barth) grounds morality in love and revelation: agape is unconditional but situational; Kantian duty is unconditional and rule-bound. Bonhoeffer's critique: ethics is not about principles (Kantian or otherwise) but about responsible action in concrete situations - his responsibility ethics rejects principles-based accounts generally while sharing Kant's seriousness about the will. Weighing point: Kantian ethics and Christian ethics converge on the dignity of persons (imago Dei; humanity as an end) but diverge on grounding (reason vs revelation) - A* essays use this convergence-divergence pattern across applied topics (euthanasia, business, sexual ethics). Applications for this section: euthanasia (Kant: perfect duty vs NL: sanctity of life - converge on prohibition but for different reasons); business (Kant: dignity vs utilitarian: outcomes); sexual ethics (Kant: never merely as a means vs agape: love decides). Name the contrast in each application.

topics.name: Natural Law and Situation Ethics
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Natural Law and Situation Ethics Explain Aquinas' Natural Law: telos, primary and secondary precepts, real vs apparent goods, interior vs exterior acts (AO1) Explain the doctrine of double effect and apply it to a case (ectopic pregnancy) (AO1) Explain Fletcher's situation ethics: four working principles, six propositions and agape (AO1) Compare Natural Law and situation ethics as legalistic vs antinomian extremes with situation ethics between (AO2) Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of both, including Hume's is-ought gap and the objection that 'natural' does not entail 'good' (AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) natural law Aquinas' deontological theory: human nature has a telos (union with God) knowable by reason; precepts derived from that telos are objective and universal. telos The end or purpose of a thing; for Aquinas the telos of human nature is eudaimonia and ultimately union with God. primary precepts Aquinas' five fundamental purposes of human nature: worship God, reproduce, live in an ordered society, learn, defend the innocent (self-preservation). secondary precepts Rules derived from the primary precepts by reason (do not steal, do not abort) - they guide action and can be refined for circumstance. real vs apparent goods Aquinas: a real good accords with human nature's telos; an apparent good (e.g. adultery) seems desirable but leads away from the telos; wrongdoing is error of reason. interior and exterior acts Aquinas: the interior act (intention) and exterior act (action done) must both be good for an act to be morally good; helping a neighbour for reward has a good exterior but bad interior act. doctrine of double effect It can be permissible to perform a good act with a foreseen but unintended bad effect if the intention is good, the bad effect is not the means to the good, and the good is proportionate. situation ethics Fletcher's theory: only one rule is absolute - agape (selfless love); each situation is decided by what love requires, rejecting fixed rules. four working principles Fletcher's methodology: pragmatism (workable), relativism (no fixed rules), positivism (love is willed, not reasoned from nature), personalism (people before rules). agape Unconditional, selfless Christian love (Greek agape); the only intrinsic good in Fletcher's theory - 'love your neighbour as yourself' applied universally. legalism vs antinomianism Fletcher's two rejected extremes: legalism (fixed rules govern decisions) and antinomianism (no principles at all); situation ethics sits between them. Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II.94): the theory rests on a telos in human nature: all things are directed to ends; human nature's end is eudaimonia (flourishing) and ultimately union with God.
