This telos is knowable by reason , not revelation alone - 'the light of natural reason, whereby we discern what is good and what is evil... is nothing else than an imprint on us of the divine light' (participation in the eternal law). Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.1.1; OCR H573/02. Primary precepts - five fundamental purposes written into human nature: (1) worship God, (2) reproduce, (3) live in an ordered society, (4) learn, (5) defend the innocent/self-preservation. Secondary precepts - rules derived from these by reason: do not steal, do not abort, keep promises; they are refinements that guide action. The structure: eternal law (God's rational order) - divine law (revealed) - natural law (human participation) - human law (civil). Real vs apparent goods: wrongdoing is an error of reason - a person who commits adultery pursues an apparent good (pleasure) that leads away from the telos; no one knowingly chooses evil. Interior and exterior acts: both intention and action must be good; giving to charity for reputation has a good exterior act but a bad interior act, so the act lacks moral worth. Casuistry: applying precepts case by case (e.g. is this lie permissible?) - though Aquinas' casuistry remains rule-governed. NL in Catholic teaching: Vatican I reaffirms that God can be known and the moral law discerned by natural reason; Humanae Vitae (1968) applies NL to contraception - each marital act must remain open to procreation; the ordered-society precept grounds Catholic social teaching (just wage, Rerum Novarum). The four levels of law in full: eternal law (God's rational ordering of the universe) - divine law (revealed scripture, needed because reason is fallible) - natural law (human participation in the eternal law) - human law (civil law derived from natural law). Casuistry in full: NL supports case-by-case application through secondary precepts - e.g. is this lie permissible? (Aquinas: lies are always wrong); is this killing permissible? (double effect decides). Doctrine of double effect: it can be permissible to perform a good act knowing it will have a bad side-effect, provided: (1) the act itself is good or neutral; (2) the agent intends only the good effect (the bad effect is foreseen but not intended); (3) the bad effect is not the means to the good effect; (4) the good effect is proportionate to the bad. Application: ectopic pregnancy - removing the damaged tube (good or neutral act) foreseeably ends the foetus, but the bad effect is not the means; abortion directly intended to end the foetus would be impermissible. Other applications: self-defence (killing an aggressor unintended), palliative sedation, bombing in war (military target with civilian deaths foreseen but unintended). Critique: the intention condition is psychologically slippery - did the agent really not intend the bad effect?; some say the distinction between intended and foreseen is morally arbitrary (the foetus dies either way). Defence: intention is morally central - a surgeon's intent differs from a bomber's even where outcomes match; the doctrine resolves conflicts without condoning intended evil. Proportionalism (Hoose, Knauer, Fuchs): a Catholic development - in real conflicts of precepts, one may act to produce a proportionately greater good; 'ontic evil' in acts may be tolerated if proportionate; this softens NL rigidity and is debated in Catholic ethics. Finnis (Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980): secular restatement - seven basic goods (life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, religion) knowable by reason without theological grounding. Self-defence in full: killing an aggressor in self-defence is permissible if the intention is to repel the attack, not to kill; proportionality limits it. Finnis' seven basic goods in full (Natural Law and Natural Rights, 1980): life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability (friendship), practical reasonableness, and religion ('transcendental' goods knowable by practical reason without theological premises); Finnis' restatement answers the secular objection to Aquinas' telos but multiplies goods, so conflicts are harder to resolve - a standard AO2 point. Fletcher (Situation Ethics, 1966): rejects two extremes: legalism (fixed rules govern every decision) and antinomianism (no principles at all, pure spontaneity). Situation ethics sits between: one absolute rule - agape - applied flexibly to each situation. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.1.2; OCR H573/02. Four working principles: (1) pragmatism - the course of action must be workable, not theoretical; (2) relativism - no fixed rules; 'it depends' is the whole of the situation; (3) positivism - love is a matter of faith and will, not derived by reason from nature; (4) personalism - people, not rules or things, come first: 'the situationist avoids words like never and perfect and always'. Six propositions: (1) only love is intrinsically good; (2) love is the only norm (love replaces rules); (3) love and justice are the same (justice is love distributed); (4) love is not liking; (5) love justifies the means (only the end can justify the means - love's end); (6) love decides situationally (there are no fixed categories). Applications: extramarital affair to save a marriage (love may require it); stealing medicine for a dying spouse (love justifies theft); abortion where the pregnancy threatens the mother's life. Fletcher's own examples: the middle-aged mother in a prisoner-of-war camp, and Mrs Bergmeier. Strengths: flexible and person-centred; fits Jesus' teaching on love over law (Sabbath healing, woman taken in adultery); avoids both rigidity and chaos. Weaknesses: agape is undefined and unmeasurable - 'what does love require?' admits conflicting answers; it may license almost anything (Fletcher's own provocations); love as the only norm is secularised in practice; critics say it collapses into act utilitarianism with a religious label. Fletcher's examples in full: Mrs Bergmeier - a German woman in a Russian POW camp deliberately becomes pregnant by a camp guard so she is released to her family; Fletcher argues love justified the act. The middle-aged mother - a POW camp mother who contracted syphilis from guards could have an abortion to avoid infecting her husband: Fletcher argues love, not the rule against abortion, decides. Agape and Jesus' teaching in full: 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44); the Sabbath healing (Mark 2-3) and the woman taken in adultery (John 8) show Jesus setting love over law - Fletcher's biblical warrant. Critique in full: the six propositions may collapse into one ('do the loving thing'); Paul Lehmann and James Gustafson questioned whether agape can be operationalised without rules - the standard AO2 point. Natural law vs situation ethics: NL is deontological and rule-based (fixed precepts from human nature's telos); Fletcher's theory is teleological in method (ends decided per situation) with one absolute (agape). NL grounds morality in nature and reason; Fletcher in faith and will (positivism). NL supports double effect and fixed secondary precepts (against contraception, abortion); Fletcher permits both where love requires. Judgement patterns for A*: NL is objective and protects the innocent, but 'natural' does not entail 'good' (Hume's is-ought gap) and rigid precepts can produce harmful outcomes; Fletcher's theory is flexible and person-centred, but agape is undefined and the theory risks collapsing into utilitarianism. Religious perspectives: Catholic tradition endorses NL (Vatican II, Humanae Vitae) - reason participates in the divine law; Protestant thinkers (Barth, Brunner) reject natural theology - morality comes from revelation and agape, not nature, which supports Fletcher's direction. Bonhoeffer: ethics is not about principles but about responsible action in concrete situations - his responsibility ethics anticipates Fletcher's flexibility while remaining theocentric. Robinson (Honest to God, 1963): popularised Fletcher's situational agape for a modern church - 'the new morality'. Vardy: agape remains a Christian ideal that secular versions cannot capture. Weighing point: the decisive questions are (1) whether fixed precepts or situational love better protect people; (2) whether morality can be grounded in nature (NL) at all in a secular age; (3) whether agape is precise enough to guide decisions - A* essays must weigh, not list. Bonhoeffer in full: Ethics (unfinished) - ethics is not about principles but about responsible action in concrete situations; 'responsible action' weighs the concrete reality, not abstract rules - anticipating Fletcher's flexibility while remaining theocentric. Robinson in full: Honest to God (1963) popularised Fletcher and Tillich for a lay audience - 'the new morality'; the church establishment reaction (1963 controversy) shows how radical the situational agape was received as being. Exam structure: AQA 7062 Paper 1 Section B: each question = 25 marks - 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'; two questions answered. OCR H573/02: extended 'Critically discuss' essays plus AO1 components. Applications to have ready: euthanasia (double effect vs agape), abortion (ectopic pregnancy case), sexual ethics (contraception, premarital sex, homosexuality - NL fixed precepts vs Fletcher's love), business (just wage - NL; honest dealing - Fletcher's person-centred agape). Command words: 'Explain' = accurate AO1 with the five primary precepts and four working principles named; 'Critically discuss' = sustained argument with verdict. Pitfalls: confusing primary and secondary precepts (five purposes vs derived rules); treating double effect as permitting intended harm (it must be unintended); saying Fletcher has 'no rules' (one absolute: agape - plus four working principles); missing Fletcher's positivism (love is willed, not reasoned) - the standard AO1 differentiator; presenting NL as purely religious (Aquinas grounds it in reason - Vatican I); ignoring Hume's is-ought gap; asserting 'natural = good' without defence. Examiner tips: memorise the five primary precepts and the four working principles as lists; quote 'never' and 'perfect' and 'always' (Fletcher) and 'the light of natural reason' (Aquinas); use the ectopic pregnancy as the double-effect case; name Bonhoeffer and Robinson for religious support of agape; use Hume's is-ought gap as the sharpest NL critique; end with a justified verdict - e.g. Fletcher better protects people but NL better secures objectivity, so the choice depends on whether morality is grounded in nature or revelation.

topics.name: Applied Ethics: Business, Sexual Ethics and Euthanasia
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Applied Ethics: Business, Sexual Ethics and Euthanasia Distinguish types of euthanasia (active/passive, voluntary/non-voluntary/involuntary) and apply ethical theories to each (AO1) Evaluate sanctity of life vs quality of life arguments, with Case studies (Tony Bland, Charlie Gard) (AO2) Explain business ethics concepts: CSR, stakeholders, whistle-blowing, good/bad practice - and apply Kant, utilitarianism and NL (AO1/AO2) Explain sexual ethics issues: pre/extra-marital sex, homosexuality, contraception, consent - religious and secular approaches (AO1/AO2) Apply Kantian dignity, utilitarian outcomes, NL precepts and agape across all three issues comparatively (AO2) Structure an applied-ethics essay with case anchors, scholars and a justified verdict (AO2/AO3) euthanasia Good death; intentionally ending a life to relieve suffering - classified as active/passive and voluntary/non-voluntary/involuntary. sanctity of life Life is sacred because given by God (imago Dei); human life has intrinsic worth regardless of quality - grounds the religious opposition to euthanasia and abortion. quality of life The value of life depends on its quality (pain, dignity, autonomy, capacity for relationships) - grounds arguments for euthanasia and resource prioritisation. corporate social responsibility (CSR) A business's duty to consider the impact of its actions on employees, consumers, society and the environment beyond legal requirement and profit. whistle-blowing Disclosure by an employee of wrongdoing within an organisation; raises conflicts between loyalty, self-interest and public duty (Kant: public duty; utilitarian: outcome). stakeholders All parties affected by a business: employees, consumers, shareholders, suppliers, community, environment - CSR widens consideration from shareholders to stakeholders. consent Informed, voluntary agreement; the secular foundation of sexual ethics (harm-based consent) and of autonomy-based arguments in euthanasia. imago Dei Doctrine that humans are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), grounding the sanctity of life and human dignity. Types: active euthanasia (deliberate act to end life - lethal injection) vs passive euthanasia (withdrawing or withholding treatment - removing a ventilator); voluntary (at the patient's competent request), non-voluntary (patient cannot decide - infant, vegetative state), involuntary (against the patient's wishes). Legal context: active euthanasia illegal in the UK; Assisted Dying Bill debates; Tony Bland (Hillsborough, 1993) - Law Lords permitted withdrawal of feeding as passive euthanasia since he was in a persistent vegetative state; Charlie Gard (2017) - withdrawal over parents' wishes raised non-voluntary and quality-of-life issues. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.2; OCR H573/02. Theories applied: Natural Law: active euthanasia is intrinsically wrong (violates defend-the-innocent/self-preservation); passive euthanasia may be permissible via double effect (foreseen but unintended death); palliative sedation permissible; sanctity of life is absolute. Critique: the intended/foreseen distinction is arbitrary - the foetus or patient dies either way. Kant: suicide is a perfect duty violation - the rational agent may not use himself as a means to escape suffering; but respect for autonomy complicates: a competent patient's rational will to die may be treated as an end - Kant himself still forbids it. Critique: cold formalism ignores suffering; a rigid Kantian outcome is monstrous. Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill, Singer): the calculus decides per case - if continued life contains only pain (hedonic calculus: intensity, duration, certainty), euthanasia maximises utility; Mill's harm principle permits voluntary choice; Singer's preference utilitarianism weighs the patient's own preference for death; quality of life over sanctity. Critique: slippery slope - resource pressure may pressure the vulnerable; non-voluntary euthanasia of the disabled violates Singer's own equal-weight principle. Situation ethics (Fletcher): agape decides per situation - love may require active euthanasia for a suffering spouse; Mrs Bergmeier example (pregnancy in a POW camp) shows Fletcher's willingness to break rules for love. Critique: agape is undefined - conflicting answers are possible. Debate landscape in full: Dignity in Dying (campaigns for assisted dying with safeguards) vs Care Not Killing (opposes on sanctity-of-life and slippery-slope grounds); Lord Falconer's Assisted Dying Bill (2014-15) and successive attempts - the standard UK context. Sanctity of life in full: the Catholic Catechism - intentional euthanasia is 'morally unacceptable'; the Church of England and other Protestant bodies similarly reject active euthanasia but accept withdrawal of futile treatment. NL double effect in full: palliative sedation and high-dose analgesics are permissible when death is foreseen but not intended and pain relief is proportionate - the standard NL distinction between passive and active cases. Concepts: corporate social responsibility (CSR) - duty to consider impact on employees, consumers, society and environment beyond legal requirement and profit; stakeholders vs shareholders - CSR widens consideration; whistle-blowing - disclosing organisational wrongdoing (raises loyalty vs public duty conflicts); good/bad practice - good: fair wages, honest advertising, sustainable sourcing, worker welfare; bad: exploitation, child labour, bribery, environmental damage, misleading claims. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.3; OCR H573/02. Theories applied: Kant: humanity as an end in itself - workers and consumers must be treated as ends, never merely as means; misleading advertising uses consumers' rationality as an instrument (deception fails universalisability); exploitative wages and child labour use workers as means; whistle-blowing is a duty to the public even against loyalty. Strengths: dignity-based; Critique: ignores outcomes - a rigid Kantian may condemn a profitable venture that benefits thousands. Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill): cost-benefit per decision - pollution permissible if aggregate benefit outweighs harm (hedonic calculus); CSR justified by long-run utility (reputation, sustainability); whistle-blowing right if it maximises utility. Critique: tyranny of the majority - exploited minorities (workers, consumers) may be sacrificed to shareholder benefit; Friedman's objection - the only social responsibility of business is to increase profit within the rules (utilitarian reply: externalities and long-run utility defeat Friedman). Natural Law: just wage, honest dealing, stewardship of creation (dominion - Genesis 1:28) are secondary precepts; CSR fits the ordered-society precept; bad practice (exploitation, bribery) violates precepts regardless of profit. Strengths: absolute; Critique: 'natural' does not entail 'good' (Hume's is-ought gap); precepts may not fit modern global markets. Situation ethics: agape per situation - love may require flexible practice (paying above the wage for a struggling employee); but the theory says little about systematic corporate duty. Whistle-blowing cases: the NHS whistle-blowers (Mid Staffordshire), Financial Sector cases (the 2008 crisis) - the standard examples of loyalty vs public duty. Consumers and good practice in full: honest advertising (Kant: universalisability of deception), product safety (utilitarian: risk calculus), fair trade sourcing (NL: just wage), environmental stewardship (NL: dominion as responsibility, Genesis 1:28; utilitarian: externalities). Kant in full: the dignity of persons grounds the prohibition on treating workers as mere labour costs - CSR's strongest theoretical grounding; utilitarian in full: cost-benefit analysis per decision - pollution permissible if aggregate benefit outweighs harm, which Friedman accepts and critics (externalities, long-run reputation) reject. Issues: premarital sex, extramarital sex (adultery), homosexuality, contraception, consent and age of consent. Spec: AQA 7062/1A section 3.2.4; OCR H573/02. Religious approaches: natural law - sex belongs within marriage oriented to reproduction (primary precept); contraception and homosexual acts violate the reproductive precept (Humanae Vitae, Vatican II); adultery violates the ordered-society precept; biblical support: Genesis 1:28 (be fruitful), 1 Corinthians 6 (flee sexual immorality), Seventh Commandment. Liberal religious approaches: agape-based (Fletcher) - love decides per situation; premarital sex permissible where love is genuine; homosexuality judged by the quality of the relationship, not the act's telos; Robinson (Honest to God) and the 'new morality' popularised this. Critique: agape is undefined; the theory may license anything. Secular approaches: harm-based consent - sex is ethical where informed, voluntary and non-exploitative (consent); Kant - humanity as an end: using a person merely as a means (prostitution without consent, deception) is wrong, but consenting adults as ends is permissible; utilitarianism - pleasure permissible if no net harm (STIs, exploitation, broken relationships weighed in the calculus); Singer - preference satisfaction, speciesism parallel for sexual orientation discrimination. Critique: consent alone may not capture exploitation within apparent consent (power imbalances); utilitarian calculus on intimacy is speculative. Judgement for A*: the decisive questions are (1) whether the telos of sex is reproduction (NL) or relational love (agape) or mutual pleasure (utilitarian); (2) whether fixed precepts or consent best protect people; (3) whether religious frameworks add anything secular consent-based ethics lacks - essays must weigh, not list. Religious detail in full: Humanae Vitae (1968) - each marital act open to procreation; the Church of England's more permissive line (contraception permissible within marriage) shows denominational variation; Genesis 1:28 (be fruitful and multiply), 1 Corinthians 6-7 (the body as temple; marriage), Hebrews 13:4 (marriage honoured). Secular detail in full: the harm principle applied to sexual ethics - only harm to others may restrict liberty; consent as the criterion (age of consent, informed consent); Kant: deception and non-consent use a person merely as a means; utilitarianism: pleasure permissible if no net harm (STIs, exploitation, relational damage weighed in the calculus). Spec coverage: AQA 7062 Paper 1 Section B sections 3.2.2 (euthanasia), 3.2.3 (business ethics), 3.2.4 (sexual ethics) - applied through the ethical theories of section 3.2.1. OCR H573/02 applied ethics - euthanasia, business ethics, sexual ethics applied through NL, situation ethics, utilitarianism and Kant. WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA include similar applied topics. Essay structure for applied questions: AQA Paper 1: 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' (set out the issue and one theory's application) then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...' (compare theories, weigh, verdict). Plan: (1) define the issue with one case anchor (Tony Bland, whistle-blowing case, contraception debate); (2) strongest theory application with scholar; (3) strongest critique; (4) comparative application of a second theory; (5) weigh and verdict. Pitfalls: confusing active and passive euthanasia (act vs withdrawal); asserting sanctity of life without naming imago Dei; confusing CSR with shareholders (stakeholders are wider); treating consent as sufficient without power-imbalance analysis; missing the double effect application in euthanasia (examiners expect it); applying only one theory (applied questions reward comparison); listing theory applications without weighing them against each other. Examiner tips: memorise one case per issue (Tony Bland for euthanasia, Friedman for business, Humanae Vitae for sexual ethics); quote 'never merely as a means' (Kant) and 'every man to count for one' (Bentham); state explicitly which theory you defend and why in your verdict; use the same theory across issues to show synthesis - e.g. NL's fixed precepts protect the vulnerable but fail in dilemmas, while agape is flexible but undefined; end with a justified comparative verdict, not a summary. Further pitfalls: confusing CSR with stakeholder theory (CSR is the duty; stakeholders are the affected parties); asserting 'consent is sufficient' without power-imbalance analysis; presenting sanctity of life as purely Christian (imago Dei grounds it, but secular absolute-life positions exist); missing the Assisted Dying Bill context in euthanasia answers; applying only one theory per issue when the mark scheme rewards comparison across at least two. Spec note: OCR H573/02 expects applied answers to reference meta-ethics where relevant - e.g. whether 'good' in 'a good death' means naturalistically good (pleasure, preference-satisfaction) or non-naturalistically good (dignity, telos); the naturalistic fallacy (Moore) and Hume's is-ought gap are the standard AO2 cross-references. AQA 7062 similarly rewards linking applied issues back to the theories of section 3.2.1 and to sanctity of life as a doctrine.

topics.name: Christianity: Death and the Afterlife, Developments and Dialogues
topics.subject: religious-studies
topics.searchText: religious-studies Religious Studies Christianity: Death and the Afterlife, Developments and Dialogues Explain Christian teaching on death, judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory, resurrection and the intermediate state (AO1) Evaluate resurrection of the body vs immortality of the soul, using 1 Corinthians 15, Aquinas and Hick (AO2) Explain Bonhoeffer's theology: costly grace, solidarity, religionless Christianity - and its critiques (AO1/AO2) Explain liberation theology: Gutierrez, orthopraxis, base ecclesial communities - and its critiques (AO1/AO2) Explain exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism (Hick's copernican revolution, Rahner's anonymous Christians) and interfaith dialogue (AO1/AO2) Explain Christianity's dialogue with science (Darwin, Polkinghorne, process thought) and secularisation (Wilson, Bonhoeffer) (AO1/AO2) Write an evaluative essay with a sustained argument and justified verdict (AO2/AO3) particular judgement The individual judgement at death - immediately after death each soul is judged (Catholic tradition), determining its destiny. final judgement The last judgement at the end of time, when Christ returns (parousia) and all are judged - Matthew 25:31-46, the sheep and the goats. purgatory Catholic doctrine: a state of purification for those who die in God's friendship but imperfectly purified; souls are cleansed before heaven (2 Maccabees 12, prayers for the dead). resurrection of the body Christian doctrine that the dead will be raised bodily at the last day (1 Corinthians 15); the body is transformed - a 'spiritual body' - not abandoned. immortality of the soul The Platonic doctrine that the soul naturally survives death; adopted by much Christian tradition but distinct from resurrection. election Calvin's doctrine: God has predestined some to salvation (the elect) and others to damnation; unconditional election is not based on merit. costly grace Bonhoeffer: grace that costs the disciple something - discipleship, sacrifice, solidarity with the suffering - contrasted with 'cheap grace': grace without discipleship. orthopraxis Right action (as opposed to orthodoxy - right belief); liberation theology's claim that Christian truth is verified in action for justice with the poor. base ecclesial communities Liberation theology: small local Christian communities reading scripture in the light of their oppression and acting for justice. anonymous Christians Rahner's inclusivist term: non-Christians who respond to God's grace in their own tradition are anonymous Christians - saved through Christ without knowing him. pluralism (religious) The view that many religions are valid paths to the same divine reality; Hick's copernican revolution - God, not Christianity, is the centre of religious plurality. secularisation The decline of religious belief, practice and institutional influence in modern societies (Wilson: 'the decline of religious practice, institutions and belief'). Spec: AQA 7062 Paper 2 section 3.3.2 (Self, death and the afterlife); OCR H573/03 (death and the afterlife). Judgement: particular judgement - at death each soul is judged (Catholic tradition; Hebrews 9:27 'it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgement'); final judgement - at the parousia (Christ's return), all are judged: Matthew 25:31-46, the sheep and the goats - judged by works of mercy ('I was hungry and you gave me food'); election - Calvin: God has predestined the elect to salvation regardless of merit; Arminian response - free response to grace matters. Heaven and hell: heaven - union with God (beatific vision); hell - separation from God; traditional imagery (fire, darkness) vs modern reinterpretations (hell as self-chosen estrangement - C.S. Lewis' locked door from the inside). Purgatory: Catholic doctrine - purification for the imperfectly purified (2 Maccabees 12; prayers for the dead); Protestant reformers rejected it as unbiblical. Resurrection vs immortality of the soul: resurrection of the body is the Christian doctrine (1 Corinthians 15 - 'sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body'; the body is transformed, not abandoned); immortality of the soul is Platonic (the soul naturally survives) and adopted into much Christian tradition via Augustine. Aquinas: the soul survives death as the form of the body (hylomorphism: the soul is not a separate substance but the body's form); the resurrected body reunites with the soul - resurrection completes the person. Hick: the replica theory - God re-creates a replica of the person at the moment of death elsewhere (possibly in a new space); identity is secured by God's act, not a naturally surviving soul; Hick's eschatological verification supports this. Critiques: the replica may not be the same person (identity problem); hylomorphism makes natural survival hard to explain; Peter Geach - resurrection requires the same body, not a replica. Intermediate state in full: between death and resurrection the soul awaits the final judgement (Catholic: particular judgement, purgatory; Protestant: the intermediate state without purgatory); 2 Corinthians 5:8 - 'away from the body and at home with the Lord' - the standard proof text for immediate presence with Christ; Luke 23:43 - the penitent thief: 'today you will be with me in paradise' - immediate vs deferred readings. Limbo: the contested Catholic doctrine for the unbaptised - formally set aside in recent theology (the International Theological Commission, 2007). Judgement by works in full: Matthew 25 (sheep and goats) grounds the Catholic-Protestant debate on faith and works (James 2 - 'faith without works is dead'); the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16) illustrates judgement and the fixed chasm after death. Bonhoeffer (1906-1945; The Cost of Discipleship, Ethics; Letters and Papers from Prison): executed by the Nazis for involvement in the resistance. Costly grace: 'cheap grace is the preaching of forgiveness without requiring repentance... costly grace is the gospel which must be sought again and again... it is costly because it costs a man his life, and it is grace because it gives a man his life' - discipleship demands sacrifice and solidarity. Solidarity: 'Christ exists as community' - the church exists for others; Bonhoeffer's own solidarity with the oppressed (Jews under Nazism) models this. Religionless Christianity: from prison letters - in a world 'come of age', Christianity must speak without the trappings of religion; the church must exist for others in the secular world. Critiques: the prison letters are fragmentary - the exact meaning of 'religionless Christianity' is disputed; costly grace may be legalistic; his involvement in the assassination plot raises moral questions (deception, violence). Liberation theology: Gustavo Gutierrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971) - theology must begin from the experience of the poor; orthopraxis over orthodoxy - Christian truth is verified in action for justice; base ecclesial communities - small local communities reading scripture in the light of oppression; preferential option for the poor (Vatican II, Medellin); the Exodus and the prophets as the biblical pattern - God sides with the oppressed. Critiques: the Vatican (1984 instruction) warned against Marxist analysis; the gospel is not a political programme; base communities can bypass the hierarchy. Defence: orthopraxis does not require Marxism - it requires action for justice; the preferential option is a Catholic principle, not a party line. Spec: AQA 7062 Paper 2 (Christianity: good conduct, key moral principles, religion and secularisation); OCR H573/03 (Christian moral action - Bonhoeffer; liberation theology). Feminist theology: Mary Daly (The Church and the Second Sex; Beyond God the Father) - 'if God is male, then male is God'; Rosemary Ruether - 'the negative theology of women's religious experience'; critiques of patriarchal language and structures; process thought: Whitehead - God evolves with the world (dipolar theism); Polkinghorne - science and theology as complementary. Feminist theology in full: Mary Daly (Beyond God the Father, 1973) - 'if God is male, then male is God'; the critique of exclusively male God-language and church structures; Rosemary Ruether (Sexism and God-Talk, 1983) - 'the negative theology of women's religious experience'; the recovery of Sophia wisdom traditions; critique: Daly's departure from theism (radical feminism) is contested; Ruether's reformist line retains Christian doctrine while critiquing patriarchy. Process thought in full: Whitehead (Process and Reality, 1929) - dipolar theism: God is primordial (unchanging potential) and consequent (evolving with the world); Hartshorne develops this; God acts by persuasion, not coercion - compatible with evolution and with Bonhoeffer's church-for-others; critique: a God who evolves cannot be the omnipotent God of classical theism - the standard AO2 point. Religious pluralism: three positions. Exclusivism: only one religion is true (Karl Barth - revelation in Christ alone; 'only in Christ'); inclusivism: one religion is fullest but others participate in its truth (Rahner - anonymous Christians : non-Christians saved through Christ without knowing him; Vatican II - elements of truth in other religions); pluralism: many religions are valid paths to the same reality (Hick - the copernican revolution in theology: God, not Christianity, is the centre; all the great faiths are culturally conditioned responses to the same divine Reality; the Real an sich is beyond all concepts). Critiques of pluralism: it flattens real doctrinal differences (Trinity vs no Trinity cannot both be true of the same God); the 'Real an sich' is unverifiable; exclusivists reply that pluralism is itself a first-order religious claim, not neutral. Interfaith dialogue: learning, witness and common action (Nostra Aetate); dialogue presupposes neither relativism nor exclusivism. Science: Darwin (On the Origin of Species, 1859) - natural selection challenges literal readings of Genesis and design arguments; responses: non-literal readings (Augustine's allegorical Genesis commentary), theistic evolution (Polkinghorne - science describes how, theology why); process thought (Whitehead) - God acts through persuasion, not coercion, compatible with evolution; Dawkins - science makes God redundant (The God Delusion). Judgement: the science dialogue is not a single conflict - it is staged as Darwin vs literalism, Polkinghorne vs Dawkins, with Augustine as the hermeneutical hinge. Secularisation: Bryan Wilson - 'the decline of religious practice, institutions and belief' in modern societies; causes: rationalisation, differentiation, pluralism; responses: Bonhoeffer's religionless Christianity - the church must exist for others without religious trappings; the secularisation thesis is contested - global Pentecostalism and religious resurgence show decline is not universal; Berger recanted his early secularisation claims ('the world today... is as furiously religious as it ever was'). Judgement for A*: secularisation in the West is real but not total; Bonhoeffer's response is prescient but his 'religionless Christianity' is fragmentary and disputed. Interfaith dialogue in full: Nostra Aetate (1965) - the Catholic church's declaration on non-Christian religions: elements of truth and holiness in other faiths; dialogue takes three forms: learning (study of other faiths), witness (sharing one's own) and common action (justice, peace) - dialogue presupposes neither relativism nor exclusivism, and Rahner's inclusivism is its standard theological grounding. Science in full: the Galileo affair and Darwin's challenge are historical anchors; modern figures: Polkinghorne (Physics and Theology - science and theology as complementary descriptions of one reality), Peacocke (theistic evolution), Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006 - science makes God redundant); process thought (Whitehead) as a metaphysical reconciliation. Secularisation in full: Weber's rationalisation ('disenchantment of the world'), Wilson's differentiation; UK data - declining affiliation and attendance since the 1960s census patterns; Bruce (God is Dead, 2002) - the strongest secularisation thesis; Berger's recantation (The Desecularization of the World, 1999) as the standard counterpoint. Spec coverage: AQA 7062 Paper 2 section 3.3.2 (Self, death and the afterlife: judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory, resurrection, election); 3.3.7 (Religion and secularisation); 3.3.8 (Religion and religious pluralism); plus good conduct and key moral principles. OCR H573/03 (Developments in Christian thought): death and the afterlife, Christian moral action (Bonhoeffer), liberation theology, religious pluralism, gender, secularisation, knowledge of God. Exam structure: AQA Paper 2: each question = 25 marks - 10-mark AO1 'Explain...' then 15-mark AO2 'Critically discuss...'; two questions answered from Section 3.3 (Study of religion). OCR H573/03: extended 'Critically discuss' essays. WJEC/Eduqas Component 3 (Christianity option) and CCEA A2 systematic study of Christianity cover similar content. Essay structure: (1) set out the doctrine/development with scripture or scholar; (2) strongest supporting point; (3) strongest critique; (4) comparative or dialoguing position (Hick, Polkinghorne, Berger); (5) weigh and verdict. Pitfalls: confusing resurrection with immortality of the soul (bodily transformation vs natural survival); presenting purgatory as biblical for all traditions (it is Catholic; Protestants reject it); treating Bonhoeffer's prison letters as a complete systematic theology (they are fragmentary); confusing inclusivism (Rahner: anonymous Christians) with pluralism (Hick: many valid paths); asserting secularisation as universal (Berger's recantation); quoting Hick's 'Real an sich' without explaining that it is beyond concepts; missing election (Calvin) in afterlife answers. Examiner tips: quote 1 Corinthians 15 ('sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body') and Matthew 25 (sheep and goats); name Bonhoeffer's three contributions (costly grace, solidarity, religionless Christianity) as separate points; distinguish exclusivism, inclusivism and pluralism explicitly with Rahner and Hick; use Polkinghorne and Berger as the dialogue counterpoints to Dawkins and Wilson; end with a justified verdict - e.g. Hick's pluralism is theologically radical but unverifiable, so inclusivism better preserves Christian doctrine while accepting other faiths.

topics.name: Epistemology: Perception, Knowledge and Gettier
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Epistemology: Perception, Knowledge and Gettier Define knowledge using the tripartite (justified true belief) view and construct Gettier-style counter-examples against it (Spec 3.1.1). Explain and evaluate direct realism, indirect realism and Berkeleian idealism, including illusion, hallucination and veil-of-perception issues (Spec 3.1.2). Explain Plato's innate knowledge thesis and Descartes' intuition and deduction thesis, with Locke's and Hume's critiques (Spec 3.1.3). Distinguish a priori from a posteriori knowledge and apply Hume's fork to a priori claims about the world. Analyse and evaluate philosophical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent'). Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays. Gettier cases show JTB is not sufficient for knowledge: true belief + justification + epistemic luck is not knowledge. Direct realism: perception is immediate awareness of physical objects; attacked by perceptual variation, illusion, hallucination and time-lag. Indirect realism (Locke): we perceive the world via sense-data; attacked by the veil of perception, answered by Russell's inference to the best explanation. Idealism (Berkeley): only minds and ideas exist; the master argument plus God's perception; attacked on the act/object conflation and pre-mind worlds. Rationalism (Plato, Descartes) grounds knowledge in reason; empiricism (Locke, Hume) in experience; Hume's fork restricts a priori knowledge to relations of ideas. Propositional knowledge Knowledge 'that' a proposition p is true (e.g. knowing that it is raining), as distinct from ability knowledge ('knowing how') and acquaintance knowledge ('knowing of' a person or place). Tripartite view (JTB) The classical definition of knowledge: S knows that p if and only if (1) p is true, (2) S believes that p, and (3) S is justified in believing that p — justification ruling out lucky guesses and wild hunches. Gettier case A counter-example in which a belief is true and justified but its truth is connected to the justification only by epistemic luck, showing the tripartite view is insufficient (Gettier 1963). No false lemmas Response to Gettier: add a fourth condition that the justification must not be inferred from (or rest on) any false proposition ('lemma'). Reliabilism Externalist theory: S knows that p iff p is true, S believes p, and S's belief is produced by a reliable cognitive process (e.g. normal perception, good memory) — associated with Goldman and Nozick's truth-tracking variant. Direct realism The view that perception gives us immediate awareness of mind-independent physical objects themselves — we see the table directly, as it is. Indirect realism Locke's view that we perceive mind-independent physical objects only indirectly, via the direct objects of perception: sense-data (ideas) caused by the objects. Primary and secondary qualities Locke's distinction: primary qualities (shape, size, motion, number, solidity) are inseparable, mind-independent features objects really have; secondary qualities (colours, tastes, sounds) are just powers objects have to produce sensations in us. Idealism (Berkeleian) Berkeley's view that only minds and their ideas exist — 'esse est percipi' (to be is to be perceived); physical objects are collections of ideas, so there is no mind-independent matter. A priori knowledge Knowledge that can be had independently of (prior to) sense experience, e.g. by intuition and deduction — '2+2=4', 'all bachelors are unmarried'. A posteriori knowledge Knowledge that depends on (is posterior to) sense experience — 'the cat is on the mat', 'water boils at 100°C'. Hume's fork Hume's division of all knowledge into relations of ideas (a priori, analytic, necessary; denying them is a contradiction) and matters of fact (a posteriori, contingent) — leaving no room for substantive a priori knowledge of the world. Three types of knowledge. The spec opens with the distinction between propositional knowledge ('knowing that' — Paris is the capital of France), ability knowledge ('knowing how' — knowing how to ride a bike) and acquaintance knowledge ('knowing of' — knowing Oxford). The tripartite analysis targets propositional knowledge only. AQA examiners regularly report candidates losing marks by illustrating 'knowledge' with skills — use propositions . The tripartite view. S knows that p iff: (1) p is true — you cannot know something false; (2) S believes that p — knowledge requires belief, not mere assent; (3) S is justified in believing that p — the belief must be backed by good grounds (perception, memory, testimony, reasoning), excluding coin-flip guesses that happen to be right. Conditions (1) and (3) must be independent: if justification consists in 'it seems true', the definition collapses. Gettier's challenge (1963). Gettier produced cases where all three conditions hold yet intuition denies knowledge. Standard case: Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket, so Smith infers and believes 'the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket'. Unknown to Smith, he gets the job and also has ten coins. The belief is true, justified — and pure epistemic luck . Zagzebski's recipe shows the problem is general: engineer any justified false belief (a false lemma), then bolt the truth on by luck; the tripartite conditions will be met. Responses. (1) No false lemmas : knowledge requires that the justification not rest on any false proposition. Smith's rests on the false 'Jones will get the job'. Critique: Gettier-style cases with no false lemmas (fake-barn variants where every belief in the chain is true) still generate luck, so the fix is incomplete. (2) Reliabilism (Goldman; Nozick's truth-tracking): knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process. In Gettier cases the belief-forming process (inference from a false lemma) is unreliable. Critique: in a field of papier-mâché barns, the one genuine barn seen in normal conditions yields a reliably-formed true belief that most still judge not knowledge — reliabilism either still admits luck or rigs the notion of 'reliable process'. (3) Virtue epistemology (Zagzebski, Sosa): knowledge is true belief because of intellectual virtue (careful perception, good reasoning); Gettier luck means the truth is not creditable to the agent's virtue. Critique: beliefs from a virtuous process in an unvirtuous environment (the barn field) still seem lucky, so 'because of' must do heavy lifting. (4) Infallibilism : strengthen the justification condition so that only beliefs beyond any possibility of error count as knowledge (Descartes' certainty standard). Critique: the bar is too high — it yields virtually no perceptual knowledge and cannot explain fallible everyday knowledge. Direct realism holds that in perception we are in immediate, direct contact with mind-independent physical objects themselves: when I look at the table, I perceive the table, and (in good conditions) as it really is. Attractions: it is the common-sense view, it invokes no hidden intermediaries, and it explains how perception straightforwardly yields knowledge of the world. Argument from perceptual variation. Russell's table: from one angle it looks distinctly brown and rectangular; from another, paler and diamond-shaped; Locke's straight stick looks bent in water. The same single object appears F to one observer and G to another; if we directly perceived the object as it is, we would contradict ourselves ('the table is brown and not brown'). Conclusion: what we directly perceive is not the object itself but an appearance (sense-data), so direct realism is false. Direct realist response: the argument shows only that objects look different from different points of view — 'looks' reports how the object appears from a perspective, not a second object perceived; there is no contradiction in one object appearing different ways from different angles. Argument from illusion. In illusion something with property F appears to have property G (the straight stick appears bent). What we are directly aware of in illusion — the bent appearance — is not the physical object as it is. But illusion is subjectively indistinguishable from veridical perception; so in veridical perception too we are directly aware only of appearances. Conclusion: we never directly perceive physical objects. Response: the inference overreaches — from 'in illusion we do not perceive a bent object' it does not follow that we never perceive objects directly; in illusion we may still perceive the very stick, with the experience merely misdescribing it (we perceive that it appears bent, not that it is bent). Argument from hallucination. A subject hallucinating a pink rat has an experience subjectively indistinguishable from really seeing one. Since in hallucination there is no pink rat being perceived, what the subject is directly aware of is a mere appearance; by indistinguishability, veridical perception is the same kind of awareness — so perception is never direct. Response: hallucination is a degenerate, abnormal case; we cannot generalise from it about what normal perception is like. (This reply is weaker than for illusion: the indistinguishability premise is harder to shift here.) Time-lag. Light and sound take time: we see the star as it was, not as it is now; so we never perceive objects as they presently are. Response: 'as it is now' sets the bar too high — seeing the star is directly seeing a (past-stage) physical object. Examiner tip: in 12-markers on this section, present the argument's premises and conclusion cleanly, then the specified response — no evaluation (AO1 only). Indirect realism (Locke). We perceive mind-independent physical objects indirectly : the direct objects of perception are sense-data caused by, and in some way representing, the objects. Locke's primary/secondary quality distinction does the representational work: primary qualities (shape, size, motion, number, solidity) are inseparable from the object and our ideas of them resemble them; secondary qualities (colours, tastes, sounds) are merely powers objects have to produce sensations in us — the redness is in the experience, not in the tomato. This underwrites a realist world of minute particles and explains illusion and perceptual variation: the senses reliably tell us 'when something has a property, it seems to have it' (Locke), even when appearance misleads. Issue: the veil of perception. If we only ever perceive sense-data, we can never 'step outside' our experiences to compare them with the objects they allegedly represent. So the claims that sense-data are caused by and resemble mind-independent objects are unverifiable — we are sealed behind a veil. Berkeley presses further: an idea can only be like another idea (the likeness principle), so mind-dependent sense-data cannot resemble mind-independent objects at all — the resemblance claim is incoherent, not merely unverifiable. Related sceptical issue: the very existence of the external world no longer follows from perception: all my experiences would be exactly as they are if caused by something else (a dream, a demon, nothing at all). Responses: (1) Inference to the best explanation (Russell): the hypothesis that mind-independent objects cause our sense-data is the best explanation of their involuntary character, their coherent cross-sensory structure (what I see, I can touch), and their patterned, partly unpredictable regularities; a dream or demon explains the pattern less well. (2) 'Resemblance' is needed only for primary qualities, where our ideas are structural (shapes, sizes) and comparison is less mysterious. Idealism (Berkeley). Esse est percipi — to be is to be perceived. Only minds and their ideas exist; there is no mind-independent matter. Berkeley first attacks the primary/secondary quality distinction: secondary qualities (colour, taste) are plainly mind-dependent — but primary qualities are no better off, since size, shape and motion are all relative to the perceiver (what looks small to me is large to a mite); so if secondary qualities exist only in the mind, primary qualities do too — both are ideas. What we call 'physical objects' are stable, lawful collections of ideas; the immediate objects of perception are exactly these ideas, so idealism takes the indirect realist's sense-data and stops inferring anything behind them. Berkeley's master argument : try to conceive a tree existing unperceived — in the very act of conceiving it, you are perceiving it; so an unperceived object is inconceivable, so mind-independent matter is impossible. Critique: this conflates conceiving a tree with conceiving a tree-unperceived : the content of the second thought is different, and it is the second that is coherent. God's role. Objects persist when no human perceives them because God perceives everything always; the regularity of our ideas reflects God's uniform will, which also explains why the world is orderly and why perception yields knowledge. Critiques of idealism: (1) it makes the existence of tables and mountains depend on minds — implausible for a world that apparently existed before any minds; God rescues continuity only by loading theology into metaphysics; (2) idealism appears to conflate the act of perceiving with the object perceived; (3) problems with God's role: Berkeley holds that God cannot feel pain or have sensations — so how can our painful, colour-like ideas exist in God's mind? God's perception explains the existence of objects but not, on Berkeley's own view of God, what our ideas are like; (4) idealism is said to lead to solipsism : if only minds and ideas exist, my evidence for other minds weakens; the veil-of-perception worry dissolves — but at the price that what exists is not the world common sense believes in. Rationalism vs empiricism. A priori knowledge is had independently of experience; a posteriori knowledge depends on experience. Rationalists (Plato, Descartes) hold that some substantive knowledge of the world is a priori; empiricists (Locke, Hume) deny this: all substantive knowledge of the world is a posteriori, with reason merely operating on material supplied by the senses. Innate knowledge (Plato). In the Meno , Socrates questions an untutored slave boy and gets him to 'discover' a geometrical truth (doubling the square). Since the boy was never taught it, his knowledge must be innate — recollected ( anamnesis ) from a prior existence; the argument from recollection generalises: learning is remembering. Locke's critique: (1) argument from ignorance : children and 'idiots' plainly do not know geometry or the supposed universal maxims — a truth universally present in the mind cannot be unknown to the person whose mind it is; (2) there is no universal consent on the speculative candidates (moral and religious principles vary across cultures), and where agreement exists (logic, mathematics) it can be explained by shared cognitive equipment plus instruction; (3) the mind at birth is white paper (tabula rasa): what feels 'innate' is merely what experience delivers very early and effortlessly. Platonist reply: innate knowledge may be dispositional — a capacity triggered rather than consciously possessed from infancy. Leibniz's argument from necessary truths (New Essays): experience only ever supplies instances — however many white swans we see, never the necessity of 'all swans are white' — yet we grasp necessary truths (mathematics, logic) whose denial is inconceivable; so necessary truths cannot come from experience and must be innate, as dispositions or 'inclinations' (Leibniz's veined marble: the veins are in the block from the start, though work is needed to reveal them). Intuition and deduction thesis (Descartes). Some truths are grasped by intellectual intuition as self-evident; from these, deduction yields further substantive knowledge. In the Meditations : the cogito — 'I think, I am' — is indubitable, since the attempt to doubt it presupposes a thinking 'I'; this establishes that I am a thinking thing (res cogitans). The trademark argument : the idea of an infinite, perfect being could not have originated in a finite, imperfect mind; by the causal principle (a cause must contain at least as much reality as its effect), only God could cause such an idea; so God exists — and the idea is God's 'trademark'. Meditation 5 adds the a priori proof from the essence of a triangle: existence belongs to God's essence as necessarily as three angles to two right angles belong to a triangle. Hume's fork (empiricist critique). Every proposition is either a relation of ideas (a priori, analytic, necessary — to deny it is a contradiction: '2+2=5') or a matter of fact (a posteriori, contingent — its denial is conceivable: 'the sun will not rise'). No proposition can be both substantive about the world and knowable a priori. Applied to Descartes: (1) the causal principle powering the trademark argument is not a relation of ideas — 'every event must have a cause' is, for Hume, a matter of fact known only from experience; (2) the cogito, if true, is singular and fleeting — it establishes a thinking self only 'while I think'; whether the self persists needs a further, a posteriori argument. Rationalist reply: intuition and deduction demonstrably yield necessity that experience never can (mathematics); Hume's fork is itself a philosophical claim not certified by his own dichotomy. Paper format. Paper 1 (3 hours, 100 marks) has Section A: Epistemology and Section B: Moral philosophy — five questions per section worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks . Every question except the 25-marker is pure AO1 ; the 25-marker is 5 AO1 + 20 AO2 . Overall the qualification weights AO1 60% / AO2 40%. Command words. 'Explain…' questions (3/5/12 marks) demand explanation only : define the key terms, set out the claim, argument or distinction, illustrate where asked. Evaluation in short questions is redundant and loses marks — examiners report penalising 'it could be objected…' material on 12-markers. The 25-marker presents a quoted claim followed by 'Evaluate this claim': here you must argue with intent — commit to a thesis in the introduction, defend it through objections, and finish with a consistent conclusion. 25-mark essay structure (top band 21–25). (1) Introduction: define key terms, state your thesis. (2) Argument for your view, with premises and conclusion; consider the best objection; respond. (3) Argument against your view; give a weak response, then the strong response showing why the weak one fails. (4) Conclusion: restate the thesis as supported by the argument — no new ideas . The mark scheme rewards 'crucial arguments clearly identified against less crucial ones': develop one or two debates in depth rather than listing everything. Common pitfalls and examiner tips (click to expand) Gettier = luck only: state that the belief is true and justified, so the failure is not about truth or justification but the lucky connection — then give a named response (no false lemmas, reliabilism, virtue epistemology) and its critique. Confusing direct and indirect realism: direct = we perceive physical objects themselves; indirect = via sense-data caused by them. Idealism denies the objects entirely — do not describe idealism as 'we cannot know reality'. Veil of perception is an objection to indirect realism — do not attach it to direct realism or idealism. Hume's fork: relations of ideas = a priori + analytic; matters of fact = a posteriori + contingent. Candidates routinely swap the labels. Timing: with 10 questions in 3 hours, budget roughly 5 minutes per 3-marker, 8–10 per 5-marker, 15 for the 12-marker and 35–40 for each 25-marker.

topics.name: Scepticism and Descartes' Meditations
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Scepticism and Descartes' Meditations Distinguish normal incredulity from philosophical scepticism and set out Descartes' method of doubt (Spec 3.1.4). Explain the dreaming and evil demon arguments with their premises and conclusions. Explain the cogito and Descartes' clear and distinct ideas thesis, including the charge of the Cartesian circle. Explain the problem of other minds with the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response (Spec 3.1.4). Evaluate sceptical arguments and their responses to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2). Answer 3/5/12-mark questions with pure AO1 explanation, using correct command-word technique. Descartes' method of doubt is a search for certainty, not an endorsement of scepticism — sceptical arguments are his tools. The evil demon is the strongest sceptical scenario because it attacks reason (mathematics) as well as the senses. The cogito survives all doubt: 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever it is thought. The Cartesian circle: clear and distinct ideas prove God; God guarantees clear and distinct ideas — Descartes' reply turns on present attention vs memory. The problem of other minds is answered by the argument from analogy and the 'best hypothesis' response — both inductive, never deductive. Philosophical scepticism The claim that we cannot know (or should doubt that we know) some or all of what we ordinarily claim to know — e.g. that there is an external world; a thesis about the limits of knowledge, not ordinary everyday doubt. Normal incredulity Everyday doubting that depends on background knowledge and is resolvable by further ordinary evidence ('is the shop shut today?') — unlike philosophical scepticism. Method of doubt Descartes' strategy in Meditation 1: withhold assent from any belief that is not indubitable, using the senses-deceive, dreaming and evil demon arguments to strip belief down to a certain foundation. Dreaming argument There are no infallible marks distinguishing waking from dreaming, and in dreams we experience things that do not exist; so for any experience we cannot know we are not dreaming — the senses cannot then give knowledge of the external world. Evil demon (malin génie) Descartes' supposition of a being of supreme power and cunning who systematically deceives him about everything, including mathematics and his own body: if even '2+2=4' could be false, nothing from the senses or from reason is certain. Cogito Descartes' indubitable intuition 'I am, I exist' (Meditation 2): necessarily true whenever it is put forward or conceived, since doubting presupposes a thinking 'I'; it establishes the self as a thinking thing (res cogitans). Clear and distinct ideas Ideas grasped by the attentive intellect as self-evident (like the cogito); Descartes' truth rule — accept only what is clearly and distinctly perceived — is certified by the proof of a non-deceiving God. Cartesian circle The objection (Arnauld) that Descartes relies on clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, but relies on God (as non-deceiver) to guarantee clear and distinct ideas — the argument is circular. Problem of other minds We cannot directly perceive others' minds, only their bodies and behaviour; so how can we know other minds exist at all, or what mental states they contain? Argument from analogy Response to the problem of other minds: my mind causes my behaviour; others' bodies and behaviour are relevantly similar to mine; so by analogy their behaviour is probably caused by minds like mine (Mill, Russell). Res cogitans 'Thinking thing' — Descartes' conclusion from the cogito: the self is essentially a thinking substance (links to substance dualism in Metaphysics of Mind). Two kinds of doubt. Normal incredulity (ordinary incredulity) is everyday doubting that depends on, and is resolved by, further beliefs: 'is the train cancelled?' — check the app. Philosophical scepticism is the claim that we cannot know things we ordinarily take ourselves to know, where no further evidence could settle the matter: e.g. that there is an external world at all. AQA expects the distinction applied, not merely stated — ordinary doubt presupposes we know how to find out; philosophical doubt questions the standards themselves. Descartes' method of doubt. In Meditation 1 Descartes seeks an unshakeable foundation for knowledge by withholding assent from anything not indubitable . The sceptical arguments — Descartes' three 'waves of doubt' — are demolition tools: (1) the senses sometimes deceive (distant towers look small; things look bent in water) — so it is prudent never to trust completely those who have deceived us even once; (2) the dreaming argument : there are no certain marks by which waking can be distinguished from sleep, and in dreams we seem to perceive things that do not exist — so for any particular experience I cannot know that I am not dreaming, and the senses cannot give knowledge of the external world; (3) the evil demon : suppose a being of supreme power and cunning devotes all his efforts to deceiving me — about my body, the world, and even simple mathematics ('2+2=4'). This is the strongest scenario: it attacks reason as well as the senses, and nothing escapes it. The cogito (Meditation 2). Even if the demon deceives me about everything else, he cannot deceive me about my doubting : to doubt is to think; to think, I must exist. 'I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.' Its certainty is performative — the proposition confirms itself in the very act of being thought. From it Descartes derives that he is a thinking thing (res cogitans): a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, imagines and senses (in the sense of 'having seemings'). Critique: the cogito yields only a momentary certainty — it is true while it is thought; whether the 'I' persists or is a substance needs further argument, and the move from 'there is thinking' to 'I (a continuing substance) exist' is a further inferential step, not part of the intuition itself. Rebuilding. With one certainty, Descartes generalises: whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly — as the attentive intellect grasps the cogito — is true. But to apply the truth rule beyond the present moment (e.g. to mathematics I am not currently attending to), he must rule out the demon, i.e. prove there is no deceiver. In Meditation 3 he argues from the idea of God: my idea of an infinite, perfect being has more objective reality than a finite mind could supply; by the causal principle (the cause of an idea must have at least as much reality as the idea's content), only God could cause it; a perfect being is non-deceiving (deception is an imperfection); so God exists and guarantees the truth of clear and distinct ideas. Meditation 5's a priori proof (from God's essence — necessary existence) underwrites the same guarantee. The Cartesian circle. The classic objection (Arnauld): to prove God, Descartes relies on clear and distinct ideas (the causal principle applied to the idea of God); but to trust clear and distinct ideas, he relies on the proved God. The guarantee is bought with the currency it was meant to buy — circular . Descartes' reply: while attending to a clear and distinct idea, its truth is self-evident and needs no guarantee; God is needed only for remembered demonstrations — to secure that the demon cannot sneak back between episodes of attention. Critique: if the guarantee is needed for memory but the proof of God itself relies on remembered premises, the circle reappears; and if self-evidence while attending suffices on its own, God looks redundant. Why this matters for the exam. The 25-marker on Descartes' epistemology typically turns on this section: know (a) the trademark/causal argument's premises, (b) the truth rule, (c) the circle charge and Descartes' remembered-vs-present reply. Note the connection to scepticism : if the circle is vicious, the evil demon is never ruled out, and Descartes ends where Meditation 1 began — with only the cogito. The problem. I know my own mind directly (by introspection); other people's minds I cannot perceive at all — I perceive only bodies and behaviour. Sceptical challenge: how do I know there are other minds at all (rather than automata), or what others feel? The stakes are high: testimony, language and most of our knowledge presuppose other thinkers. Argument from analogy. (Mill, Russell.) (1) I know by introspection that my mental states cause my bodily behaviour (I feel embarrassed; I blush). (2) Other bodies are relevantly similar to mine, and their behaviour is similar. (3) The best explanation of similar behaviour in similar bodies is that it is caused by mental states like mine. Conclusion: probably, other minds exist. Critique: the analogy is a single-case induction — one mind (mine) is a tiny sample; and the reasoning is inductive, so at most probable, never certain — it cannot answer the philosopher's sceptic who demands deductive proof. Best hypothesis response. The existence of other minds is the best explanation of the complexity, purposiveness and linguistic creativity of others' behaviour: treating people as thinkers explains and predicts their conduct far better than any automaton hypothesis. Critique: same epistemic ceiling — inference to the best explanation is still inductive; and the automaton hypothesis is not clearly worse, since a sufficiently complex machine would behave indistinguishably. Connections. In Meditation 6 Descartes argues that I have a 'great inclination' to believe my sensations come from bodies existing independently of me, divinely guaranteed; but other minds are not so guaranteed. Note also the dualist link: if minds are non-extended substances (Metaphysics of Mind), the epistemic gap between my mind and other minds is wider still — dualism intensifies the problem. Examiner tip: 12-markers here ask you to explain the problem and one response — premises, conclusion, response, and stop. Reliabilism as a response. If knowledge is true belief produced by a reliable process rather than belief that is internally demonstrable, the sceptic's demand for indubitability is misplaced. My perceptual beliefs are formed by reliable processes in normal conditions; that I cannot rule out dreaming or demons does not show those processes are unreliable. Critique: reliabilism concedes that I cannot tell whether I know — an externalist cost ('I know, but I could not say why'); and in abnormal conditions the same internal evidence would be misleading, so the intuition that knowledge must be certain fights back. Localising scepticism. A further response: philosophical scepticism is idle — it questions everything at once and so cannot be acted on; ordinary inquiry proceeds by ordinary standards. The Moore-style 'here is a hand' proof is the classic gesture: if the proof fails, the sceptic's premises ('I cannot rule out that I am dreaming') are less certain than the conclusion they deny ('I am not dreaming') — a pragmatic asymmetry that weakens the sceptic's case. For AQA the evaluative point is: the sceptic's premises must be more certain than the ordinary beliefs they overthrow, and it is not obvious that they are. What survives. Even the harshest assessment leaves: (1) the cogito — the one proposition that defeats the demon by being thought; (2) the a priori/a posteriori structure of what is under attack — the demon attacks a posteriori beliefs via dreaming and a priori beliefs via false mathematics; (3) the insight that perception and knowledge of other minds are never demonstrative. A* answers connect these: scepticism is defeated only if either the cogito generalises (Descartes' route) or the standard for knowledge drops from certainty to reliability (reliabilist route) — and each route has a named cost (the circle; the externalist opacity). Where it lands. Scepticism sits in Epistemology (Spec 3.1.4, 'The limits of knowledge') on Paper 1 Section A: five questions worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks . Short questions are pure AO1; the 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2) presents a quoted claim + 'Evaluate this claim'. 25-mark essay structure. Introduction: define philosophical scepticism, state your thesis. Then argue with intent — e.g. that Descartes' sceptical arguments fail to establish global scepticism: (1) argument for the thesis: the cogito survives all doubt, and the dreaming argument only localises doubt to particular experiences; consider the best objection: the evil demon attacks mathematics too, so the cogito is the only survivor; respond. (2) Argument against the thesis: the Cartesian circle means God never guarantees clear and distinct ideas, so the demon is never ruled out; weak response, then strong response. Conclusion consistent with the introduction, no new ideas. Mark scheme top band (21–25): 'crucial arguments clearly identified against less crucial ones' — develop the demon and the circle in depth; the senses-deceive argument is less crucial and can be one line. Common pitfalls and examiner tips (click to expand) Method ≠ creed: Descartes uses sceptical arguments to find certainty — answers that treat him as a sceptic miss the point; describe the method of doubt as a tool. The cogito is conditional: 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever it is thought — do not claim it proves an enduring soul by itself. Cartesian circle: state both halves (clear and distinct ideas prove God; God guarantees clear and distinct ideas), then Descartes' remembered-vs-present reply, before evaluating. Other minds ≠ mind–body problem: the problem of other minds is epistemic (how do I know?); do not swap it for interactionism. Command words: 'Explain the dreaming argument' (12 marks) = premises + conclusion + response only; writing 'but Descartes replies that scepticism is false…' here loses marks for redundancy. Timing: ~35–40 minutes per 25-marker, ~15 for the 12-marker; leave five minutes to check the conclusion matches the introduction.

topics.name: Moral Philosophy: Utilitarianism, Kant and Aristotelian Virtue Ethics
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Moral Philosophy: Utilitarianism, Kant and Aristotelian Virtue Ethics Explain and evaluate Bentham's act utilitarianism (hedonism, felicific calculus) and Mill's qualitative, rule-based refinement (Spec 3.2.1). Explain and evaluate Kantian deontology: the good will, duty, the categorical imperative's formulations and clashing-duty issues (Spec 3.2.1). Explain and evaluate Aristotelian virtue ethics: eudaimonia, the function argument, the doctrine of the mean and phronesis (Spec 3.2.1). Apply utilitarianism, Kantian deontology and virtue ethics to stealing, eating animals, simulated killing and telling lies (Spec 3.2.2). Compare the three theories' decision procedures, strengths and weaknesses to form reasoned judgements (AO2). Write 25-mark essays 'arguing with intent' with balanced argument sandwiches and consistent conclusions. Bentham: quantitative hedonism + felicific calculus; Mill: qualitative pleasures + rule utilitarianism + competent-judges 'proof'. Kant: act from duty via the categorical imperative — universal law, humanity as an end, kingdom of ends; consequences are irrelevant to rightness. Aristotle: eudaimonia via the function argument; virtues are means between vices, hit by practical wisdom and habituation. Classic critiques: tyranny of the majority and integrity (utilitarianism); clashing duties and rigidity (Kant); circularity and guidance (Aristotle). Applied ethics on spec: stealing, eating animals, simulated killing, telling lies — each theory delivers a different verdict. Eudaimonia Aristotle's highest human good: flourishing or living well — a complete, final end desired for its own sake, achieved over a whole life by exercising virtue. Hedonism The view (Bentham) that pleasure (and absence of pain) is the only thing good in itself; morality maximises pleasure summed over everyone affected. Felicific (hedonic) calculus Bentham's decision procedure: measure each option's pleasure by seven criteria — intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent. Higher and lower pleasures Mill's qualitative distinction: pleasures of the intellect, imagination and moral sentiment are higher in kind than bodily pleasures; competent judges who have experienced both prefer the higher. Rule utilitarianism The view that the right act is what conforms to rules whose general acceptance maximises utility — avoiding the act-theory's case-by-case licence for injustice. Good will (Kant) The only thing good without qualification: a will that acts from duty, out of respect for the moral law, rather than from inclination or for consequences. Categorical imperative Kant's supreme principle of morality, binding unconditionally (unlike hypothetical imperatives, which bind only given a desired end). Universal law formulation 'Act only according to that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law' — test maxims for contradiction in conception (universalised) or in the will. Humanity formulation 'Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means' — persons have absolute, non-negotiable worth. Kingdom of ends Kant's third formulation: act as a law-making member of an ideal community of rational agents, each legislating universal laws for all. Doctrine of the mean Aristotle's thesis that each virtue is a mean between two vices — excess and deficiency relative to us (courage between rashness and cowardice). Phronesis Practical wisdom: the intellectual virtue of perceiving what a situation requires and deliberating well about how to act — what makes the mean hit reliably. Bentham's act utilitarianism. Hedonism: nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure; pleasure is the only intrinsic good. An act is right iff it produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. The felicific calculus operationalises this: weigh each option's pleasure/pain by seven criteria — intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (how soon), fecundity (will it produce more of the same), purity (will it be followed by pain), extent (how many affected). Act utilitarianism assesses each act individually by its consequences. Mill's refinement. Mill accepts the consequentialist core but answers the doctrine of swine objection (that the theory makes humans no better than pigs) with a qualitative hedonism: pleasures of the intellect, imagination and moral sentiment are higher in kind ; the test is the verdict of competent judges who have experienced both — they invariable prefer the higher. His 'proof' that happiness is desirable: the only proof something is desirable is that people actually desire it; everyone desires their own happiness; so general happiness is desirable — a fallacious slide (each person's happiness from my perspective vs everyone's ). Mill also moves towards rule utilitarianism : acts are right if they conform to rules (e.g. keep promises, tell the truth) whose general acceptance maximises utility — the rules encode long-run, whole-society consequences. Preference utilitarianism. The modern variant (Singer): maximise the satisfaction of preferences rather than pleasure — it avoids measuring pleasure and better handles diverse goods, at the cost of counting maladaptive or immoral preferences. Issues. (1) Tyranny of the majority : aggregating happiness permits sacrificing individuals — punishing an innocent person to stop a riot maximises utility but is unjust. (2) Calculation : consequences are unknowable in advance; the calculus is impractical in real time (Mill's reply: rules summarise millennia of experience — the 'dead-weight' of calculation is already done). (3) Fairness/utility monster (Nozick): a being that gains enormous utility from any resource would justify total sacrifice of others. (4) Integrity (Williams): Jim and the Indians — shooting one hostage to save twenty maximises utility but destroys the agent's integrity; utilitarianism alienates agents from their own projects. (5) Motives/means: it assesses acts by outcomes, so a malicious act with good consequences comes out right. (6) Experience machine (Nozick): if pleasure were all that matters, we should plug in — most would not, suggesting we value contact with reality and authenticity. The good will and duty. Kant: nothing is good without qualification except a good will — talents, wealth and even happiness can be used for evil. An act has moral worth only when done from duty (out of respect for the law), not merely in accordance with duty (the shopkeeper who is honest only because honesty profits). Hypothetical imperatives ('if you want X, do Y') bind conditionally and are hypothetical counsel of skill or prudence; morality needs an unconditional command: the categorical imperative . Three formulations. (1) Universal law : act only on maxims you can will as universal laws.
