Worship ranged across Panhellenic (Zeus at Olympia, Apollo at Delphi), localised (Athena Polias at Athens, city-specific cults) and personal (household gods, private vows) — the spectrum the whole component measures. The Olympian roster is fixed by tradition: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and (in the Athenian list) Hestia or Dionysus — twelve names worshipped Panhellenically, but each with local cults, iconographies and festivals. Hesiod's Theogony supplies the genealogy that orders them; his Works and Days supplies their justice — Zeus who watches all and punishes wrongdoing. Hero cult fills the space between gods and the dead: exceptional mortals received tombs, offerings and prayers for aid — Herakles was worshipped as both hero and god across Greece; city founders (Theseus at Athens) and war dead (Brasidas at Amphipolis) drew cult; and the chthonic register (offerings poured into the earth, at dusk, to the dead below) contrasts with Olympian sacrifice (burnt on the altar, by day, to the gods above). Mystery cults inverted the communal norm: participation was a matter of personal choice and initiation, open across the usual barriers. The Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone (whose Homeric Hymn explains the myth) promised initiates better prospects — for the harvest and for death; the ritual was secret, with two grades (mystes, then epoptes at a later Great Eleusinia). The prescribed red-figure plaque of the cult of Eleusis (c.400–300 BC) shows Demeter and Persephone with initiates — the evidence base. Mystery cults offered what the polis could not: individual religious experience, hope and a personal relationship with the divine. The healing cult of Asclepius blurs the god/hero boundary: a mortal healer deified, worshipped as both god and hero, with incubation (ritual sleep) and miracle cures recorded in the iamata inscriptions at Epidaurus. The prescribed marble anatomical votive from the shrine of Asclepius (British Museum) shows the body parts dedicated in thanks — private piety made material. The oracle at Dodona (Zeus and Dione, in Epirus) served private individuals : questions scratched on lead tablets — will the child be mine? whom should I marry? should I sail? — asked for personal help and advice, contrasted with Delphi's state business. The prescribed Kodros Painter kylix (c.440–430 BC) depicts a consultation of the Pythia at Delphi — the oracle in use, not just in myth. Together these three show the personal face of Greek religion that the polis-centered festivals hide; A* answers use them to complicate any claim that religion was purely civic. The Eleusinian Mysteries rest on the myth of the Homeric Hymn to Demeter: Persephone abducted by Hades, Demeter's grief and withdrawal, the famine that forces Zeus' settlement, and the gift of the Mysteries to Eleusis. The officials are hereditary priestly families: the hierophant (revealer of the sacred things) and the dadouchos (torch-bearer), with the kykeon drink and the two grades of initiation. Asclepius' cult spread from Epidaurus across the Greek world (a temple in Piraeus by 420 BC); his characterisation as both god and hero — a deified mortal healer — and the iamata inscriptions (patients' cures recorded for public display) make the healing cult the best-documented personal religion. At Dodona, the oak's rustling and the bronze cauldrons' humming were read as Zeus' voice; the lead tablets record questions on marriage, children, travel and property — the private questions the polis' festivals never ask. Levels of participation : household (Zeus Ktesios, Hestia, the herm at the door, ancestors), deme (local festivals — the Rural Dionysia, Thesmophoria for women), polis (state sacrifices and festivals, funded by deme and polis) and Panhellenic (Olympia, Delphi, Isthmia, Nemea). Religious authority lay with the polis, its laws and customs — there was no church, no scripture, no dogma; asebeia was a legal offence (Socrates 399 BC; the Mysteries scandals of 415 BC). Politics and religion were intertwined: assemblies consulted oracles before wars (the Sicilian expedition's omens); Sparta's kings needed Delphic approval; sacred wars were fought over Delphi — political decisions were sometimes made on the basis of divine intervention. The Panathenaia is the component's set festival. Structure: the Lesser (annual) and Greater (every four years, penteteric) Panathenaia; contests in athletics, music and (from the 6th century BC) the apobates race, with prizes of Panathenaic amphorae filled with sacred olive oil (the prescribed black-figure Panathenaic amphora, 333–332 BC, British Museum 1856,1001.1, shows the armed Athena between columns and the prize event); the procession (pompe) from the city gate up the Panathenaic Way to the Acropolis, with the hecatomb, the girls (kanephoroi, arrephoroi, ergastinai) who carried baskets and wove the peplos, and the presentation of the robe to Athena Polias. Significance for Athens: Panhellenic spectacle (athletes and visitors from across the Greek world), civic unity (the procession represented all Athenians — the Parthenon frieze depicts it as an eternal procession), and political power (Peisistratus used it; the fifth-century BC Acropolis made it the image of the polis). The impiety cases define the limits of authority: Andocides was prosecuted over the Mysteries scandal of 415 BC (the herms' mutilation and the profanation of the rites); Socrates was tried and executed in 399 BC. Politics and religion intertwined in the other direction too: the Athenian assembly consulted oracles before the Sicilian expedition, Nicias' lunar eclipse delayed the retreat, and Sparta's kings needed Delphic approval for their wars — political decisions were sometimes made on the basis of divine oracular intervention. The Panathenaia's programme also included the ship-cart — the peplos of Athena hoisted like a sail and processed to the Acropolis — and the musical contests added under Pericles; the festival's representation of all Athenians (all tribes, ages and sexes in the procession) is monumentalised in the Parthenon frieze. The prescribed sites are three sanctuaries with different functions. The Athenian Acropolis (Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaia) is the polis' civic and religious heart: Athena Polias' cult statue, the city's treasury, the image of Athens to the world. Delphi is the Panhellenic oracle: the Temple of Apollo with its adyton and the Pythia, consulted in a fixed process (purification, fee, lot-order, state business first); the Sacred Way lined with state treasuries and votives (the Siphnian Treasury); the theatre and stadium (Pythian games) — prophecy embedded in festival. Olympia is the Panhellenic games: the Temple of Zeus with Pheidias' chryselephantine statue, the ash altar of Zeus (the hecatombs' ash mound), treasuries, the Echo Stoa and stadium — competition between poleis under a sacred truce (ekecheiria), Panhellenic identity in action. Ritual and priests. Blood sacrifice (thusia) is the central rite — purpose: honour, thanksgiving, communion, divination; process: victim selected and processed, water and barley scattered, the knife concealed, the throat cut, the gods' portion (bones and fat) burned, the meat eaten as a communal feast; significance: the whole social order rehearsed. Libations (wine, water, oil) renewed reciprocity daily, at oaths and symposia; votive offerings — from anatomical models at the Asclepieion to state treasuries — made gratitude permanent. Priests and priestesses were part-time ritual experts, not a preaching class: the priest conducted the rite, often as a hereditary or elected honour; aristocratic families monopolised key posts (the Eteoboutads held the priestess of Athena Polias and the priest of Poseidon-Erechtheus; the Eumolpids and Kerykes ran the Mysteries); women held prominent posts (the Pythia; Athena Polias; the Thesmophoria's priestesses) — religion was the one public arena open to women. Religion and philosophy. From the 6th century BC, philosophical thinking challenged the traditional gods: Xenophanes mocked anthropomorphism — Ethiopians draw their gods snub-nosed, horses would draw horse-gods; there is one god, not like mortals in body or thought. Socrates spoke of a personal divine sign (daimonion), rejected the Homeric gods' immoral behaviour, and was tried and executed for impiety in 399 BC (not believing in the city's gods, introducing new divinities, corrupting the young) — ideas the exam treats as genuinely radical in context, though note the counter-view: philosophers inherited the gods' vocabulary (Xenophanes still posits a god; Socrates still swears by Zeus), temples kept being built, and philosophy coexisted with cult rather than destroying it. The tension — a religion of ritual and reciprocity meeting a philosophy of reason — is the thought half's core evaluation. Delphi's consultation process was fixed and public: purification in the Castalian spring, the pelanos fee, the order by lot with state business first, the Pythia's response from the adyton — and the scholarly debate over how she prophesied (the vapours, the laurel, the verses' ambiguity) is itself examinable. Olympia's games ran under the sacred truce (ekecheiria) with events from the footrace through the combat sports to the chariot races; the ash altar's mound grew with each hecatomb, and Pheidias' Zeus — one of the ancient world's wonders — sat within the temple. On philosophy, the exam's evaluation is the extent to which the ideas were 'truly new': Xenophanes' monotheism still posits a god; Socrates still swears by Zeus and dies obeying the city's gods; Anaxagoras' nous still orders a cosmos — philosophical thinking inherited the gods' vocabulary even as it criticised their stories, and temples kept being built.

topics.name: Greek Art
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Art kouros An archaic Greek free-standing marble statue of a nude youth, standing frontal with one foot advanced; developed from geometric rigidity (New York Kouros, c.600 BC) towards naturalism (Aristodikos, c.500 BC). kore The female counterpart — a draped standing maiden, usually a votive offering in a sanctuary (e.g. the Peplos Kore from the Athenian Acropolis); flesh painted white. contrapposto The classical stance: weight on one leg, so hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions — the naturalistic balance of the Doryphoros. chiastic composition Symmetrical, A-B-B-A balance of body parts (tense/relaxed alternating) that organises Polykleitos' Doryphoros and his Canon of proportions. canon (kanon) Polykleitos' treatise on ideal proportions (symmetria), exemplified by the Doryphoros — 'the' statue by which sculptors learned proportion. foreshortening Representing depth on a two-dimensional surface — receding limbs and shields drawn in perspective (Euthymides' experiments on the Three Men Carousing amphora). torsion Twisting of the torso to imply violent movement in space — Euphronios' Herakles and Antaios; Myron's Diskobolos. black-figure Vase-painting technique: figures painted in slip silhouette on the clay, details incised, added white (female flesh) and purple; dominant to c.530 BC. red-figure The reverse: figures reserved in clay against a black slip ground; details painted with brushes and diluted slip — finer line, foreshortening, emotion; dominant from c.530 BC. chryselephantine A cult statue of gold and ivory over a wooden core — Pheidias' Athena Parthenos (Parthenon) and Zeus at Olympia. Free-standing sculpture had four functions: cult statue (the god's image in a temple — chryselephantine Athena Parthenos, Zeus at Olympia), votive (a dedication to a god — most kouroi and korai stood in sanctuaries), grave marker (the Anavysos Kouros for Kroisos; the Aristodikos) and memorial (the Delphic Charioteer commemorates Polyzalos' victory). Architectural sculpture worked by position: Doric metopes (relief panels between triglyphs, usually fighting scenes), Ionic friezes (continuous narrative bands — the Siphnian Treasury, the Parthenon) and pediments (the gable tympana, where a centrepiece anchors flanking figures that shrink towards the corners). Pot shapes map uses: amphorae for storage and transport, kraters for mixing wine, hydriai for water, oinochoai for pouring, kylikes for drinking, lekythoi for oil — shape dictates which scenes suit which vessel (symposium scenes on kraters and cups; maenads on wine vessels). Materials : marble (block-carving; luminous, but heavy and inflexible) vs bronze (lost-wax casting, hollow and strong — allowing free-standing action poses, chased detail, added metals for lips, teeth and eyes: the Delphic Charioteer's inlaid glass eyes and copper lashes). Limestone survives at Corcyra's pediment; marble dominates later. In vase-painting, clay, slip and added colour (white, purple) carry the design. Limitations drive the exam: damaged pieces (the Antikytheran Youth; the Peplos Kore's missing arm — attribute debated), reconstructions (the Hermes and Dionysus' right arm is a restoration controversy) and copies (most classical bronzes survive only as Roman marble copies — the Diskobolos and Doryphoros; the copy preserves pose and proportion but loses the bronze's surfaces, eyes and balance). Always ask what a piece can and cannot tell us. The Parthenon metopes show the four great battles in position: the Gigantomachy (east), the Amazonomachy (west), the Centauromachy (south — the prescribed XXVI–XXVIII among them) and the Ilioupersis (north) — gods over giants, Greeks over Amazons, Lapiths over Centaurs, Greeks over Trojans. Grave markers could be kouroi (the Anavysos) or stelai with relief scenes; memorial sculpture (the Delphic Charioteer) commemorated victory rather than death. Panathenaic prize amphorae are the shape-function link in action: the shape (wide shoulders, black-figure, armed Athena between columns) was fixed by convention for the prize oil, and prize amphorae kept black-figure long after red-figure conquered the market. The kouros develops from geometric rigidity to naturalism: the New York Kouros (c.600 BC) is frontal, block-like, with geometric anatomy; Kleobis and Biton (c.580 BC, Delphi — Herodotus 1.31 tells their story of a blessed death) are Argive, stockier; the Anavysos Kouros (Kroisos, c.530 BC) shows fleshed musculature and the archaic smile; the Aristodikos Kouros (c.500 BC) is shorter-haired, more proportional — the formula dissolving before the classical pose. The kore develops through drapery and adornment: the Berlin Standing Goddess (c.570 BC) wears layered drapery; the Peplos Kore (c.530–540 BC, Acropolis) is plainer, with painted patterns and added-white flesh — colour, now lost, was central. Bronze moves to action: the Delphic Charioteer (c.470 BC, Severe style, inlaid eyes) stands at rest within his chariot; the Artemision Zeus (or Poseidon — the attribute is debated; c.460 BC) strides with arms extended; the Diskobolos (Myron, c.450 BC) twists at the instant before release; the Doryphoros (Polykleitos, c.440 BC) perfects contrapposto and the Canon; the Antikytheran Youth (c.340 BC) shows late proportional change; the Aphrodite of the Agora, Eirene and Ploutos (Kephisodotos, c.370 BC — allegory of peace and wealth), Hermes and Dionysus (Praxitelean S-curve), the Aphrodite of Knidos (Praxiteles, c.340 BC — the first monumental female nude) and the Apoxyomenos (Lysippos, c.330 BC — smaller head, new eight-head proportions, arms breaking into the viewer's space) complete the arc. Black-figure develops through line and pattern: the Gorgon Painter's dinos (frontal Gorgon faces, profile bodies); Sophilos' dinos and the François Vase (Kleitias, c.570 BC — miniaturist, labelled figures, multiple myth cycles); the Amasis Painter's neck amphora (refined line); Exekias' Achilles and Ajax playing dice (c.540 BC — psychological tension, dignity, the spears' verticals) and Dionysus sailing on the ocean kylix (full-frontal innovation; the mast becomes a vine). Red-figure inverts the technique and unlocks drawing: the Andokides Painter's bilingual amphora (both techniques on one pot); the Pioneers — Euphronios (Herakles and Antaios: torsion, musculature, foreshortened feet; Herakles and the Amazons) and Euthymides (Three Men Carousing — foreshortening 'as never Euphronios [did]'; Hector arming) — compete in experiments and sign their work; the Berlin Painter (Achilles and Hector/Memnon — single figures on black ground) refines; the Kleophrades Painter (the Trojan War hydria — pathos in the sack of Troy; Dionysus and the Maenads) and the Pan Painter (Perseus and Medusa; Boreas pursuing Oreithyia — wit and movement) extend the range. Mannerists deliberately revive archaic manner in red-figure after 480 BC. For each work: appearance, style, content, original location, and what it can and cannot tell us. Details the exam expects: Kleobis and Biton were dedicated by Argos at Delphi, and Herodotus (1.31) tells their story — they drew their mother's cart to the temple and died in their sleep, blessed by the goddess; the Peplos Kore's missing arm once held an attribute that is debated (a bow, a pomegranate, a bird); the Artemision Zeus (or Poseidon) is identified by the attribute the empty hand once held — thunderbolt or trident; the Doryphoros survives through copies (Naples; Pompeii) that transmit pose and proportion; the Aphrodite of Knidos' fame is recorded by Pliny (Natural History 36), with the Knidians' refusal to sell her; the Apoxyomenos' scraping pose breaks the figure's bounds — the arms extend into the viewer's space, completing Lysippos' new proportions (smaller head, taller body). Section A commentary questions reward a fixed method . Analyse in this order: Composition — dominant verticals, horizontals and diagonals: Exekias' dice amphora builds a triangle of cloaks under the spears' verticals; the Doryphoros' chiastic balance (tense right leg/relaxed right arm; relaxed left leg/tense left arm); contrapposto in every classical stance. Pose, anatomy and movement — portrayal of the body from geometric outline (New York Kouros) to musculature (Anavysos) to idealised harmony (Doryphoros); torsion (Diskobolos; Euphronios' Antaios); foreshortening (Euthymides' shields and feet); movement captured between poses (the Artemision Zeus' stride). Emotion — pathos: the Kleophrades Painter's Trojan War hydria (women's grief); Exekias' dice players' concentration; the Hermes and Dionysus' tenderness; the archaic smile's ambiguity. Evaluation — what the piece tells us about function, technique and context, and what it cannot; the range of ancient and modern interpretations. A* answers link technique to effect and effect to context: contrapposto is not just a stance but a claim about the ideal body; foreshortening is not just a trick but a claim about the picture plane. The paper's question types (short answer, 10-mark stimulus, 20- and 30-mark essays) reward this structure at every length. Use the method on the whole range: the Berlin Painter refines red-figure to single figures on the black ground (Achilles and Memnon on the volute krater — the figures' edges against the black field are the technique's clarity at its height); the Kleophrades Painter's Trojan War hydria (a water pot — the sack of Troy on the vessel women used) places pathos at the centre: Neoptolemos swings Astyanax onto Hector's blood; the women grieve; Priam's figure closes the scene. Emotion's portrayal develops with the techniques: the archaic smile's ambiguity, the Severe style's gravity, the classical pathos of the late 5th century BC (the hydria) and the 4th century's grace (Hermes and Dionysus). Mythology dominates, but everyday life is reflected inside it: the Wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Sophilos; the François Vase) mirrors Athenian wedding processions; maenads and symposiasts decorate wine vessels for symposium use; Achilles arming (Euthymides) mirrors the hoplite's own kit. Free-standing themes : mortals and gods (the Delphic Charioteer as a mortal's dedication; the Artemision Zeus' attribute debate); 4th-century concepts — the Aphrodite of Knidos (sensuality and religion; Pliny records the Knidians refusing to sell her), Eirene and Ploutos (peace and wealth as allegory after the Peloponnesian War). Architectural themes : Medusa (Corcyra's west pediment — apotropaic, terrifying at the threshold); the Centauromachy (Olympia and the Parthenon metopes — order over barbarism, read by many as a Persian Wars subtext); the Trojan War (Aphaia's east and west pediments — Greek vs Trojan heroes; the Parthenon's metopes); Olympia's pediments (the chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus; the Lapiths and Centaurs) and Herakles' labours in its metopes. Vase themes : Achilles (Exekias' dice players; the Berlin Painter's Achilles and Memnon), Athena (on the Panathenaic-type amphorae), Dionysus (Exekias' sailing kylix; the Kleophrades Painter's maenads), Herakles (Euphronios' Antaios and Amazons), and the Trojan War (the Kleophrades Painter's hydria). Contextual analysis is the A* skill. The social, political and religious context shaped the art: the Persian Wars (480–479 BC) turned battle myths (Centauromachy, Amazonomachy, Gigantomachy) into allegories of Greek order over Persian chaos; the Acropolis' rebuilding after the Persian destruction (the Perserschutt buried and preserved the korai); symposium culture dictated vessel shapes; sanctuary economies funded votives. Limits : original paint is lost — the modern white marble and terracotta are illusions; workshop practice is inferred; female painters are unknown. Interpretations differ ancient and modern: cult statues awed worshippers, museums aestheticise them; the Aphrodite of Knidos scandalised and attracted in equal measure (Pliny's anecdote); modern scholarship (Woodford, Boardman, Moignard) reads style chronologically. A* answers evaluate usefulness — what the sources prove about technique, function and context — and mark their limitations honestly. Olympia's pediments pair a local myth with a Panhellenic one: the east pediment's chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus (the sanctuary's founding myth of the games) and the west's Centauromachy (Lapiths vs Centaurs — order over barbarism); the metopes show the labours of Herakles (the Cretan Bull, the Garden of the Hesperides, the Stables of Augeas among the prescribed) — the Panhellenic hero at the Panhellenic games. The Perserschutt detail is the exam's best example of context preserving art: the Athenians buried the damaged korai and kouroi of the destroyed Acropolis, which preserved them for us; the rebuilt Parthenon replaced the damaged old temple of Athena. On interpretations: cult statues' awe (Pheidias' Zeus) vs museum aesthetics; the Aphrodite of Knidos' scandal and fame (Pliny); and the modern scholarly readings (Woodford's chronological method, Boardman's stylistic surveys, Moignard's vase analysis, Jenkins' architectural sculpture) — cite them to support, not to decorate.

topics.name: Love and Relationships
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Love and Relationships epithumia Desire or appetite — the bodily longing that Plato and Seneca distinguish from love (which they give a rational or spiritual definition). sophrosyne Self-control, moderation — the virtue Greek thought demanded of both sexes, but especially policed in women. paiderastia Institutionalised Greek homoerotic courtship between an older lover (erastes) and a younger beloved (eromenos), with norms of gift, shame and restraint. kyrios The male guardian (father, husband, nearest male kin) with legal authority over an Athenian woman and her property. patria potestas The Roman father's legal power over his descendants — life and death authority that marriage (cum manu or sine manu) modified for the wife. pudicitia Roman sexual modesty and chastity — the matrona's defining virtue, policed by law and iconography (the veil; the Head of Livia's imagery). lex Iulia de adulteriis Augustus' adultery law (18 BC): criminalised adultery, gave fathers and husbands the duty to prosecute — the legal double standard against female sexuality. monodic lyric Sappho's genre: songs for solo performance with lyre/aulos accompaniment, composed for her circle of female companions — distinct from public choral poetry. praeceptor amoris 'Teacher of love' — Ovid's didactic persona in the Ars Amatoria, parodying the instructional manuals of farming and rhetoric. apatheia The Stoic ideal of freedom from passion (pathos) — passions as false judgements to be corrected by reason; the frame for Seneca's treatment of love. Greek ideals. The ideal man is self-controlled, brave, publicly useful (andreia and sophrosyne); the ideal woman is chaste, obedient, silent indoors — Pericles' funeral oration gives the classic statement: the best woman's reputation is not to be talked of among men, good or bad (Thucydides 2.45). Status is legally and civically unequal: an Athenian woman needs a kyrios (guardian), cannot vote or own property outright, and her citizen status matters only as the conduit of citizen children (Pericles' citizenship law, 451/450 BC); her public outlets are religious (the Thesmophoria, priesthoods). Roman women sit under patria potestas , though marriage sine manu (without hand) left them in their birth family and, by the late Republic, legally freer than Greek counterparts; the matrona's virtue is pudicitia, the ideal the univira (one-man woman) embodies. Marriage. A good marriage produces legitimate children, joins properties (dowry) and joins families; its joys are companionship and civic continuity. Sexual freedom is double-standard : men in Greece could frequent hetairai and slaves and practise paiderastia; Roman men meretrices; women in both cultures faced enforced monogamy — Augustus' lex Iulia de adulteriis (18 BC) criminalised female adultery and placed prosecution on the family. Adultery is thus theft of another man's property-rights in the Greek frame, and a crime against the state's moral order in the Roman one. Ideal vs reality is the recurring evaluation: funerary monuments and laws praise the silent matron, but literature records real voices — Medea's speech on the desperate bargain of marriage (Euripides, citable as context), Sappho's women who feel, Ovid's women who manipulate. The thought half's question — what makes a 'good' or 'bad' way to love — runs through all four topics. Greek women's religious outlets were real power: the Thesmophoria (the women's festival of Demeter) was organised and run entirely by citizen women; the priestess of Athena Polias (from the Eteoboutad family) held one of the city's most important posts. Xenophon's Oeconomicus gives the Greek training of the wife: Ischomachus marries a girl of fifteen and trains her to run the household — the ideal in a manual, citable as context. Roman women's legal position improved across the Republic: marriage sine manu left them in their birth family's potestas; they could appear in court and manage property; the matrona's veil (the flammeum) and pudicitia remained the ideal, and Augustus' laws (the ius trium liberorum privileges; the adultery courts) policed the ideal by law. Definitions of love — the Symposium stages a competition of speeches: Eryximachus (love as harmony balancing opposites, medical and cosmic); Pausanias (two Aphrodites — Common Love, bodily and venal, vs Heavenly Love, the noble love of character that grounds respectable paiderastia); Aristophanes (the myth of split beings: humans were doubles, cut apart by Zeus, and love is the desire and pursuit of the whole — the physical symptom is the yearning of halves to melt together); Agathon (love as the youngest, most beautiful and virtuous god); and Socrates, reporting Diotima : love is not a god but a great daimon, intermediate between mortal and immortal — the desire for the perpetual possession of the good, expressed as reproduction in beauty, and ascending by the ladder of love from one beautiful body, to all bodies, to souls, to practices and laws, to knowledge, to Beauty itself. Love vs desire. Desire (epithumia) is appetite — for food, drink, sex; love, on Diotima's account, is desire rationally redirected to the good and the everlasting. The distinction grounds the control and resistance of desire: desire should be controlled because it misjudges the good (aiming at the mortal, not the everlasting) and resisted through education, shame and philosophy — the beloved in respectable paiderastia restrains the lover with shame (aidos) and law (nomos), and Socrates resists even Alcibiades' attempt to seduce him (the final speech, where the roles reverse). Homoerotic relationships are thus both the norm being theorised (erastes/eromenos courtship, age asymmetry, gifts) and the object of Plato's refinement: Heavenly Love ennobles them, Common Love disgraces them. Context and reception. Plato's contemporary context shaped the ideas: classical Athens' symposium culture, its elite paiderastia, the aftermath of the Sicilian expedition (Agathon's victory dinner, c.416 BC). His contemporaries would have heard much that was familiar (Pausanias' defence of paiderastia) and much that was new (Diotima's ladder; love as philosophy rather than sex); the women's absence — the flute-girl sent away — is itself evidence of whose relationships the theory is about. A* answers weigh the ladder against the myth: Aristophanes' romantic picture has proved more famous than Diotima's rigorous one — which reception itself is examinable. The Symposium's frame matters for reception: Apollodorus retells the party from a friend's memory; the speeches are staged at Agathon's victory dinner (c.416 BC), with the flute-girl sent away so the men can talk — the women's absence is itself evidence of whose relationships the theory theorises. Socrates' resistance of Alcibiades is the final speech's climax: Alcibiades' drunken entrance (beauty's prize arrives to indict beauty's teacher), his attempt to seduce Socrates (under the cloak), and Socrates' refusal — desire resisted by reason, the theory performed in a character. Note the ambiguity: Socrates' resistance is not pure — he praises and flirts; the exam expects you to weigh the performance against the theory. Stoicism frames everything. The Stoics define passion (pathos) as a false judgement — an impulse that runs ahead of reason; the four categories are distress, fear, appetite and pleasure. Love, for Seneca, belongs to the appetites unless disciplined into rational affection: the Stoic ideal is apatheia, freedom from passion, with virtue as the only good and the body, beauty and pleasure as indifferents (adiaphora). Definitions : love is the desire for union with what appears good — but since beauty is not good (it is indifferent), erotic love is a misjudgement; friendship, by contrast, is rational affection between virtuous partners. Physical symptoms of desire — pallor, trembling, sleeplessness — are evidence of the mind's assent to a false appearance; the first involuntary movements (the blush, the startle) are not yet passions: assent makes them so, and reason can stop the assent. Control and resistance : Stoic technique — premeditation of future ills, habituation away from banquets and luxury, the refusal of the first assent — makes desire resistible; the answer to 'why should desire be controlled' is that passion enslaves the sage's sovereignty of reason. Homoerotic relationships meet the Roman frame: male-male sex was tolerated only in the active role; the passive adult male (the cinaedus of Roman invective) was disgraced — Seneca's moralising reflects and sharpens this; the Stoic critique cuts across both: passion of any direction enslaves. Context and reception. Seneca's contemporary context is Neronian Rome — imperial luxury, the court's excesses, and his own ambiguous position (a Stoic moralist of vast wealth); his contemporaries received the ideas as elite ethics against the court's example, and the irony (Nero as the pupil) is examinable. Good and bad conduct : marriage is a rational partnership (contrast Ovid's game); desire should be governed by judgement, not extinguished by force; the ideal is the sage who feels the first movement and refuses the second. A* answers evaluate the Stoic programme against the reality of Neronian Rome and against Plato: Seneca offers control as therapy; Diotima offers redirection as philosophy. Seneca's Stoic sources matter: the passion taxonomy (distress, fear, appetite, pleasure) comes from the Stoic school; his De Ira is the model treatment — anger as a passion governed by the same techniques (delay, avoid the stimuli, judge the appearance before assent); his Letters apply the method to wealth, grief and love. The context sharpens the irony: Neronian Rome's court (Nero's excesses, the pupil-teacher relationship) makes the therapy political — the sage's self-control against the emperor's license; and Seneca's own vast wealth is the examinable contradiction. Sappho (Lesbos, late 7th–early 6th century BC) is the component's female voice: monodic lyric composed for performance by and for her circle of female companions. The prescribed fragments show the range: fr. 1, the Hymn to Aphrodite — a prayer in ring composition, the goddess's amused epiphany ('once again?'), and the request 'whom shall I persuade to lead you back?'; fr. 16 — 'some say cavalry, others infantry... but I say the most beautiful thing is whatever one loves', proved by Helen's choice of Paris over family; fr. 31 — the triangular scene of desire's physical symptoms: the voice fails, fire runs under the skin, the eyes see nothing, the ears hum, sweat pours, 'I am greener than grass, and little short of dying'; fr. 44 — the wedding of Hector and Andromache in epic style; fr. 58 — old age, via Tithonus, with the claim that love of the sun's light persists; frr. 94 and 96 — parting and the absent companion remembered through sensuous detail. Devices to cite: apostrophe, imagistic compression, myth as exemplum, irony and humour (Aphrodite's teasing; Sappho's self-deprecation). The issues of fragmentary material are examinable: papyrus scraps, torn lines and restored words mean interpretation is provisional — and that fragility is part of the poems' modern fame. Ovid, Ars Amatoria Book 3 (c.AD 1–2) reverses the didactic frame: Books 1–2 taught men to seduce; Book 3 teaches women — the praeceptor amoris addresses the pupil female. Cite the didactic style: imperatives, catalogues, mock-scholarly digressions (cosmetics, hair, dress in moderation); the venues — the theatre, the porticos, the games as hunting grounds; the tactics — reading and writing elegies, timed arrivals, calculated coldness; the mythological examplars (Myrrha; Pasiphae; Atalanta run down by Hippomenes' apples); and the humour — irony, self-mockery, bathos (the teacher who admits his own failures). Themes : love as art and game, not fate; manipulation as skill; gender roles reversed inside a patriarchal frame — the pupil is empowered to hunt, but the quarry is still male approval. The Roman context is Augustan morality legislation (the same laws Imperial Image studies) — Book 3's tolerance of affairs was, tradition says, part of the carmen et error behind Ovid's exile (AD 8). Comparisons are the Section B core: Sappho's earnest, imagistic desire vs Ovid's playful technique; Plato and Seneca's control vs Ovid's indulgence; Diotima's objective Beauty vs fr. 16's subjective 'whatever one loves'; Greek paiderastia vs Roman marriage economics; and the societal frame — ideal vs reality — against which every text measures 'good' and 'bad' love. Sappho's devices reward close reading: fr. 1's ring composition (prayer — epiphany — request — closing invocation) and Aphrodite's teasing tone; fr. 16's exemplum structure (the general list, Helen's choice, the personal application to Anactoria); fr. 31's escalating symptoms (sight, sound, fire, sweat) broken off in the fragment's gap; fr. 58's Tithonus myth (the dawn-goddess's lover aged into immortality without youth) turned to Sappho's own old age. Ovid's Book 3 rewards the same: the didactic structure (cosmetics, dress, deportment, then tactics), the exemplars (Myrrha and Pasiphae as desire's warnings; Atalanta run down by Hippomenes' apples — the praeceptor's approval of the trick), and the humour that undercuts the teacher (his own failures admitted, the irony of a man teaching women to outwit men).

topics.name: Earth Structure and Plate Tectonics
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Earth Structure and Plate Tectonics Lithosphere The rigid outer shell of the Earth comprising the crust and the uppermost mantle, roughly 100 km thick (thicker beneath cratons), broken into the tectonic plates. Asthenosphere The mechanically weak, partially molten zone in the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere (roughly 100-350 km depth) on which the plates move. Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho) The seismic velocity boundary between crust and mantle, where P-wave velocities jump from about 6-7 km/s to about 8 km/s; about 7 km deep beneath oceans, 30-70 km beneath continents. Gutenberg discontinuity The boundary between the mantle and the liquid outer core at about 2890 km depth, marked by the disappearance of S waves and a sharp drop in P-wave velocity. Shadow zone The belt 105-140 degrees from an earthquake focus where direct P waves are refracted away by the core and S waves are absent, because S waves cannot travel through liquid. Benioff zone An inclined zone of earthquake foci, dipping from the trench down to about 700 km, tracing the descending oceanic slab at a destructive margin. Palaeomagnetism The record of the Earth's past magnetic field preserved as aligned magnetic minerals (e.g. magnetite) cooling through their Curie point in igneous rocks. Magnetic reversal (chron) A period during which the Earth's magnetic field polarity was reversed relative to the present; reversals are irregular in timing, the last (Brunhes-Matuyama) at about 780,000 years ago. Seafloor spreading The generation of new oceanic lithosphere at mid-ocean ridges by upwelling partial melting, producing symmetrical magnetic anomaly stripes that record reversals as the plates diverge. Slab pull The gravitational force exerted by the dense, cold subducting slab on the rest of the plate; widely regarded as the dominant plate-driving mechanism. Exams expect two parallel classifications of the interior. Compositional layers : the crust (oceanic about 7 km thick, basaltic and gabbroic, density about 3.0 g/cm3; continental 30-70 km, granitic in composition, about 2.7 g/cm3), the mantle (peridotite, about 3.3 g/cm3, extending to the Gutenberg discontinuity at 2890 km) and the core (iron-nickel, 10-13 g/cm3; liquid outer core 2890-5150 km, solid inner core 5150-6371 km, separated by the Lehmann discontinuity). Mechanical layers : the rigid lithosphere (crust plus uppermost mantle, about 100 km) rides on the weak asthenosphere , which is why plates can move. The evidence is seismic and you must be able to link each observation to an inference: P waves (primary, compressional) travel fastest (6-8 km/s in crust), pass through solids and liquids, and are refracted at velocity boundaries. S waves (secondary, shear) travel at 3.5-4.5 km/s, are slower, more destructive and cannot pass through liquid . S waves are absent beyond about 105 degrees from the focus: the outer core is liquid . Direct P waves are absent in the P-wave shadow zone (105-140 degrees) because they are sharply refracted downwards on entering the lower-velocity core. Velocity jumps at the Moho (6-7 to 8 km/s) and the drop at Gutenberg locate those boundaries; travel-time curves of refracted and direct arrivals allow crustal thickness to be calculated. Know the refraction calculation used in Component 3 papers: H = (D/2) x sqrt[(V2-V1)/(V2+V1)] , where H is crustal thickness, D the crossover distance of the two travel-time lines, V1 and V2 the P-wave velocities in crust and mantle. Practise substituting values (e.g. D = 100 km, V1 = 6.5, V2 = 8.0 km/s gives H of about 20 km) and state assumptions: layers are homogeneous and horizontal. Exam trap: Moho depth varies Never quote a single Moho depth. Say about 7 km beneath oceans and 30-70 km beneath continents, thickening under mountain belts (up to 70 km under the Himalaya) because of crustal thickening during orogeny. Interpreting travel-time curves is a routine numerical skill: the direct wave plots as one straight line of slope 1/V1; the refracted wave (critically refracted along the Moho) plots as a second, shallower line of slope 1/V2 that overtakes the direct at the crossover distance D. Beyond D the refracted arrival arrives first. Deeper crust shifts D to greater distances. Isostasy explains the thick crust of mountain belts: the low-density crust floats on the denser mantle like an iceberg (Airy model), so elevated belts have deep roots of up to 70 km and gravity measurements are close to zero over them (isostatic compensation). Travel-time drill Two lines on a travel-time graph: steep line = direct wave in the crust (slower); shallow line = refracted wave along the Moho (faster, arrives first at distance). Crossover distance D increases with crustal thickness. Quote velocities: about 6-7 km/s crust, about 8 km/s mantle. Mechanical vs compositional distinction is itself examinable: the lithosphere INCLUDES the uppermost mantle (it is not just crust) and behaves rigidly; the asthenosphere is solid but weak (near its melting point), flowing slowly by solid-state creep - allowing plate motion. Seismic velocities decrease in the asthenosphere (the low-velocity zone) - direct evidence for its weakness. State this distinction precisely: questions ask why plates are defined mechanically, not compositionally, and the low-velocity zone is the evidence. Learn the three boundary types as process + product + example triplets, because compare-and-contrast questions are routine: Boundary Processes Products Example Divergent (constructive) Decompression partial melting of upwelling peridotite; dyke injection; normal faulting Mid-ocean ridge, axial rift valley, pillow basalts, sheeted dykes, shallow earthquakes (less than 30 km), black smoker VMS deposits Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Iceland (ridge above hotspot) Convergent (destructive) Subduction; flux melting as water leaves the slab; accretionary prism construction; partial melting of crust Trench, Benioff zone (foci to 700 km), island arc or Andean arc, andesitic-rhyolitic volcanism, granite plutons, back-arc basin Japan and Mariana (ocean-ocean); Andes (ocean-continent) Conservative (passive) Strike-slip shear; no creation or destruction of lithosphere Fault-line valleys, offset ridge segments, shallow but powerful earthquakes, no volcanism San Andreas Fault; Alpine Fault, New Zealand Continent-continent collision (Himalaya, from closure of the Tethys Ocean) produces no subduction of continental material (too buoyant): instead crust doubles in thickness, generating regional metamorphism, granites and the highest seismicity on Earth. Distinguish island arcs (oceanic crust subducting beneath oceanic crust: thin, basaltic-andesitic, e.g. Aleutians) from marginal (Andean) arcs (thicker crust, large granodiorite plutons). SAMs questions ask you to judge whether arc plutons are likely to be intermediate - argue from magma contamination by continental crust versus crustal thickness, and note the limitation: pluton composition alone cannot prove arc type. Why deep foci only occur at Benioff zones Rocks at 300-700 km depth in normal mantle are too hot and ductile to store elastic strain, so earthquakes only occur where cold, brittle oceanic slab is carried to that depth - diagnostic evidence for subduction. Refine the margin comparison further: back-arc basins form by extension behind island arcs (Sea of Japan, Lau Basin) - spreading behind subduction, with its own ridge and magnetic stripes. Subduction polarity controls margin type: steep slab dip (old, cold ocean floor - Marianas) gives oceanic island arcs; shallow dip (young, buoyant slab - Chile) gives marginal Andean arcs and shallow seismicity. Transform faults offset ridge segments into short spreading cells - the zig-zag ridge pattern of the Atlantic - and their first-motion studies confirm strike-slip sense. Cite these when comparing margins: the full evidence chain (foci distribution, volcanism, heat flow, magnetic stripes) is what earns A* credit. Igneous minerals such as magnetite align with the ambient field as they cool through the Curie point (about 580 C for magnetite), then freeze the record in place - this is palaeomagnetism . Two independent lines of evidence underpin plate tectonics: Magnetic anomaly stripes : Vine, Matthews and Morley (1963) showed that the ocean floor carries symmetrical bands of alternately normal and reversed polarity parallel to ridge axes. Because reversals are global and time-parallel, symmetrical stripes can only be explained by new crust forming at the ridge and moving outwards symmetrically. This is the classic evidence for seafloor spreading - learn to argue it, not just state it. Apparent polar wander curves : palaeomagnetic inclination fixes palaeolatitude; declination fixes the palaeomeridian. Rocks of different ages on the same continent give different pole positions, tracing a wander path; different continents give divergent paths, proving the continents (not the poles) have moved. Supporting observations all co-vary with distance from the ridge and should be quoted together: age of the crust (oldest ocean floor only about 200 Ma, Jurassic), sediment thickness (zero at the axis, increasing outwards), water depth (shallowest at the hot, buoyant ridge, deepening with age as the plate cools and contracts), and heat flow (highest at the axis). Spreading rate calculation : measure the distance from the ridge axis to a dated anomaly (e.g. the 780 ka Brunhes-Matuyama reversal), then rate = distance / time. Example: an anomaly 30 km from the axis gives 30,000 m / 780,000 yr = about 3.8 cm/yr. State whether you quote the half-rate (one flank) or full rate (both flanks). Atlantic full rates are about 2-4 cm/yr; the East Pacific Rise reaches about 15-18 cm/yr. Fast-spreading ridges are smoother and topographically subdued; slow ridges have deep axial rift valleys. The field evidence for spreading strengthens into a complete case: palaeomagnetic measurements (declination and inclination) are made with a magnetometer on oriented cores; averaging many samples removes secular variation. The geomagnetic polarity time scale is built by tying anomaly patterns to radiometrically dated ash horizons and basalt flows, converting the stripes into a dated reversal sequence (the current normal chron, Brunhes, spans about 780 ka). The geodynamo itself operates in the liquid outer core - convecting iron generates the field - so the same seismic evidence that proved the liquid core underpins palaeomagnetism. Tomographic imaging of slabs (cold, fast seismic anomalies descending into the mantle) provides direct confirmation of subduction. A* answers evaluate mechanisms rather than list them. Slab pull is now regarded as dominant: the cold subducting slab is denser than the surrounding asthenosphere and drags the trailing plate; it explains why plates with long subducting margins (Pacific) move fastest. Ridge push contributes: elevated, buoyant ridge lithosphere slides away on the asthenosphere. Basal shear from mantle convection drags the plate base but is too weak alone. Hotspots are not plate-boundary features: fixed mantle plumes build trails of volcanoes whose ages increase along the chain - the Hawaii-Emperor chain youngs towards the present island, with a bend at about 47 Ma recording a change in Pacific plate motion. The Wilson cycle sequences ocean basin evolution and is a reliable essay framework: Embryonic - continental rifting, fault-block grabens, volcanism (East African Rift). Juvenile - narrow linear sea, oceanic crust formed (Red Sea). Mature - wide ocean with mid-ocean ridge and passive margins (Atlantic). Declining - subduction begins, trenches and volcanic arcs (Pacific). Terminal - closing sea, collision imminent (Mediterranean). Suturing - collision, orogenic belt and suture zone (Himalaya; Iapetus suture in Scotland), after which the cycle may restart by rifting. Link each stage to its rocks: rifting gives continental flood basalts and red beds; mature oceans give ophiolite sequences eventually obducted onto margins; collision gives regional metamorphic belts and granites. Examiners reward tying structure, process and rock type into one line of reasoning - the Quality of Extended Response (QER) marking in Component 2 rewards exactly this coherence. Measure plate motion directly and historically: GPS networks record present rates (cm/yr) that match the magnetic-anomaly rates; hotspot chains record motion over tens of millions of years. In extended-response answers, combine evidence scales: present GPS rates + anomaly-derived average rates + palaeomagnetic polar wander = a coherent case that plates move and the mechanisms are gravity-driven. When sequencing a Wilson cycle, attach rates: rifting (East African Rift, a few mm/yr), mature spreading (Atlantic 2-4 cm/yr), fast closing basins (Pacific up to 15-18 cm/yr) - and note the Himalaya sutures at similar rates, closing the Tethys.

topics.name: Rock Forming Processes
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Rock Forming Processes Bowen's reaction series The order in which minerals crystallise from a cooling basic melt: discontinuous ferromagnesian series (olivine-pyroxene-amphibole-biotite), continuous plagioclase series (calcic to sodic), then late residual minerals (orthoclase, muscovite, quartz). Fractional crystallisation The separation of early-formed crystals (e.g. by crystal settling or filter pressing) from the remaining melt, so the residual liquid evolves to a more silica-rich composition. Lithification (diagenesis) The conversion of sediment to sedimentary rock by compaction, dewatering and cementation by calcite, silica or iron oxides. Facies The total character of a rock reflecting its formative environment (sedimentary facies, e.g. fluvial, aeolian, reef) or its pressure-temperature conditions (metamorphic facies, e.g. greenschist, amphibolite). Graded bedding A bed in which grain size decreases upwards, formed by rapid deposition from a decelerating density (turbidity) current; indicates the way-up of the bed. Oolite A limestone composed of ooids - concentrically coated carbonate grains precipitated in warm, shallow, agitated water. Slaty cleavage A low-grade regional metamorphic fabric of closely spaced parallel planes formed by alignment of platy minerals perpendicular to the maximum compressive stress. Index mineral A mineral whose presence brackets a range of metamorphic grade (chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite in the Barrovian regional sequence). Porphyroblast A large metamorphic crystal (e.g. garnet, staurolite) grown within a finer matrix during metamorphism - the metamorphic analogue of a phenocryst. Porphyritic texture An igneous texture of large phenocrysts in a finer groundmass, recording two stages of cooling (slow at depth, then rapid on eruption or emplacement). Magma originates by partial melting of mantle peridotite (decompression at ridges and hotspots; flux melting by water from slabs at destructive margins) and of lower continental crust. Evolution of composition is examined through Bowen's reaction series : as a basic melt cools, olivine, then pyroxene, amphibole and biotite form by reaction with the melt (discontinuous series) while plagioclase changes continuously from calcic (anorthite) to sodic (albite); the late residual melt crystallises orthoclase, muscovite and quartz. Fractional crystallisation - crystal settling of dense early minerals, filter pressing, or sidewall accretion - removes early crystals from contact with the melt so the residual liquid becomes progressively more silica-rich, explaining suites from gabbro to granite in one pluton and layered basic intrusions (e.g. the Skaergaard intrusion, Greenland). Assimilation of country rock and magma mixing add further variety. Classification is by silica content and texture, and examiners require justification of both. Eduqas uses ultrabasic (under 45% SiO2), basic (45-52%), intermediate (52-66%), acid (over 66%) . Grain size reflects cooling rate: coarse-grained (phaneritic) plutonic rocks cool slowly at depth (granite, diorite, gabbro, peridotite); fine-grained (aphanitic) volcanic rocks cool rapidly at the surface (rhyolite, andesite, basalt). Learn the standard grid: Setting Acid Intermediate Basic Ultrabasic Plutonic Granite Diorite Gabbro Peridotite Volcanic Rhyolite Andesite Basalt Komatiite Textures carry the interpretation marks: porphyritic (two-stage cooling), vesicular (gas escape - basalt, pumice), glassy (obsidian, chilled too fast for crystals), pyroclastic (fragmental - tuff, agglomerate from explosive eruption), plus flow banding and amygdaloidal (vesicles later infilled). For minor intrusions know dykes (discordant, fine chilled margins), sills (concordant, baked country rock above and below, e.g. the Whin Sill) and the field evidence distinguishing a sill from a lava flow (baked contacts on both surfaces, no weathered top, feeder relationships). Tie composition to tectonic setting - the synoptic link examiners test: tholeiitic basalts (low K) dominate ridges; alkali basalts (higher K, Na) characterise hotspots and continental rifts; andesites mark subduction zones; rhyolites come from crustal melting above subducting slabs or fractionated continental magma. Crystal settling is directly observable: layered basic intrusions show graded modal layers and cumulate textures (e.g. the Bushveld Complex) - the same deposits exploited for chromite and platinum (see the Geological Resources topic). Magma stoping (blocks of country rock sinking into the magma) explains xenoliths and further contamination; chilled marginal facies mark the original magma composition before fractionation. Revise the process chain in order and attach products to each stage: weathering (physical - freeze-thaw, exfoliation, salt weathering; chemical - hydrolysis of feldspars to clay, carbonation of limestone, oxidation; biological - root wedging, chelation) produces regolith and detritus; erosion detaches and removes it; transport by traction (bedload rolling), saltation (bouncing sand), suspension (silt and clay) and solution sorts the load - wind and water sort better than glaciers, so sorting and rounding record transport history and textural maturity; deposition occurs when energy falls below threshold; lithification by compaction, dewatering and cementation (calcite, silica, iron oxide cements) converts sediment to rock. Classification of clastics by grain size (Wentworth): rudaceous (over 2 mm - conglomerate rounded, breccia angular), arenaceous (2-0.063 mm - sandstone: quartz sandstone, arkose, greywacke), argillaceous (under 0.063 mm - mudstone, shale with fissility from compaction-aligned micas). Carbonates : classify by texture - micrite (lime mud), oolite, calcirudite/shell gravel, bioclastic limestone, chalk (coccoliths), reef limestone (coral, in situ framework). Chemical sediments : evaporites (halite, gypsum - precipitated by evaporation in restricted basins) and chert (silica from radiolaria/sponges). Note the carbonate compensation depth : below about 4-5 km carbonate dissolves faster than it is supplied, so deep-ocean sediments are siliceous or clay - a routine AO2 point. Sedimentary structures are the way-up and environment toolkit: graded bedding (turbidity currents; youngs upwards), cross-bedding (dune/ripple migration in rivers, deltas, deserts; tops truncated), ripple marks (asymmetric current ripples, symmetric wave ripples), mudcracks (desiccation - exposure), flute and load casts on sole surfaces. Facies analysis links assemblage to environment: red beds + cross-bedding = desert or river; graded greywackes + sole marks = deep marine turbidites; coal + rootlets + seat earth = swamp; oolite + marine fossils = warm shallow shelf. Exam questions give a description or specimen and expect a justified environment with evidence. Extend the facies analysis to basin-scale patterns : facies belts parallel the shoreline (shoreface sandstone - offshore mudstone - deep-water turbidite), so lateral facies changes record the depth gradient; transgression (sea-level rise) shifts facies belts landward (deepening-upward sequence), regression the reverse. Carbonate settings build a Darwin-style reef sequence: fringing reef , then barrier reef , then atoll as the volcano subsides. Evaporite cycles (restricted basins: Zechstein salt) show repeated carbonate-sulfate-halite bands as salinity rises. Red beds record oxidising terrestrial palaeoclimates - another palaeoclimate pointer examined in the Quaternary theme. Exam questions may supply a log or map of facies belts: infer the environment from the assemblage, then state whether sea level rose or fell from the vertical trend. Chemical classification details that earn marks: silica content controls mineralogy - basic rocks are dominated by calcic plagioclase and pyroxene/olivine (no quartz); acid rocks by sodic plagioclase, alkali feldspar, mica and quartz (no olivine); intermediate rocks by zoned plagioclase, hornblende and biotite. Colour index (percentage of dark minerals) tracks silica inversely - a hand-specimen clue for classification. Volcanic equivalents of ultrabasic rocks ( komatiites ) are almost entirely Archaean, recording hotter Precambrian mantle. When justifying an identification, quote TWO observed features plus the inference: e.g. visible quartz + alkali feldspar = granite (acid, plutonic); vesicles + fine grain + pyroxene = basalt (basic, volcanic). Rote naming without features scores half. Metamorphism changes rocks in the solid state under heat , pressure/stress and chemically active fluids (water carrying ions in solution). Learn the three types with diagnostic products: Contact (thermal) metamorphism : baked margin (aureole) around an intrusion; high temperature, low pressure, no foliation. Products: hornfels , spotted slate, marble (from limestone), quartzite (from sandstone); aureole zones narrow outwards from the contact. Dynamic (dislocation) metamorphism : intense directed stress along fault zones; products cataclasite (fragmented) and mylonite (sheared, fine, banded). Regional metamorphism : orogenic belts, combined heat and stress. Barrovian sequence in pelitic rocks: slate (chlorite) - phyllite (biotite; silky sheen) - schist (garnet, staurolite, kyanite; visible micas) - gneiss (banding; migmatite at highest grade) . Index minerals track increasing grade; isograds can be mapped across an orogen (e.g. the Dalradian of Scotland). Fabrics : foliation records the compressive stress direction - slaty cleavage (aligned chlorite/mica, perpendicular to compression, commonly oblique to bedding), schistosity (coarser aligned micas), gneissose banding (segregation of light and dark minerals). Distinguish cleavage from bedding in the field (cleavage cuts across bedding) and use this in fold analysis. Lineation and stretched pebbles or fossils record the strain direction. Reactions are prograde with dehydration (clay + quartz gives mica + water); retrograde alteration follows if fluids return during cooling. Metamorphic facies (zeolite, greenschist, amphibolite, granulite, hornfels, blueschist) classify P-T fields - glaucophane-bearing blueschist identifies the high-pressure, low-temperature conditions of subduction zones, a classic applied point. Thermal and regional metamorphism sit on different P-T paths, and examiners test the discrimination: contact metamorphism is high-T/low-P (hornfels facies; no directed stress, hence no foliation); regional metamorphism combines both (Barrovian facies series). Real aureoles are zoned - the Comrie aureole (Scotland) shows spotted slates grading outwards from hornfels at the contact; Skiddaw shows knotted micaschists around the granite. Impure limestones give skarns (calc-silicate minerals - diopside, wollastonite) where hot fluids react with the carbonate; pure limestone gives marble. Burial metamorphism (low grade, no stress) affects thick sedimentary or volcanic piles - zeolite minerals in deeply buried basalt. Quote these when justifying a metamorphic rock identification: mineral + fabric + inferred P-T conditions. Synoptic skill: place every rock in the cycle and its tectonic setting. Igneous rocks form from melt at ridges (basalt), hotspots (flood basalts), subduction zones (andesite, granite) and within plates (minor intrusions). Uplift exposes them to weathering and erosion , producing sediments deposited in environments from desert to deep sea; burial lithifies them into sedimentary rocks. Burial plus heat and stress, or contact with intrusions, produces metamorphic rocks; further heating causes partial melting and the cycle restarts. Exam questions ask you to construct or complete such pathways, so practise writing gabbro-to-migmatite and sandstone-to-gneiss chains with the process named at each arrow. Mineral stability unites the topic. The Goldich stability series for weathering is essentially the inverse of Bowen's series: minerals crystallising at highest temperature (olivine, calcic plagioclase) are least stable at surface conditions and weather first, while quartz survives to form mature sandstones - explaining why beach sands are quartz-rich and why basic igneous rocks weather to clay faster than granites. The same logic explains residual deposits (bauxite from intense leaching). In metamorphism, stability fields (index minerals, facies) map P-T conditions; in igneous systems, Bowen's series maps crystallisation order. Explaining why each series runs as it does - mineral structures in equilibrium with their environment - earns the evaluation marks. Specimen-identification routine for Component 1 Work in order: (1) crystalline or clastic? (2) grain size and alignment (equigranular, porphyritic, vesicular, foliated, fossiliferous)? (3) composition tests (hardness, acid reaction on calcite, streak). Name the rock, then justify with two observed features and state the process and setting. Answers justified from observations score; rote names alone do not. Synthesis drill: the complete cycle on one diagram Draw the cycle with three boxes (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) and label every arrow with a process AND a tectonic setting: melt generation (decompression at ridges; flux melting at slabs), cooling/crystallisation, uplift, weathering/erosion, transport, deposition, lithification (burial), burial metamorphism, contact metamorphism (intrusions), regional metamorphism (orogeny), partial melting. Examiners award the process label, not just the arrow - a bare diagram of boxes scores little.

topics.name: Geological Time and Stratigraphy
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Geological Time and Stratigraphy Principle of superposition In an undeformed sedimentary or volcanic sequence, each bed is younger than the one beneath it. Principle of cross-cutting relationships A rock unit, fault or intrusion is younger than any rock it cuts; an inclusion is older than the host rock that contains it. Faunal succession Fossil organisms succeed one another in a definite, non-repeating vertical order, so fossil assemblages can be used to order and correlate strata. Unconformity A buried erosion surface separating younger rocks above from older rocks below, representing a gap in the geological record (types: angular, disconformity, nonconformity, paraconformity). Half-life The time for half of the atoms of a radioactive parent isotope to decay to its daughter product; constant for each isotope regardless of temperature or pressure. Radiometric dating Absolute dating by measuring parent:daughter isotope ratios in a mineral or rock and applying the decay equation age = (1/lambda) x ln(1 + D/P). Index fossil A fossil species ideal for correlation: abundant, geographically widespread, easily identified, and with a short vertical (stratigraphical) range due to rapid evolution. Biozone A body of rock defined by its fossil content, e.g. a range zone (total range of one species), assemblage zone (association of species) or acme zone (peak abundance). Correlation Establishing equivalence in age between rock units in different areas, using lithostratigraphic, biostratigraphic, magnetostratigraphic, chemostratigraphic or tephrochronological evidence. Mass extinction A geologically short interval of globally elevated extinction; the Big Five are end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous (K-Pg). Event-ordering questions on maps and sections are marked by the principle quoted for each relationship. Know all six and apply them explicitly: superposition (youngest at top in undeformed sequences), original horizontality (sediments deposit on near-horizontal surfaces; tilted or folded beds show later deformation), lateral continuity (a bed once extended until it thinned out or was truncated - allows displaced sequences to be matched across faults), cross-cutting relationships (faults, intrusions and veins are younger than the rocks they cut), inclusions (fragments in a host are older than the host - e.g. xenoliths in granite, clasts in conglomerate) and faunal succession (fossils order the strata). Always write the reasoning: state the principle as well as the event order. Unconformities represent gaps in the record (time missing = erosion and/or non-deposition) and must be classified: Type Recognition Implication Angular Older beds tilted/folded, younger beds lie across them at an angle Deformation + uplift + erosion + subsidence + renewed deposition Disconformity Beds parallel either side but an erosion surface (relief, palaeosol, basal conglomerate) separates them Uplift/erosion or non-deposition without deformation Nonconformity Sediments rest on igneous/metamorphic basement Long erosion unroofed deep-seated rocks Paraconformity Parallel beds, no visible relief - gap proved only by fossils/ages Non-deposition or subtle erosion On sections, sequence the full event history: deposition, deformation, erosion (unconformity), renewed deposition, intrusion, faulting - in that logical order, with each principle named. The way-up structures from sedimentology (graded bedding, cross-bedding) also matter here: inverted limbs of folds are identified by way-up evidence, which changes the whole event sequence. Event-ordering drill - a sequence question wants exactly this structure. Given: mudstone, overlain by sandstone, cut by a dyke, intruded by granite with xenoliths of both sediments, all unconformably overlain by conglomerate: (1) mudstone deposited; (2) sandstone deposited (superposition); (3) dyke intruded (cross-cutting - younger than both sediments); (4) granite intruded (contains inclusions of both sediments AND the dyke - younger than all three); (5) uplift and erosion; (6) conglomerate deposited (unconformity - youngest). Note the inclusion logic: the dyke fragments appear in the granite, so the granite post-dates the dyke even though both cut the sediments - the classic discriminating mark. Absolute (numerical) ages come from radiometric dating : radioactive parent isotopes decay to stable daughters at a fixed half-life , so the measured parent:daughter ratio gives the age. Learn the examinable systems and their applications: System Half-life Use U-238 to Pb-206 4.47 Ga Oldest rocks, Earth age (4.567 Ga from meteorites); zircon U-Pb is the gold standard U-235 to Pb-207 704 Ma Old Palaeozoic rocks; concordant U-Pb pairs cross-check K-40 to Ar-40 1.25 Ga Igneous rocks containing K-feldspar, mica, hornblende; volcanic ash (tephra) horizons Rb-87 to Sr-87 48.8 Ga Whole-rock dating of granites; isochron method corrects initial daughter Sr C-14 to N-14 5730 yr Organic remains (peat, wood, shell); useful to about 50-60 ka - Quaternary only Half-life calculations are routine: after n half-lives, parent remaining = (1/2)^n. Example: a rock with 12.5% of its original K-40 has lost 87.5% = 3 half-lives, so age = 3 x 1.25 Ga = 3.75 Ga. Reverse problems (given age, find fraction remaining) are equally common - practise both. Assumptions and limitations earn the evaluation marks: the system must have remained closed (no gain/loss of parent or daughter - argon especially is lost on reheating, so K-Ar dates the last cooling, not crystallisation); the initial daughter content must be zero or corrected (the Rb-Sr isochron solves this by plotting 87Sr/86Sr against 87Rb/86Sr for several co-magmatic whole-rock samples: slope = e^(lambda t) - 1, intercept = initial ratio); the half-life must suit the age range (C-14 useless beyond about 50-60 ka; Rb-Sr poor for young rocks). Metamorphism can reset or partially reset systems - a granite giving a K-Ar mica age younger than its U-Pb zircon age records cooling after metamorphism, not a contradiction. Non-radiometric absolute methods for the Quaternary: dendrochronology (tree rings, calibrates C-14), varves (annual glacial lake couplets), ice cores. Choosing the right system is the applied skill: zircon survives metamorphism and gives U-Pb crystallisation ages - the system of choice for ancient rocks; K-Ar on mica/hornblende dates cooling through about 300-350 C, so it dates metamorphism or the last heating event; Rb-Sr whole-rock suits granites but needs an isochron; C-14 suits only young organic material (peat, shell) to about 50-60 ka. Quote precision: modern U-Pb gives about +/-0.1% (about 1 Ma at 1 Ga); K-Ar on young volcanics to about +/-1-2%. Errors and interpretation matter: a K-Ar age younger than a U-Pb age on the same granite records slow cooling after intrusion or later metamorphism - not a failed analysis. Link to the Quaternary: dendrochronology (tree-ring counts to about 14 ka) and varves calibrate the C-14 scale; ice cores count annual layers to about 100 ka. Fossilisation is exceptional: it requires rapid burial and usually hard parts , commonly in low-oxygen (anoxic) sediment. Modes of preservation: unaltered shells/teeth, permineralisation (pore spaces filled - petrified wood), replacement (original material dissolved and replaced - pyritised, silicified, calcitised ammonites), carbonisation (volatiles distilled leaving black film - graptolites, fish, plants), moulds and casts (external/internal impressions filled to form natural casts). Life assemblages (in life position, e.g. crinoids rooted, oysters in clusters) vs death assemblages (transported, sorted, broken) are examined in Component 1 - use orientation, breakage and size sorting as evidence. Index fossils must be: abundant , widespread geographically , easy to identify , and short-ranging (rapid evolution). The classic British macrofossil index groups by era: graptolites (Ordovician-Silurian), trilobites (Palaeozoic), brachiopods and corals (Palaeozoic), ammonites (Mesozoic, with lineage zones), belemnites (Mesozoic). Microfossils serve hydrocarbon exploration: foraminifera, conodonts, pollen and spores - recovered from borehole cuttings. Biozones formalise correlation: range zones, assemblage zones, acme zones. Correlation uses multiple independent methods - know their reliability ranking: lithostratigraphic correlation (matching rock type) is least reliable alone (same facies can repeat in time - facies is diachronous); biostratigraphic (fossil zones) is the backbone of the Phanerozoic; magnetostratigraphic (reversal chrons matched to the global polarity time scale); chemostratigraphic (d18O, d13C, Sr isotope curves); tephrochronology (instantaneous volcanic ash markers, e.g. the Vedde Ash). Exam questions ask you to correlate boreholes or field sections and justify the method - always prefer fossil/isotope evidence to lithology and say why. Evolution : know gradualism versus punctuated equilibrium (long stasis punctuated by rapid speciation, often after extinctions - fits the fossil record's abrupt appearances), adaptive radiation after extinctions (mammals after K-Pg), and the Cambrian explosion (about 541 Ma; sudden appearance of most animal phyla, preceded by the Ediacaran biota). The Big Five mass extinctions with approximate dates and causes: end-Ordovician (445 Ma, glaciation), Late Devonian (372 Ma, ocean anoxia), end-Permian (252 Ma, the largest - about 96% of marine species; Siberian Traps volcanism, ocean anoxia, climate change) , end-Triassic (201 Ma, CAMP volcanism), K-Pg (66 Ma - iridium anomaly, shocked quartz, Chicxulub impact crater; ammonites, belemnites, non-avian dinosaurs lost) . Mass extinctions mark era boundaries and are used as correlation events. Fossil identification is examined in Component 1 with specimens - know the diagnostic morphology of the classic index groups: graptolites (colonial, carbonised films - rhabdosome of parallel stipes with thecae; Ordovician-Silurian); trilobites (three-lobed arthropods, head/middle/tail shields, compound eyes; Palaeozoic); ammonites (planispirally coiled, chambered shells, complex suture lines where septa meet the shell wall; sexual dimorphism; Mesozoic); belemnites (bullet-shaped internal guards; Jurassic-Cretaceous); brachiopods (two-valved but unequal, symmetry plane through both valves; Palaeozoic-dominated). Microfossils serve industry: foraminifera and conodonts (tooth-like elements of an extinct chordate - Palaeozoic index fossils, used in borehole cuttings for hydrocarbon exploration); pollen and spores for Quaternary climate reconstruction (the Llyn Gwernan pollen diagram in the SAMs). Pair the fossil with its era and environment every time. The scale is hierarchical: eons (Hadean, Archaean, Proterozoic, Phanerozoic), eras within the Phanerozoic (Palaeozoic 541-252 Ma, Mesozoic 252-66 Ma, Cenozoic 66 Ma-present), periods (Cambrian, Ordovician, Silurian, Devonian, Carboniferous, Permian, Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous, Palaeogene, Neogene, Quaternary) and epochs (e.g. Pleistocene 2.58 Ma-11.7 ka, Holocene 11.7 ka-present). The Precambrian occupies about 88% of geological time - a standard one-mark fact. Boundaries are chosen at globally recognisable events (extinctions, reversals, isotopic excursions) and fixed by GSSPs (golden spikes). Apply the scale synoptically to British geological evolution - the map-and-time combination the Eduqas themes examine: Precambrian : Lewisian gneisses (NW Scotland, about 3.0-1.7 Ga), Torridonian sandstones, Dalradian sediments metamorphosed in the Grampian event. Paleozoic : Iapetus Ocean closes - Caledonian orogeny (Ordovician-Silurian into Devonian, about 490-390 Ma) sutures Scotland to England (Iapetus suture), produces Dalradian/Southern Uplands deformation and the Devonian Old Red Sandstone continent; marine Carboniferous limestones and Coal Measures swamps; Variscan (Hercynian/Armorican) orogeny (about 380-290 Ma) folds SW England, intrudes Cornish granites (tin), forms the Hercynian unconformity. Mesozoic : desert Triassic, marine Jurassic (ammonite-rich, Portland Stone, Kimmeridge Clay source rock), Chalk Cretaceous - the opening Atlantic and North Sea rifting control facies. Cenozoic : Alpine orogeny folds and inverts southern England; Paleogene volcanism builds the Hebridean volcanoes and intrudes the Tertiary dyke swarms; Quaternary (2.58 Ma) glacial/interglacial cycles shaped the landscape - tills, moraines, periglacial deposits. Epoch-level Quaternary detail (the Eduqas optional theme): Pleistocene glacial stages and interglacials paced by Milankovitch cycles (eccentricity about 100 ka, obliquity 41 ka, precession about 21 ka), evidenced by oxygen-isotope curves from deep-sea cores; Holocene post-glacial warming and sea-level rise. Exam technique: when a question names a period, attach the fossils, rocks and events - e.g. Jurassic = ammonites, marine mudrocks/limestones, Kimmeridge Clay. Cross-reference to the mapwork topic for how these events appear on maps (unconformities, orogenic fold trends). Period Index fossils British rocks/events Cambrian Trilobites Quartzites, shales (Wales) Ordovician Graptolites, trilobites Volcanic ashes, Welsh Basin Silurian Graptolites, brachiopods Limestones (Wenlock Edge); Iapetus closing Devonian Fish, plants Old Red Sandstone; Caledonian granites Carboniferous Corals, brachiopods, crinoids Limestones, Coal Measures; Variscan folding Permian-Triassic Bivalves; end-Permian extinction Desert sandstones, red beds, Zechstein salt Jurassic Ammonites, belemnites Oolites, Kimmeridge Clay, Portland Stone Cretaceous Chalk coccoliths; K-Pg extinction Chalk; North Sea rifting Quaternary Mammals, pollen Tills, moraines; Milankovitch cycles

topics.name: Geological Mapwork
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Geological Mapwork Strike The compass bearing of the line of intersection between an inclined plane (bedding, fault) and the horizontal; perpendicular to the true dip direction. Dip The maximum angle between an inclined plane and the horizontal, measured in the vertical plane perpendicular to the strike, together with the dip direction. Apparent dip The dip of a bed measured in any vertical plane not perpendicular to the strike; always less than the true dip. Plunge The angle between the hinge line of a fold and the horizontal, measured in the vertical plane containing the hinge; the outcrop nose points in the plunge direction. Axial plane (surface) The plane joining the hinge points of the folds in a fold train, bisecting the limbs; its trace on a map is the axial trace. Limb The part of a fold between the hinge and the next fold's hinge; in an overfold both limbs dip in the same direction and one is inverted. Throw The vertical component of displacement on a fault; heave is the horizontal component (heave = throw / tan of fault dip). Structure contour A line joining points of equal altitude on an inclined plane such as a bedding surface or fault plane; spacing gives the horizontal equivalent of the dip. Outcrop The area on a map or at the surface where a rock unit is exposed at bedrock level (solid or drift). V-rule Where a dipping bed crosses a valley its outcrop forms a V: the apex points in the direction of dip if the dip is steeper than the valley gradient, and up-dip if it is gentler. Strike is the bearing of the line a bed makes with the horizontal (e.g. 045 degrees); dip is the maximum inclination of the plane, measured perpendicular to strike in a vertical plane (e.g. 30 degrees south-east). Every mapwork answer starts here: state dip DIRECTION as well as amount. Outcrop patterns discriminate dip from topography: Horizontal beds : outcrops follow the contours exactly (parallel bands); the youngest bed is at the highest ground. Vertical beds : outcrops are straight lines crossing topography at right angles regardless of relief; width of outcrop = true thickness. Dipping beds : V-rule - where a bed crosses a valley the outcrop forms a V; the apex points in the dip direction if the dip is steeper than the valley gradient, and points up-dip (opposite to dip) if the dip is gentler than the gradient. On ridges the V reverses.
