Practise reading the common patterns: a homoclinal dip-slope/scarp sequence (regional dip one direction); inliers (older rocks surrounded by younger, e.g. through an unconformity or in a dome) and outliers (younger rocks surrounded by older, e.g. an eroded dome remnant). Unconformities on maps: older rocks below the unconformity surface are truncated by it, younger beds above overlap them at an angle (angular unconformity) or parallel (disconformity/paraconformity); basal conglomerate commonly overlies the surface. Exam questions often ask you to prove an unconformity from a map: quote the truncation of strike directions plus a way-up/fossil age difference. Scarp and vale topography is the surface expression of regional dip: alternating hard (scarp-forming: Chalk, limestone, gritstone) and soft (vale-forming: clay) beds dip gently one way, giving a steep scarp face and gentle dip slope (the Chalk scarps of southern England). Read dip from the landscape: steep scarp faces the up-dip direction; dip slopes descend in the dip direction. On BGS maps, the legend gives lithology colours and symbols; the scale and contour interval set what precision of dip calculation is possible. Apparent dip on any cross-section not perpendicular to strike is less than true dip - state this when projecting dips onto sections at an angle to strike: tan(apparent) = tan(true) x sin(angle between the section line and the strike). Fold recognition from outcrop pattern and dip arrows: anticlines (oldest rocks in the core) and synclines (youngest in the core); antiform/synform where way-up is unknown. Plunge : a plunging fold's outcrop pattern closes to a nose (U-shape) - the nose points in the direction of plunge; for a plunging anticline the OLDEST beds form the nose , for a plunging syncline the YOUNGEST . Non-plunging folds produce parallel, endless outcrops. Vertical (isoclinal, overturned) folds show both limbs dipping the same way; identify inverted limbs from way-up structures (graded bedding, cross-bedding) or from cleavage-bedding relations (cleavage steeper than bedding on the normal limb). Terminology to deploy: hinge, limbs, axial trace (the line joining hinges on the map), axial plane dip, vergence (direction of overturning - asymmetric folds verge towards the foreland, e.g. Caledonian folds verge NW in the Scottish Highlands). Culminations and basins : domes (oldest at centre, concentric outcrops) and structural basins (youngest at centre). Parasitic folds on the limbs of major folds record shear sense (S/Z asymmetry). Mapwork questions ask you to state fold type, axial trace orientation, plunge amount/direction and to label a section accordingly - practise sketching anticlines/synclines with plunge shown by the closure direction and dip symbols. Quick drill Closure with oldest rocks in the nose = plunging anticline. Closure with youngest = plunging syncline. Concentric rings with oldest at centre = dome. Youngest at centre = basin. Straight parallel bands with alternating old-young-old = non-plunging fold train. Fold-recognition workflow for exam answers: (1) establish way-up from sedimentary structures (graded bedding, cross-bedding) or cleavage-bedding relations - cleavage transecting bedding proves younging direction; (2) read dip arrows on both limbs; (3) identify the axial trace (line through the hinge points); (4) determine plunge from outcrop closure. Vergence - the direction the asymmetric folds overturn - records the shear sense of the orogeny: Caledonian folds in the Scottish Highlands verge NW towards the foreland. Culminations and basins : map-scale domes (oldest at centre) and basins (youngest at centre) show concentric outcrops; plunging fold trains show repeated noses. Parasitic folds (S on one limb, Z on the other, M on the hinge) record which limb of the major fold they sit on - a genuine A* discriminator. Classify faults by the relative movement of the hanging wall (rock above the fault plane) and footwall (below): normal faults (hanging wall down - extension), reverse faults (hanging wall up - compression) and thrusts (reverse faults dipping under 45 degrees), plus strike-slip (wrench) faults with horizontal dextral/sinistral offset. On sections, mark the fault plane, hade (angle from vertical) and the displaced beds. Recognising faults on maps : straight or curved fault lines truncating outcrops; offset of beds or dykes across the fault; omission (missing beds at the surface on the downthrow side, where the fault plane dips the same way as the beds) or repetition of strata; fault-line valleys along weaker fault rocks (breccia, gouge). Determining downthrow - the routine exam method: (1) match a distinctive marker bed either side of the fault; (2) project its dip across the fault; the side on which the sequence sits lower is the downthrow side. Alternatively: where strata are cut out (omitted) at the surface, the downthrow side is the direction towards which the missing beds dip; where beds are repeated, the downthrow is in the opposite sense. Quote the marker-bed method in answers and label the throw. Throw and heave : throw = vertical displacement; heave = throw / tan(dip of fault) (horizontal displacement). Example: a fault dipping 60 degrees with 100 m throw has heave = 100 / tan60 = about 58 m. Horsts and grabens (paired normal faults - rift valleys, North Sea fault blocks) and the tectonic setting of each fault type (normal = rifts/extension; reverse/thrust = collision zones; wrench = conservative margins) earn the synoptic marks. Faults control ore localisation, aquifer boundaries and landslide risk - a standard applied point in Component 3. Structure contours on fault planes give the most rigorous downthrow determination: construct contours on the fault surface by the three-point method from where it intersects two beds plus its dip; then compare the altitude of a marker bed on each side projected to the fault - the difference in altitude is the throw . Hadé is the complement of the fault dip (angle between the fault plane and the vertical); a 60 degree dip has a 30 degree hade. Fault regimes link to tectonics: normal faults and graben (paired listric faults) dominate rifts and the North Sea rotated fault blocks; reverse faults and thrusts dominate collision zones (Moine Thrust); wrench faults dominate conservative margins. Fault-line scenery: fault-line valleys follow weaker fault rocks (breccia, gouge); reactivated faults may juxtapose resistant against weak lithology, controlling escarpment lines. Structure contours join points of equal altitude on a planar surface (bed, unconformity, fault plane). From three spot heights on the same bed (the three-point problem ): draw the contour through the intermediate point, spaced between the high and low points, then compute dip = tan-1(vertical interval / horizontal equivalent) . Contour spacing gives the horizontal equivalent: closer contours = steeper dip. If a structure contour and an outcrop line intersect, the bed at that point is at the contour's altitude - use this to find the depth to a horizon anywhere on the map: depth = contour altitude at the point minus ground height. Thickness calculations are examined numerically: vertical thickness (measured down a vertical borehole between the top and base of a bed) = true thickness / sin(dip) ; so true thickness t = vertical thickness x sin(dip) . On flat ground the horizontal outcrop width w gives t = w x sin(dip). Example: a bed with 40 m vertical thickness dipping 30 degrees has true thickness 40 x sin30 = 20 m. For inclined boreholes the downhole interval is not the vertical thickness - correct using the borehole angle (standard AO3 trap). Cross-section construction - the routine Component 3 practical: (1) draw the section line on the map; (2) mark every topographic detail (use the contour profile) and every geology boundary at its intersection with the section line; (3) project dips at each boundary - for folds, use the dip arrows and axial trace; (4) extend boundaries smoothly downwards, keeping thicknesses constant and honouring the data (extrapolate no deeper than about equal to the width of exposure); (5) draw faults with their dip, mark downthrow, and restore displaced sections if asked. Borehole data : logs record depths, lithologies, dips of beds, groundwater strikes; correlate marker beds between boreholes to build the subsurface picture (the same logic as field correlation - biostratigraphic matching preferred to lithological). Exam questions give borehole depths for a marker bed in two holes plus its outcrop dip - expect a three-point calculation for structure/dip and a statement of the assumptions (beds planar, no folding between holes). Worked three-point problem : spot heights on the base of a sandstone are A (200 m), B (150 m) and C (100 m), with B between A and C horizontally 200 m from each. The contour through B runs parallel to strike; the vertical interval A-B = 50 m over 200 m horizontal, so dip = tan-1(50/200) = about 14 degrees towards C. Depth-to-horizon : at any point, depth = structure-contour altitude at that point minus ground height - draw contours across the whole map by interpolating from the outcrop intersections. Cross-section rules : mark true dips (correct apparent dips first), keep bed thicknesses constant down-section, honour all data, and extrapolate downward no deeper than roughly the width of exposure; show faults with downthrow arrows and the displaced beds. Borehole correlation : match marker beds (or better, fossil/isotope-dated horizons) between holes, draw dips from the logs, and state assumptions: beds planar between holes, no undetected folding or faulting.

topics.name: Geological Hazards
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Geological Hazards Focus (hypocentre) The point within the Earth where an earthquake rupture begins; the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it. Elastic rebound The mechanism of earthquakes: elastic strain accumulates across a locked fault until it exceeds friction, rupture occurs and the rock rebounds, releasing energy as seismic waves. Moment magnitude (Mw) Magnitude scale based on the seismic moment (rigidity x slip x ruptured area); logarithmic and accurate for large earthquakes, unlike the Richter (local) scale which saturates. Mercalli intensity A I-XII scale of earthquake effects observed at a location (damage, perception); intensity varies with distance, ground conditions and building quality, unlike magnitude. Liquefaction Loss of shear strength in water-saturated unconsolidated sediment during shaking, when grains temporarily float in pore water; buildings sink and sand volcanoes erupt. Pyroclastic flow A gravity-driven, incandescent density current of hot gas, ash and pumice moving at up to 200 km/h from a collapse of an eruption column or dome - the deadliest volcanic hazard. Lahar A volcanic mudflow/debris flow of ash and water, triggered by rainfall on fresh ash or melting snow/ice; can travel far beyond the volcano. Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) A 0-8 logarithmic scale of eruption size based on ejecta volume and column height; each unit is about ten times more erupted volume. Factor of safety On a slope, the ratio of shear strength to shear stress; values above 1 are stable, below 1 the slope fails. Reduced by pore-water pressure, undercutting and loading. Tsunami A series of long-period sea waves generated by sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor (large shallow earthquakes, submarine landslides, volcanic collapse); wave speed c = sqrt(gd). Elastic rebound : strain accumulates across a locked fault segment until friction is overcome; rupture propagates and the stored elastic energy radiates as seismic waves from the focus . Depth classes: shallow ( P (compressional, 6-8 km/s, through any material) , S (shear, 3.5-4.5 km/s, solids only, more destructive) ; surface waves ( Love - horizontal shearing; Rayleigh - rolling) travel slowest but shake buildings hardest. Liquefaction in saturated unconsolidated sediment amplifies damage - a standard secondary-hazard point alongside landslides, fires and tsunami. Magnitude vs intensity - the classic discriminating question: moment magnitude (Mw) measures the seismic moment at source and is logarithmic (each unit = about 32 times more energy); the Richter (local) scale saturates above about M7. Mercalli intensity (I-XII) is observed damage at a location - it varies with distance, ground conditions and building quality, so one earthquake produces a range of intensities but one magnitude. Examiners want both scales contrasted, not confused. Prediction and mitigation : earthquakes cannot be reliably predicted in time or size - the Eduqas mark scheme credits exactly this evaluation. Some success in location (known active faults, seismic gaps, palaeoseismology); monitoring uses background seismicity rates (increases or decreases as micro-fractures open and water influxes, with pore pressure rising to failure), P/S wave velocity anomalies through the fault zone, radon emission and ground tilt - but anomalies give false alarms and missed events. Mitigation is engineering-led: building codes (cross-bracing, reinforced frames, base isolation on rubber/steel bearings to absorb energy, low centre of gravity, symmetric design), safety cut-off valves on gas/water and reinforced tanks (preventing fire and flooding), early-warning systems (P-wave detection gives seconds before S-wave arrival - Japan), and land-use zoning away from fault traces. Case examples: Christchurch 2011 (M6.3, shallow focus directly under the city, liquefaction) versus Kobe 1995 (elevated highway collapse) - compare damage against building quality. Locating an epicentre is a routine calculation: three or more seismograph stations measure the S-P arrival time difference; the distance to the focus comes from travel-time curves (S-P interval scales with distance); circles of those radii intersect at the epicentre. Depth classes matter for hazard: shallow ( Aftershocks follow main ruptures for months (Christchurch 2011 followed the September 2010 Darfield event) and finish damaged buildings - a standard secondary-hazard point. Global distribution maps are examinable: belts of shallow foci along ridges and transforms, inclined Benioff zones under arcs, and diffuse continental zones (Himalaya, Mediterranean) - link each belt to its boundary type. Eruption style is controlled by magma composition, viscosity and gas content - the core exam relationship: low-viscosity, low-gas basaltic magma degasses easily, giving effusive Hawaiian (shield volcanoes, lava fountains) and fissure eruptions (Laki 1783, Iceland - flood basalts, famine); higher-viscosity, gas-rich andesitic-rhyolitic magma retains pressure until catastrophic Vulcanian and Plinian eruptions (Vesuvius AD 79) with eruption columns and pyroclastic flows (Mont Pelee 1902 - peléan domes). Classify volcano types with the relationship: shield (basaltic, gentle slopes, non-explosive), stratovolcano/composite (alternating lava and pyroclastic layers, andesitic, steep, explosive), cinder/scoria cone (monogenetic), caldera (collapse after evacuation of a magma chamber - Yellowstone, Santorini), lava domes (acid, endogenous growth, collapse to pyroclastic flows). Hazards ranked by deadliness: pyroclastic flows and surges (St Helens 1980), lahars (Nevado del Ruiz 1985 - 23,000 deaths in Armero), ash fall (Eyjafjallajokull 2010 - European airspace closure; respiratory and roof-collapse effects), lava flows (slow, property not life), jokulhlaups (glacial outburst floods where eruptions melt ice), toxic gas (CO2 limnic eruption, Lake Nyos 1986 - about 1,700 deaths; SO2 vog). Explosivity is ranked by VEI (0-8, logarithmic ejecta volume): St Helens VEI 5, Pinatubo VEI 6, Toba VEI 8. Forecasting volcanoes works - contrast with earthquakes: eruptions are preceded by weeks-months of seismicity (harmonic tremor as magma moves), ground deformation (tiltmeters, EDM, GPS, InSAR - inflation of the edifice), gas monitoring (rising SO2 as magma nears surface) and thermal anomalies. Pinatubo 1991 : monitoring identified the pre-eruption inflation and tremor, about 60,000 people evacuated, deaths limited to a few hundred; 20 Mt of SO2 caused global cooling of about 0.5 C for a year. St Helens 1980 : flank bulge and earthquake swarm monitored, access zones reduced deaths to 57, but the lateral blast (from flank collapse) exceeded the designated zones. Vesuvius/Naples : forecasting is good but evacuation of up to a million people is the limiting factor - the classic exposure/vulnerability point for A* answers. Eruption column dynamics explain pyroclastic flow formation: gas-rich magma fragments as it exits the vent; the column rises buoyantly while convecting, but if the eruption rate falls or the column density exceeds air, it collapses - pyroclastic density currents race down the flanks at up to 200 km/h. Plinian eruptions (Vesuvius AD 79 - Pliny the Younger described the pine-tree column; Herculaneum and Pompeii buried by ash and pyroclastic surges) are the textbook case. Temperatures: basaltic lava about 1,000-1,200 C (fluid, Pahoehoe and Aa flows); rhyolitic lava about 700-900 C (viscous domes). Link viscosity to silica: polymerised silica tetrahedra in acid melts resist flow - the chemistry-physics link examiners reward. Slope stability is a balance: shear strength (friction + cohesion of the material) against shear stress (weight of material on the slope). Factor of safety = shear strength / shear stress ; failure below 1. Pore-water pressure from heavy rainfall is the common trigger (water reduces effective normal stress), alongside stream undercutting, earthquake shaking, and loading (building, tip waste). Lithology matters: bedding dipping out of the slope planes failure surfaces (Vaiont 1963); clays lose strength when remoulded; jointed chalk fails as blocks. Classify mass movements by material and speed: falls (rockfall from cliffs - jointed limestone), slides - rotational slump (curved slip surface in clay/regolith, back-tilted blocks) and translational slide (planar surface - bedding, joint), flows (mudflow, debris flow, earthflow - saturated), and complex movements (rotational slump mobilising into a flow). UK case: Aberfan 1966 (coal-tip waste slid on saturated ground onto a school - 144 deaths; tipping practice and drainage) and coastal Folkestone Warren slumps. Vaiont 1963 (Italy): a 270 million m3 reservoir slope failed after rising water pore pressures, displacing the reservoir and overtopping the dam - about 2,000 deaths; the classic case of geological understanding (bedding dipping into the valley, clay layers) ignored. Mitigation : drainage (cut-off drains, adits - most effective and cheapest), slope reprofiling (reducing angle), pinning/bolting of jointed rock, retaining walls, grouting, toe loading, and hazard zoning/planning based on geological survey. Tsunami : generated by sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor - large shallow earthquakes (Mw > 7 at Propagation : a shallow-water wave with speed c = sqrt(gd) - about 200 m/s in 4 km deep ocean, slowing to tens of m/s onshore; wavelength hundreds of km, amplitude small at sea ( shoals and amplifies at the coast, with run-up to tens of metres. Case pair : Indian Ocean 2004 (Sumatra-Andaman Mw 9.1 - about 230,000 deaths; no regional warning system existed) versus Tohoku 2011 (Mw 9.0 megathrust - run-up to about 40 m, seawalls overtopped, Fukushima Daiichi meltdown; the Pacific warning system gave warnings but the magnitude and run-up exceeded design). Evaluation points: warnings work for distant tsunamis (hours of travel time) but near-field tsunamis arrive in minutes - hence natural warnings (ground shaking, sea withdrawal) and vertical evacuation are needed. Landslide hazard mapping underpins mitigation: geological surveys map slopes by lithology, dip of bedding relative to slope, drainage and historic movement (BGS landslide databases); hazard zoning then restricts building on unstable ground. The Hong Kong landslides (Sau Mau Ping 1972 and 1976 - fill slopes failed in rainstorms, about 150 deaths) drove a systematic slope-safety programme: cut slopes engineered with drainage and soil nails, registration of every slope - the textbook success of mitigation after failure. Tsunami distance warning : distant tsunamis give hours of travel time (Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre from 1949), so the 2004 Indian Ocean disaster was principally a failure of warning infrastructure (no Indian Ocean system then) - one was installed afterwards; near-field tsunamis (Tohoku, minutes) need natural warnings and vertical evacuation. Synoptic framing for the extended-response questions: risk = hazard x exposure x vulnerability (mitigated by capacity/resilience). Examiners reward candidates who separate what CAN be done (engineering, planning, warning systems) from what CANNOT (reliable earthquake prediction in time and size). The Eduqas mark scheme for earthquake prediction credits: limited success in predicting size/timing; some success in location; background seismicity rate anomalies; seismic gaps; P and S velocity changes through the fault zone; dilatancy models (micro-fractures open, water influx, pore pressure rises to failure); duration of anomaly related to magnitude. Quote these to show depth - then evaluate: anomalies give false positives and missed events, so prediction cannot yet drive evacuation policy. Comparing case examples is the highest-tariff skill - practise three-way comparisons on: (1) prediction success : Pinatubo (evacuation before eruption) vs St Helens (zones, but exceeded by lateral blast) vs earthquakes (no prediction; Kobe 1995 sudden rupture); (2) mitigation effectiveness : building codes and base isolation (Christchurch 2011 vs Kobe 1995 highway collapse), lahar warning sirens (Ruiz failed - Armero), tsunami walls and education (Tohoku - overtopped but evacuation saved many lives); (3) exposure and vulnerability : Naples (good forecasting, impossible evacuation), Iceland (small exposed population, excellent monitoring). Structure extended answers: define the hazard mechanism, give the case with named facts (dates, magnitudes, VEI, deaths), then evaluate mitigation against prediction limits - a coherent line of reasoning with evidence is what QER marking rewards. Case example quick facts to memorise St Helens 18 May 1980, VEI 5, 57 deaths, lateral blast. Pinatubo 15 June 1991, VEI 6, 20 Mt SO2, about 0.5 C global cooling, 60,000 evacuated. Nevado del Ruiz 1985, lahar, 23,000 deaths. Lake Nyos 1986, CO2, about 1,700 deaths. Laki 1783, fissure, famine. Indian Ocean 2004, Mw 9.1, about 230,000 deaths. Tohoku 2011, Mw 9.0, run-up 40 m. Christchurch 2011, M6.3, liquefaction. Hazard perception and capacity complete the risk equation: populations that have recently experienced a hazard (Japan, Chile) support strict building codes; hazard fatigue and short memories undermine compliance (Armero 1985 - warnings issued but not acted on). Economic development increases capacity to mitigate but also concentrates exposure (coastal megacities). For the QER, balance: engineering (codes, base isolation), planning (zoning on geological evidence), warning systems (volcanic monitoring; tsunami buoys; earthquake early warning) and education/drills - then judge which combination the named cases used, and what the residual risk was. This evaluative structure is what levels-based marking rewards above description.

topics.name: Geological Resources
topics.subject: geology
topics.searchText: geology Geology Geological Resources Ore A rock or mineral deposit containing a metal (or other material) in sufficient concentration and tonnage, at the prevailing price, to be mined economically. Grade The concentration of metal in an ore, usually quoted as a percentage or grams per tonne; the cut-off grade is the lowest concentration that can be mined at a profit. Porosity The percentage of a rock's volume that is void space (pores, fractures); determines storage capacity for water or hydrocarbons. Permeability The ease with which a fluid can flow through a rock, controlled by the connectedness and size of pores/fractures; measured in darcies or millidarcies. Aquifer A permeable rock body that stores and transmits useful quantities of groundwater (e.g. Chalk, Permo-Triassic sandstones); aquitards (e.g. London Clay) transmit water slowly; aquicludes effectively not at all. Source rock An organic-rich (kerogen-bearing) fine-grained sediment, e.g. the Kimmeridge Clay, which generates hydrocarbons when heated through the oil window (about 60-120 C for oil; gas at higher temperatures). Oil window The burial depth/temperature range (roughly 60-120 C, about 2-4 km) in which kerogen matures to liquid oil; above it gas and condensate form and beyond about 150 C oil is destroyed. Structural trap A trap formed by deformation - anticlinal crest, fault block or salt dome - that stops migrating hydrocarbons; stratigraphic traps (pinch-outs, unconformity overlaps) are formed by depositional change. Placer deposit A surficial concentration of dense, chemically resistant heavy minerals (gold, cassiterite) sorted and deposited by flowing water (alluvial, beach, or ancient palaeoplacers such as Witwatersrand). Acid mine drainage Sulfuric acid and iron hydroxide runoff formed when pyrite in mine waste and workings oxidises on exposure to air and water, contaminating streams and groundwater. An ore is metal in economic concentration - grade x tonnage at the prevailing price defines profitability ( cut-off grade ). Learn each ore-forming process with its diagnostic setting and examples: Process Mechanism Deposits/examples Magmatic segregation Dense oxide/sulfide crystals settle in layered basic intrusions or magma immiscibility Chromite and PGMs (Bushveld Complex, South Africa); Ni-Cu (Sudbury, Canada) Hydrothermal Hot metal-bearing fluids precipitate in fractures, porphyries or on the sea floor Porphyry Cu-Mo (huge tonnage, low grade); epithermal Au-Ag; skarns; volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) at ridges - black smokers Sedimentary/exhalative Chemical precipitation or basin brines exhaled onto the sea floor Banded iron formations (Precambrian, Hamersley); SEDEX Pb-Zn-Ba (Silvermines, Ireland) Residual/weathering Intense leaching leaves insoluble residues Bauxite (tropical weathering of aluminous rocks); lateritic Ni Placer Water sorts dense resistant grains into surficial concentrations Gold (Witwatersrand palaeoplacer); cassiterite (Cornish stream tin) Metamorphic and tectonic links earn synoptic marks: hydrothermal fluids are commonly driven by granites (Cornwall: tin-tungsten-copper zoned around granite cupolas) or by circulating seawater at ridges; BIFs record Precambrian anoxic oceans; ophiolite-hosted deposits (Cyprus) mark former ocean floor. Exam questions supply an ore description or locality and expect the process, the mechanism and one piece of supporting evidence - practise arguing from texture (banded, massive, disseminated) and setting. Ore textures diagnose the process: disseminated (fine grains spread through the host - porphyry copper), massive sulfide (near-solid metal sulfide - VMS), banded (alternating iron oxide and silica/chert layers - BIF), vein (hydrothermal fluids filling fractures, often with a zoned mineral sequence), disseminated cumulate (settled crystals - Bushveld chromitite layers). Zonation around granites is the classic Cornwall case: skarns/tungsten at the contact, then copper, then lead-zinc, then iron and manganese outwards, with cassiterite close to the cupola - the sequence records falling fluid temperature with distance. Hydrothermal fluids originate from the granite itself (late-stage magmatic water), from circulating groundwater heated by the intrusion, or from seawater circulating at ridges (VMS) - state the fluid source when explaining a deposit. Revise the petroleum system as a chain of elements, each examined in turn: source rock - organic-rich mudrock (kerogen) such as the Kimmeridge Clay (Late Jurassic, North Sea); maturation - burial heats kerogen through the oil window (about 60-120 C; deeper, gas and condensate; beyond about 150 C oil is cracked/destroyed); primary migration out of the source and secondary migration through permeable carrier beds driven by buoyancy; reservoir - porous AND permeable rock (clean sandstone, e.g. Brent Group; oolitic/fractured carbonate) holding oil in its pore space; seal - impermeable caprock (salt, shale, e.g. the Zechstein evaporites of the Southern North Sea gas fields); trap - structural (anticlinal crest, fault-block - the rotated fault blocks of the North Sea), stratigraphic (pinch-out, unconformity overlap, reef) or combination ; plus timing - the trap must exist before migration. Sketch an anticlinal trap with oil-gas-water contacts: gas on top, oil beneath, water below (buoyancy stratification). Exploration : seismic reflection surveys (2D/3D) image subsurface structure by recording two-way travel times of reflections - depth = velocity x time/2; identify anticlines, fault blocks, pinch-outs. Well logs identify reservoirs and fluids downhole: gamma ray (distinguishes shale - high K - from clean sandstone), resistivity (high in hydrocarbon-filled pores - fluids are insulators), sonic and density-neutron (porosity; crossover indicates gas), caliper. Drilling (rotary, mud logging, cuttings and core) tests the prospect. Unconventional resources : shale gas by hydraulic fracturing (Bowland Shale, Lancashire), coal-bed methane, oil sands - know that fracking injects water/sand/chemicals at pressure to open fractures, and the environmental concerns (groundwater, induced seismicity). These questions link directly to the mapwork topic (seismic sections, fault blocks) and to stratigraphy (source/reservoir ages). Extend the North Sea case with its thermal history - the timing element examiners reward: rifting (Permian-Triassic and Jurassic) created rotated fault blocks and deposited the Jurassic Kimmeridge Clay source; Cenozoic burial of the source into the oil window generated oil that migrated (Tertiary) into pre-existing traps - Paleocene/Eocene sandstone reservoirs (Forties) and Jurassic fault-block traps (Brent province). The Southern Gas Basin differs: Carboniferous Coal Measures generate gas, trapped beneath the impermeable Zechstein salt seal in Permian Rotliegendes sandstone. Maturation evidence : vitrinite reflectance and burial/thermal history curves show when the source entered the window; a trap formed after migration is barren - timing is the mark. Sketch the anticlinal trap with gas-oil-water contacts: gas top (lowest density), oil middle, water below. Migration and trapping detail : primary migration is expulsion of oil from the compacting source rock into carrier beds (driven by overpressure from compaction and hydrocarbon generation); secondary migration is buoyant flow up-dip through permeable beds until stopped by a seal - oil accumulates in the trap crest with gas on top. Impermeable seals depend on capillary entry pressure (fine-grained clay, evaporite); fault seals can both trap (clay smearing) and leak (open fractures) - a standard AO2 point. If the seal fails or the trap is breached, hydrocarbons seep to the surface (oil seeps, tar pits) - historically the first indicators of petroleum provinces. Hydrogeology : porosity (void percentage - storage) versus permeability (connectedness - flow). Clay is porous but effectively impermeable (pores too small); the Chalk stores water in its matrix but transmits it through fractures - a classic discriminating point. Aquifer types : unconfined (water table open to the surface, recharge by rainfall), confined (aquifer bounded above and below by aquitards - water under pressure) giving artesian wells where the piezometric surface is above ground (historically in the London Basin, where Chalk is confined by London Clay); perched water tables above local aquitards. The major UK aquifers are the Chalk and the Permo-Triassic sandstones - know their characters: Chalk fissure flow and high storage; sandstones intergranular flow. Exploitation and problems : wells, springs and boreholes; over-abstraction lowers the water table (dry wells, reduced baseflow to rivers, land subsidence - London's historic decline and recovery) and causes saline intrusion along coasts (sea water replaces drawn-down fresh water under London). Contamination : nitrates from agriculture, hydrocarbons (LNAPLs float on the water table - petrol; DNAPLs sink - solvents), landfill leachate; protection via source protection zones and aquifer vulnerability mapping (BGS/Evironment Agency mapping). Engineering geology of construction: aggregates (crushed limestone/gritstone; sand and gravel - the largest UK quarry product), dimension stone (Portland Stone, granite - Aberdeen), slate (Welsh quarries - Penrhyn), brick clay, gypsum (plaster), and cement (limestone + clay calcined). Foundations: rock strength, dip of bedding out of slope, perched water and mined ground (shafts) control site suitability - standard Component 3 applied questions give a site description and ask for hazards and suitability judgments. Water table behaviour : unconfined water tables rise with recharge (winter) and fall with drought and abstraction - contour maps of the water table show flow directions perpendicular to the contours, from recharge to discharge areas (springs, river baseflow, the sea). Groundwater age can be dated by C-14 (dating the dissolved carbonate) - deep Chalk groundwater may be thousands of years old, meaning slow recharge and slow recovery from over-abstraction: a genuine A* synthesis link to radiometric dating. Building stone durability : limestones suffer sulphation in polluted cities (SO2 forms gypsum crusts that spall), sandstones resist; Portland Stone weathers to a honeyed patina in clean air - stone selection is a classic applied question. Aggregate quality : strength (crushing value), polish resistance for road stone (gritstone, not limestone) and alkali-silica reactivity control use - exam questions give a proposed quarry site and ask for the quality tests and market. Exploration sequence (learn as an ordered workflow with the purpose of each stage): (1) desk study - geological maps, borehole records, archives (BGS GeoReports); (2) remote sensing - satellite/aerial imagery, lineaments; (3) geophysical surveys - magnetic (magnetite ores, dykes), gravity (dense ores, salt domes - low gravity), electrical resistivity (aquifers, clays), induced polarisation (disseminated sulfides), seismic reflection (basins, traps); (4) geochemical surveys - stream sediment, soil and lithogeochemistry trace ores to source (anomalies); (5) drilling - percussion/rotary (cheap testing) and diamond core (structural and grade data); (6) evaluation - resource estimation, grade-tonnage curves, feasibility. Evaluate each: geophysics covers ground cheaply without drilling but is ambiguous (non-uniqueness - multiple geologies fit one anomaly); geochemistry localises but not quantifies; drilling is definitive but expensive and point-sampled - hence the sequence from cheap-wide to expensive-narrow. Exam questions give a scenario (e.g. suspected porphyry copper beneath soil cover) and expect the chosen techniques justified in order. Sustainability : resources are finite; demand rises with population and the energy transition (lithium from brines and pegmatites, cobalt, copper for electrification, rare earth elements for magnets - monazite/bastnasite). Evaluate: recycling extends supply but cannot fully replace mining; new exploration opens environmentally sensitive areas; mining impacts include acid mine drainage (pyrite oxidation producing sulfuric acid and iron hydroxides), subsidence (coal fields), tailings dam failures and habitat loss; rehabilitation (restoration to agriculture/wetland), water management and planning conditions mitigate. Examiners reward balanced judgment: economic benefit versus environmental cost, the role of geological survey data (BGS) in responsible land-use decisions, and the difference between renewability (groundwater - recharge rate matters) and finite stocks (ores, hydrocarbons). Link back to hazards (tailings, subsidence) and mapwork (site evaluation) for the synoptic marks. Evaluation depth for the exploration sequence: state the non-uniqueness of geophysical anomalies (one magnetic anomaly could be a dyke, a magnetite body or buried iron - only drilling resolves it), the point-sample problem of drilling (grade between holes interpolated, hence grade-tonnage curves), and the cost logic that drives the sequence from cheap-wide (desk study, remote sensing) to expensive-narrow (diamond drilling). BGS role in the UK: regional mapping, borehole records, GeoReports and landslide/ground stability data underpin both exploration and planning decisions - cite it in sustainability answers. Sustainability synthesis : groundwater is renewable only if abstraction stays below recharge (the aquifer over-abstraction point cross-links to the hydrogeology section); ores and hydrocarbons are finite stocks, so recycling, substitution and efficiency extend them; the energy transition creates new demand (lithium, cobalt, rare earths) whose mining carries the same environmental management duties - balance economic benefit against environmental cost, with named impacts, for the evaluation marks.

topics.name: Sampling and Data
topics.subject: statistics
topics.searchText: statistics Statistics Sampling and Data Population The entire set of items or individuals relevant to the statistical enquiry; every member must be identifiable to take a census or use a sampling frame. Sampling frame A numbered list of all members of the population from which a sample is drawn, e.g. an electoral register or class register. Simple random sample A sample in which every member of the population has an equal chance of selection, chosen using random numbers so there is no bias. Systematic sample Selecting every kth member of an ordered sampling frame after a random start, where k = N/n; simple but risks periodicity in the list. Stratified sample The population is split into strata that differ in a relevant way, and each stratum is sampled in proportion to its size: n_h = (N_h / N) x n. Quota sample A non-random sample where interviewers fill quotas of respondents in each group; needs no sampling frame but is prone to interviewer bias. Cluster sample Randomly selecting whole groups (clusters, e.g. schools or streets) and sampling within them; cheap for geographically spread populations but clusters may be unrepresentative. Standard deviation The root mean square deviation from the mean, s = sqrt( sum of (x - mean)^2 / (n - 1) ), measuring spread in the same units as the data. Frequency density For a histogram, frequency divided by class width; the area of each bar is proportional to frequency. Outlier A value lying more than 1.5 x IQR beyond the quartiles, i.e. below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR; discard only with a justifiable reason such as a recording error. A census measures every member of the population; a sample measures only a subset. Exams expect you to weigh these up: a census gives complete information and no sampling variation, but is expensive, time-consuming, and destructive testing (e.g. crash-testing cars) rules it out entirely. A sample is cheaper and quicker, but smaller samples give less precise estimates. Random methods need a sampling frame . Simple random sampling uses random numbers from a calculator or tables to pick n members, giving equal selection probability and no bias; its weakness is the requirement for a complete, up-to-date frame, which is impractical for large or scattered populations. Systematic sampling picks every kth item after a random start (k = N/n); it is quick and spreads through the frame, but if the list has a periodic pattern the sample can be badly biased. Stratified sampling divides the population into strata that differ in a way relevant to the enquiry (e.g. year group, region) and samples each in proportion to its size, guaranteeing every stratum is represented and often improving precision. Quota sampling is non-random: interviewers fill predetermined quotas (e.g. 20 men over 60). It needs no sampling frame and is fast, but the choice of respondents within a quota is left to the interviewer, introducing bias. Cluster sampling randomly selects whole clusters and samples within them, cutting travel costs, but a cluster may not resemble the population. Opportunity (convenience) sampling and self-selected samples (volunteers) are almost always biased towards particular types of respondent and attract easy marks when asked to criticise a design. Worked stratified calculation A school of 800 students has 300 in Year 12 and 500 in Year 13. For a stratified sample of 40: Year 12 gives (300/800) x 40 = 15 students; Year 13 gives (500/800) x 40 = 25 students. Check: 15 + 25 = 40. State the method, the formula, the arithmetic and the total - that sequence earns full marks. Method-choice questions follow a decision order. Ask: does a sampling frame exist? If not, quota or opportunity sampling is forced. If yes, do distinct groups matter to the enquiry? If so, stratify. Otherwise, is the frame large and ordered? Systematic sampling may then be the efficient choice. Whatever you choose, the highest marks come from a two-part justification: a correct property of the method (e.g. random, unbiased, proportionally representative) linked to the specific context of the question. Also be ready to calculate k = N/n for a systematic sample and to explain why a random start is needed - without it the sample could systematically miss part of the frame. Categorical (qualitative) data are descriptions (blood group, brand); if the categories can be ordered they are ordinal (exam grade, satisfaction rating). Quantitative data are numerical: discrete data take exact, countable values (number of siblings, goals scored), while continuous data arise from measurement and can take any value in an interval (height, time). Choosing the right chart and the right average depends on this classification, so state the type explicitly when asked. Primary data are collected first-hand by the enquirer: fully relevant, defined for the purpose, and you control the method - but collection is slow and costly. Secondary data were collected by someone else (government statistics, published surveys): instantly available and often large-scale, but possibly out of date, collected for a different purpose, and of unknown reliability. Questions frequently ask for one advantage and one disadvantage of each - learn those pairs. Three quality words carry precise meanings in 9ST0. Reliability : the method would give consistent results if repeated. Validity : the data actually measure what the enquiry intends to measure. Bias : systematic distortion in one direction, from a poor sampling frame, leading questions, non-response or unrepresentative sampling. A pilot study is a small-scale trial run used to check that questions are understood, test the timing of the collection process, and refine the design before the main enquiry - quote at least two of these purposes. When asked to criticise a data collection method, scan a checklist: sample size too small; sampling frame incomplete or absent; non-random selection; leading or ambiguous question wording; low response rate; data recorded inaccurately; secondary data of unknown reliability or age. One developed criticism per mark, each tied to the specific context. Two further ideas appear in 9ST0 questions on data quality. Accuracy concerns how close a measurement is to the true value, while precision concerns the level of detail recorded (e.g. heights to the nearest centimetre); more precision is not automatically more accurate. Data cleaning - removing impossible values, correcting mis-keyed entries, deciding what to do about missing responses - should be done before any calculation, and exam questions expect you to state a rule (e.g. discard if clearly a recording error, otherwise keep) rather than silently delete. Link every quality discussion back to its effect on conclusions: biased or invalid data make estimates untrustworthy however large the sample. The three averages have distinct jobs. The mean , sum of x divided by n, uses every data value and is needed for standard deviation, but is distorted by outliers and skew. The median is the middle value when ordered - resistant to outliers, so preferred for skewed data. The mode is the most frequent value, the only sensible average for categorical data. For a frequency table the mean is sum of fx divided by sum of f; for grouped data use class midpoints and state that the answer is an estimate. Dispersion measures: the range uses only two values and is distorted by outliers; the interquartile range (Q3 - Q1) is resistant; the standard deviation uses every value and pairs with the mean. Edexcel 9ST0 uses the sample formula s = sqrt( sum of (x - mean)^2 / (n - 1) ) - the (n - 1) divisor is a mark-scheme point; calculator SD functions may default to a different divisor, so quote 3 significant figures and state the formula used. Coding appears in exam questions: if y = (x - a)/b then the mean of y is (mean of x - a)/b and the SD of y is SD of x divided by the absolute value of b. Division affects spread; subtraction does not. Expect a question asking you to recover the original mean or SD from coded summary statistics. Skewness is measured from the averages: if mean > median the distribution has positive (right) skew; if mean Choosing the measure for an exam answer is a two-step decision. First, is the data categorical? Then the mode is the only option. Second, is the distribution skewed or does it contain outliers? Then pair the median with the IQR. Only for roughly symmetric data without outliers should the mean with standard deviation be reported. A quick sanity check that earns marks: compare mean and median - if they differ noticeably, the distribution is skewed and the median should be quoted. A typical exam item gives coded or summary statistics and asks which average is appropriate and why; the answer is graded on the reasoning, not the choice alone. An outlier is any value below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. Show the fence calculations explicitly, then decide: discard an outlier only with a justifiable reason (mis-keyed data, impossible value), otherwise keep it and say why (a genuine extreme value still part of the population). A discarded outlier changes the mean and SD but not the median or IQR. A box plot displays the five key values - minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum - with outliers marked as crosses beyond the whiskers. It makes location (position of the median), dispersion (width of the box = IQR) and skew (asymmetry of the box and whiskers) visible at a glance. Comparison questions are guaranteed marks if you write in context: state which group has the higher average (median), which is more consistent (smaller IQR or range), and comment on skew - never just quote numbers without interpretation. Histograms represent continuous, grouped data. The vertical axis is frequency density = frequency / class width , and the area of each bar is proportional to frequency. With unequal class widths, plotting raw frequency is a classic error; with equal widths the densities are proportional to frequencies anyway. You can estimate how many observations lie in any interval by finding the corresponding area, and you should describe the shape: unimodal, symmetric, or positively/negatively skewed. A high-mark comparison paragraph has a fixed skeleton: (i) compare medians in context - on average...; (ii) compare spread in context - the IQR/SD for... is smaller, so more consistent; (iii) comment on outliers or skew and what they imply for the choice of average. Practise writing all three sentences with the context nouns in every one. Box plots can also be constructed from a cumulative frequency curve : read the quartiles at cumulative frequencies of n/4 and 3n/4 and the median at n/2, then draw the box plot from those five values. Edexcel marks quartiles from cumulative frequency graphs leniently for reading accuracy but strictly for method - plot points at class upper boundaries, join with a smooth curve, and draw horizontal and vertical construction lines. Finally, remember the two marks that most candidates drop in comparison questions: interpreting every number in context (the mark scheme usually rejects uninterpreted values), and stating which distribution is more consistent rather than only which has the greater spread.

topics.name: Probability
topics.subject: statistics
topics.searchText: statistics Statistics Probability Trial A single performance of an experiment whose outcome is uncertain, e.g. one roll of a die. Sample space The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment; probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1. Mutually exclusive Events that cannot occur together: P(A intersection B) = 0, so P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B). Exhaustive Events that together cover the whole sample space: their union has probability 1. Complement The event A-prime (not A): P(A-prime) = 1 - P(A); used to convert at-least-one questions into one-minus-none. Conditional probability The probability of A given that B has occurred: P(A given B) = P(A intersection B) / P(B), for P(B) > 0. Independence Events A and B are independent if P(A intersection B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A given B) = P(A) and P(B given A) = P(B). Union The event that A or B (or both) occurs; probability found with the addition rule. Intersection The event that both A and B occur; found with the multiplication rule or read from a Venn overlap. Tree diagram A diagram with branches whose first level carries unconditional probabilities and later levels carry conditional probabilities; multiply along branches and add between complete cases. Probabilities live on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Two structural facts do most of the early work: the complement , P(A-prime) = 1 - P(A), which converts questions such as at least one into one minus none; and the addition rule , P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A intersection B), which requires the overlap to be subtracted because it is counted twice. If A and B are mutually exclusive the overlap is zero, so P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B). If events are exhaustive their union is the whole sample space, probability 1. Venn diagrams turn wordy descriptions into region arithmetic. Draw the universal set, place the intersection first when it is known, and label every region including outside both circles. Learn the standard translations: only A means P(A) minus the overlap; A or B means the union; both means the intersection; neither means 1 minus the union; exactly one means the two non-overlapping parts of A and B added. Exam questions often describe frequencies (e.g. of 60 students, 35 study French...) - convert frequencies to probabilities only when the question asks, and otherwise work in counts and divide at the end. A recurring mark-earning skill is finding the intersection from a conditional statement. If the question gives P(A given B) and P(B), then P(A intersection B) = P(A given B) x P(B); write that multiplication down explicitly - it is usually a dedicated method mark. Check any finished Venn by adding all region probabilities: the total must equal 1 (or the total frequency). Two-way tables are the Venn diagram's twin and often quicker when data are given as counts. Rows and columns carry the marginal totals; each cell is an intersection. The same translations apply: only A is a single cell, neither is the grand total minus the row-plus-column sum. When a question gives a table and asks for a conditional probability, cover the rows outside the condition and read within the condition row or column - this physical restriction is what conditioning means, and writing the restricted fraction (e.g. 30 out of 55) before simplifying earns the method mark. Be ready to complete a partially given table first, using the fact that rows and columns sum to their totals. Conditional probability restricts the sample space. Given that B has occurred, only outcomes inside B are possible, and A given B is the part of A inside B relative to B: P(A given B) = P(A intersection B) / P(B). Rearranged, this is the multiplication rule : P(A intersection B) = P(A given B) x P(B). In Venn or two-way table questions, conditioning physically means covering up the rest of the table: P(tea given female) is the tea column read only within the female row. Independence is tested, not assumed. A and B are independent if and only if P(A intersection B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A given B) = P(A) or P(B given A) = P(B) - knowing one event gives no information about the other. Exam questions supply numbers and expect you to compute both sides and state a conclusion in context: since P(A given B) = 0.545 but P(A) = 0.45, the events are not independent. Show both computations; the comparison alone is the answer. The most reliable mark-earner in this topic is the distinction between mutually exclusive and independent . They are different conditions and cannot both hold for two non-zero probabilities: if A and B are exclusive then P(A given B) = 0, but independence would demand P(A given B) = P(A) > 0. Questions deliberately test whether you know that exclusive events are dependent, and that independence requires the multiplication rule to hold exactly. A second family of questions asks you to find a conditional probability when the conditioning event has already happened in the data. Two classic setups: sampling without replacement, where the second draw is made from a reduced population and every branch probability must be updated; and given-that questions on two-way tables, where the denominator is the condition total rather than the grand total. In both, state what the sample space has become before calculating - the sentence for the second draw there are 7 counters remaining is itself a marking point. Finally, use complements inside conditional questions too: P(at least one red given the first was red) is 1 minus the probability of no red on the second draw, which is often a one-step calculation. A tree diagram is the safest machine for multi-step problems. The first level of branches carries unconditional probabilities; every later level carries conditional probabilities (the probability of the new outcome given the path taken so far). Multiply along a complete path to get the probability of that case; add between paths when a final event can occur in several ways. With replacement , the branch probabilities stay constant; without replacement , they change because the population shrinks - e.g. from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue counters, the second draw is from 7 counters, so P(red then blue) = (5/8)(3/7). Bayes-style questions reverse the conditioning: the natural order of the tree gives P(path), but the question asks P(early event given late outcome). The method is fixed and full marks are available for writing it out: list the complete cases that make up the late outcome, add their probabilities to get the denominator, and divide the relevant case by that total. For a disease test with P(positive given disease) = 0.98 and P(positive given no disease) = 0.05 in a population where 2 percent have the disease: P(disease and positive) = 0.02 x 0.98 = 0.0196, P(no disease and positive) = 0.98 x 0.05 = 0.049, so P(positive) = 0.0686 and P(disease given positive) = 0.0196 / 0.0686 = 0.286. Two habits make tree answers bulletproof. First, label every branch with its event and its probability, and annotate the end of each complete path with the product - examiners award method marks for structure even if arithmetic slips. Second, work in exact fractions where possible and round only the final answer to 3 significant figures; premature decimal rounding in the denominator is the most common cause of lost accuracy marks. Choosing between a tree and a Venn is itself an exam skill. Use a tree when events happen in stages or when you need to reverse a conditional (Bayes); use a Venn or two-way table when a single collection is split by two characteristics and the question gives counts. If a question offers a choice, state yours in one sentence - the examiner cannot award structure marks for a method you did not show. And when a tree grows beyond two levels, do not multiply across everything blindly: identify which complete paths correspond to the event asked about, add only those, and check that the selected cases are exhaustive for that event. This topic punishes rushed reading, so audit every answer against a fixed checklist. (i) Did you answer the conditioning the right way round? P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different numbers, and Bayes questions exist precisely because they differ. (ii) Did you use the addition rule when events overlap? Subtracting the intersection is a named method mark. (iii) Did you confuse mutually exclusive with independent? Test with the multiplication rule and say so in context. (iv) Did your tree keep conditional probabilities on later levels? Constant probabilities throughout the tree only apply with replacement. Context sentences carry marks in 9ST0 probability. Conclusions should name the events: for example, the probability that a customer buys tea given that she is female is 0.545, which is higher than the overall probability of 0.45, so buying tea and gender are not independent. Numbers without the context nouns typically score zero for interpretation marks. Finally, exploit the checking structure that examiners build in. All probabilities in a distribution or Venn must sum to 1 - verify before moving on. Complements convert hard questions into easy ones: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none) is almost always faster than adding the individual cases. And when a question chains conditionals (given that the first draw was red, find...), do not recompute from scratch: the condition has changed the sample space, so work within it. A final word on presentation. Examiners reward answers that set out notation before calculation: define A, B, write the rule you will use, substitute, then answer. This costs seconds and secures method marks even when arithmetic slips later. In longer questions, keep each part of the working on its own line - merged working hides where the marks are. Practise writing the conclusion sentence for every interpretation mark: name the events, give the probability, and say what it means in the context of the question.

topics.name: Probability Distributions
topics.subject: statistics
topics.searchText: statistics Statistics Probability Distributions Random variable A variable whose value is a numerical outcome of a random experiment, conventionally denoted by a capital letter such as X. Discrete random variable A random variable taking countable values, described by a probability function p(x) with p(x) at least 0 for all x and the sum of p(x) = 1. Expected value E(X) The mean of a random variable over many repetitions: E(X) = sum of x times p(x). Variance of a random variable Var(X) = E(X squared) - (E(X)) squared; the standard deviation is its square root. Binomial distribution The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials, each with success probability p: X ~ B(n, p), with mean np and variance np(1 - p). Bernoulli trial A single trial with exactly two outcomes, success (probability p) and failure (probability 1 - p). Normal distribution A continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution X ~ N(mu, sigma squared) determined by its mean and standard deviation. Standard normal variable Z Z = (X - mu)/sigma for X ~ N(mu, sigma squared); Z ~ N(0, 1) and is used with normal tables. Continuity correction The adjustment made when a discrete distribution is approximated by a continuous one, e.g. P(X less or equal a) becomes P(Y < a + 0.5). Inverse normal Working backwards from a probability to the value of X, using x = mu + sigma z with the z-value from normal tables. A discrete random variable X takes countable values, each with a probability. Two conditions define a valid distribution: every probability is between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Exam questions typically give a distribution with one probability written as k, ask you to find k using the sum-to-1 condition, then calculate E(X) = sum of x times p(x) and Var(X) = E(X squared) - (E(X)) squared. Write the tables out with a row for x and a row for p(x); the sum-to-1 equation is always a method mark. The linear results save time and are directly examinable: E(aX + b) = a E(X) + b, and Var(aX + b) = a squared times Var(X) - the shift b does not affect spread, the scale a does. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it is Var(X), not E(X squared) minus something else - state which you are quoting. A typical high-mark part asks for the expected value of a transformed variable, e.g. E(5X - 2): apply the rules to the E(X) you found first. Remember what expectation means in context: E(X) is the long-run average per trial, so an answer of 2.1 goals per match is sensible even though no single match can score 2.1 goals - a favourite interpretation point. Similarly, Var(X) measures the spread of the distribution over many repetitions, in squared units. Some questions build the distribution from a situation rather than presenting it: for the sum of two fair dice, list the 36 outcomes, count the ways for each total, and divide by 36 - the sample space listing is the method mark. Others ask for the distribution of a transformed variable or for probabilities from a described game. In every case the workflow is identical: identify the values, find each probability with the rules of probability, check the two conditions, then compute E(X) and Var(X). Keep the distribution table visible throughout; answers computed from an unlisted distribution usually lose the structure marks even when the arithmetic is right. A distinct family of 9ST0 questions gives E(X) or Var(X) and asks for a missing probability or for E of a function of X. Work backwards through the same formulae: if you know E(X) and E(X squared), the variance follows; if you know E(2X + 1) = 7, then E(X) = 3 by reversing the linear rule. Keep the two conditions (probabilities between 0 and 1, summing to 1) in mind throughout - a found value of k that violates either signals an earlier slip. State the standard deviation separately from the variance, with units, and quote 3 significant figures unless the value is exact. The binomial distribution X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials, each with the same success probability p. Four conditions, all examinable: a fixed number n of trials; each trial has exactly two outcomes (success/failure); trials are independent; p is constant. Typical binomial contexts: number of defective items in a batch, number of sixes in a set of dice rolls, number of patients responding to treatment. When asked to state why the binomial model applies, quote the conditions in context - e.g. each item is defective independently with the same probability. The formula is P(X = r) = C(n, r) p to the power r times (1 - p) to the power (n - r), but in practice you use the cumulative binomial tables in the formula booklet or a calculator. Three standard conversions from cumulative values: P(X greater or equal a) = 1 - P(X less or equal a - 1); P(X greater a) = 1 - P(X less or equal a); P(a less or equal X less or equal b) = P(X less or equal b) - P(X less or equal a - 1). The off-by-one in each is the classic error - always rewrite the event in terms of less-or-equal before touching the tables. The mean and variance follow immediately: E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 - p). Questions ask you to state or use them - e.g. find the expected number of successes in 50 trials with p = 0.3 (answer 15). Note the variance uses (1 - p), not p squared, and that for a binomial variable the mean, variance and their relationship to the mode can be examined; know that the distribution is skewed when p is far from 0.5 and becomes more symmetric as n grows with p near 0.5. Two table habits avoid lost marks. First, always rewrite the event as less-or-equal before reading: examiners set the off-by-one deliberately, and the rewritten inequality line is a method mark in its own right. Second, when the tables in the booklet do not cover the required n and p, use the binomial cumulative function on the calculator instead - but show the converted inequality either way. For context questions, connect the model to the situation: if trials might not be independent (e.g. sweets eaten from the same bag without replacement), the binomial model is questionable and saying so earns the AO3 mark. The normal distribution N(mu, sigma squared) is continuous, symmetric about the mean, bell-shaped, with tails that approach the horizontal axis without touching it. It models naturally symmetric measurements - heights, masses, times in large populations. Every normal calculation should start with a sketch: draw the curve, mark mu, shade the required area. The notation matters: the second parameter is the variance, so N(52, 9) has standard deviation 3. Probabilities are found by standardising : Z = (X - mu)/sigma converts to the standard normal N(0, 1), whose probabilities come from normal tables or a calculator. For P(X a) use the complement 1 - P(X Inverse normal questions reverse the flow: given a probability, find the value of X. Find the z-value from the tables for the given tail probability, then convert back with x = mu + sigma z. Example: for X ~ N(40, 36), the value exceeded with probability 0.10 has z = 1.2816, so x = 40 + 6 x 1.2816 = 47.7. Percentages must be converted to probabilities first (10 percent becomes 0.10), and symmetrical phrasings (the middle 90 percent) need two z-values or one with the symmetry of the curve. Symmetry questions are frequent and worth practising as a set. For the middle 90 percent of a distribution, the two tails each hold 5 percent, so find z for an upper-tail probability of 0.05 (z = 1.6449) and state both endpoints x = mu plus-or-minus sigma z. For within-one-standard-deviation questions, z = plus-or-minus 1 and the answer is 2 x 0.8413 - 1 = 0.6826, a value worth memorising as a check. When a question mixes units (masses in grams, times in minutes) standardise in the units given and never convert the distribution parameters themselves; and when a value is described in words (two standard deviations above the mean), translate it into a z-value before any table work. When n is large, binomial calculations by formula or tables become impractical, so X ~ B(n, p) is approximated by a normal distribution: X approximately N(np, np(1 - p)) - the mean and variance of the binomial become the parameters of the normal. The standard conditions quoted by Edexcel are that n is large with np > 5 and n(1 - p) > 5; state both when asked to justify the approximation, and expect an AO3 mark for explaining why: the binomial becomes symmetric and bell-shaped for large n, matching the normal shape. Because the binomial is discrete and the normal continuous, a continuity correction is essential: whole-number values become intervals of width 1. The three conversions: P(X less or equal a) becomes P(Y a - 0.5); P(X = a) becomes P(a - 0.5 Worked structure for a full-mark answer: (i) state the approximation with its parameters, e.g. X ~ B(120, 0.4) is approximately N(48, 28.8); (ii) apply the continuity correction to rewrite the event; (iii) standardise and use tables; (iv) answer to 3 significant figures. For X ~ B(120, 0.4), P(X greater or equal 55): mu = 48, sigma = the square root of 28.8 = 5.37 (3 sf); the event becomes P(Y > 54.5); z = (54.5 - 48)/5.37 = 1.21; P(Z > 1.21) = 1 - 0.8939 = 0.106. Accuracy questions compare the approximation with the exact binomial answer and ask for a comment. The approximation is close for large n but slightly out because the normal is continuous; the continuity correction removes most but not all of the gap, and as n grows the approximation improves. Expect an AO3 mark for explaining why the approximation is needed (tables impractical, computation heavy) and one for the conditions. Also be ready to reverse the process: given a normal model claimed as an approximation to a binomial, recover n and p from the parameters - the mean np and variance np(1 - p) give two equations in two unknowns, since the variance divided by the mean equals 1 - p.

topics.name: Correlation and Regression
topics.subject: statistics
topics.searchText: statistics Statistics Correlation and Regression Bivariate data Paired observations of two variables recorded for each item, e.g. height and weight of each person. Explanatory variable The variable x plotted on the horizontal axis, used to explain or predict the response variable. Response variable The variable y plotted on the vertical axis, whose values may be explained by the explanatory variable. Product moment correlation coefficient (PMCC) r, measuring the strength and direction of linear association: r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx Syy), with r always between -1 and 1. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient A rank-based measure of monotonic association, rs = 1 - (6 x sum of d squared) / (n(n squared - 1)), where d is the difference in ranks. Least squares regression line The line y = a + bx minimising the sum of squared vertical residuals, with b = Sxy/Sxx, passing through the mean point (mean of x, mean of y). Interpolation Using the regression line to predict within the range of the observed x-values; generally reliable. Extrapolation Using the regression line to predict outside the range of the observed x-values; unreliable because the linear pattern may not continue. Confounding variable A third variable associated with both x and y that could explain an observed correlation between them. Bivariate data record two variables per item. Plot them first: the explanatory variable x goes on the horizontal axis and the response variable y on the vertical. The scatter diagram reveals the shape of any relationship - linear or curved, tight or loose - and exposes outliers that would distort summary statistics. Exam questions often ask what the scatter diagram shows before any calculation: describe direction, strength and shape, always naming the variables. The product moment correlation coefficient quantifies linear association: r = Sxy / sqrt(Sxx Syy), where Sxy, Sxx and Syy are the sums of squared deviations. In practice r comes from the calculator statistics mode. It always lies between -1 and 1: r = 1 means perfect positive linear correlation, r = -1 perfect negative, r = 0 no linear correlation. Interpretation must be in context with both words - direction and strength: for example, r = 0.82 for hours of revision and exam score indicates strong positive linear correlation, so students who revise for longer tend to score higher. Two limits of r are examined directly. First, r measures linear association only: a perfect curved relationship (e.g. y = x squared) can give r close to 0, so r near 0 does not mean no relationship - plot the data. Second, r is sensitive to outliers: one extreme point can change r dramatically, so check the scatter diagram and consider recalculating without the outlier, stating what you did. A further AO3 point: a large sample can make a tiny r significant, so statistical significance is not the same as a strong relationship - interpret the size of r as well as testing it. Interpreting the size of r is a skill in its own right. Common conventions describe values above about 0.8 as very strong, 0.6 to 0.8 strong, 0.4 to 0.6 moderate, and below 0.4 weak - but the mark scheme rewards the direction plus a contextual sentence rather than a memorised band. Exam questions also ask you to compare two coefficients (e.g. r = 0.62 for one pair of variables and r = 0.31 for another): state which indicates the stronger linear association and what that means in context, and be ready to explain that different strengths in different samples do not contradict each other. When r is calculated by hand from Sxy, Sxx and Syy, quote intermediate sums - the substituted formula line is the method mark. Spearman's rank correlation coefficient , rs, measures monotonic association on the ranks of the data. Rank each variable separately from 1 (smallest or best, state your convention and use it consistently), compute the differences d between paired ranks, then rs = 1 - (6 x sum of d squared) / (n(n squared - 1)). It lies between -1 and 1 and is interpreted like r, but it detects any consistent increasing or decreasing relationship, not just linear ones. Use Spearman rather than the PMCC in three standard situations: the data are ordinal (ranks, grades, ratings) rather than genuine measurements; the relationship is monotonic but not linear (consistently increasing but curved); or the data contain outliers , because ranking limits their influence. Exam questions test the choice: state which coefficient and justify with the data type or shape of the scatter diagram. Spearman is also robust when one variable is subjective, e.g. judges' placements in a competition. Tied ranks need care: when two values share a rank, give each the average of the ranks they would have occupied (e.g. two values tied for 3rd and 4th place both get 3.5). The formula is then approximate, so quote rs to 2 or 3 significant figures and note that ties make the formula inexact. A classic high-mark item gives ranks with ties and asks for rs plus an interpretation; show the d column and the sum of d squared explicitly - that table is the method mark. The workflow for a full Spearman answer is mechanical and worth automating in revision. (i) Rank both variables, stating the convention (e.g. rank 1 = smallest). (ii) Build the d column and its squares. (iii) Substitute into rs = 1 - (6 x sum of d squared)/(n(n squared - 1)). (iv) Interpret in context with direction and strength. Marks appear at each stage, and the most commonly dropped is the final interpretation sentence. Note also that Spearman uses ranks only, so the actual size of differences between values is ignored - two datasets with the same ranks give the same rs however different the underlying numbers are, which is both the strength of the method (robustness) and its weakness (loss of information). The least squares regression line of y on x is y = a + bx, chosen to minimise the sum of squared vertical distances (residuals) from the points to the line. The gradient is b = Sxy/Sxx, and the line always passes through the mean point (mean of x, mean of y) - a fact used to find the missing coefficient in exam questions. It exists and is meaningful only when the scatter diagram shows a roughly linear pattern, so check the correlation first. Interpret the coefficients in context, every time . The gradient b is the predicted change in y per unit increase in x: for y = 22.0 + 4.8x with x = hours of revision and y = exam score, each additional hour of revision predicts 4.8 more marks. The intercept a is the predicted value of y when x = 0: here 22 marks, sensible in context; but for a line predicting plant height from days, an intercept could be negative and meaningless physically - state that a should be interpreted only where x = 0 is meaningful in the context. Predictions use the line directly: substitute the given x. The reliability distinction is examined every year: interpolation (predicting within the range of observed x-values) is generally reliable; extrapolation (predicting outside it) is unreliable because the linear pattern may not continue beyond the data. When asked to predict and comment, give the value and then one sentence - the prediction is an interpolation/extrapolation, and extrapolated values should be treated with caution. Never swap the variables: the regression line of y on x predicts y from x; predicting x from y needs a different line. Two regression facts are directly examinable and worth memorising. First, the line of y on x passes through the mean point (mean of x, mean of y): given a gradient and the means, the intercept follows immediately - a = mean of y - b x (mean of x). Second, the gradient satisfies b = Sxy/Sxx, and r and b are linked: r = b x (sd of x / sd of y), so the gradient and the correlation have the same sign. Questions occasionally ask for the regression line from summary statistics alone (means, Sxy, Sxx) without the raw data - set up both formulas, substitute, and state the line in the form y = a + bx with the context variables named. Correlation does not imply causation - the most examined AO2 sentence in this topic. An observed correlation between x and y has four possible explanations: x causes y; y causes x (reverse causation); a confounding variable drives both (e.g. temperature drives both ice-cream sales and drowning incidents); or the pattern is coincidence. A full-mark answer names the correlation in context, states that correlation alone does not establish a causal link, and gives at least one plausible alternative explanation tied to the context. Interpretation questions have a fixed skeleton worth rehearsing. For a correlation: direction, strength, context. For a regression line: gradient meaning, intercept meaning (if sensible), prediction with the interpolation/extrapolation caveat. For a comparison of two coefficients or two lines: say which indicates the stronger association and what changes in gradient imply. Every sentence should contain the context nouns - bare numbers and bare adjectives (strong, weak) without the variables named typically score zero. Two technical traps to close the topic. First, the regression line should not be used when the scatter diagram shows a non-linear pattern: fitting a straight line to curved data gives misleading predictions even if r is moderate - say the relationship is not linear and suggest a change of variable or a curve. Second, correlation coefficients measure association in the observed sample only; different samples (different countries, time periods) can show different strengths, so be cautious about generalising a conclusion beyond the data - another standard AO3 mark. When a question asks whether two variables are related, structure the answer around what you have: the scatter diagram (shape, direction), the PMCC or Spearman coefficient (strength of linear or monotonic association), and any regression line (a model for prediction). A complete AO2 paragraph uses at least two of these together: for example, the scatter diagram shows a linear pattern and r = 0.82, indicating strong positive linear correlation between the variables, so the regression line y = 22.0 + 4.8x is appropriate for prediction within the observed range. Practice pairing the evidence with the conclusion in one sentence - that habit converts calculation marks into interpretation marks and is the difference between grade B and A/A* answers on this topic.

topics.name: Hypothesis Testing
topics.subject: statistics
topics.searchText: statistics Statistics Hypothesis Testing Null hypothesis H0 The default assumption being tested, usually of no change or no effect, always containing an equality, e.g. p = 0.5 or mu = 20. Alternative hypothesis H1 What is being tested for: p > or < a value (one-tailed) or p is not equal to a value (two-tailed). Significance level The probability threshold alpha (usually 0.05 or 0.01) below which H0 is rejected; the probability of rejecting a true H0.
