Bill Nichols systematised the genre into six modes , and the spec's set films map onto them precisely. Poetic — expressive, associative organisation over argument (fragments of tone and image). Expository — voiceover, titles and interviews organise footage to a thesis; the classic broadcast mode; 'the voice-of-God' narration that answers questions before the spectator asks them. Observational — fly-on-the-wall capture of reality with minimal intervention; Sisters in Law is the most conventional of the set films, an observational documentary committed to capturing the reality played out in front of the camera. Participatory — the filmmaker interacts with subjects through interviews and encounters; Broomfield and Moore are the spec's exemplars. Performative — subjective, expressive engagement; knowledge as personal experience; For Sama combines performative and observational modes. Reflexive — the film's own construction becomes the subject; Stories We Tell 's self-reflexive investigation into her family, and Exit Through the Gift Shop 's provocation about the nature of documentary film, are the cases. Conventions to analyse as film language: voiceover (presence, authority, reliability), formal interviews (framing, eyeline, staging), archive footage (authorship, ethics, context), reconstruction (Watkins' docu-drama method), observational camera (handheld, available light), captions and graphics, and the near-absent score of observational work. Each convention is a choice about the film's relationship to truth — bind every one to meaning and response. Modes are not boxes — films combine them, and the spec's set films do: For Sama is performative-observational; Stories We Tell is reflexive-participatory; Amy is expository in structure but archival in method; Exit Through the Gift Shop is reflexive with a participatory core. For the exam, name the dominant mode, note the combination, and analyse what the combination does — e.g. For Sama 's performative voiceover inside observational footage means subjective testimony and witnessed reality reinforce each other, so the film's claim to truth is doubled. Also know the genre's history as context in one sentence: actuality films of the Lumière brothers vs the fantasy films of Méliès — the earliest documentary debate, later systematised by Grierson's British documentary movement and Bazin's realism. The documentary is explored in relation to key filmmakers from the genre ; two of the following theories must be chosen for study — the film studied may directly embody aspects of them or strongly challenge them. In either case the theories provide the means of exploring different approaches to documentary. Kim Longinotto ( Sisters in Law ): 'I don't think of films as documents or records of things. I try to make them as like the experience of watching a fiction film as possible, though, of course, nothing is ever set up.' Her work finds characters the audience will identify with — 'you can make this jump into someone else's experience'. Unlike Moore and Broomfield, Longinotto is invisible , with very little use of voice-over, formal interviews, captions or incidental music. As the 'eyes' of her audience, she doesn't like to zoom or pan; she says she doesn't want her films to have conclusions but to raise questions . Sisters in Law embodies this theory: observational, immersive, judgement-free, built on identification with its subjects (the judges Vera Ngassa and Beatrice Ntuba, and the women and girls whose cases they resolve). Michael Moore : a very visible presence; participatory and performative; highly committed — overtly polemical, taking up a clear point of view, agit-prop documentary. He justifies his practice as providing 'balance' for mainstream media which, in his view, provides false information; his humour lampoons subjects and recognises that documentaries must entertain . Exit Through the Gift Shop challenges Moore's model from a different direction: Banksy's film is itself a provocation — its narrator-author relationship (Thierry Guetta's transformation into 'Mr Brainwash') may be a stunt, forcing the spectator to question the nature of documentary film. Nick Broomfield : participatory, performative investigative documentarist with a distinctive interview technique used to expose people's real views; keeps the filmmaking presence minimal (crew of no more than three); his films are 'like a rollercoaster ride... a diary into the future'. Peter Watkins : established his reputation with the docu-dramas Culloden and The War Game (both documenting events using actors and reconstruction), asking questions of conventional documentary out of deep concern with mainstream media, which he calls the 'monoform' . How to use the theories in the exam. The question will ask about your documentary in relation to the debates and the theories. The method: state the theory (with its key claims, and the spec's quotations where memorable); test the film against it — embodies, extends or challenges; then analyse film language as evidence. Sisters in Law is the cleanest embodiment of Longinotto: no zooms or pans (she is the 'eyes' of her audience), no incidental music or captions, conclusions replaced by questions — so spectators make the judgements the judges make. Exit Through the Gift Shop is the cleanest challenge to all four theories: its authorship is the question, so no theory explains it fully — and arguing that is a strong evaluative move. If you study Moore or Broomfield, be ready to contrast the visible filmmaker's polemic with Longinotto's invisibility as alternative ethics of documentary address. Sisters in Law (Ayisi and Longinotto, Cameroon/UK, 2005) is the most conventional of the choices — an observational documentary set in Cameroon, following women working in the legal system as judges and lawyers, focusing on resolving family cases including wife abuse and child cruelty. Its film language is Longinotto's theory in practice: available-light handheld camera, no zooms or pans, near-absent score, no captions or voiceover — so spectators judge as the judges do, watching reality unfold. Stories We Tell (Polley, Canada, 2012) engages in an investigation into Polley's own family — specifically the identity of her genetic father — innovative in its commitment to a self-reflexive approach: reconstruction, home-movie pastiche, interviews with family members who sometimes contradict the film itself, so the film's own construction becomes its subject and the fact/fiction divide dissolves by design. Amy (Kapadia, UK, 2015) takes a different approach to a singer's life: composed almost entirely of home video footage , brought together to offer a compelling portrait of its subject — an archival film whose authorship lies in selection and sequencing, whose intimacy is genuine, and whose ethics (Winehouse's exploitation by media, management and family) are carried by the assembly itself. For Sama (Al-Kateab, UK, 2019) combines performative and observational modes to document a young mother's experience during the Battle of Aleppo — five years of footage shot inside the siege, structured as a letter to her daughter, so the subjective voice is the film's form. Exit Through the Gift Shop (Banksy, UK, 2010) is the street artist's provocative statement about the value of art that forces the spectator to question the nature of documentary film — is Guetta's story real, staged, or both? All five 'frequently make the division between fact and fiction ambiguous and exploit digital technology' — the spec's phrasing. Map each film to its mode(s), its filmmaker-theory relationship, and two sequences where film language carries its claim to truth. Ethics per film — one sentence each, exam-ready: Sisters in Law represents suffering (wife abuse, child cruelty cases) through observation — consent and dignity are its ethical questions, and its subjects' agency (the judges' authority) is part of its answer. For Sama films a war from inside a family's life — the ethics of filming a child in a siege, resolved by the film's own framing as a mother's letter. Amy constructs a portrait from archive the subject never consented to as a film — its ethics lie in indicting the exploitation it also participates in. Stories We Tell films family members without full control of the outcome — consent to the process, not the result. Exit Through the Gift Shop makes its subject's consent itself the puzzle. Weave one of these into any response-analysis paragraph — ethics is where documentary's meaning and response meet. Critical Debate 2 (Area 8): the significance of digital technology in film , studied in relation to the documentary film. The debate: some commentators argue that although digital technology could potentially transform cinema, narrative films designed for cinema release have changed little from pre-digital times; others consider the impact of digital filmmaking is only beginning to emerge, in high-concept Hollywood and in low-budget experimental work. Documentary is the genre where the digital's impact is clearest — apply it to your film: Access : lightweight digital cameras enabled For Sama 's five years of footage inside a siege — physically impossible on film stock with a crew. Archive : digital storage and home video enabled Amy 's composition from found footage; digital restoration makes archive usable at feature length. Distribution/exhibition : streaming and online release changed documentary's audience and economics — For Sama premiered at Cannes/SXSW and reached global audiences via Channel 4 and PBS; Stories We Tell and Amy built their reputations partly online. Manipulation : digital editing and (increasingly) synthetic imagery make the fact/fiction divide harder to police — Stories We Tell 's fabricated home movies exploit exactly this; Exit Through the Gift Shop stages the question. Realism and ethics complete the analysis. Documentary claims a relationship to the real — observational camera, natural light and absence of reconstruction are realism's grammar ( Sisters in Law ), while voiceover, staging and reconstruction signal construction ( Stories We Tell , Watkins' docu-dramas). Ethics: consent, representation of suffering (the abuse cases in Sisters in Law ; the siege in For Sama ), the subject's exploitation ( Amy ), and the filmmaker's presence (Moore's polemic vs Longinotto's invisibility). The 20-mark question assesses AO1 and AO2 in equal measures: define the terms, apply the theories, analyse film language, and reach a reasoned judgement on the debate or statement offered. Realism's grammar, expanded. The realist vs expressive debate (Bazin's lineage: the Lumière actuality vs Méliès fantasy; German Expressionism and Soviet Montage against cinema's 'realist calling') underwrites documentary's choices: observational camera, natural light and long takes are realist; stylisation, reconstruction and expressive score are expressive. For Sama and Sisters in Law sit at the realist pole; Stories We Tell and Exit Through the Gift Shop weaponise the expressive pole against the genre's own claims. Band awareness for 2B: 20 marks in roughly 25-30 minutes — AO1 (define, locate, know the theory) and AO2 (apply, analyse, judge) in equal measures. Middle-band answers assert the debate; top-band answers apply it to specific film-language evidence and weigh both sides in the verdict. Prepare your documentary in terms of: dominant mode, filmmaker-theory relationship, two sequences, and one digital-technology application — that quadruple coverage answers either of the two offered questions.

topics.name: Filmmaking and Screenwriting (NEA)
topics.subject: film-studies
topics.searchText: film-studies Film Studies Filmmaking and Screenwriting (NEA) Non-exam assessment (NEA) Component 3: Production — internally assessed, externally moderated coursework worth 30% of the qualification (40 marks for the production, 20 for the evaluative analysis). Production brief The annually-set brief offering four options, of which one must be chosen — two based on narrative elements and two on character-led elements of the short film. Master scene script The standard screenplay format: single column, wide margins, sequential page numbering, centred dialogue with character names in upper case, sluglines in upper case, Courier 12-point, action in present tense. Slugline The scene heading: interior/exterior indicator (INT., EXT., INT/EXT), location descriptor and lighting descriptor (DAY, NIGHT or TIME), followed by the scene/action descriptor. Digitally photographed storyboard The screenplay option's companion: a photographed storyboard of a key section of the screenplay (up to 2 minutes of screen time, approximately two pages, approximately 20 storyboard shots). Storyboard conventions Shot number plus indicative image incorporating intended framing; duration of shot; mise-en-scène detail and camera movement; specific editing techniques (e.g. DISSOLVE TO); sound details (diegetic or non-diegetic, but not dialogue); landscape mode; up to five credited found shots. Evaluative analysis The 1600-1800 word written analysis of the production in relation to professionally produced films, including at least three short films totalling a minimum of 80 minutes from the WJEC compilation. Narrative arc The overall shape of a story from setup through conflict to resolution — the practical screenwriting concept behind the commonly used three-act structure (Area 5). Character-led option A production brief option grounded in character-driven narrative elements, where dramatic qualities, motivation and psychological insight drive the story rather than plot events. Film poetics What elements of film filmmakers select and how they combine them to create meaning (Area 5) — the concept underpinning both the production and its evaluative analysis. Component 3 is a synoptic NEA worth 30% of the qualification : one production and its evaluative analysis. You produce either a short film (4-5 minutes) or a screenplay for a short film (1600-1800 words) plus a digitally photographed storyboard of a key section from the screenplay — and an evaluative analysis (1600-1800 words) . The production is marked out of 40, the evaluative analysis out of 20, using the marking criteria in Appendix A of the specification. The production brief (set for a defined period, e.g. first assessment Summer 2023, last Summer 2026; the Summer 2027 brief publishes on the WJEC Portal) offers four options, of which one must be chosen — two based on narrative elements and two on character-led elements of the short film. Read the brief precisely: your production must demonstrably answer the option chosen. Conditions : complete the production within approximately 13-15 weeks to balance NEA against the exam components; all production work must be individual and demonstrably your own, unaided work ; teacher support is limited to general advice on one draft of the evaluative analysis — no specific guidance, no creative decisions from teachers. Misuse of AI is malpractice — follow the Eduqas 'Misuse of AI in Assessment' guidance. Filmmaking option : you must be responsible for the camerawork and editing ; it is recommended that you do not act in your own film (performance is not assessed); unassessed participants may act; unassessed assistants may operate lighting/sound under your direction; live action or animation is permitted, but animation must not use video-game software or pre-populated characters/backgrounds. Screenplay option : the screenplay must be for a live action film (to fulfil the storyboard), in standard master scene script format. Marks and weighting in detail. The production is marked out of 40 and the evaluative analysis out of 20 , using the criteria in Appendix A; AO3 (apply knowledge and understanding of elements of film to the production of a film or screenplay) is the NEA's own objective, but AO2 applies through the evaluative analysis — analysing and evaluating your own work in relation to professionally produced work. Internally assessed by your centre (standardised if more than one teacher), externally moderated by WJEC; sample assessed work is made available on the Eduqas website. Timing discipline: the recommended 13-15 weeks splits roughly into research/scripting (4-5 weeks), production (4-5 weeks) and the evaluative analysis (3-4 weeks) — and the evaluative analysis should be written while the production is fresh, not as an afterthought. Check the coversheet requirements early: the short films analysed must be listed on it, and both teachers and learners authenticate the conditions on it. The spec sets a compilation of contrasting short films for study (Appendix A: e.g. Meshes of the Afternoon , La Jetée , The Grandmother , Elephant (Clarke, 1989), The Wrong Trousers , About a Girl , Wasp , Two Cars, One Night , Night Fishing , Pitch Black Heist , Curfew , Swimmer , the Wild Tales compilation, Stutterer , The Silent Child , Hair Love , The Human Voice ) to develop knowledge of the short film form, particularly its distinctive narrative . Study the set shorts for what they teach: economy of setup, single-location or single-relationship focus, the dramatic weight of endings, how dialogue is rationed, and how images and sound carry narrative without exposition. Screenwriting craft (Area 5) : the narrative arc and the commonly used three-act structure (setup — confrontation — resolution); how narrative construction provides psychological insight into character ; how the dramatic qualities of a sequence are constructed, including through dialogue ; and the narrative conventions of mainstream screenwriting — construction of dialogue, character, and the use of images and sound to convey narrative. For a 4-5 minute short film, structure compresses: establish a character and a want within 30-60 seconds, escalate through one central conflict, and land an ending that re-frames what came before (the Curfew / Stutterer model). In screenplay format: each scene numbered with a slugline (INT./EXT. + location + DAY/NIGHT/TIME), action in present tense , dialogue centred with character names in upper case, Courier 12-point — and screenplays do not include camera directions except essential instructions in exceptional circumstances (e.g. SLO-MO). Dialogue craft deserves its own attention because the spec singles it out — how the dramatic qualities of a sequence are constructed, including through dialogue . In short film, dialogue is rationed: every line either reveals character, escalates conflict, or withholds — the Curfew model (a phone call reframed by an ending) or Stutterer (a voice heard but not spoken) demonstrate dialogue as dramatic structure rather than exposition. The Silent Child makes silence itself the dramatic device — BSL signing as performance and the hearing world's failure as theme. For the screenplay option, dialogue centred with upper-case speaker names is also where format is most visible to markers. And for both options, images and sound carry narrative: a sound bridge across a cut, a recurring diegetic noise (the kettle, the clock), a visual motif (a doorway, a reflection) — the spec's film poetics concept: what you select and how you combine it is the meaning. Keep an unassessed portfolio throughout the course (electronic — a blog or Pinterest page) consisting of: notes on or visuals from the short films studied that could inform your production; character(s) and narrative ideas; examples of cinematography, mise-en-scène, editing and sound that could inform the production; effective screenplay techniques (for the screenplay option); and examples of storyboards (if taking the screenplay option). The log is not marked, but it is the raw material for the evaluative analysis — and evidence of authentic, individual development. The evaluative analysis (1600-1800 words) must analyse and evaluate the production in relation to other professionally produced films or screenplays, including at least three short films totalling a minimum of 80 minutes from the compilation set by WJEC — listed on the coversheet. Its three required strands: Narrative structure of the short film — analyse how the narrative features and dramatic qualities of all short films studied are constructed, including through dialogue, highlighting key ideas which informed your own production. Cinematic influences — analyse how key visual/audio elements of other professionally produced films or screenplays, including the short films studied, influenced your short film. Creating meaning and effect — an evaluative analysis of how your production creates meanings and generates responses for the spectator in relation to other professionally produced films or screenplays. What examiners reward : specific, named influences applied precisely (not genre mentions); film-language precision in describing your own work (shot types, editing techniques, sound design choices — by their proper names); the three strands each substantively addressed; honest evaluation — what worked, what did not, and why, in relation to the professional films; extended word-processed writing (sub-headings permitted, screen shots may illustrate). One teacher-annotated draft is permitted; the evaluative analysis is completed under supervised conditions (not exam conditions), and must be listed on the coversheet with the short films analysed. Worked example of strand logic — a production about an isolated teenager in a coastal town, choosing a character-led brief option: Strand 1 would analyse About a Girl 's monologue-driven structure, Wasp 's observational family realism and Curfew 's reveal-ending, drawing from each a structural principle (monologue as spine; environment as character; ending as reframe) and stating how each informed the production. Strand 2 would name precise influences: Wasp 's available-light handheld staging informing the town's restricted follow shots; The Silent Child 's sound design (silence against diegetic detail) informing the film's soundscape; Saint Maud -style God's-eye framing (a feature film may also be referenced) informing the final aerial insert. Strand 3 would evaluate: how the restricted framing generates the spectator's enclosure, where the reveal-ending re-frames the film, and honestly — which techniques worked and which did not, judged against the professional films. Specific, named, precise — that is the difference between the middle and top bands. The screenplay option's digitally photographed storyboard must cover a key section of the screenplay — up to 2 minutes of screen time, corresponding to approximately two pages and approximately 20 storyboard shots — and demonstrate how the screenplay will be realised. Images may be indicative and need not employ a realistic mise-en-scène; Photoshop of backgrounds is permitted but not assessed; up to five found shots may be used where photography would not be possible (source must be credited); images are presented in landscape mode ; a template is available on the Eduqas website. Storyboard conventions — the storyboard must include: shot number plus indicative image of the main shot (e.g. close-up of face); the image must incorporate the intended framing (e.g. close-up of face ranged right); duration of shot (or a timeline); visual details including mise-en-scène detail and any camera movement within the shot; specific editing techniques beyond simple cuts (e.g. DISSOLVE TO); sound details referencing diegetic or non-diegetic sound — but not dialogue . Filming rules for the short-film option : you are responsible for camerawork and editing ; it is recommended you do not act in your own film (unassessed participants may act; performance skills are not assessed); lighting and sound may be operated by unassisted assistants under your direction; live action or animation is permitted, but animation must not use video-game software or software with pre-populated characters and backgrounds. The production encourages an appropriate range of camera shots and editing techniques , applying your knowledge and understanding of cinematography, mise-en-scène, editing and sound — the AO3 criteria reward application of film language, not production values alone. Plan coverage of the micro-elements deliberately: a film that shows controlled framing, motivated camera movement, purposeful editing (beyond cuts) and designed sound scores across the production criteria. Common mistakes to avoid — worth knowing as a checklist before submission: acting in your own film (recommended against; keep performance to unassessed participants); including camera directions liberally in the screenplay (permitted only exceptionally); dialogue in storyboard sound details (excluded — storyboard sound is diegetic/non-diegetic detail only); portrait-mode storyboard images (must be landscape); uncredited found shots (must be credited, maximum five); evaluative analysis that describes the production without relation to the professional films (the relation is the assessment); evaluative analysis under or over the 1600-1800 word band (stay inside it); and missing coversheet details (short films analysed must be listed). Finally, keep the unassessed portfolio current as you go — it is the raw material of the evaluative analysis, and examiners' sample work on the Eduqas website shows that top-band productions are planned around the micro-elements (cinematography, mise-en-scène, editing, sound) rather than assembled around a story alone.

topics.name: Choreography
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Choreography Motif A short movement phrase with significance to the dance idea; the building block that is developed through choreographic devices. Motif development Altering a motif through changes of action, space or dynamics (e.g. retrograde, inversion, augmentation, transference to another body part) to create unity with interest. Repetition Exact restatement of movement material to reinforce the dance idea and give the audience a recognisable anchor. Contrast Juxtaposition of opposing movement material (fast/slow, high/low, solo/ensemble) to create interest and mark structural change. Highlight A moment choreographed to catch the eye and direct audience attention, e.g. unison, stillness or a lift. Climax The point of greatest intensity in the dance; its placement is a deliberate structural decision. Transition The link between phrases, sections or formations; may be fluid (continuity) or abrupt (contrast). Binary Two-part structure (AB) built on contrast between its sections. Ternary Three-part structure (ABA) in which a return to altered opening material provides resolution. Episodic Structure of linked, often non-chronological episodes connected by thematic threads. Assessment Task 3 requires you to create a complete, original group dance lasting a minimum of three minutes and a maximum of four minutes for three, four or five dancers , in response to an externally set task (spec 3.2). AQA publishes three set tasks on Centre Services by 15 September in the academic year of assessment; you respond to one task in its entirety - tasks must not be edited, changed or abridged. The choreography is assessed by an external AQA visiting examiner during a visit to your centre (normally between March and May) and is worth 40 marks , contributing 25% of the A-level through AO2: create dance applying choreographic skills to communicate artistic intention . Own unaided work: you must be wholly responsible for the creation of a complete dance; you select and develop the movement material rather than the teacher. You may perform in your own dance if you wish, or act as, for example, accompanist or sound operator - the mark rewards choreography, not your performance. Programme note (maximum 300 words): must clearly inform the examiner of the choreographic intention of the work and how it relates to the selected task; handed to the examiner at the start of the live assessment. Timing penalty: choreography under three minutes or over four minutes incurs a penalty scaled to the severity of the infringement. Evidence: a single-camera, unedited audio-visual recording from an audience perspective, identifying you by name and candidate number, submitted with a signed candidate record form. The group choreography assessment grid divides the 40 marks into five criteria worth 8 marks each, and every criterion is judged in relation to the dance idea(s) : Criterion What exceptional (7-8) looks like Selection of movement components (action, spatial, dynamic) Components selected appropriately and consistently for the dance idea(s) Manipulation through choreographic devices Devices develop the idea with imagination and control Structuring of movement material Coherent sectional structure that communicates the idea Aural setting (and physical setting where appropriate) Sound, costume, set, lighting used aptly to embody the idea Use of dancers Dancers' skills and attributes fully utilised in the service of the idea Mark bands and penalties Bands run exceptional (7-8), highly refined (5-6), proficient (3-4), adequate (1-2) per criterion. A mark of 0 is awarded where no work is presented or nothing is worthy of credit. Duration penalties apply to the total mark. Examiners only conduct assessments where health and safety requirements are securely in place, so a formally risk-assessed space and warm-up time are non-negotiable. The specification names two strands of choreographic process: researching, developing and experimenting with dance ideas through studio and non-studio investigation, and the rehearsal process . Non-studio investigation includes stimulus research (image, text, music, observation of people), task-setting and recording of ideas; the rehearsal process converts material into performance - refining dynamics, fixing spatial patterns, cleaning timing and gathering dancer feedback. Manipulation of movement happens through choreographic devices . Learn each device with a definition, an example and a reason for its use in relation to the dance idea(s) - examiners credit manipulation that develops the idea, not decoration: Motif: a short movement phrase or sequence with significance - the dance idea in miniature. A strong motif is simple enough to be recognised after development. Motif development: altering the motif through changes of action, space or dynamics - e.g. retrograde, inversion, augmentation, diminution, transference to another body part, embellishment, or changes of level, direction and dynamics. Development creates unity while maintaining interest. Variation: a restatement of material with notable changes, usually longer than a single developed motif. Repetition: restating movement exactly; reinforces the idea and gives the audience a hook. Contrast: placing opposing material (fast/slow, high/low, solo/group) side by side to create interest and mark structural change. Highlights: moments that catch the eye - a sudden stillness, unison, lift or change of direction - used to direct the audience's attention. Climax: the point of greatest intensity; its placement is a structural decision (commonly, but not always, late in the work). Transitions: the links between phrases and sections; fluid transitions create continuity, abrupt ones create contrast. An A* response uses a small number of devices thoroughly : one motif developed in many ways across the work is more creditable than many motifs developed superficially. Expect to justify why each device serves the intention stated in your programme note - the grid criterion is manipulation in relation to the dance idea(s) , so a device that does not develop the idea earns nothing. Anchor devices in the practitioners you study rather than inventing in a vacuum: Bruce's Rooster takes one movement idea - the strutting, chest-forward walk - and develops it through dynamics (swagger to sudden bursts), number (unison verses broken into duet variations) and spatial patterning (circular parades around a central pair). That development logic - one idea, many manipulations, each signposted to the audience - is exactly the pattern the grid rewards, and it can be transplanted into your own group choreography without borrowing the material itself. Device-to-effect map Device Effect on the audience Typical use in a group work Motif development Recognition plus freshness Open each section with a new variant of the signature motif Repetition Reinforcement Close a section by restating its motif exactly Contrast Interest; section boundary Break unison into opposing duos Highlights Directed attention A sudden stillness before the climax builds Climax Emotional peak Full-cast unison at maximum intensity in the final section Transitions Flow or fracture Travelling pathways that re-form the cast during a section change Structuring of movement material is a separate assessment criterion: the examiner rewards material structured in a coherent way through sectional use of choreographic structures: Binary (AB): two contrasting sections; effective for opposing moods or question-and-answer material. Ternary (ABA): a return to opening material gives resolution; the reprise should be recognisably altered to avoid pointless repetition. Rondo (ABACA): a recurring principal section alternating with contrasting episodes; strong for group works built on a signature motif. Theme and variation: a theme stated then varied successively; mirrors motif development at structural scale. Narrative: order dictated by a story; the dance idea and the set task's stimulus control the sequence. Episodic: linked episodes, often non-chronological, connected by thematic threads. Chance: ordering determined by chance procedures (associated with Merce Cunningham); if you use chance deliberately, coherence must still be communicated to the audience. Choose the structure that serves the set task and state the intention clearly in the programme note. A common weakness is a structure that exists only on paper: the audience must be able to see section boundaries - through changes of spatial organisation, dynamics, aural setting or use of dancers. Study how practitioners in your area of study structure works (for example, the sectional construction of Bruce's Rooster , one section per Rolling Stones song) and borrow the logic, not the material. Handle transitions as material in their own right: travelling pathways that re-form the cast during a section change keep the work continuous, while a deliberate freeze or blackout break announces a new section. Decide which reading you want and be consistent - an A* choreography shows intentional structure throughout, and the examiner can see every section boundary from the auditorium. If you use an episodic or chance structure, thread a recurring motif or aural cue through the sections so the fragments read as one work. Choosing structure for the task Match structure to stimulus: contrast-rich stimuli suit binary or ternary; a strong recurring idea suits rondo or theme and variation; a story suits narrative; linked episodes suit episodic. Whatever you choose, the set task's wording must still be answered - re-read the task and check your structure delivers every demand it makes. Choreographic intent is the through-line of every criterion: what you want the dance to communicate and how each decision serves it. The programme note (maximum 300 words) must tell the examiner the intention and its relation to the selected task; the choreography must then deliver exactly what the note promises. The aural setting is the dominant constituent feature in group choreography. Know these music-movement relationships and use at least two deliberately: Direct correlation: movement matches the music's beat, phrasing and accents exactly. Music visualisation: movement makes visible the music's colours, textures and instrumentation. Mutual coexistence: music and dance develop independently yet complement one another. Disassociation: movement deliberately ignores or opposes the music - effective for irony or tension. Narrative aural setting: the soundtrack carries or advances the story. Call and response: one voice or part initiates, another answers - mirrored in movement exchange. Also consider tempo, rhythm, mood and atmosphere of the accompaniment, and use physical setting (costume, properties, set, lighting) where appropriate to the task. Dancers are a constituent feature too: communicate with and organise your dancers, utilising their individual skills and attributes (flexibility, partnering strength, performance presence, musicality) to develop the artistic intention - the grid rewards this specifically. Safe practice (spec 3.1.1) applies throughout creating and rehearsing: awareness of correct alignment; technical accuracy; appropriate dancewear and presentation of self; and a healthy approach to training, including the lifestyle of a dancer. Give dancers warm-up time, develop lifts and contact work progressively on a risk-assessed floor, and never choreograph beyond the safe physical capability of your cast. Finally, the specification expects the study of the choreographic approaches (historical or current) of named practitioners in the areas of study to inform your practical work - a synoptic link that also feeds the written paper. Anchoring your process in a practitioner's approach (for example, Bruce's synthesis of Graham and Cunningham techniques, or Alston's Cunningham-based clarity) demonstrates theory informing practice, which is precisely what synoptic assessment demands. Work the rehearsal process in phases: early studio investigation (improvisation tasks from the stimulus, recording promising fragments), then selection and refinement (fixing motif variants, structuring the sections), then production rehearsal (spatial patterns, timing, lifts developed progressively, full runs with the aural setting). Keep the programme note in draft from the start - an intention stated early keeps every later decision answerable to it, and the final version (maximum 300 words) should read as the plan the examiner has just watched, not a retro-fit.

topics.name: Performance
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Performance Alignment The correct stacking of head, ribcage, spine, pelvis, knees and ankles; the foundation of safe, efficient technique. Transference of weight Controlled shifting of body weight between points of support; underpins locomotion, falls and partnering. Locomotion Travelling movement across space (walk, run, leap, slide) executed with clear direction and momentum. Elevation Height achieved in jumps and leaps, with controlled, quiet landings. Kinaesthetic awareness The dancer's internal sense of body position, weight and movement in space, enabling continuous self-correction. Neuromuscular coordination The nervous system and muscles working together to produce smooth, accurate movement. Projection Directing movement energy outward to reach the audience; sustaining performance presence to the back of the space. Musicality Sensitivity to the music beyond the beat - phrasing, texture, accent and silence - embodied in movement. Dynamic variation Command of contrast in attack, weight, flow and tempo within performance. Isolation Precise independent movement of one body part while the rest of the body remains controlled or still. Component 1 assesses AO1: perform dance through the application of physical, technical, interpretative and performance skills through two tasks, each marked out of 20 by an external AQA visiting examiner (visits normally March-May): Assessment Task 1 - solo in the style of a specified practitioner: minimum two , maximum three minutes. The practitioner must be the choreographer of a prescribed set work or a named practitioner within one of the prescribed areas of study, from any area of study, and may be the same as or different from your Component 2 choices. The solo can be choreographed by you, your teacher, a dance artist, or a collaboration - but it must encapsulate the practitioner's style without being a reconstruction of existing repertoire. Assessment Task 2 - performance within a quartet: minimum three , maximum four minutes, in any style relevant to the defined genres (modern, ballet, jazz). No practitioner is required; if you use one, it must differ from your solo practitioner. If fewer than four candidates are entered, the centre may add non-examined dancers (including students from other year groups) of appropriate standard and physical maturity. Both tasks require a programme note of no more than 150 words : the solo note identifies the practitioner and reveals insight into the stylistic features explored; the quartet note references the style(s) and the dance idea(s) if applicable. The performance must take place in a live setting, formally risk assessed , with sufficient warm-up time, under teacher supervision for authentication, in the academic year of certification. Under-length or over-length performance incurs a timing penalty scaled to the severity of the infringement. Evidence: a single-camera, unedited recording from an audience perspective, name and candidate number at the start. Choosing your solo practitioner strategically Pick a practitioner whose stylistic vocabulary you can genuinely embody: Graham (contraction and release, floorwork), Alston (Cunningham-based clarity and speed), Bruce (theatrical synthesis of modern, ballet and folk colour), Bournonville (ballon and quick petit batterie) or Fosse (angled lines, isolations, hunched posture). The examiner marks style-embodiment in every column of the grid, so half-embodying a stylistically distant practitioner caps your mark. In the quartet, casting is a performance decision: additional non-examined dancers must have the physical maturity and standard to complete the choreography, and examined dancers must rehearse sensitivity - matching timing, sharing weight safely, holding spacing - since the quartet grid credits spatial awareness including sensitivity to other dancers as its own column. A quartet of strong soloists who ignore each other cannot reach the top band. Task logistics checklist Externally set tasks: the solo and quartet tasks remain unchanged for the lifetime of the specification; the choreography task list is published on Centre Services by 15 September. Live assessment in the academic year of certification; formally risk-assessed setting; sufficient warm-up; teacher supervision for authentication. Evidence: single-camera, audience-perspective, start-to-finish, unedited recording; student named with candidate number; candidate record form signed. Programme notes handed to the examiner at the start of the live assessment. Timing penalties: applied for infringement of minimum/maximum duration, scaled to severity. The specification lists physical skills that underpin both tasks : flexibility, strength, cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, agility, neuromuscular coordination and kinaesthetic awareness. These are trained conditions - the examiner sees their product as precision and control. Build them through supplementary conditioning, class technique and progressive rehearsal, not on assessment day. Technical skills credited in the grids: Correct alignment - the stacking of head, ribcage, pelvis, knees and ankles that makes movement safe and efficient. Flexion, extension, rotation - controlled joint actions executed with the range the style demands (turn-out maintained in ballet vocabulary; parallel in much modern work). Whole body participation and/or isolation - integrated movement versus precise isolation of body parts (central to jazz technique). Transference of weight - smooth, controlled shifts between support points; underpins partnering and falls. Locomotion - travelling actions (walk, run, leap, slide) with clarity of direction and momentum. Elevation - height in jumps and leaps, with controlled landing. Balance - sustained stillness on one or few points of support, in the style's required alignment. The grid language matters: top bands demand exceptional and safe demonstration of precision and control in relation to the specified practitioner (solo) or in relation to style/genre (quartet). Safety is embedded in the descriptor - a technically showy but unsafe performance cannot reach the top band. Train each physical skill deliberately: flexibility through progressive stretching after class; strength through resistance and body-conditioning work (core for alignment, legs for elevation); cardiovascular and muscular endurance through sustained full runs of the assessed material; agility through rapid direction-change drills; neuromuscular coordination and kinaesthetic awareness through class technique, partner feedback and video review. The grid's top bands describe a sustained state, not a flash - conditioning underpins everything the examiner sees. Pre-assessment skills audit Check each grid column in rehearsal video: precision and control of technique; spatial control or awareness; dynamics; timing and musicality; focus, projection, emphasis, expression. Any column you cannot evidence in the footage is the one to drill - the grid marks columns separately, so one weak column caps the task. Spatial elements: the solo grid rewards spatial control (personal and stage space) - direction, levels, shape/form - meaning you command both your kinesphere and the stage picture. The quartet grid rewards spatial awareness including sensitivity to other dancers : maintaining formations and spacing, safe partnering, and adapting to the quartet in real time. Dynamic elements (solo): rhythmic control and dynamic variation - command of attack, weight, flow and tempo change, matching the practitioner's dynamic signature (Fosse's controlled isolations against sudden bursts; Graham's percussive contraction against sustained release). Interpretative/performance skills exist to communicate the dance idea(s) in a clear and considered manner - the specification lists projection, focus, expression, emphasis, timing and musicality: Projection: energy reaching the audience; performing to the back row even in a small studio. Focus: deliberate direction of the eyes - focal shifts shape meaning (inward focus for introspection, outward for confrontation). Expression: facial and physical expression consistent with the dance idea and style. Emphasis: giving certain moments weight so the audience reads what matters. Timing: accurate response to the aural setting and to other dancers. Musicality: sensitivity to the music beyond the beat - phrasing, texture, accent, silence. Note the grid splits interpretative skills into two credited columns - timing and musicality , and focus, projection, emphasis and expression - so neglecting one pair caps the mark regardless of brilliance elsewhere. Solo grid (20 marks) at a glance Five columns, 4 marks each: physical/technical skills; spatial elements (personal and stage space); dynamic elements; interpretative skills (timing and musicality); interpretative skills (focus, projection, emphasis and expression). Bands: exceptional (4), highly articulate (3), proficient (2), adequate (1), nothing worthy of credit (0). Quartet grid (20 marks) at a glance Four columns, 5 marks each: physical/technical skills; spatial awareness (including sensitivity to other dancers); timing and musicality; focus, projection, emphasis and expression. Bands: exceptional (5), highly articulate (4), proficient (3), sound (2), adequate (1), nothing worthy of credit (0). Train expressive skills as deliberately as technique: projection through performing phrases to a distant point and filming from the back of the room; focus through rehearsing deliberate focal shifts marked into the choreography; timing and musicality through clapping phrases, marking accents and dancing to silence. In the solo, match your interpretative choices to the practitioner: Fosse's fixed, inward gaze; Graham's dramatic intensity; Alston's clean musical phrasing. Expression inconsistent with style reads as decoration and caps the interpretative columns. Safe practice (spec 3.1.1) is examinable knowledge and a condition of assessment. Know all four requirements: awareness of correct alignment ; technical accuracy (executing movement as intended - inaccurate technique is itself unsafe); appropriate dancewear and presentation of self (correct footwear or barefoot convention for the style, hair secured, no jewellery); and a healthy approach to training, including the lifestyle of a dancer (progressive warm-up and cool-down, hydration, nutrition, sleep, load management, injury reporting). The examiner will only conduct assessments where health and safety requirements are securely in place. Rehearsal process converts skill into performance: learn material accurately, mark through for spacing and safety, build full runs to develop stamina, then rehearse in performance conditions - same floor, same aural setting, entrances and exits rehearsed. For the quartet, rehearse sensitivity deliberately: blind-spot awareness, counterbalance and lift progressions, and recovery from slips without breaking the ensemble picture. Performance environment: the assessed performance happens in a live, formally risk-assessed setting, and the recording must be the performance being assessed - one take, single camera, audience perspective, unedited, in the academic year of certification. Adapt projection and focus to the venue: a studio assessment needs less force than a theatre, but never perform flatly. Treat the examiner as an audience member; do not perform to the examiner. Finally, embodying a specified practitioner means evidencing their style in every credited column: alignment, rotation and balance executed as Graham, Alston, Bruce, Bournonville or Fosse would demand; dynamics matching their signature; timing and musicality inside their aural world; expression consistent with their choreographic intent. Study film of the practitioner's repertoire, take class in the style, and let the programme note signal precisely which stylistic features the examiner should expect to see. The lifestyle of a dancer is named in the spec: sleep for recovery, hydration and nutrition for energy, load management to avoid overuse injury, and honest reporting of niggles before they become injuries. In the performance environment, plan the space: rehearse entrances, exits and spacing to the actual room, check the floor is risk assessed and fit for the style (sprung floor for elevation work), and agree how the aural setting will be played. Walk in as a performer: warm-up complete, dancewear and presentation right, focus already on the dance idea - the assessment begins the moment you enter the space.

topics.name: Dance Appreciation
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Dance Appreciation Constituent features The four analytically separable features of a dance: movement components; dancers; aural setting; physical setting. Movement components The action, spatial and dynamic elements of the movement itself. Dynamic elements Qualities of movement - attack, weight, flow, tempo - as distinct from what is done (action) and where (space). Aural setting Everything heard: music, sound, the spoken word, the audible aspect of dance and silence. Physical setting Everything seen that surrounds the movement: costume, properties, set, lighting design, performance environment, film. Choreographic approach A choreographer's particular technique, movement style and choreographic style. Genre A category of dance defined by style, technique and history - modern dance, ballet and jazz dance in AQA 7237. Subject matter The theme or topic of the dance and its treatment. Form The structure of the dance - phrases and sections - and its effectiveness in communicating the subject matter. Leitmotif A recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, incorporated into ballet scores during the romantic period. Component 2: Critical engagement is a written exam of 2 hours 30 minutes , 100 marks , 50% of the A-level , assessing AO3 (knowledge and understanding of performance and choreography from different periods and genres) and AO4 (critically appreciating and assessing performance and choreography through analytical, interpretative and evaluative judgements). You study two set works : one compulsory, one chosen from four options. Section A (50 marks) - compulsory: short answer questions (25 marks) and one essay (25 marks) on the compulsory set work and area of study: Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) and Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 . Section B (50 marks) - two essays, 25 marks each: one on your optional set work and one on its corresponding area of study. Options: Giselle / the romantic ballet period; Appalachian Spring / the origins of American modern dance 1900-1945; Singin' in the Rain / American jazz dance 1940-1975; Sutra / the independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current. The assessment is synoptic : you must draw together knowledge from across the course, demonstrating the relationships between theory and practice - examiners reward answers that connect set works to choreographic and performance understanding, not isolated recall. Command words determine depth demanded: identify/state (recall), describe (account of features), explain (give reasons - how and why), discuss/analyse (interrogate features and their effect), evaluate (AO4 judgement with justification). Short answers reward precise, dated facts; essays reward a thesis supported by constituent-feature evidence and secured by judgement. Timing plan for 2h30 Section A: short answers (25 marks) in about 30 minutes; essay (25 marks) in about 30-35 minutes. Section B: two essays (25 marks each) in about 30-35 minutes each; keep 10 minutes to check dates and terminology. At roughly 1.2 marks per minute, every minute must produce dated, interpretable content - plan each essay in its first two minutes (thesis plus three evidence points) rather than after writing. Also know how the two AOs divide the paper: AO3 (knowledge and understanding of performance and choreography from different periods and genres) dominates the short answers; AO4 (critically appreciating and assessing performance and choreography through analytical, interpretative and evaluative judgements) dominates the essays. An essay with no judgement is capped at mid-band however dense its recall. Command words ladder Identify/state = recall a fact (1-2 marks). Describe = give a precise account of features using action, spatial and dynamic vocabulary. Explain = give reasons - how and why features work. Discuss/analyse = interrogate features, weigh their effect, make links across the work. Evaluate = reach a justified judgement (AO4). Match paragraph length to the command word: short answers earn marks per accurate point; essays earn them per developed, evidenced, judged point. Spec 3.3.1 defines four constituent features - learn this framework as the skeleton of every analysis answer. Each feature must be interpreted in relation to the subject matter , not merely described: Constituent feature Elements Movement components action, spatial and dynamic elements Dancers number, gender, role, physique Aural setting music, sound, the spoken word, the audible aspect of dance, silence Physical setting costume, properties, set, lighting design, performance environment, film Analyse in three moves: describe the feature precisely (what is seen/heard, using action, space and dynamic vocabulary); interpret (what the feature communicates about the subject matter or the character of the dance); evaluate (how effectively it embodies the subject matter - AO4). For example, in Rooster : the men's strutting, cock-of-the-rooster carriage (action) performed with swaggering, syncopated attack (dynamics) to Rolling Stones tracks (aural setting) in 1960s-inspired costume (physical setting) embodies the sexual politics and swagger of the decade - description becomes interpretation once linked to the work's subject matter. Also know the language of form (phrases, sections) and the significance of the character of the dance - both named in the spec as things you must understand about each set work: whether the work is abstract or has a character, how form communicates subject matter, and how the sections build. Build movement vocabulary you can deploy in any work: action - travel, turn, gesture, elevation, stillness, fall, jump, contract, extend; spatial - pathway, direction, level, formation, symmetry/asymmetry, personal versus stage space; dynamic - attack, weight, flow, tempo, sustained/percussive/suspended/swinging. Every set-work answer should name the feature, describe it precisely and interpret its effect on the subject matter in one move. Test the framework on a second work: in Sutra (2008), the dancers move among Antony Gormley's wooden boxes - the physical setting is simultaneously apparatus (boxes are carried, stacked, tipped) and metaphor (a hut, a wall, a void), and the audible aspect of the dance (knocking, sliding) merges with Szymon Brzoska's composed score; in Appalachian Spring (1944), Isamu Noguchi's sculptural set reduces a farmhouse to suggestion, and Graham's dancers work in contraction and release to Aaron Copland's Americana. Both show constituent features embodying subject matter - the pattern every 25-mark answer must expose. Give the dancers feature full treatment too: number (why this many - ensemble weight, symmetry, opposition), gender (casting as meaning - the flirtatious gender play of Rooster ), role (principal, corps, ghost, outsider) and physique (the physique a style demands and displays). Casting choices are interpretation: connect them to the subject matter rather than listing them. Quick check before any set-work answer Can you name: the action, spatial and dynamic features of a key moment; the dancers' number, gender, role and physique; the aural setting elements heard; the physical setting elements seen? If not, that feature is your next revision target - every 25-mark answer draws on all four. Choreographic approach = the choreographer's particular technique, movement style and choreographic style . For each set work you must know the approach, the influences affecting its development , the origins of the dance , its importance in the development of the choreographer and the genre , and similarities and differences with other works by the choreographer. This requires understanding of other related works - selected by your teacher from visual and/or written sources - to place the set work in context within the area of study and the genre. For each area of study you must know the stylistic features of the genre and the choreographic approach of a minimum of two named practitioners , showing the range within the genre, with at least two works from each (subject matter, treatment, form, constituent features of each). The three genres are defined by AQA: Modern dance: theatrical dancing that began in the early 20th century, originally in opposition to the formality of ballet; the term is now sometimes replaced by other labels, e.g. contemporary. Ballet: dancing focused on the technique and style of the danse d'ecole - port de bras, the five positions of the feet, turn-out of the legs. Jazz dance: dancing of African origins focused on complex rhythms and techniques including isolation of body parts; a wide range of styles has evolved, e.g. lyrical jazz and urban dance. Named practitioner lists: Rambert 1966-2002 - Glen Tetley, Robert North, Richard Alston, Siobhan Davies, Ashley Page; romantic ballet - Filippo Taglioni, August Bournonville, Arthur Saint-Leon; American modern 1900-1945 - Loie Fuller, Isadora Duncan, Ruth St Denis, Doris Humphrey; American jazz 1940-1975 - Agnes de Mille, Jack Cole, Jerome Robbins, Bob Fosse; independent contemporary Britain 2000-current - Shobana Jeyasingh, Matthew Bourne, Jasmin Vardimon, Akram Khan, Hofesh Shechter. Structure practitioner comparison by influence, then approach, then work : state the practitioner's influences (training, teachers, companies), define their approach (technique, movement style, choreographic style), then evidence it in two works with subject matter, treatment, form and constituent features. To show the range within the genre, pair practitioners whose approaches genuinely oppose - within the Rambert list, for example, pair a Cunningham-derived, abstract approach with a more theatrical, dramatic one - and make the contrast itself your argument. The spec also asks for similarities and differences between the set work and other works by the choreographer - a cheap source of AO3 content once prepared: Rooster 's celebratory social-dance register against the political gravity of Bruce's other repertoire; Appalachian Spring 's celebratory Americana against Graham's darker psychological works; Sutra 's ritual austerity against Cherkaoui's more overtly theatrical pieces. Prepare one similarity and one difference per set work, each grounded in subject matter, form or constituent features. You must understand the relationship between the dance and its context - the position of the genre within history, culture and society - and the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society . This is where top-band essays separate from mid-band: connect the work's features to its world. Rooster only makes full sense against 1960s social dance and gender politics; Giselle against Romanticism's supernatural and the ballerina cult; Appalachian Spring against American modern dance's individualism and Copland's American sound; Sutra against Britain's independent, collaborative contemporary scene. Essay craft for the 25-mark questions: Open with a thesis that answers the question directly (one sentence). Build 3-4 paragraphs, each anchored in precise, dated evidence - choreographer, work, year, company, constituent feature. Interpret: link every feature to subject matter, form or character. Judge (AO4): how effectively, how significantly - use evaluative language (the most striking embodiment; this changed the company's direction because...). Use terminology specific to the genre (contraction and release; ballon; isolation; Bharatanatyam) accurately. Cross-reference across the course where possible - synopticity is credited. Practise by converting every fact into a claim: not 'Morrice changed the company in 1966' but 'Morrice's 1966 changes - reducing company size, introducing Graham technique into training, engaging guest choreographers - reoriented Ballet Rambert from ballet towards modern dance, which is why a Bruce work using Rolling Stones and social dance idiom could enter its repertoire by 1994.' Facts + consequence + judgement = AO3 + AO4. Prepare AO4 language deliberately: evaluative sentence openers (the most significant; the decisive change; this crystallised the company's identity), consequence links (which meant that; as a result), and balanced judgement (however; the exception being). Address the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society with concrete cases: the romantic ballet reflected its era's cult of the unattainable yet, by elevating the ballerina above the male dancer, eventually narrowed ballet's expressive range; jazz on screen democratised dance for mass audiences while drawing on racialised popular forms; Bruce's Rooster both celebrates and gently satirises the sexual politics it reconstructs.

topics.name: Set Works and Anthology
topics.subject: dance
topics.searchText: dance Dance Set Works and Anthology Set work A professional dance work prescribed by AQA for in-depth study in Component 2: Critical engagement. Area of study A prescribed genre-focused period (e.g. Rambert Dance Company 1966-2002) providing historical, cultural and social context for the set work. Compulsory set work Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) with the Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 area of study - required of all candidates. Romantic ballet 19th-century ballet style peaking in the 1830s-40s: focus on the ballerina, reality/fantasy contrast, supernatural mystery, illusion of weightlessness, gas lighting, folk colour; formulaic by 1870. Modern dance Theatrical dancing begun in the early 20th century in opposition to ballet's formality; the label is now sometimes replaced by contemporary. Jazz dance Dance of African origins focused on complex rhythms and isolation of body parts; evolved into lyrical jazz, urban and theatre styles. Denishawn The school and company founded by Ruth St Denis and Ted Shaw; students included Martha Graham, Doris Humphrey and Charles Weidman. Contraction and release Martha Graham's technique, based on the act of breathing - percussive contraction of the torso and its release. Fall and recovery Doris Humphrey's technique, built on the arc between surrendering to and resisting gravity. Leitmotif A recurring musical theme associated with a principal character, incorporated into ballet scores during the romantic period. Component 2 requires in-depth knowledge of two set works and their corresponding areas of study . One is compulsory: Rooster (Christopher Bruce, 1991) with Rambert Dance Company (formerly Ballet Rambert) 1966-2002 . One is selected from four options. Learn the credits precisely - short answers reward dated facts: Option Set work Music Area of study 1 Giselle (Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot, 1841) - libretto Gautier, Saint-Georges and Coralli; decor Pierre Ciceri Adolphe Adam The romantic ballet period 2 Appalachian Spring (Martha Graham, 1944) - set Isamu Noguchi; costumes Edythe Gilfond Aaron Copland The origins of American modern dance 1900-1945 3 Singin' in the Rain (Stanley Donen and Gene Kelly, 1952) - lyrics Arthur Freed; screenplay Comden and Green Nacio Herb Brown American jazz dance 1940-1975 4 Sutra (Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, 2008) - design Antony Gormley; lighting Adam Carree Szymon Brzoska The independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current Choose by genuine comparative strength: your Section B essays need a minimum of two named practitioners plus two works each from the area of study, so pick the area whose practitioner list and repertoire you can evidence best. Professional works studied must be in the public domain and easily accessible to examiners. For your selected set work you must know: the significance of the character of the dance; the subject matter and its treatment; the form (phrases, sections) and its effectiveness; the constituent features and their relevance to subject matter; the choreographic approach; the influences affecting the development of the choreographer; the origins of the dance; the relationship between the dance and its context; the importance of the dance in the development of the choreographer and the genre; and the similarities and differences between the dance and other works by the choreographer. For short answers, credits win marks: know each work's choreographer, year, company and premiere, music and designers cold. Section A short answers ask for exactly this recall plus constituent-feature identification; the essays ask you to convert it into argument. Also note the spec's list of what you must know about each area of study: the stylistic features of the genre and how they relate to it; the choreographic approach of a minimum of two named practitioners (influences, technique, movement style, choreographic style) with at least two works each; the relationship between the genre's development and its context; the genre's capacity to reflect and challenge society; and terminology specific to the genre. Rooster credits: choreography Christopher Bruce; music - songs recorded by the Rolling Stones; costume designs Marian Bruce; lighting designs Tina MacHugh. First performed 10 October 1991 by the Ballet du Grand Theatre de Geneve; British premiere 28 October 1992 by London Contemporary Dance Theatre; first performance by Rambert Dance Company 8 December 1994 . The work: a suite of sections, each built on one Rolling Stones song, reviving the social dance idiom of the 1960s - strutting, twist- and jitterbug-derived actions, flirtatious gender play. The subject matter is the swagger and sexual politics of the decade: the men preen, the women counter with knowing control, and the mood shifts from celebratory to darker across the sections. The form - one section per song - communicates the decade's shifting moods; the aural setting works through direct correlation and music visualisation with the Stones' syncopated drive. Bruce's approach: technique rooted in Graham-based training with Cunningham influence - the two techniques Rambert institutionalised after 1966; movement style synthesising modern dance, ballet and social dance colour; choreographic style theatrical, musical and humanist - his works frequently address political and social themes (cf. Ghost Dances , 1981, Ballet Rambert, responding to oppression in Latin America). Rooster 's celebratory register shows the range within Bruce's output - a contrast examiners like to see argued. Rambert 1966-2002 chronology - learn as a chain of consequences: 1966: Norman Morrice (associate director) encourages Marie Rambert to change the company - company size, preservation and creation of works, Graham technique in training, involvement of guest choreographers and teachers, development of the touring schedule. The modern-dance reorientation begins. 1974: Morrice leaves; John Chesworth continues his policies - promotes new work from company members, expands the repertoire through guest choreographers, develops Rambert's educational activities. 1975: Christopher Bruce becomes associate director; 1979 associate choreographer. 1975-1985: links between Ballet Rambert and London Contemporary Dance Theatre through choreographers such as Robert North and Richard Alston. 1980s: repertoire focuses on three British choreographers - North, Bruce and Alston. North directs 1981-1986, keen to develop the physicality, musicality and dramatic quality of the dancers. Alston: resident choreographer 1980, artistic director 1986 - consolidating the Cunningham influence. 1987: company renamed Rambert Dance Company . 1994-2002: Bruce returns as artistic director - inclusion of a range of techniques, new works, guest choreographers, and a repertoire of neo-classical and modern works. Rooster enters the repertoire (December 1994). Named practitioners (know two in depth, two works each): Glen Tetley (1926-2007), Robert North (born 1945), Richard Alston (born 1948), Siobhan Davies (born 1950), Ashley Page (born 1956). Option 1 - The romantic ballet period (with Giselle ): Romanticism rebelled against Classicism's focus on form, balance and order, emphasising creativity, emotion and subjectivity; ballet was the last art affected. The romantic ballet peaked in the 1830s-40s. Characteristics: focus on the ballerina; contrast between reality and fantasy; the supernatural and mystery via the illusion of weightlessness, gas lighting and the characteristic romantic tutu; folk or national dances for local colour; leitmotifs for principal characters. Taglioni, Perrot and Bournonville led development - Bournonville alone maintained balance between male and female dancing. The style became formulaic by 1870; female dancers performing male roles signalled decline. Practitioners: Filippo Taglioni (1777-1871), August Bournonville (1805-1879), Arthur Saint-Leon (1821-1870). Option 2 - The origins of American modern dance 1900-1945 (with Appalachian Spring ): America had no tradition of professional ballet; innovators performed barefoot to concert music in freer costume. Loie Fuller led the way in modern stage lighting; Isadora Duncan developed natural movement. Ruth St Denis (eclectic styles, the Delsarte system) with Ted Shawn created a company and the Denishawn school - students included Graham, Humphrey and Weidman. Modern dance stressed individualism: angular asymmetries, aggressive and earthy qualities; early works minimised the importance of music and art; from the 1930s choreography addressed psychological and social issues. German modern dance (Mary Wigman) reached America via tours and via Hanya Holm's branch of the Wigman school. Graham, encouraged by Louis Horst, built technique on breathing - contraction and release ; Humphrey on fall and recovery . University support (e.g. Bennington) accelerated acceptance of modern dance as a distinct art form. Practitioners: Fuller (1862-1928), Duncan (1877-1927), St Denis (1879-1968), Humphrey (1895-1958). Option 3 - American jazz dance 1940-1975 (with Singin' in the Rain ): early 1900s jazz performed by African-American artists showed links to minstrelsy and ragtime via new syncopated rhythms; from the 1930s-60s it became a theatre-based form requiring trained dancers, with choreography from the ballet and modern worlds. Jack Cole developed jazz dance technique and its theatrical form (inspiring Matt Mattox, Jerome Robbins and Bob Fosse); Katherine Dunham founded the anthropological dance movement, introducing African and Caribbean ritual into American choreography; Matt Mattox's teaching shaped future generations' training. Gene Kelly - physique and personality, acrobatic and athletic training, camera-conscious choreography in collaboration with Stanley Donen; Jerome Robbins combined social dance with classical ballet for characterisation, rhythmic complexity and dynamic variation, following Agnes de Mille in making dance of equal importance to drama and music in the storyline; Bob Fosse's style - angled lines, inverted limbs, hunched-over posture. Practitioners: de Mille (1905-1993), Cole (1911-1974), Robbins (1918-1998), Fosse (1927-1987). Option 4 - The independent contemporary dance scene in Britain 2000-current (with Sutra ): several generations of practitioners have achieved international recognition through their own work and commissions for different companies; the work embraces cultural similarities and differences, enhanced by collaborations with designers (Antony Gormley, Anish Kapoor) and composers (Nitin Sawhney, Szymon Brzoska), and responds to social, political and historical issues. Shobana Jeyasingh: Bharatanatyam foundation, multicultural themes of personal identity, relationships and heritage; Matthew Bourne: choreographed body language and a variety of dance and movement styles for storytelling, supported by design and music; Jasmin Vardimon: observations of human behaviour through physical theatre, inventive characterisation, technology, text and dance; Akram Khan: Kathak and contemporary training, constantly exploring other styles through collaborators from a range of backgrounds; Hofesh Shechter: composer involvement - soundscapes providing powerful backgrounds for his contemporary movement and interest in aspects of contemporary life; Cherkaoui: yoga and jazz backgrounds explored from a theatrical starting point. Practitioners: Jeyasingh (born 1957), Bourne (born 1960), Vardimon (born 1971), Khan (born 1974), Shechter (born 1975). Section B demands two essays: one on your optional set work, one on its corresponding area of study (25 marks each). Strong essays do three things the mark scheme rewards: Argue through features: every paragraph anchored in a constituent feature or formal detail of a named work, interpreted in relation to subject matter. Show the range within the genre: contrast two practitioners' approaches (technique, movement style, choreographic style) with at least two works each - e.g. Bournonville's gender-balanced virtuosity against the ballerina-centred romantic norm; Khan's Kathak-contemporary hybridity against Shechter's rock-inflected ensemble drive. Situate and judge: place the genre in history, culture and society, and discuss its capacity to reflect and challenge society - jazz on screen democratised dance but traded on racialised popular forms; the romantic ballet worshipped the unattainable yet narrowed opportunities for male dancers. Use comparison sentences that carry facts : 'Where Graham's Appalachian Spring (1944) stripped the setting to Noguchi's sculptural shorthand, Cherkaoui's Sutra (2008) made Gormley's wooden boxes both set and apparatus - both physical settings concentrate meaning, but Sutra 's is also choreographic infrastructure.' Compare across the two set works you study for synopticity: Bruce's social-dance revival and Cherkaoui's intercultural ritual both reconstruct borrowed movement idioms, but to opposite effect - nostalgia versus inquiry. Finally, connect to practice: the specification states that study of the choreographic approaches of named practitioners in the areas of study informs practical work. Knowing how Graham built material through contraction and release, or how Kelly choreographed for the camera, feeds directly into AO2 decisions in your group choreography - theory informing practice is the stated aim of the area-of-study design.

topics.name: Materials and Performance
topics.subject: design-and-technology
topics.searchText: design-and-technology Design and Technology Materials and Performance Physical property A characteristic measured without changing the composition of the material, e.g. density, thermal conductivity, electrical conductivity. Mechanical property How a material responds to an applied force, e.g. tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, elasticity. Toughness The ability of a material to absorb sudden shock or impact without fracturing; the opposite of brittleness. Hardness Resistance of a surface to scratching, indentation and wear. Malleability The ability of a material to be deformed by compression (hammering, rolling, pressing) without cracking. Thermoset polymer A polymer that cures permanently when heated or mixed with a hardener and cannot be remelted, e.g. epoxy resin, urea formaldehyde. Elastomer A polymer that can be stretched and returns to its original shape, e.g. natural rubber, neoprene, silicone, TPE. Composite Two or more materials combined so the resulting properties are enhanced beyond those of the individual components, e.g. CFRP, GRP, reinforced concrete, glulam. Smart material A material that responds to an external stimulus - a change in temperature, light level or pressure - e.g. shape memory alloy (Nitinol), thermochromic pigment. Case hardening A heat treatment that adds carbon to the surface of a low carbon steel component, producing a hard, wear-resistant skin over a tough core. Paper 1 expects instant, accurate classification. Learn the categories and one or two examples each - examiners award marks for named materials, not vague ones.
